questions.stem: The percentage of ALUMINA in ordinary Portland cement is about:
questions.solution:
**About 3 to 8 per cent.**

**The oxide composition of ordinary Portland cement:**

| Oxide | Chemical name | Percentage |
|---|---|---|
| **CaO** | **LIME** | **60-67 %** |
| **SiO₂** | **SILICA** | **17-25 %** |
| **Al₂O₃** | **ALUMINA** | **3-8 %** ← |
| **Fe₂O₃** | **Iron oxide** | **0.5-6 %** |
| **MgO** | **Magnesia** | **0.1-4 % (limited to 6 % maximum)** |
| **SO₃** | **Sulphur trioxide (from the gypsum)** | **1-3 %** |
| **Alkalis (Na₂O, K₂O)** | — | **0.4-1.3 %** |

> **Note that options (a) and (b) are the LIME and SILICA percentages — the two largest constituents — offered for alumina.**

> **So the option set requires the specific oxide in the stem to be matched, and a candidate who recalls only "lime is about 63 per cent" will pick the wrong one.**

> **The order worth holding is simply LIME > SILICA > ALUMINA > IRON, with roughly 63, 21, 6 and 3 per cent as the central values.**

**What each oxide contributes, since the percentages alone are inert facts:**

| Oxide | Effect of an EXCESS | Effect of a DEFICIENCY |
|---|---|---|
| **LIME** | **UNSOUNDNESS — free lime hydrates later and expands, cracking the concrete** ← | **Reduced strength; the cement sets too quickly** |
| **SILICA** | **Strength is high but the SETTING is SLOW** | Low strength |
| **ALUMINA** | **QUICK SETTING — and reduced chemical resistance** ← | Slower setting |
| **Iron oxide** | Gives the grey COLOUR; acts as a flux in the kiln | — |
| **MAGNESIA** | **UNSOUNDNESS, like free lime — hence the 6 % limit** | — |
| **Alkalis** | **ALKALI-AGGREGATE REACTION with reactive silica in the aggregate** | — |

> **The ALUMINA entry answers why this question matters: alumina is what makes cement set QUICKLY, and its proportion is a principal control on setting behaviour.**

> **And the EXCESS LIME entry is the most consequential: FREE LIME — lime that did not combine in the kiln — hydrates slowly AFTER the concrete has hardened, expanding as it does so and cracking the set paste from within.**

> **That is UNSOUNDNESS, and it is why the Le Chatelier and autoclave tests exist and why the kiln's burning must be complete.**

> **MAGNESIA causes the same defect by the same mechanism, which is why it is capped rather than merely specified.**

**The BOGUE COMPOUNDS, which are what the oxides actually form:**

> **The oxides combine in the kiln into four principal compounds, and it is these — not the oxides — that determine the cement's behaviour:**

| Compound | Formula | Abbreviation | Typical % | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tricalcium silicate** | **3CaO·SiO₂** | **C₃S (alite)** | **25-50 %** | **EARLY strength; hardens rapidly; considerable heat** ← |
| **Dicalcium silicate** | **2CaO·SiO₂** | **C₂S (belite)** | **20-45 %** | **LATE strength; hardens slowly; little heat** ← |
| **Tricalcium aluminate** | **3CaO·Al₂O₃** | **C₃A (celite)** | **5-12 %** | **FLASH SET if uncontrolled; most heat of all; poor SULPHATE resistance** |
| **Tetracalcium aluminoferrite** | **4CaO·Al₂O₃·Fe₂O₃** | **C₄AF (felite)** | **6-12 %** | **Contributes little to strength; acts as a flux** |

> **The C₃S / C₂S balance is the single most useful thing to understand here, because it explains every variety of Portland cement:**

| Cement | Composition adjustment | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **ORDINARY Portland (OPC)** | Balanced | Normal strength gain |
| **RAPID HARDENING** | **MORE C₃S, finer grinding** | **High EARLY strength; more heat** |
| **LOW HEAT** | **LESS C₃S and C₃A, MORE C₂S** | **Slow strength gain, LOW heat — for mass concrete in dams** ← |
| **SULPHATE RESISTING** | **C₃A limited to 5 %** | **Resists sulphate attack — for foundations in sulphate soils** ← |
| **HIGH ALUMINA** | Not a Portland cement at all | Very rapid strength; refractory |

> **The LOW HEAT cement case is worth understanding because it explains a real engineering problem: a large concrete pour generates heat as the cement hydrates, and the interior cannot lose it.**

> **A temperature difference between the hot core and the cool surface produces tensile stresses at the surface, which crack it — THERMAL CRACKING.**

> **So a dam or a thick raft uses a cement deliberately formulated to hydrate SLOWLY, generating the same total heat over a much longer period so it can escape as it is produced.**

> **The cost is very slow strength gain, which a dam can tolerate and a building programme cannot** — which is why the two applications use different cements for the same nominal strength.

> **And the SULPHATE RESISTING case explains why C₃A content is specified at all: C₃A reacts with sulphates in groundwater to form ETTRINGITE, which occupies a far greater volume than the compounds it replaces and disrupts the concrete.**

> **Limiting C₃A to 5 per cent removes most of the material the reaction needs, which is a direct and effective remedy — and one available only because the compound composition can be controlled at the works.**
tags: low heat and sulphate resisting cement

examTip.trick: **Order: LIME 63 % > SILICA 21 % > ALUMINA 6 % > IRON 3 %.** Options (a) and (b) are the lime and silica figures offered for alumina.
examTip.trap: **Excess LIME or MAGNESIA causes UNSOUNDNESS** — free lime hydrates after hardening and expands, cracking the paste from within. That is why the Le Chatelier test exists and why MgO is capped at 6 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **C₃S gives EARLY strength, C₂S gives LATE strength, C₃A causes flash set and poor sulphate resistance.** Low-heat cement cuts C₃S and C₃A for mass concrete; sulphate-resisting cement caps C₃A at 5 %.

questions.stem: The defect in timber consisting of a lengthwise separation between adjacent layers of annual rings is called:
questions.solution:
**A SHAKE — specifically a CUP or RING shake when it follows the annual rings.**

**The natural defects in timber, classified:**

| Defect | Description |
|---|---|
| **SHAKE** | **A lengthwise SEPARATION or split in the wood** ← |
| **Cup (ring) shake** | **Separation BETWEEN adjacent annual rings — curved, following a ring** |
| **Heart shake** | **Radial cracks starting at the PITH and spreading outward — from the decay of the heartwood in an over-mature tree** |
| **Star shake** | **Radial cracks from the BARK inward, in a star pattern — from heat or frost** |
| **KNOT** | **The base of a branch enclosed in the trunk; a hard, dark, cross-grained inclusion** |
| **RIND GALL** | **A curved swelling where a branch was improperly cut off; the wood there is weak and irregular** |
| **UPSET (rupture)** | **Fibres crushed and buckled ACROSS the grain, from compression while the tree stood — usually from wind or from felling** |
| **Twisted fibres** | Fibres wound spirally, from wind twisting a young tree |
| **Foxiness** | Yellow or red stain from incipient decay in over-mature timber |
| **Druxiness** | White decayed spots, from fungus entering through wounds |
| **Burls (excrescences)** | Warty growths from injury in early growth |
| **Chemical stain** | Discolouration from chemical action |

> **The stem's phrase "between adjacent layers of annual rings" identifies it precisely as a CUP or RING shake, which is a kind of SHAKE.**

> **Option (d) UPSET is the most instructive distractor because it is also a fibre discontinuity — but it runs ACROSS the grain from compression, not ALONG it from separation.**

**The classification of timber defects by CAUSE, which organises the whole list:**

| Cause | Defects |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL (growth) defects** | **Knots, shakes, rind galls, upsets, twisted fibres, burls, curl** |
| **Defects from SEASONING** | **Bow, cup, twist (warp), split, check, honeycombing, case hardening, collapse** ← |
| **Defects from CONVERSION (sawing)** | **Chip mark, torn grain, diagonal grain, wane, machine burn** |
| **Defects from FUNGI** | **Dry rot, wet rot, brown rot, white rot, blue stain, heart rot, sap stain** |
| **Defects from INSECTS** | **Beetle, marine borer and TERMITE damage** |

> **The SEASONING defects deserve attention because they are the ones a designer can actually prevent:**

| Seasoning defect | Description |
|---|---|
| **BOW** | Curvature along the length, in the plane of the wide face |
| **CUP** | Curvature ACROSS the width |
| **TWIST** | **Spiral distortion — the most troublesome, since it cannot be pulled flat** |
| **SPLIT** | **A crack extending through the whole thickness** |
| **CHECK** | **A crack that does NOT go through the whole thickness — the milder form** |
| **HONEYCOMBING** | **INTERNAL cavities from the outside drying and shrinking faster than the inside** ← |
| **CASE HARDENING** | **The outer surface dries and sets hard while the core is still wet — the timber then distorts when finally cut** |
| **COLLAPSE** | Cell walls buckle from too rapid drying |

> **HONEYCOMBING and CASE HARDENING share one cause: DRYING TOO FAST.**

> **When the surface dries much faster than the core, it shrinks while the core cannot, and the resulting internal stresses tear the wood apart inside or lock the surface into a strained condition.**

> **The remedy is controlled, gradual seasoning — which is precisely what kiln seasoning does, and why it is preferred over air seasoning where quality matters:**

| | **AIR (natural) seasoning** | **KILN (artificial) seasoning** |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | **6 months to 2 years or more** | **Days to weeks** ← |
| **Control of temperature and humidity** | **NONE** | **FULL** |
| **Moisture content achievable** | **About 15-20 %, set by ambient humidity** | **Any required value, down to 6-8 %** ← |
| **Cost** | Low, but ties up capital in stock |Higher |
| **Defects** | More, and less predictable | **Fewer, if the schedule is correct** |
| **Kills insects and fungi?** | **NO** | **YES — the temperature sterilises the timber** ← |

> **The MOISTURE CONTENT point is the practically decisive one: air seasoning cannot dry timber below the ambient equilibrium, which in Nepal's humid climate is around 15 to 18 per cent.**

> **Timber for interior joinery in a heated or air-conditioned building must be at 8 to 12 per cent, or it will SHRINK after installation — doors will develop gaps, panels will split, and floors will open.**

> **Air-seasoned timber installed in a dry interior WILL move, and no amount of workmanship prevents it.**

> **So the choice of seasoning method is determined by where the timber will be used, and the commonest cause of joinery failure is timber seasoned to the wrong moisture content for its destination.**

**And a note on the STRUCTURAL significance of the defects, since that is what a grading standard addresses:**

| Defect | Structural effect |
|---|---|
| **KNOTS** | **Reduce strength, particularly in TENSION and in bending when on the tension face** ← |
| **SHAKES and splits** | **Reduce SHEAR strength; admit water and fungi** |
| **Sloping (diagonal) grain** | **Reduces strength substantially — a 1 in 10 slope can cost 20 % of bending strength** |
| **Wane (missing edge)** | Reduces the section |
| **Decay** | Disqualifies the piece entirely |

> **The KNOT rule is the one worth carrying into design: a knot on the TENSION face of a beam is far more damaging than the same knot on the compression face, because wood in tension depends on continuous fibres and a knot interrupts them.**

> **So timber grading rules limit knot size by location, and a beam should be installed with its better face DOWN** — a detail that costs nothing and is routinely got wrong on site.

examTip.trick: **A SHAKE is a lengthwise SEPARATION; "between adjacent annual rings" makes it a CUP or RING shake.** Heart shakes run radially from the pith, star shakes from the bark inward.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) UPSET is also a fibre discontinuity but runs ACROSS the grain from compression**, not along it from separation.
examTip.mnemonic: **HONEYCOMBING and CASE HARDENING both come from DRYING TOO FAST.** And air seasoning cannot go below ambient equilibrium (15-18 % in Nepal), so interior joinery needing 8-12 % must be KILN seasoned — otherwise it shrinks after installation.

questions.stem: As per IS 1077, the minimum compressive strength of a common burnt clay building brick of the lowest class is:
questions.solution:
**3.5 N/mm².**

**The IS 1077 brick classification by compressive strength:**

| Class designation | Minimum average compressive strength |
|---|---|
| **35** | **35 N/mm²** |
| **30** | **30 N/mm²** |
| **25** | **25 N/mm²** |
| **20** | **20 N/mm²** |
| **17.5** | **17.5 N/mm²** |
| **15** | **15 N/mm²** |
| **12.5** | **12.5 N/mm²** |
| **10** | **10 N/mm²** |
| **7.5** | **7.5 N/mm²** |
| **5** | **5 N/mm²** |
| **3.5** | **3.5 N/mm² — the LOWEST class** ← |

> **The class designation IS the minimum strength in N/mm², which makes the system entirely transparent — a class 10 brick has a minimum strength of 10 N/mm².**

> **Options (b) 7.5 and (c) 5.0 are the next two classes up, and option (a) 10.5 is close to class 10 — so every option is near a real class value.**

> **The specific fact asked for is the FLOOR of the range: 3.5 N/mm².**

**How the strength is measured, since the figure depends on the procedure:**

| Aspect of the test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Number of bricks tested** | **FIVE, and the AVERAGE is taken** |
| **Frogs and voids** | **FILLED with 1:1 cement mortar and cured, so the load is applied evenly** ← |
| **Immersion before test** | 3 days in water at room temperature |
| **Rate of loading** | **14 N/mm² per minute** |
| **Result** | **The average of five; no individual result may fall more than 20 % below the class value** |

> **The FROG FILLING requirement matters: a brick tested with its frog empty would be loaded on a reduced and uneven area and would fail prematurely, giving a result that describes the test rather than the brick.**

> **So the preparation is not a formality — it is what makes the result a property of the material.**

**The other IS 1077 requirements, since a brick is specified on several counts:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Compressive strength** | **3.5 N/mm² minimum, by class** ← |
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **Not more than 20 % by weight for classes up to 12.5; not more than 15 % for higher classes** ← |
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | **"NIL" to "SLIGHT" for a first class brick; "moderate" tolerated in lower classes** |
| **Dimensional tolerance** | **On 20 bricks measured in a row, within a stated range** |
| **Standard (modular) size** | **190 × 90 × 90 mm** |
| **Nominal size (with 10 mm mortar joint)** | **200 × 100 × 100 mm** |
| **Traditional (non-modular) size** | **230 × 110 × 70 mm** |

> **The MODULAR and NOMINAL size distinction is worth being exact about: the BRICK is 190 mm long, and with a 10 mm mortar joint the repeating MODULE is 200 mm.**

> **That is what makes a modular brick convenient: wall lengths, openings and returns all work out in round hundreds of millimetres, so a drawing dimensioned in multiples of 100 mm can be built without cutting bricks.**

> **The traditional 230 mm brick has no such property, which is why it produces the cut bricks and awkward closures that characterise older work.**

**WATER ABSORPTION — why it is limited, since the reason is not obvious:**

> **A highly absorbent brick is a poorly burnt, porous brick, and porosity brings several problems:**

| Consequence of high absorption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Low strength and poor DURABILITY** | Porosity and strength are inversely related |
| **It SUCKS WATER OUT OF THE MORTAR before it can set** | **The mortar is starved of water, does not hydrate properly, and the JOINT is weak** ← |
| **Frost damage where freezing occurs** | Absorbed water expands on freezing |
| **Dampness transmitted through the wall** | Rising and penetrating damp |
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | Water carries soluble salts to the surface |

> **The SECOND row is the one bricklayers know and engineers sometimes forget: this is why bricks are SOAKED before laying.**

> **A dry, absorbent brick laid on fresh mortar draws the water out of it within minutes, and the mortar sets without adequate hydration — giving a joint far weaker than the mortar mix would suggest.**

> **So bricks are soaked until they cease absorbing (or for a stated period), and the soaking is a genuine requirement rather than a tradition.**

> **The complementary error is also real: a SATURATED, dripping brick will FLOAT on the mortar bed and the joint will not adhere. So the brick should be wet but surface-dry when laid.**

**EFFLORESCENCE, since it is the third specified property:**

> **Soluble salts in the brick — chiefly sulphates of sodium, magnesium and calcium — dissolve in water, migrate to the surface, and CRYSTALLISE there as the water evaporates, leaving a white deposit.**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Origin of the salts** | **The clay itself, the fuel, the mortar, or groundwater** |
| **Appearance** | **A white or greyish powdery bloom on the face** |
| **Direct harm** | **Chiefly APPEARANCE — but see below** |
| **CRYPTO-florescence** | **Salts crystallising WITHIN the brick rather than on its surface — this DOES cause damage, spalling the face off** ← |
| **Test** | **A brick stood in water in a shallow dish and allowed to dry; the deposit is graded nil, slight, moderate, heavy or serious** |

> **The distinction between EFFLORESCENCE (on the surface, unsightly) and CRYPTO-FLORESCENCE (within the brick, destructive) is the one worth knowing, because it explains why a merely cosmetic-seeming defect is specified at all.**

> **Salt crystallising inside the pores exerts pressure enough to spall the brick's face, and the damage is progressive.**

> **So a brick with a heavy salt content will not merely look poor — it will lose its face over some years, particularly in a wall subject to wetting and drying.**

examTip.trick: **The class designation IS the minimum strength in N/mm², and the lowest class is 3.5.** Options (b) and (c) are the next two classes up.
examTip.trap: **Frogs must be FILLED with 1:1 mortar before testing** — an unfilled frog gives a reduced, uneven bearing area and a result that describes the test rather than the brick.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bricks are SOAKED because a dry absorbent brick sucks water out of the mortar before it hydrates**, giving a weak joint — but a dripping brick floats on the bed. Wet, surface-dry. And CRYPTO-florescence (salts inside the brick) spalls the face, unlike surface efflorescence.

questions.stem: In the standard test on coarse aggregate, the FLAKINESS INDEX is the percentage by weight of particles whose:
options: Length is greater than 1.8 times their mean dimension
Least dimension (thickness) is less than 0.6 times their mean dimension
Volume exceeds that of a sphere of the same mean dimension
Surface area exceeds a specified value per unit weight
questions.solution:
**Whose LEAST dimension (thickness) is less than 0.6 times their mean dimension.**

**The two shape indices, which are a matched pair:**

| Index | Definition | Measured with |
|---|---|---|
| **FLAKINESS index** | **Percentage by weight of particles whose THICKNESS is less than 0.6 × their mean dimension** ← | **A THICKNESS GAUGE — a plate with elongated slots** |
| **ELONGATION index** | **Percentage by weight of particles whose LENGTH is more than 1.8 × their mean dimension** | **A LENGTH GAUGE — a device with pegs at set spacings** |

> **Option (a) is the ELONGATION index definition, which makes it the designed distractor — the two are constantly interchanged.**

> **The way to keep them apart is to reason from the words: a FLAKE is THIN, so the flakiness index concerns the THICKNESS and the criterion is a FRACTION (0.6) — thickness LESS than.**

> **An ELONGATED particle is LONG, so the elongation index concerns the LENGTH and the criterion is a MULTIPLE (1.8) — length MORE than.**

> **Fraction with thickness, multiple with length. That pairing is enough to reconstruct both.**

**The "mean dimension" — worth clarifying, since it is not the average of three dimensions:**

> **The MEAN DIMENSION of a particle is the average of the two SIEVE SIZES between which it is retained.**

> **So a particle passing a 40 mm sieve and retained on a 25 mm sieve has a mean dimension of (40 + 25)/2 = 32.5 mm.**

> **It is therefore a property of the SIEVE FRACTION, not of the individual particle — which is what makes the test practicable: the whole fraction is gauged against one setting rather than each stone being measured.**

> **For that fraction, the flakiness thickness gauge slot is 0.6 × 32.5 = 19.5 mm, and every particle passing through it is counted as flaky.**

**Why particle shape matters — the consequences:**

| Effect of FLAKY and ELONGATED particles | Note |
|---|---|
| **They BREAK easily under load and under compaction** | **A thin flake is a weak element whatever the rock's strength** ← |
| **Poor INTERLOCK, so lower stability in an unbound layer** | They lie flat and slide over one another |
| **They orient FLAT during compaction, creating planes of weakness** | And they shield the material beneath from compaction |
| **Higher SURFACE AREA per unit weight, so more binder or cement is needed** | Directly raises cost |
| **Poor workability in concrete; harsh mixes** | More water needed for the same slump |
| **Voids increase, density falls** | Weaker layer for the same material |

> **The FIRST row is the essential one: a flaky particle fails by BREAKING rather than by the rock being crushed, so a flaky aggregate performs far below the parent rock's strength.**

> **That is why shape is specified alongside strength, and why a strong rock badly crushed can make a poor aggregate.**

> **The IRC limits:**

| Application | Maximum flakiness index (or combined index) |
|---|---|
| **Bituminous surface courses** | **25 %** |
| **Bituminous bases and binder courses** | **30 %** |
| **Water bound macadam (WBM)** | **15 % (combined flakiness and elongation)** |
| **Wet mix macadam (WMM)** | **35 % (combined)** |
| **Concrete** | **Commonly 30-35 %** |

> **The COMBINED INDEX — flakiness plus elongation — is what most modern specifications use, since a particle may be both and the two defects have the same consequences.**

> **Note the ORDER in which the combined index must be determined: FLAKINESS FIRST, then elongation on the NON-FLAKY portion.**

> **The reason is that a particle that is both flaky and elongated would otherwise be counted twice, and the combined index would exceed 100 per cent for a badly shaped aggregate — which is arithmetically absurd.**

> **So the sequence is prescribed, and getting it the wrong way round is a genuine error rather than a matter of preference.**

**What CAUSES flaky aggregate, since the remedy lies there:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The PARENT ROCK's structure** | **Foliated and laminated rocks — slate, shale, schist, some gneisses — break into flakes by nature** ← |
| **The type of CRUSHER used** | **A JAW crusher tends to produce flaky material; an IMPACT or CONE crusher produces cubical particles** ← |
| **The reduction ratio in one stage** | Too great a reduction in one pass produces poor shape |
| **Insufficient crushing stages** | — |

> **The CRUSHER point is the practically actionable one: aggregate shape is largely determined by the crushing plant, and a quarry producing flaky material can often improve it by adding an impact crusher as a final stage rather than by changing rock.**

> **And the PARENT ROCK point is a genuine constraint: a foliated metamorphic rock will produce flakes however it is crushed, because the flakes are how it breaks.**

> **That matters in Nepal, where much of the available hard rock in the hills is metamorphic and foliated, and where good cubical aggregate is correspondingly valuable and worth hauling for.**

**And the ANGULARITY NUMBER, the third shape measure, for completeness:**

> **ANGULARITY NUMBER = 67 − (percentage solid volume when compacted in a standard way)**

> **The 67 is the solid volume percentage of the most rounded gravel** — so a perfectly rounded aggregate has an angularity number of ZERO.

| Angularity number | Character |
|---|---|
| **0** | **Perfectly rounded** |
| **0-11** | **The normal range for practical aggregates** |
| **Higher** | More angular |

> **ANGULARITY is desirable for INTERLOCK and hence for stability, and undesirable for WORKABILITY and water demand — so it is a genuine trade-off rather than something to be maximised.**

> **Angular crushed rock is preferred for bituminous and unbound layers, where mechanical interlock carries the load; rounded gravel gives better workability in concrete, where the paste does the binding.**

examTip.trick: **FLAKY means THIN, so flakiness uses THICKNESS with a FRACTION (< 0.6 × mean). ELONGATED means LONG, so elongation uses LENGTH with a MULTIPLE (> 1.8 × mean).**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the ELONGATION definition.** And for the COMBINED index, determine FLAKINESS FIRST and elongation on the non-flaky remainder — otherwise a particle that is both gets counted twice.
examTip.mnemonic: **A flaky particle fails by BREAKING, so a strong rock badly crushed makes a poor aggregate.** Shape is largely set by the CRUSHER — jaw crushers give flakes, impact and cone crushers give cubes — and by foliated parent rock, which is much of Nepal's hill rock.

questions.stem: In brick masonry, the vertical joints in alternate courses must not coincide. This requirement is met by:
options: Providing a proper BOND, using queen or king closers as required
questions.solution:
**By providing a proper BOND, using queen or king closers as required.**

**What bond is and why it is essential:**

> **BOND is the arrangement of bricks in successive courses so that the VERTICAL JOINTS DO NOT LINE UP between one course and the next.**

> **The vertical joints must be STAGGERED — normally by a quarter or half a brick — and the reason is structural:**

| Without bond (continuous vertical joints) | With proper bond |
|---|---|
| **The wall is a set of INDEPENDENT vertical piers, side by side** | **The wall acts as ONE monolithic element** ← |
| **A load on one pier is carried by that pier alone** | **The load SPREADS sideways through successive courses** |
| **A continuous vertical joint is a ready-made CRACK** | No continuous plane of weakness |
| **No resistance to lateral or out-of-plane forces** | The courses tie the wall together |
| **A settlement or a point load splits the wall** | The wall redistributes |

> **So bond is what turns a stack of bricks into a wall, and it is not a matter of appearance.**

> **The mortar is far weaker than the brick, so a continuous line of mortar is the plane on which any crack will run — and bond exists to ensure no such continuous line exists.**

**The CLOSERS — the cut bricks that make bond possible:**

| Closer | Description | Where used |
|---|---|---|
| **QUEEN closer (half)** | **A brick cut in HALF along its LENGTH, giving a piece 45 mm wide and full length** | **Next to the quoin header, to start the quarter-brick lap in English bond** ← |
| **Queen closer (quarter)** | Half of a queen closer | Where a quarter lap is needed |
| **KING closer** | **A brick with one corner cut off diagonally, leaving half a header and half a stretcher face** | **At jambs of openings, and in some bonds** |
| **BEVELLED closer** | **The full length of one face bevelled off** | Splayed jambs, angled work |
| **Mitred closer** | An end cut at an angle | Corners other than 90° |
| **BAT (half bat, three-quarter bat)** | **A brick cut across its WIDTH, giving a shorter full-width piece** | **In Flemish bond and at stopped ends** |

> **The QUEEN CLOSER against the BAT is the distinction most often muddled, and the difference is the direction of the cut:**

> **A CLOSER is cut along the LENGTH — it is narrower but still full length.**

> **A BAT is cut across the WIDTH — it is shorter but still full width.**

> **The queen closer's purpose in English bond is specific and worth understanding: placed next to the corner header, it shifts the whole header course by a quarter brick, which produces the quarter lap that English bond requires.**

> **Without it, the joints would align and the bond would fail — so a cut brick a bricklayer might be tempted to omit is in fact what makes the bond work.**

**The principal bonds:**

| Bond | Arrangement | Strength | Appearance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **STRETCHER bond** | **All stretchers; every course the same** | **Only for HALF-BRICK walls — no headers, so it cannot tie a thicker wall** | Plain |
| **HEADER bond** | **All headers** | For curved walls and footings | — |
| **ENGLISH bond** | **Alternate courses of headers and stretchers; quarter lap** | **The STRONGEST for a thick wall** ← | Less decorative |
| **FLEMISH bond** | **Headers and stretchers ALTERNATING in the SAME course** | **Weaker than English — more internal cut bricks and less continuity** | **Better appearance — the reason it is used** ← |
| **Double Flemish** | Flemish appearance on BOTH faces | — | Both faces good |
| **Single Flemish** | Flemish face, English backing | A compromise: appearance and strength | — |
| **Rat-trap bond** | **Bricks on edge, forming cavities** | **Saves about 25 % of bricks and gives insulation** | — |
| **Garden wall, English cross, raking, herringbone** | Decorative and special-purpose | — | — |

> **The ENGLISH against FLEMISH comparison is the classic examination question and the answer is worth stating precisely:**

> **ENGLISH bond is STRONGER; FLEMISH bond LOOKS BETTER.**

> **The reason English is stronger is that its header courses are continuous across the wall's full thickness, tying the two faces together in every alternate course.**

> **Flemish bond's headers are interrupted by stretchers within the same course, so the through-thickness tie is intermittent, and the bond requires more cut bricks internally — each cut brick being a small discontinuity.**

> **So English bond is specified for structural walls and Flemish for exposed facework, and SINGLE FLEMISH — a Flemish face with an English backing — is the practical compromise that gives both.**

> **The RAT-TRAP bond deserves a note for Nepal and for low-cost construction generally: laying bricks on edge to form a cavity within the wall thickness saves roughly a quarter of the bricks and a similar proportion of the mortar, and the cavity gives useful thermal insulation.**

> **Its limitations are that it needs good-quality bricks of accurate size and careful workmanship, and that it is unsuitable where heavy loads or seismic detailing require solid masonry** — so it suits single-storey and boundary work rather than load-bearing multi-storey construction.

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real practice serving a different purpose:**

| Option | Its actual purpose |
|---|---|
| **(a) Damp proof course** | **Prevents RISING DAMP from the ground into the wall — a moisture barrier, nothing to do with joint alignment** |
| **(b) Raking the joints** | **Prepares the joint for POINTING by removing mortar to a depth of 10-20 mm, so the pointing mortar has a key** |
| **(d) Soaking the bricks** | **Prevents the brick absorbing water from the mortar before it hydrates — a mortar-strength measure** |

> **All three are genuine and necessary practices, which is what makes the option set well formed: the candidate must identify which one addresses the STAGGERING OF JOINTS specifically, and only bond does.**

examTip.trick: **BOND is the arrangement that staggers the vertical joints, and CLOSERS are the cut bricks that make it work.** A queen closer next to the quoin header creates the quarter lap English bond requires.
examTip.trap: **CLOSER is cut along the LENGTH (narrower, full length); BAT is cut across the WIDTH (shorter, full width).** The two are constantly muddled.
examTip.mnemonic: **ENGLISH bond is STRONGER (continuous header courses tie the faces); FLEMISH LOOKS BETTER.** Single Flemish — Flemish face, English backing — gives both. And a continuous vertical joint is a ready-made crack, which is why bond is structural, not decorative.

questions.stem: A damp proof course in a wall built at ground level is provided principally to:
options: Prevent rising damp from the foundation into the wall above
Provide a level bed for the first course of brickwork
questions.solution:
**To prevent RISING DAMP from the foundation into the wall above.**

**The mechanism it interrupts:**

> **Masonry and concrete are POROUS, and their pores are fine enough to act as CAPILLARIES.**

> **Groundwater is therefore drawn UPWARD through the foundation and into the wall by capillary action, against gravity.**

> **The capillary rise formula shows why it is significant:  h = 4σ cos θ / (ρ g d)**

> **The finer the pore, the higher the rise — and masonry pores are fine enough to lift water a metre or more.**

> **A DAMP PROOF COURSE is an IMPERVIOUS LAYER placed across the full thickness of the wall, which BREAKS the capillary path.**

> **Water can rise up to it and no further, so the wall above stays dry.**

**The consequences of rising damp — why the DPC is not optional:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Damp patches, staining and a tide mark on the wall** | The visible symptom |
| **Plaster and paint failure, blistering and flaking** | The first practical damage |
| **EFFLORESCENCE and salt damage** | **The rising water carries dissolved SALTS from the soil, which crystallise in the masonry and spall it** ← |
| **Fungal growth, mould and an unhealthy interior** | A health matter, not merely cosmetic |
| **Timber DECAY where joists or frames meet damp masonry** | **Dry rot and wet rot need moisture; a damp wall supplies it** ← |
| **Corrosion of embedded metal** | Cramps, ties, conduit |
| **Loss of thermal insulation** | Wet masonry conducts heat far better than dry |

> **The SALT damage entry is the reason rising damp is progressively destructive rather than merely unsightly: the water evaporates from the wall face and leaves its dissolved salts behind, concentrating them over years until crystallisation pressure breaks the surface away.**

> **And the TIMBER DECAY entry is the most serious in a traditional building: a floor joist built into a damp wall will rot at its bearing, and the failure is concealed inside the wall until the floor moves.**

**Where DPCs are required — not only at the plinth:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL DPC at plinth level** | **Against RISING damp — the case in this question** ← |
| **Under the floor slab (a membrane over the fill)** | Against damp rising into the floor |
| **VERTICAL DPC on the earth-retaining face of a basement wall** | **Against LATERAL penetration from the surrounding soil** |
| **DPC over openings, and cavity trays** | Against water tracking down and inward |
| **Under and over window sills, at jambs** | At the details where water is directed |
| **At the junction of a parapet and a roof** | Against downward penetration |
| **Under a coping or a chajja** | — |

> **The essential principle governing all of them: A DPC MUST BE CONTINUOUS AND MUST BE CONNECTED TO THE ADJACENT DPCs.**

> **A gap of a few centimetres in a horizontal DPC lets damp bypass the whole barrier, and the resulting damp patch may appear metres away from the gap.**

> **So the failures of damp proofing are almost always failures of CONTINUITY at junctions and penetrations rather than failures of the material** — a pipe passing through, a bolt fixed through, a lap not sealed, a corner not turned.

**The materials used, and their characters:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete (1:1½:3), 40-75 mm thick, often with a waterproofing admixture** | **The commonest at plinth level; also serves as a level bed** |
| **Mastic asphalt** | **The best material — completely impervious, and it self-heals minor cracks** ← |
| **Bitumen felt / bituminous sheeting** | **Cheap and flexible; must be LAPPED properly, and it can be punctured** |
| **Polythene or PVC sheeting** | Cheap, effective, easily punctured |
| **Metal sheets — lead, copper, aluminium** | Durable, expensive; lead must be protected from cement |
| **Bricks of very low absorption, in cement mortar** | Traditional; only partially effective |
| **Stone slabs (in traditional construction)** | Slate or dense stone |

> **MASTIC ASPHALT is the best of them and it is worth knowing why: it is applied hot as a plastic mass, it has no laps or joints once laid, and it remains slightly plastic in service — so a small movement or settlement crack in the wall does not tear it, and it flows to close.**

> **A rigid material such as cement concrete, by contrast, cracks where the wall cracks, and the crack is a capillary path straight through the barrier.**

> **Which is a general lesson about waterproofing: a FLEXIBLE barrier survives movement and a RIGID one does not, and buildings move.**

**Why option (d) is not simply wrong — the qualification worth making:**

> **A cement concrete DPC at plinth level DOES also provide a level bed for the brickwork above, and that is a genuine incidental benefit.**

> **But it is not the PURPOSE, and a DPC of bitumen felt or polythene provides no such bed at all while still being a perfectly good DPC.**

> **So the levelling is a property of one material rather than a function of the element** — and the question asks for the principal purpose, which is the moisture barrier.

> **Option (a) is likewise not absurd: a dry wall insulates better than a wet one, so a DPC does improve thermal performance indirectly.**

> **But that is a CONSEQUENCE of keeping the wall dry, not the reason for the DPC — and no one would install a DPC for insulation.**

**And the remedy where a DPC was omitted or has failed, since it is a common problem in older buildings:**

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHEMICAL injection DPC** | **A water-repellent silicone or siloxane injected into a line of drilled holes, forming a barrier in situ** ← the usual modern approach |
| **Physical insertion — cutting a slot and inserting sheeting** | Effective and disruptive; done in sections to avoid destabilising the wall |
| **Electro-osmotic systems** | A small potential difference opposing the capillary rise; mixed reputation |
| **Atmospheric siphon (porous tubes)** | Encourages evaporation at low level; limited effect |
| **Improving external drainage and lowering the adjacent ground** | **Often the cheapest partial remedy — and frequently the actual cause** ← |

> **The last row deserves emphasis because it is the first thing to check: rising damp is very often caused or aggravated by GROUND LEVEL HAVING BEEN RAISED against the wall — a new path, a paving, a flower bed, or accumulated soil bridging the DPC from outside.**

> **In such a case no injection is needed; lowering the ground below the DPC and providing drainage cures it.**

> **Diagnosing before treating is worth a great deal here, because the expensive remedies are useless if the DPC is being bridged.**

examTip.trick: **A DPC is an impervious layer that BREAKS the capillary path** through which groundwater is drawn up into the wall. Masonry pores are fine enough to lift water a metre or more.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (d) are real incidental effects, not the purpose** — a dry wall does insulate better, and a concrete DPC does give a level bed. But a bitumen-felt DPC gives no bed and is still a good DPC.
examTip.mnemonic: **DPC failures are almost always failures of CONTINUITY at junctions and penetrations, not of the material.** And check first whether the ground has been RAISED against the wall, bridging the DPC from outside — no injection cures that.

questions.stem: The radius of gyration of a circular section of diameter d about a diameter is:
questions.solution:
**d/4.**

**The derivation:**

> **r = √(I/A)**

| Quantity | For a circle of diameter d |
|---|---|
| **I about a diameter** | **π d⁴/64** |
| **A** | **π d²/4** |

> **r = √[(π d⁴/64) / (π d²/4)] = √[(d⁴/64) × (4/d²)] = √(d²/16) = d/4** ✓

> **So the radius of gyration of a circle is a QUARTER of its diameter, or HALF its radius.**

**What the radius of gyration MEANS:**

> **It is the distance from the axis at which the whole area could be CONCENTRATED without changing the second moment of area.**

> **That is, a thin ring of the same area at radius r = d/4 would have the same I as the solid circle.**

> **So it is a measure of how far the material is spread from the axis — a purely geometric property with dimensions of LENGTH.**

> **And it is the property that determines BUCKLING, through the slenderness ratio λ = L_e/r.**

**The radii of gyration worth having:**

| Section | r about the axis stated |
|---|---|
| **CIRCLE, diameter d, about a diameter** | **d/4 = 0.25 d** ← |
| **Hollow circle, D and d** | **√(D² + d²)/4** |
| **THIN ring / thin tube, mean diameter D** | **D/(2√2) = 0.354 D** |
| **RECTANGLE b × d, about the axis parallel to b** | **d/√12 = 0.289 d** |
| **Square, side a, about a centroidal axis** | **a/√12 = 0.289 a** |
| **Triangle, base b, height h, about the centroidal axis** | **h/√18 = 0.236 h** |

> **The comparison in the first and fourth rows is instructive: for the same overall depth, a RECTANGLE has a LARGER radius of gyration (0.289 d) than a CIRCLE (0.25 d).**

> **The reason is that a circle tapers toward its extremities — there is little material near the top and bottom of a circle, where it would do most good — while a rectangle has its full width there.**

> **So a square column is slightly more efficient against buckling than a circular one of the same overall size, which is a small but real result.**

**And the THIN RING result, which is the important one:**

> **A thin ring of mean diameter D has r = 0.354 D — considerably better than a solid circle's 0.25 d for the same overall size.**

> **That is why HOLLOW SECTIONS are so efficient in compression: all the material sits at the maximum distance from the axis, where it contributes most to I, and none is wasted near the centre where it contributes almost nothing.**

| Section, same AREA | r | Relative buckling capacity |
|---|---|---|
| **Solid circle, diameter d** | **0.25 d** | **1** |
| **Tube of the same area, mean diameter 2d** | **≈ 0.71 d** | **≈ 8** |

> **Roughly EIGHT TIMES the buckling capacity for the same weight of steel, from geometry alone.**

> **That is the single strongest argument for hollow structural sections, and it is why scaffold tubes, masts, bicycle frames and space-frame members are tubular.**

> **The limit is that a tube's wall can BUCKLE LOCALLY if it is made too thin — so the efficiency cannot be pushed indefinitely, and codes limit the diameter-to-thickness ratio to prevent it.**

> **Which is a general feature of structural optimisation: pushing one failure mode away eventually brings another one forward, and the optimum sits where they meet.**

**The related section properties, since they form a set:**

| Property | Symbol | Expression for a circle | Dimensions |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Area** | **A** | **π d²/4** | **L²** |
| **Second moment of area (moment of inertia)** | **I** | **π d⁴/64** | **L⁴** |
| **Section modulus** | **Z = I/y_max** | **π d³/32** | **L³** |
| **RADIUS OF GYRATION** | **r = √(I/A)** | **d/4** | **L** ← |
| **POLAR moment of inertia** | **J = I_x + I_y** | **π d⁴/32** | **L⁴** |
| **Polar section modulus** | **Z_p = J/r_max** | **π d³/16** | **L³** |

> **The dimensions column is the most useful check available: I is L⁴, Z is L³, r is L¹.**

> **So any expression offered for r that has dimensions other than length is wrong on sight — and the same test catches errors in I and Z.**

> **The POLAR moment J = I_x + I_y is worth noting, and for a circle the two are equal so J = 2I = πd⁴/32.**

> **It governs TORSION: the shear stress in a circular shaft is τ = T r / J, and the twist is θ = T L / (G J).**

> **The PERPENDICULAR AXIS THEOREM — that J = I_x + I_y for any plane section — is what makes that relation so easy for a circle, and it is worth remembering alongside the parallel axis theorem I = I_G + A h².**

> **The two theorems between them let almost any composite section's properties be assembled from the standard shapes**, which is what makes the standard results above worth knowing in the first place.

examTip.trick: **r = √(I/A) = √[(πd⁴/64)/(πd²/4)] = d/4** — a quarter of the diameter, half the radius.
examTip.trap: **Check the DIMENSIONS: r is a LENGTH (L¹), I is L⁴, Z is L³.** Any offered expression with the wrong dimensions is wrong on sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **A hollow section of the same AREA can have eight times the buckling capacity** — all the material at maximum distance from the axis. Limited only by LOCAL buckling of the wall, which is why codes cap the diameter-to-thickness ratio.

questions.stem: A T-section has a flange 150 mm wide and 50 mm thick and a web 50 mm wide and 150 mm deep. The distance of its centroid from the top of the flange is:
questions.solution:
**75 mm from the top of the flange.**

**Step 1 — split the section into two rectangles and tabulate, measuring every centroid from ONE datum: the top of the flange.**

| Part | Dimensions | Area A (mm²) | ȳ from the TOP OF THE FLANGE (mm) | A ȳ (mm³) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FLANGE** | **150 × 50** | **7500** | **50/2 = 25** | **187,500** |
| **WEB** | **50 × 150** | **7500** | **50 + 150/2 = 125** | **937,500** |
| **TOTAL** | — | **15,000** | — | **1,125,000** |

**Step 2 — take the first moment about the datum:**

> **ȳ = Σ(A ȳ) / ΣA = 1,125,000 / 15,000 = 75 mm** ✓

**The shortcut, worth spotting:**

> **The two areas are EQUAL — 7500 mm² each, since 150 × 50 = 50 × 150.**

> **When two parts have equal areas, the composite centroid is the SIMPLE ARITHMETIC MEAN of their individual centroids, with no weighting needed:**

> **ȳ = (25 + 125)/2 = 75 mm** ✓

> **This section is deliberately proportioned to have equal areas, so recognising it turns the problem into one addition.**

> **The general relation ȳ = Σ(Aȳ)/ΣA must be used whenever the areas differ.**

**The two checks always available:**

> **FIRST — the distances from the top and from the bottom must sum to the total depth.**

> **Total depth = 50 + 150 = 200 mm, and 75 + 125 = 200** ✓

> **SECOND — with equal areas and a centroid midway between them, the two offsets h must be equal: 75 − 25 = 50 and 125 − 75 = 50** ✓

**Why the distractors are placed as they are:**

| Option | Origin |
|---|---|
| **(a) 100 mm** | **HALF THE TOTAL DEPTH — the centroid of the overall bounding rectangle. A T-section is UNSYMMETRICAL, so its centroid is NOT at mid-depth** ← |
| **(b) 62.5 mm** | The result of a mis-set datum — for instance averaging 25 and 100 |
| **(c) 125 mm** | **The distance from the BOTTOM, not from the top** |
| **(d) 75 mm** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is the conceptual trap: it assumes symmetry the section does not have.**

> **And option (c) is the right number measured from the wrong end — which is why the datum must be stated in the working, as it is in the column heading above.**

> **MIXING DATUMS is the error this class of problem is built to catch: measuring the web's centroid from the top of the WEB gives 75 instead of 125, and the answer then comes out wrong by exactly the flange thickness.**

> **Tabulating with the datum named in the heading makes that error impossible.**

**The MOMENT OF INERTIA, since the centroid is found in order to compute it:**

> **By the parallel axis theorem, I_G = Σ(I_own + A h²) about the composite centroid at 75 mm:**

| Part | I_own = bd³/12 (mm⁴) | h (mm) | A h² (mm⁴) | Total (mm⁴) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Flange 150 × 50** | **150 × 50³/12 = 1.563 × 10⁶** | **50** | **7500 × 2500 = 18.75 × 10⁶** | **20.31 × 10⁶** |
| **Web 50 × 150** | **50 × 150³/12 = 14.06 × 10⁶** | **50** | **7500 × 2500 = 18.75 × 10⁶** | **32.81 × 10⁶** |
| **I_G total** | — | — | — | **53.13 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |

> **Note that the two A h² terms come out EQUAL at 18.75 × 10⁶, which follows from the equal areas and the symmetric 50 mm offsets — a further confirmation that the centroid was correctly located.**

> **And note which part contributes more: the WEB, at 32.81 × 10⁶ against the flange's 20.31 × 10⁶ — because although the areas are equal, the web's own depth of 150 mm gives it nine times the flange's I_own.**

**Why a T-section's asymmetry matters — the design consequence:**

> **A symmetrical section has its centroid at mid-depth and equal stresses top and bottom. A T-section does not:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **y_top** | **75 mm** |
| **y_bottom** | **125 mm** |
| **Z_top = I/y_top** | **53.13 × 10⁶/75 = 708,000 mm³** |
| **Z_bottom = I/y_bottom** | **53.13 × 10⁶/125 = 425,000 mm³** ← the smaller |

> **Since σ = M/Z, the SMALLER section modulus gives the LARGER stress — so the bottom of the web is the critical fibre, reaching its limit first.**

> **That has a direct consequence for how a T-section should be oriented:**

> **For a material equally strong in tension and compression (steel), the section is simply governed by Z_bottom, whichever way up it is used.**

> **For a material MUCH STRONGER IN COMPRESSION THAN IN TENSION — concrete, cast iron, masonry — the flange should be on the COMPRESSION side, so the weak tensile capacity is required only at the fibre NEARER the neutral axis, where the stress is lower.**

> **Which is exactly the reinforced concrete T-beam: the slab forms a wide compression flange where the concrete is strong, and the tension is carried by steel concentrated low in the web where the concrete would be useless.**

> **So the asymmetry is not an inconvenience to be tolerated but the feature that lets each material work where it is strong** — and locating the centroid is the first step in exploiting it.

examTip.trick: **Fix ONE datum — the top of the flange — and measure every part from it: flange 25 mm, web 125 mm.** The areas are equal (7500 each), so ȳ = (25 + 125)/2 = **75 mm.**
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 100 mm assumes symmetry the section does not have**, and option (c) 125 mm is the right number measured from the BOTTOM. Mixing datums — taking the web's centroid from the top of the web — is the error this problem is built to catch.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two checks: distances from top and bottom sum to the total depth (75 + 125 = 200), and equal areas give the simple mean.** And the unequal section moduli (Z_bottom smaller, so critical) are why an RC T-beam puts its flange in COMPRESSION.

questions.stem: In levelling, the difference between the sum of the back sights and the sum of the fore sights should equal:
options: The sum of the rises minus the sum of the falls
The last reduced level minus the first reduced level
Both of the above, and both checks must agree
The sum of the intermediate sights
questions.solution:
**Both of the above, and both checks must agree.**

**The arithmetical check on a level book (the rise and fall method):**

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = Σrise − Σfall = Last RL − First RL**

> **All three quantities must be EQUAL, and computing them is the standard check applied at the foot of every page of a level book.**

**Why the identity holds — the reasoning in each part:**

> **FIRST — ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL.**

> **Every back sight RAISES the instrument's height of collimation relative to the point sighted, and every fore sight LOWERS it.**

> **Summing them over the whole line, the accumulated difference is exactly the net rise of the ground from the first point to the last.**

> **SECOND — Σrise − Σfall = Last RL − First RL.**

> **Each rise or fall is the change in level from one point to the next, so summing them algebraically along the line gives the total change from start to finish.**

> **That is a statement so nearly self-evident that it might seem to prove nothing — and yet it is a real check, because it tests whether every individual rise and fall was correctly computed and correctly signed.**

**What the check DOES and DOES NOT detect — the essential caution:**

| The check DETECTS | The check does NOT detect |
|---|---|
| **ARITHMETICAL errors in reducing the levels** | **A MISREAD STAFF — a wrong reading entered consistently** ← |
| **A rise entered as a fall, or vice versa** | **A wrongly BOOKED reading (a fore sight entered as a back sight is caught; a misread number is not)** |
| **An omitted or duplicated entry in the reduction** | **An instrument out of ADJUSTMENT (collimation error)** |
| **A transposed digit in the reduction** | **A staff not held VERTICAL** |
| — | **A settled or moved change point** |
| — | **A staff read on the wrong graduation (the 1 m or 2 m error)** |

> **So the arithmetical check verifies the ARITHMETIC and nothing more.**

> **A level book that checks perfectly may still contain a completely wrong level, if the staff was misread at a change point — because the wrong reading is used consistently in both the back sight and the fore sight computations and cancels out of the check.**

> **That is the single most important thing to understand about the check, and it is why field procedure matters as much as arithmetic:**

| Field safeguard | Guards against |
|---|---|
| **CLOSE the level line back onto its starting point, or onto another known bench mark** | **Detects all the errors the arithmetical check cannot** ← |
| **Keep back sight and fore sight distances EQUAL at each setup** | **Cancels COLLIMATION error, curvature and refraction** ← |
| **Choose FIRM change points** | Prevents staff settlement |
| **Read the staff to the correct graduation and book immediately** | Misreading |
| **Use a bubble or rock the staff, taking the minimum reading** | Non-vertical staff |

> **The BALANCED SIGHT DISTANCES safeguard is the elegant one and deserves explanation:**

> **If the instrument's line of sight is not exactly horizontal — a collimation error — the reading is in error by an amount PROPORTIONAL TO THE DISTANCE.**

> **With the back sight and fore sight at EQUAL distances, the two errors are EQUAL and of the same sign, so they CANCEL when the difference is taken.**

> **The same cancellation removes the effects of earth CURVATURE and atmospheric REFRACTION, which likewise depend on distance.**

> **So a simple field discipline — pace out roughly equal distances either side of the instrument — removes three systematic errors at once, without any adjustment of the instrument and without any computation.**

> **That is worth more than most corrections, and it is why the practice is insisted upon.**

**The two methods of reduction, since the check differs slightly:**

| | **HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION method** | **RISE AND FALL method** |
|---|---|---|
| **Procedure** | **RL = HI − staff reading; HI = RL + BS** | **Compute the rise or fall between consecutive readings, then apply it** |
| **Speed** | **FASTER — fewer computations** | **Slower — every reading is differenced** |
| **Check** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL only** | **The FULL THREE-WAY check** ← |
| **Checks INTERMEDIATE sights?** | **NO — intermediate sights are NOT verified by the check** ← | **YES — every reading enters the rise/fall computation** |
| **Suits** | **Longitudinal sections, cross-sections — many intermediate sights** | **Precise levelling; where a complete check is wanted** |

> **The fourth row is the decisive difference and the reason both methods survive:**

> **In the HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION method, an intermediate sight is reduced independently and appears NOWHERE in the arithmetical check — so an error in an intermediate reduction passes undetected.**

> **In the RISE AND FALL method every reading is differenced against its neighbour, so every reading participates in the check.**

> **So the height of collimation method is faster and less thoroughly checked; the rise and fall method is slower and fully checked.**

> **The practical rule follows directly: use HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION where there are MANY INTERMEDIATE SIGHTS and speed matters (profile and cross-section levelling), and RISE AND FALL where PRECISION matters and the intermediate sights are few.**

> **Which is a good example of choosing a method for the job rather than adopting one from habit — and of the fact that a faster method's cost is usually a weaker check.**

examTip.trick: **ΣBS − ΣFS = Σrise − Σfall = Last RL − First RL.** All three must agree, and all three are computed at the foot of every page.
examTip.trap: **The check verifies the ARITHMETIC and nothing else.** A misread staff at a change point is used consistently in both the BS and FS computations, cancels out of the check, and leaves a perfectly checking level book with a wrong level in it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep BS and FS distances EQUAL and three systematic errors cancel at once — collimation, curvature and refraction** — because all three are proportional to distance. And the HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION method does NOT check intermediate sights; the RISE AND FALL method does.

questions.stem: In the analysis of rates for an item of work, the contractor's PROFIT AND OVERHEAD is conventionally added as:
options: 15 % of the cost of materials and labour
10 % of the cost of materials and labour
5 % of the total estimated cost of the work
1.5 % of the total estimated cost of the work
questions.solution:
**10 per cent of the cost of materials and labour.**

**The build-up of a rate in RATE ANALYSIS:**

| Component | Basis |
|---|---|
| **MATERIALS** | **Quantity per unit of work × the rate at site, INCLUDING wastage and carriage** |
| **LABOUR** | **Number of each category of worker per unit of work × the daily wage** |
| **PLANT and machinery** | Hire or ownership cost per unit of output |
| **SUNDRIES / tools and plant (T&P)** | Commonly 1.5 to 2.5 % of the labour cost |
| **WATER charges** | Commonly 1 to 1.5 % |
| **CONTRACTOR'S PROFIT and OVERHEAD** | **10 % of the above** ← |
| **TOTAL** | **The RATE for the item** |

> **So the 10 per cent is added to the DIRECT COSTS (materials, labour, plant and sundries) at the end of the build-up.**

**The other percentages in estimating, since all four options are real figures:**

| Allowance | Conventional percentage | Applied to |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTOR'S PROFIT and overhead** | **10 %** ← | **The direct cost in a rate analysis** |
| **CONTINGENCIES** | **3-5 %** | **The estimated cost of works** |
| **WORK-CHARGED ESTABLISHMENT (supervision)** | **1.5-2 %** | The estimated cost |
| **Tools and plant (T&P)** | **1-1.5 %** | The estimated cost |
| **Petty supervision, sundries** | **1.5-2.5 %** | The labour cost |
| **Water charges** | **1-1.5 %** | The cost of materials and labour |

> **Option (d) 1.5 per cent is the WORK-CHARGED ESTABLISHMENT or T&P figure, and option (c) 5 per cent is the CONTINGENCY figure — both real, both applied to a different base and for a different purpose.**

> **So the option set requires both the PERCENTAGE and its BASE to be right, which is the substance of this topic.**

**Why CONTINGENCY is applied to the total and PROFIT to the item — the distinction that matters:**

> **PROFIT AND OVERHEAD is part of the RATE. It is what the contractor is paid for each unit of work, and it is embedded in every item of the bill.**

> **CONTINGENCY is part of the ESTIMATE, not of any rate. It is money the EMPLOYER sets aside for the unforeseen — quantities greater than estimated, minor additional items, price variation.**

> **So contingency belongs to the employer and profit to the contractor, and the two are never mixed:**

| | **PROFIT and OVERHEAD (10 %)** | **CONTINGENCY (3-5 %)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Whose money** | **The CONTRACTOR'S** | **The EMPLOYER'S** ← |
| **Where it appears** | **Inside each item RATE** | **As a separate line in the ESTIMATE** |
| **Paid out** | **With every measured item** | **Only if and when the contingency is actually needed** |
| **Purpose** | Overheads, establishment, risk and return | **Cover for the unforeseen** |
| **If not needed** | It is still paid — it is part of the price | **It is SAVED and returned to the budget** ← |

> **The last row is the crucial one and it explains why contingency must be a SEPARATE, VISIBLE line rather than buried in the rates:**

> **A contingency shown separately can be released when the risk does not materialise, and the project comes in under budget.**

> **A margin hidden inside inflated quantities or rates cannot be released — it is spent whatever happens, because the contractor is paid the rate for the work measured.**

> **Which is exactly the point made against "safer" estimating: inflating quantities to be cautious is not conservatism, it is inaccuracy, and it converts a recoverable contingency into an unrecoverable cost.**

**What the 10 per cent actually covers, since "profit" understates it:**

| Included in the contractor's 10 % | Note |
|---|---|
| **SITE overheads** | **Site office, storekeeper, watchman, site engineer, temporary works** |
| **HEAD OFFICE overheads** | **Estimating, accounts, management, office rent — spread across all the firm's work** ← |
| **Financing cost** | Working capital between doing the work and being paid |
| **Insurance, bonds and guarantees** | Bank charges on the performance security |
| **RISK** | **Weather, ground conditions, price movement, dispute** |
| **PROFIT proper** | The return on the contractor's capital and enterprise |

> **So the 10 per cent is chiefly OVERHEAD AND RISK, and the actual profit within it is a small fraction — commonly 2 to 4 per cent of turnover for a construction firm.**

> **That is worth understanding because it explains why contractors' margins are thin and why a badly estimated job loses money quickly: a 5 per cent error in a rate can consume the whole profit on an item.**

> **And it explains why contractors resist unbalanced risk allocation so strongly — a risk transferred to the contractor and not priced simply comes out of a margin that cannot absorb it.**

**A worked rate analysis, to show the build-up concretely:**

> **Take 1 m³ of brickwork in 1:6 cement mortar:**

| Item | Quantity | Rate | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bricks (with 5 % wastage)** | **500 nos** | **Rs 15 each** | **Rs 7,500** |
| **Cement** | **1.1 bags** | **Rs 800/bag** | **Rs 880** |
| **Sand** | **0.25 m³** | **Rs 1,600/m³** | **Rs 400** |
| **Mason** | **0.9 day** | **Rs 1,200/day** | **Rs 1,080** |
| **Labourer** | **1.5 day** | **Rs 800/day** | **Rs 1,200** |
| **Water and sundries, say 1.5 %** | — | — | **Rs 166** |
| **SUBTOTAL (direct cost)** | — | — | **Rs 11,226** |
| **Contractor's profit and overhead, 10 %** | — | — | **Rs 1,123** |
| **RATE per m³** | — | — | **Rs 12,349** |

> **The figures are illustrative, but the STRUCTURE is what matters, and two features of it are worth noting.**

> **First, MATERIALS dominate — about Rs 8,780 of the Rs 11,226 direct cost, nearly 80 per cent. So a rate analysis is chiefly an exercise in getting the material quantities and prices right, and an error in the brick rate matters far more than an error in the mason's output.**

> **Second, the WASTAGE allowance on materials is a real and specified figure — 5 per cent on bricks, 2 to 3 per cent on cement, more on sand — and it belongs in the QUANTITY rather than in the rate, because it is a physical loss rather than a price.**

> **That is the same separation of concerns as keeping contingency out of the measurements: each allowance sits where it belongs, visible and auditable, rather than being absorbed into a neighbouring figure.**

examTip.trick: **Contractor's profit and overhead: 10 % of the direct cost (materials + labour + plant + sundries), added at the end of the rate build-up.**
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real percentage with a different BASE** — 5 % is CONTINGENCY on the estimate, 1.5 % is work-charged establishment or T&P. Get both the figure and its base right.
examTip.mnemonic: **Profit is the CONTRACTOR'S and sits inside each rate; CONTINGENCY is the EMPLOYER'S and sits as a separate line** — which is why it can be RELEASED if unneeded, while a margin hidden in the rates is spent whatever happens.

questions.stem: A soil has D₆₀ = 0.60 mm and D₁₀ = 0.15 mm. Its uniformity coefficient is:
questions.solution:
**4.0.**

**The definition:**

> **C_u = D₆₀ / D₁₀ = 0.60 / 0.15 = 4.0** ✓

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **D₆₀** | **The particle size such that 60 % of the soil by weight is FINER** |
| **D₁₀** | **The size such that 10 % is finer — the EFFECTIVE SIZE** |
| **D₃₀** | The size such that 30 % is finer |

> **Option (c) 0.25 is the ratio inverted, and since D₆₀ is by definition LARGER than D₁₀, the uniformity coefficient is ALWAYS GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO 1.**

> **So any answer below 1 can be rejected on sight — which eliminates option (c) without arithmetic.**

**What C_u tells you:**

| C_u | Grading | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **= 1** | **The theoretical limit — all particles the same size** | Never achieved in nature |
| **< 4 (sands) or < 6 (gravels)** | **UNIFORM / POORLY GRADED** | **Particles of similar size; large voids; poor packing** ← |
| **> 4 (sands) or > 6 (gravels)** | **WELL GRADED, if C_c is also satisfactory** | **A range of sizes; small particles fill the voids between large ones** |
| **Very high with a missing fraction** | **GAP GRADED** | Two sizes present, the middle range absent |

> **So C_u = 4.0 sits exactly ON the boundary for a sand — the minimum value for it to be classed as well graded.**

> **And note that a HIGH C_u alone does NOT prove good grading, which is why the second coefficient exists.**

**The COEFFICIENT OF CURVATURE, which completes the description:**

> **C_c = (D₃₀)² / (D₁₀ × D₆₀)**

> **For a WELL-GRADED soil, C_c must lie between 1 and 3.**

> **The reason both coefficients are needed is that C_u measures only the SPREAD between two points on the curve and says nothing about what happens BETWEEN them.**

> **A GAP-GRADED soil — say a coarse gravel mixed with a fine sand, with nothing in between — can have a large C_u and yet pack badly, because the missing intermediate sizes are exactly the ones that would fill the voids.**

> **C_c detects it: with the middle of the curve missing, D₃₀ sits close to D₁₀, and C_c falls outside the 1 to 3 range.**

> **So the two coefficients together describe both the RANGE of sizes and the CONTINUITY of the distribution, and a soil is well graded only if BOTH conditions are met.**

**Why grading matters — the engineering consequences:**

| Property | WELL-graded soil | UNIFORM (poorly graded) soil |
|---|---|---|
| **Packing and density achievable** | **HIGH — fines fill the voids between coarse particles** ← | **LOW — large uniform voids remain** |
| **Shear strength** | **Higher** | Lower |
| **Compressibility** | **Lower** | Higher |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **LOWER — the fines block the flow paths** | **HIGHER** |
| **Compaction** | **Easier to compact to a high density** | Harder |
| **Suits** | **Subbase, base, engineered fill, concrete aggregate** | **DRAINAGE layers and filters — where permeability is WANTED** ← |

> **The last row is worth emphasising because it corrects a natural assumption: WELL GRADED IS NOT ALWAYS BETTER.**

> **A drainage blanket or a filter layer needs to be PERMEABLE, and a well-graded material's fines are precisely what would block it.**

> **So a drain is deliberately built of a uniform, single-sized material — and specifying a well-graded aggregate for a drain would defeat its purpose entirely.**

> **Which is the general point: a grading is specified for a PURPOSE, and "good" grading means "appropriate to the purpose".**

**The EFFECTIVE SIZE D₁₀, since it has uses of its own:**

| Use of D₁₀ | Note |
|---|---|
| **HAZEN'S formula for permeability: k ≈ C D₁₀² (cm/s, with D₁₀ in cm, C ≈ 100)** | **A rough estimate for clean sands** ← |
| **Filter design criteria** | Expressed in terms of D₁₅ and D₈₅ of filter and base |
| **Frost susceptibility assessment** | Fine fractions govern |
| **Grouting and injection assessment** | Whether grout can penetrate |

> **HAZEN'S formula is worth noting because it shows why the SMALL particles govern permeability: k goes as D₁₀², the size of the SMALLEST tenth, not as the average size.**

> **The physical reason is that flow through a soil is controlled by its NARROWEST passages — the constrictions between the fine particles — exactly as a pipeline's capacity is governed by its narrowest section.**

> **So adding a small percentage of fines to a clean sand can reduce its permeability by orders of magnitude, while adding coarse gravel changes it very little.**

> **For this soil, D₁₀ = 0.15 mm = 0.015 cm, so k ≈ 100 × 0.015² = 0.0225 cm/s = 2.25 × 10⁻⁴ m/s — a medium sand, freely draining.**

**The FILTER CRITERIA, since they are the practical application of grading:**

> **A filter must be coarse enough to DRAIN freely and fine enough to RETAIN the soil it protects:**

| Criterion | Requirement | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **PERMEABILITY (drainage) criterion** | **D₁₅(filter) / D₁₅(base) ≥ 4 to 5** | **The filter must be MORE permeable than the soil** |
| **RETENTION (piping) criterion** | **D₁₅(filter) / D₈₅(base) ≤ 4 to 5** | **The filter's voids must be small enough to hold the soil's particles** ← |
| **Uniformity** | **The filter should be reasonably uniform, and NOT gap graded** | So it does not segregate |
| **No more than 5 % passing 75 μm** | The filter itself must not contain fines | — |

> **The two criteria pull in OPPOSITE directions — one wants the filter coarse, the other wants it fine — so a filter grading is a band between two limits rather than a target.**

> **Where a single filter cannot satisfy both against a very fine base soil, a GRADED FILTER of two or more layers is used, each layer filtering the one before it.**

> **That is how a chimney drain in an earth dam is built, and it is one of the most safety-critical gradings in civil engineering: a filter that fails to retain the core material allows PIPING, and piping destroys dams.**

examTip.trick: **C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀ = 0.60/0.15 = 4.0.** Since D₆₀ > D₁₀ always, C_u is ALWAYS ≥ 1 — so option (c) 0.25 can be rejected on sight.
examTip.trap: **A high C_u alone does not prove good grading** — a GAP-graded soil can have a large C_u and pack badly. That is why C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀ D₆₀) must also lie between 1 and 3.
examTip.mnemonic: **WELL GRADED IS NOT ALWAYS BETTER** — a drainage layer needs to be PERMEABLE, and a well-graded material's fines are exactly what would block it. And Hazen's k ≈ 100 D₁₀² shows the SMALLEST tenth governs flow, because the narrowest passages control.

questions.stem: The compactive effort applied in the MODIFIED Proctor test, compared with that in the standard Proctor test, is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 4.5 times.**

**The two tests compared:**

| Parameter | **STANDARD Proctor (light compaction)** | **MODIFIED Proctor (heavy compaction)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rammer mass** | **2.6 kg** | **4.89 kg** |
| **Height of drop** | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| **Number of layers** | **3** | **5** |
| **Blows per layer** | **25** | **25** |
| **Mould volume** | **1000 cm³** | **1000 cm³** |
| **Compactive energy** | **About 595 kJ/m³** | **About 2700 kJ/m³** |
| **Ratio** | **1** | **≈ 4.5** ← |

**The computation, since the ratio can be derived rather than recalled:**

> **Energy = (mass × g × drop) × blows per layer × number of layers ÷ mould volume**

> **STANDARD:  2.6 × 9.81 × 0.310 × 25 × 3 = 593 J in 0.001 m³ = 593 kJ/m³**

> **MODIFIED:  4.89 × 9.81 × 0.450 × 25 × 5 = 2699 J in 0.001 m³ = 2699 kJ/m³**

> **Ratio = 2699/593 = 4.55 ≈ 4.5** ✓

> **Three factors contribute, and it is worth seeing how they multiply: the rammer is 1.88 times heavier, the drop is 1.45 times greater, and there are 1.67 times as many layers.**

> **1.88 × 1.45 × 1.67 = 4.55** ✓

> **So no single change accounts for the ratio — it is the product of three, which is why estimating "about twice" (option b) is so far out.**

**What the extra energy achieves — the effect on the compaction curve:**

| Effect of increasing the compactive effort | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maximum DRY DENSITY increases** | **The soil packs tighter** |
| **OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT DECREASES** | **Less water is needed to reach the peak** ← |
| **The curve becomes SHARPER (more peaked)** | Density is more sensitive to moisture near the optimum |
| **The peaks lie on a line roughly parallel to the zero-air-voids curve** | The line of optimums |

> **The SECOND row is the counter-intuitive one and the most useful to understand:**

> **HEAVIER compaction requires LESS water, not more.**

> **The reason is that water acts as a LUBRICANT allowing particles to slide into a denser arrangement. With a heavy rammer, mechanical energy does more of that work, so less lubrication is needed.**

> **And beyond the optimum, water OCCUPIES VOLUME that solids could occupy — so too much water reduces the dry density however hard the soil is compacted.**

> **Hence the characteristic peaked curve: too dry and the particles will not move; too wet and water takes their place.**

> **The practical consequence on site: if a heavier roller is brought in, the moisture content must be REDUCED, not increased — and a crew that responds to a heavier roller by watering more will get a lower density than before.**

**The ZERO AIR VOIDS line, since it bounds the curve:**

> **γ_d = G γ_w / (1 + wG)**  at 100 per cent saturation.

> **This is the theoretical maximum dry density for a given water content, corresponding to ALL the air having been expelled.**

> **No compaction curve can touch or cross it, and every real curve lies BELOW it — typically at 80 to 95 per cent saturation at the optimum.**

> **That is a genuinely useful check on laboratory results: a plotted compaction curve that crosses the zero-air-voids line contains an error, and the check costs one calculation.**

> **It also explains why the optimum is not at full saturation: expelling the last of the air requires more energy than any practical compaction delivers, so a compacted soil always retains a few per cent of air voids.**

**Which test to use, since the choice reflects the loading:**

| Application | Test |
|---|---|
| **Earth dams, embankments, general fill** | **STANDARD Proctor — the soil will carry moderate loads** |
| **HIGHWAY subgrades, airfield pavements, heavily loaded fill** | **MODIFIED Proctor — heavier compaction plant is available and heavier loads will be applied** ← |
| **Field control** | **Compare the field density against the LABORATORY maximum from the appropriate test** |

> **The principle is that the LABORATORY test should represent the FIELD compaction plant.**

> **Specifying standard Proctor and then compacting with a heavy vibratory roller means the field density may exceed 100 per cent of the "maximum" — which looks like an error but is simply the wrong reference having been chosen.**

> **Conversely, specifying modified Proctor where only light plant is available sets a target the site cannot reach, and the specification is then either broken or the work is impossibly slow.**

> **So matching the test to the plant is a real decision, and mismatching it produces either meaningless compliance or unachievable requirements.**

**RELATIVE COMPACTION, which is how the result is used:**

> **Relative compaction = (field dry density / laboratory maximum dry density) × 100**

| Application | Typical requirement |
|---|---|
| **Highway subgrade and embankment** | **95-100 % of modified Proctor** |
| **Earth dam core** | **95-98 % of standard Proctor, at a controlled moisture content** ← |
| **General fill** | **90-95 %** |
| **Backfill to structures** | 95 % |

> **The EARTH DAM entry deserves its note: for a dam core the MOISTURE CONTENT is controlled as tightly as the density, and often to slightly WET of optimum.**

> **The reason is that a core compacted DRY of optimum has a more brittle, flocculated structure and can CRACK on differential settlement — and a crack in a dam core is a seepage path.**

> **Compacted slightly WET of optimum, the clay is more plastic and can deform without cracking.**

> **So the dam core is deliberately compacted to a density slightly below the achievable maximum, in exchange for a material that will yield rather than crack — which is a clear instance of choosing ductility over strength, exactly as in structural design.**

examTip.trick: **Three factors multiply: rammer 4.89/2.6 = 1.88, drop 450/310 = 1.45, layers 5/3 = 1.67. Product = 4.55 ≈ 4.5.** No single change accounts for it, which is why "about twice" is far out.
examTip.trap: **Heavier compaction needs LESS water, not more** — water lubricates, and mechanical energy substitutes for it. A crew that waters more when a heavier roller arrives will get a LOWER density.
examTip.mnemonic: **No curve can cross the ZERO AIR VOIDS line γ_d = Gγ_w/(1+wG)** — a one-calculation check on any plotted result. And a dam core is compacted slightly WET of optimum, trading density for a material that yields rather than CRACKS.

questions.stem: A concentrated load of 1000 kN acts at the ground surface. By Boussinesq's theory, the vertical stress at a depth of 5 m directly beneath the load is:
questions.solution:
**19.1 kPa.**

**Boussinesq's expression for a point load, directly beneath it (r = 0):**

> **σ_z = (3 Q) / (2 π z²) = 0.4775 Q / z²**

**The computation:**

> **σ_z = 0.4775 × 1000 / 5² = 477.5 / 25 = 19.1 kPa** ✓

> **The constant 0.4775 is simply 3/(2π), and it is worth recognising rather than memorising: 3/6.2832 = 0.4775.**

> **Option (d) 63.7 kPa is 0.4775 × 1000 / (5 × √5) or a similar mishandling of z², and option (b) 40 kPa is Q/z² without the 0.4775.**

> **Option (c) 12.7 kPa is roughly the value at 6 m, or Q/(2πz²) — the constant taken as 1/(2π) rather than 3/(2π).**

**The general form, since the stress off the axis is often wanted:**

> **σ_z = (3 Q z³) / (2 π R⁵) = (Q / z²) × K_B**

> **where R = √(r² + z²) and the INFLUENCE FACTOR is:**

> **K_B = (3/2π) × [1 / (1 + (r/z)²)]^{5/2}**

| r/z | K_B |
|---|---|
| **0 (directly beneath)** | **0.4775** ← |
| **0.5** | **0.2733** |
| **1.0** | **0.0844** |
| **1.5** | **0.0251** |
| **2.0** | **0.0085** |
| **3.0** | **0.0015** |

> **The decay with lateral distance is very rapid: at r = z the stress is only 18 per cent of the value beneath the load, and at r = 2z it is under 2 per cent.**

> **So a point load's influence is confined to a narrow cone — which is the physical basis of the familiar rule that a footing's stress influence extends to a depth of about 1.5 to 2 times its width and little further laterally.**

**The two assumptions of Boussinesq's theory, and their honest consequences:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **The soil is HOMOGENEOUS, ISOTROPIC and semi-infinite** | **Real soil is LAYERED and often anisotropic** ← |
| **The soil is LINEARLY ELASTIC** | **Soil is not elastic, and certainly not linear** |
| **The soil is WEIGHTLESS** | The stresses computed are those DUE TO THE LOAD ONLY; overburden is added separately |
| **The load is applied at the surface of a half space** | — |

> **The most reassuring feature of the theory is one worth stating: for the VERTICAL stress, POISSON'S RATIO DOES NOT APPEAR in the expression.**

> **So the computed vertical stress is INDEPENDENT of the soil's elastic properties entirely — it depends only on the geometry.**
