> **That is why Boussinesq's solution is used with confidence for a material that is manifestly not elastic: the elastic assumption enters the derivation but drops out of the result for the quantity most needed.**

> **The horizontal and shear stresses, and the DISPLACEMENTS, do contain μ and E — so those must be treated with much greater caution.**

**WESTERGAARD'S alternative, since layered soil is the common case:**

> **Westergaard's solution assumes the soil is reinforced by thin, rigid, horizontal sheets that prevent lateral strain — a model of a layered deposit such as a varved clay.**

| | **BOUSSINESQ** | **WESTERGAARD** |
|---|---|---|
| **Soil model** | **Homogeneous, isotropic elastic half space** | **Laterally restrained, layered** |
| **σ_z directly beneath a point load** | **0.4775 Q/z²** | **0.3183 Q/z² (for μ = 0)** |
| **Stress beneath the load** | **HIGHER** | **LOWER — about two thirds** ← |
| **Lateral spread** | Narrower cone | Wider spread |
| **Suits** | **Sand and homogeneous deposits** | **Layered and stratified deposits** |

> **Boussinesq gives the LARGER stress beneath the load, so using it is CONSERVATIVE for a layered soil — which is one reason it is the default in practice despite Westergaard being the better model for a varved clay.**

**Where the point-load solution leads — the practical results built on it:**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| **Point load** | **σ_z = 0.4775 Q/z²** ← |
| **Line load** | By integration along a line |
| **UNIFORM load on a CIRCULAR area, on the axis** | **σ_z = q [1 − (1/(1+(R/z)²))^{3/2}]** |
| **Uniform load on a RECTANGULAR area, under a corner** | **Newmark's influence chart or tables in m = B/z, n = L/z** |
| **Any shape** | **NEWMARK'S INFLUENCE CHART — the plan is drawn to scale and the influence areas counted** |
| **Approximate, for practical use** | **The 2:1 method — the load spread over an area widening at 2 vertical to 1 horizontal** ← |

> **The 2:1 METHOD is worth knowing because it is quick and adequate for many purposes:**

> **σ_z = Q / [(B + z)(L + z)]** for a rectangular footing B × L.

> **For a 1000 kN load on a 2 m square footing at z = 5 m: σ_z = 1000/(7 × 7) = 20.4 kPa — very close to the 19.1 kPa from Boussinesq for a point load, which is reassuring.**

> **And the NEWMARK CHART deserves mention as a genuinely ingenious device: the chart is divided into a number of areas — usually 200 — each contributing an EQUAL influence.**

> **The loaded plan is drawn on tracing paper to a scale set by the depth, laid over the chart with the point of interest at the centre, and the influence areas covered are simply COUNTED.**

> **σ_z = q × (number of areas counted) × (influence value per area)**

> **So an arbitrary loaded shape — an L-shaped raft, a curved tank — is handled by counting squares, with no integration at all.**

> **It is a pre-computer device and it remains the clearest way to understand what a stress influence factor actually is.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) 40 kPa omits the 0.4775 entirely** and option (c) uses 1/(2π) instead of 3/(2π). Recognising the constant as 3/(2π) prevents both.
examTip.mnemonic: **POISSON'S RATIO does not appear in the vertical-stress expression** — so σ_z depends only on geometry, which is why the elastic theory is trusted for a non-elastic material. The 2:1 method σ_z = Q/[(B+z)(L+z)] gives 20.4 kPa here, a useful check.

questions.stem: The laboratory test most suitable for determining the coefficient of permeability of a CLAY is the:
questions.solution:
**The FALLING HEAD permeability test.**

**The two laboratory tests and where each applies:**

| | **CONSTANT HEAD test** | **FALLING (variable) HEAD test** |
|---|---|---|
| **Head maintained** | **CONSTANT throughout** | **Allowed to FALL, and the time recorded** |
| **Measures** | **The VOLUME collected in a measured time** | **The TIME for the head to fall between two marks** ← |
| **Suits** | **COARSE-grained soils — sands and gravels (k > 10⁻⁴ m/s)** | **FINE-grained soils — silts and clays (k < 10⁻⁴ m/s)** ← |
| **Expression** | **k = QL/(A h t)** | **k = (a L)/(A t) × ln(h₁/h₂)** |
| **Why it suits that soil** | **A permeable soil passes a MEASURABLE VOLUME in a reasonable time** | **An impermeable soil passes almost nothing — but the SLOW FALL of a head in a thin standpipe IS measurable** ← |

**Why the constant head test fails on a clay — the practical reason:**

> **A clay's permeability is of the order of 10⁻⁹ to 10⁻¹¹ m/s.**

> **Through a specimen of 50 cm² area under a metre of head, the flow would be a few cubic millimetres PER DAY.**

> **That volume cannot be collected and measured — it would evaporate from the collecting vessel faster than it arrived.**

> **The FALLING HEAD test solves it by a change of what is measured: instead of collecting the outflow, a THIN STANDPIPE is used, so that even a minute volume of flow produces a MEASURABLE DROP in the head.**

> **The narrower the standpipe, the greater the drop for the same flow — so the test's sensitivity is adjusted by choosing the standpipe area a.**

> **That is an elegant piece of experimental design: the quantity measured is changed from a volume to a LENGTH, which is far easier to measure precisely at small magnitudes.**

**Why options (b) and (d) are wrong — they are not laboratory tests:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **(b) PUMPING OUT test** | **A FIELD test — a well is pumped and the drawdown observed in observation wells. It measures the MASS permeability of the deposit in situ, and it is the most reliable method for a coarse aquifer** ← |
| **(d) Plate load test** | **A FIELD test for BEARING CAPACITY and SETTLEMENT, not permeability at all** |

> **Option (b) deserves the note it gets, because the PUMPING TEST is in fact the BEST way to determine permeability — just not in a laboratory:**

| | **LABORATORY tests** | **FIELD (pumping) test** |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume of soil tested** | **A small specimen — perhaps 100 cm³** | **A large mass of the actual deposit** ← |
| **Sample disturbance** | **Present, and it changes the structure** | **NONE — the soil is undisturbed** |
| **Represents** | **The soil's own material permeability** | **The deposit's MASS permeability, including fissures, layers and sand seams** ← |
| **Cost and time** | Low | High |

> **The MASS PERMEABILITY point is the fundamental one, and it explains why laboratory permeability values must be used with caution:**

> **A natural deposit is not homogeneous. A clay containing thin SAND SEAMS or FISSURES will conduct water along them at a rate many times the clay's own permeability.**

> **A laboratory specimen 100 mm across may miss those features entirely, and its measured permeability then describes the clay matrix rather than the deposit.**

> **Field measurements of mass permeability commonly exceed laboratory values by one to three ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE for exactly that reason.**

> **So for a seepage or dewatering problem — where what matters is how much water the ground will actually pass — a field test is worth far more than a laboratory one, and a laboratory value alone can underestimate the pumping requirement disastrously.**

**The typical permeability values, since the choice of test follows from them:**

| Soil | k (m/s) | Drainage | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Clean gravel** | **10⁻¹ to 10⁻²** | **Very good** | **Constant head; pumping test** |
| **Clean sand** | **10⁻² to 10⁻⁵** | **Good** | **Constant head** |
| **Silty sand, fine sand** | **10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁷** | **Poor** | **Either** |
| **Silt** | **10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁹** | **Very poor** | **Falling head** |
| **CLAY** | **Below 10⁻⁹** | **PRACTICALLY IMPERVIOUS** | **Falling head; consolidation test** ← |

> **The range spans some TEN ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE — from gravel to clay — which is a wider range than almost any other engineering property.**

> **That enormous range is why permeability governs so much of soil behaviour: it determines whether a soil drains during construction or years afterward, and hence whether a design is governed by drained or undrained conditions.**

**The CONSOLIDATION test as a permeability method, worth noting:**

> **For a clay, the permeability can be obtained INDIRECTLY from an oedometer (consolidation) test:**

> **k = c_v m_v γ_w**

| Symbol | From |
|---|---|
| **c_v** | **The coefficient of consolidation — from the time-settlement curve** |
| **m_v** | **The coefficient of volume compressibility — from the pressure-void ratio curve** |
| **γ_w** | Unit weight of water |

> **That route is often preferred in practice because the consolidation test must be done anyway for settlement analysis, so the permeability comes free — and because the specimen is tested under a realistic stress, which the direct permeability tests are not.**

> **It is a good illustration of a general principle worth carrying: a test done for one purpose frequently yields a second property, and recognising it saves both time and specimen.**

examTip.trick: **CONSTANT head for COARSE soils (measure the VOLUME); FALLING head for FINE soils (measure the TIME for the head to fall in a thin standpipe).**
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) are FIELD tests** — and the pumping test is in fact the BEST permeability method, just not a laboratory one. The plate load test measures bearing capacity, not permeability at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Field values exceed laboratory values by one to three ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE**, because a small specimen misses the sand seams and fissures that actually conduct the water. For dewatering, a laboratory value alone can badly underestimate the pumping needed.

questions.stem: For a cohesionless soil with an angle of internal friction of 30°, the failure plane is inclined to the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE at an angle of:
questions.solution:
**60°.**

**The relation:**

> **The failure plane is inclined at  α = 45° + φ/2  to the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE.**

> **α = 45° + 30°/2 = 45° + 15° = 60°** ✓

**Where the relation comes from — the Mohr circle geometry:**

> **On the Mohr circle, the point of tangency with the failure envelope represents the stress state on the failure plane.**

> **The angle subtended at the centre between the major principal stress point and the tangency point is 90° + φ.**

> **Angles on the Mohr circle are DOUBLE the physical angles, so the physical inclination is:**

> **α = (90° + φ)/2 = 45° + φ/2** ✓

> **For φ = 0 (a saturated clay tested undrained) the failure plane is at 45°, which is option (c) — and that is the designed distractor, since it is the correct answer for a different soil.**

> **And as φ increases the failure plane becomes STEEPER relative to the major principal plane:**

| φ | α = 45° + φ/2 |
|---|---|
| **0°** | **45°** |
| **20°** | **55°** |
| **30°** | **60°** ← |
| **40°** | **65°** |

**A caution about which plane the angle is measured FROM — this is where errors arise:**

> **In a standard triaxial test the MAJOR PRINCIPAL STRESS is VERTICAL (the axial load), so the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE — the plane on which it acts — is HORIZONTAL.**

> **So a failure plane at 60° to the major principal plane is at 60° TO THE HORIZONTAL.**

> **Equivalently, it is at 30° to the vertical, and at (45° − φ/2) = 30° to the plane of the MINOR principal stress.**

> **A question asking for the angle "to the horizontal", "to the major principal plane" or "to the direction of the major principal stress" wants three different numbers from the same geometry:**

| Measured from | Angle for φ = 30° |
|---|---|
| **The MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE (horizontal in a triaxial test)** | **60°** ← as asked |
| **The MINOR principal plane (vertical)** | **30°** |
| **The DIRECTION of the major principal stress (the vertical axis)** | **30°** |
| **The direction of the minor principal stress (horizontal)** | **60°** |

> **So reading the stem carefully is the whole task once the formula is known, and the confusion between a PLANE and the STRESS DIRECTION NORMAL to it accounts for most wrong answers.**

> **The safeguard: sketch the specimen with the axial load vertical, draw the failure plane, and mark the angle asked for.**

**Why the failure plane is NOT at 45° for a frictional soil — the physical reason:**

> **For a material with NO friction (φ = 0), failure occurs on the plane of MAXIMUM SHEAR STRESS, which is at 45°.**

> **But when friction is present, the shear strength available on a plane DEPENDS on the NORMAL STRESS acting on it — and the normal stress varies with the plane's orientation.**

> **A plane at 45° has the maximum shear stress but also a substantial normal stress holding it together.**

> **A STEEPER plane has slightly less shear stress but considerably LESS normal stress, so LESS available resistance.**

> **Failure occurs where the RATIO of applied shear to available shear strength is greatest — which for a frictional material is at 45° + φ/2, not at 45°.**

> **So friction ROTATES the failure plane away from the plane of maximum shear, and the amount of rotation is exactly φ/2.**

> **That is a genuinely instructive result: the failure plane is not where the stress is worst but where the MARGIN is smallest, and the two coincide only for a frictionless material.**

**The MOHR-COULOMB relation, since it is the same geometry expressed algebraically:**

> **From the Mohr circle at failure:**

> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)**

> **The factor tan²(45° + φ/2) is the FLOW VALUE or the coefficient of PASSIVE earth pressure:**

> **N_φ = tan²(45° + φ/2) = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = K_p**

> **For φ = 30°:  N_φ = tan²60° = 3** ✓

> **And its reciprocal is K_a = 1/3 — the ACTIVE coefficient met in retaining wall design.**

> **So the same expression tan²(45° ± φ/2) appears in three places:**

| Appearance | Expression |
|---|---|
| **The FAILURE PLANE inclination** | **45° + φ/2** ← |
| **PASSIVE earth pressure coefficient** | **K_p = tan²(45° + φ/2)** |
| **ACTIVE earth pressure coefficient** | **K_a = tan²(45° − φ/2)** |
| **The failure wedge behind a retaining wall** | **Inclined at 45° + φ/2 to the horizontal** |

> **The last row connects the two topics directly and is worth seeing: the RANKINE FAILURE WEDGE behind a retaining wall is bounded by exactly this plane.**

> **So the 60° computed here is also the slope of the failure surface behind a wall retaining this soil — which is why a wall's backfill must extend at least that far, and why a surcharge placed within that wedge adds to the thrust while one placed outside it does not.**

> **That is a practical design consequence flowing directly from a Mohr circle result, and it is the clearest demonstration that shear strength theory and earth pressure theory are one subject rather than two.**

examTip.trick: **α = 45° + φ/2 = 60°**, measured from the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE — which is HORIZONTAL in a triaxial test, since the axial load is vertical.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 45° is the answer for φ = 0** (undrained clay). And read the stem's datum: from the major principal plane it is 60°, from the minor plane or from the direction of σ₁ it is 30°. Sketch it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Failure occurs where the MARGIN is smallest, not where the shear stress is greatest** — friction rotates the plane away from 45° by exactly φ/2. And the same 45° + φ/2 bounds the RANKINE FAILURE WEDGE behind a retaining wall.

questions.stem: For the stability analysis of a non-homogeneous slope in which pore water pressures must be taken into account, the most appropriate method is:
questions.solution:
**BISHOP'S SIMPLIFIED METHOD OF SLICES.**

**Why the method of slices is required here:**

> **The stem specifies two conditions, and each rules out the alternatives:**

> **NON-HOMOGENEOUS — the slope contains more than one soil, so a single c and φ cannot describe it.**

> **PORE WATER PRESSURES — the analysis must work in EFFECTIVE stresses, with u varying along the failure surface.**

> **The METHOD OF SLICES handles both naturally, because it divides the failure mass into vertical slices and treats EACH SLICE SEPARATELY:**

| Feature of the method of slices | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Each slice has its OWN c and φ, taken from the soil at its base** | **Non-homogeneous slopes handled directly** ← |
| **Each slice has its OWN pore pressure u at its base** | **Effective stress analysis throughout; a phreatic surface or a flow net can be used** ← |
| **Each slice has its own weight and base inclination** | Irregular slope profiles handled |
| **External loads and surcharges can be applied to individual slices** | Flexible |
| **Seismic force can be applied slice by slice** | — |

> **So the method of slices is the general-purpose tool, and the others are special cases with restrictive assumptions.**

**Why the other options do not fit:**

| Option | What it is, and its limitation |
|---|---|
| **(a) CULMANN'S method** | **Assumes a PLANE failure surface through the toe. Reasonable for a STEEP slope or a vertical cut, but a real slope fails on a CURVED surface, so it is only a first approximation** |
| **(b) TAYLOR'S stability number** | **A CHART solution for a HOMOGENEOUS slope with a single c and φ, and no pore pressure. Very quick, and inapplicable here by both counts** ← |
| **(c) FRICTION CIRCLE method** | **For a HOMOGENEOUS soil with both c and φ; handles a circular surface but assumes one soil throughout** |
| **(d) BISHOP'S simplified method of slices** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) is the designed distractor because Taylor's stability number is the method most candidates meet first, and it is genuinely useful — for the case it covers.**

> **Its charts give the stability number N = c/(F γ H) as a function of the slope angle and the depth factor, and a slope's factor of safety follows in one step.**

> **But the whole apparatus assumes a SINGLE HOMOGENEOUS soil with no pore water pressure, which is precisely what the stem excludes.**

> **So it is not a weaker method but an inapplicable one — and recognising the boundary of a method's validity is the point of the question.**

**BISHOP'S method against the ORDINARY (Fellenius/Swedish) method:**

| | **ORDINARY method of slices (Fellenius)** | **BISHOP'S simplified method** |
|---|---|---|
| **Inter-slice forces** | **NEGLECTED entirely** | **The NORMAL inter-slice forces are included; the shear ones neglected** ← |
| **Equilibrium satisfied** | **Moment equilibrium of the whole mass only** | **Moment equilibrium of the whole mass AND vertical equilibrium of each slice** |
| **Solution** | **DIRECT — one pass** | **ITERATIVE — F appears on both sides of the equation** |
| **Accuracy** | **CONSERVATIVE, sometimes very much so — errors of 10-20 % on the low side, and worse with high pore pressures** ← | **Within about 5 % of rigorous methods** |
| **Effort** | Least | Modest, and trivial with a computer |

> **The ORDINARY method's error deserves a note because it is systematically in one direction: it UNDERESTIMATES the factor of safety, and the error grows with the pore pressure and with deep failure surfaces.**

> **An error of 20 per cent on the safe side sounds acceptable until its cost is considered: it means a slope that is actually adequate may be judged unsafe, and expensive stabilisation works may be built that are not needed.**

> **So conservatism is not free, and Bishop's method is preferred not because the ordinary method is unsafe but because it is WASTEFUL.**

> **Bishop's ITERATION is the reason it was little used before computers: F appears on both sides, so a value is assumed, the equation evaluated, and the result fed back until it converges — typically in three or four cycles.**

> **With a spreadsheet or any slope-stability program that is instantaneous, which is why Bishop's method is now the practical default.**

**The more rigorous methods, for completeness:**

| Method | Equilibrium satisfied | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Ordinary / Fellenius** | **Moment only** | Conservative |
| **BISHOP'S simplified** | **Moment + vertical** | **The practical default** ← |
| **JANBU'S simplified** | **Force equilibrium** | Suits non-circular surfaces |
| **SPENCER'S** | **BOTH force and moment, with a constant inter-slice force inclination** | **Rigorous** |
| **MORGENSTERN-PRICE** | **Both, with an assumed inter-slice force function** | **Rigorous and general** |
| **Sarma** | Both; suits seismic analysis | — |

> **The rigorous methods (Spencer, Morgenstern-Price) satisfy ALL the equilibrium conditions and are used for important works — and they typically give a factor of safety within a few per cent of Bishop's.**

> **Which is worth knowing, because it means Bishop's simplified method is accurate enough for most purposes, and the extra rigour buys certainty rather than a different answer.**

**The critical practical point that no method addresses — finding the CRITICAL surface:**

> **Every method computes the factor of safety FOR AN ASSUMED FAILURE SURFACE.**

> **The slope's actual factor of safety is the MINIMUM over all possible surfaces — and finding it requires a SEARCH.**

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **Trial circles on a grid of centres and radii** | **The standard approach; the computer tries hundreds** ← |
| **Non-circular surface search** | **Necessary where a WEAK LAYER exists — failure follows the weak layer, not a circle** ← |
| **Engineering judgement to bound the search** | Essential, or the search misses the critical case |

> **The WEAK LAYER case is the one that catches analyses out: where a slope contains a thin soft seam, a bedding plane or an old slip surface, the critical failure surface is NOT circular — it runs along the weak layer.**

> **A circular search will never find it, and will report a comfortable factor of safety for a slope that is on the point of failure.**

> **So the search must be told to look for non-circular surfaces where the geology suggests one, and that instruction comes from the site investigation and the engineer's judgement rather than from the software.**

> **Which returns to a theme worth repeating: the analysis answers the question it is asked, and asking the right question is the engineer's work.**

examTip.trick: **The METHOD OF SLICES handles both conditions: each slice takes its own c, φ and pore pressure u.** The other three methods all assume a single homogeneous soil.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) Taylor's stability number is not a weaker method but an INAPPLICABLE one** — its charts assume a homogeneous slope with no pore pressure, which the stem explicitly excludes.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ordinary (Fellenius) method underestimates F by 10-20 %, so its conservatism is WASTEFUL, not merely safe.** And where a WEAK LAYER exists the critical surface is NOT circular — a circular search will report comfort for a slope about to fail.

questions.stem: The minimum depth of exploration for a foundation is generally taken as:
options: 1.5 times the width of the loaded area
0.5 times the width of the loaded area
5 times the width of the loaded area
Equal to the depth of the footing
questions.solution:
**About 1.5 times the width of the loaded area** (commonly stated as 1.5 to 2 times).

**Why that depth and not more or less:**

> **The exploration must reach the depth to which the foundation's load produces STRESSES LARGE ENOUGH TO MATTER.**

> **The conventional criterion is the depth at which the imposed stress falls to about 10 PER CENT of the applied bearing pressure — or to 5 per cent of the existing overburden stress, whichever is shallower.**

> **For a square or rectangular footing, that depth works out at roughly 1.5 to 2 times the footing width.**

| Depth below the footing | Vertical stress as a fraction of the applied pressure (square footing) |
|---|---|
| **0.5 B** | **≈ 0.70** |
| **1.0 B** | **≈ 0.34** |
| **1.5 B** | **≈ 0.18** |
| **2.0 B** | **≈ 0.11** ← about 10 % |
| **3.0 B** | **≈ 0.05** |

> **So below about 2B the footing's influence is small enough that the soil there contributes little to settlement, and exploring deeper adds cost without information.**

> **Option (b) 0.5 B would stop while 70 per cent of the pressure is still acting — clearly inadequate, and it is the error of exploring only as deep as the excavation.**

> **Option (c) 5 B is unnecessary for a shallow foundation, though it may be appropriate for a pile group or a raft.**

> **Option (d) — the depth of the footing itself — is the worst: it explores only the soil that will be REMOVED and none of the soil that will carry the load.**

**The depths for different foundation types, since the rule scales with the LOADED AREA:**

| Foundation | Minimum depth of exploration |
|---|---|
| **Isolated spread footing or raft, width B** | **1.5 B below the base** ← |
| **Adjacent footings with clear spacing less than twice the width** | **Treated as ONE loaded area, so the depth is based on the TOTAL width** ← |
| **Pile foundation** | **1.5 times the width of the pile GROUP, measured below the pile TOE** |
| **Roads and airfields** | **Commonly 1.5-2 m below the formation, or to a firm stratum** |
| **Deep excavations** | **1.5 times the excavation depth** |
| **Earth dams and embankments** | **Twice the height of the embankment** |

> **The SECOND row is the one most often got wrong and it matters a great deal:**

> **Closely spaced footings do NOT behave as separate footings. Their stress bulbs OVERLAP and merge, and the combined loaded area behaves as one large footing.**

> **So a group of 2 m footings at 3 m centres over a 20 m building has an effective loaded width of 20 m, not 2 m — and the exploration must reach 30 m, not 3 m.**

> **A site investigated to 3 m under such a building may be entirely adequate for each individual footing and completely miss a soft layer at 15 m that will settle under the building as a whole.**

> **That is a documented failure mode: buildings that have settled uniformly and severely on ground that was investigated only to shallow depth, because each footing's own bulb was considered and their sum was not.**

**Why exploring DEEP ENOUGH matters more than exploring PRECISELY — the honest priority:**

> **Site investigation costs are typically 0.1 to 0.5 per cent of a project's cost, and inadequate investigation is a leading cause of construction cost overrun and of foundation failure.**

> **So the economics are lopsided in an unusual way: the cheapest item in the budget controls the risk on the most expensive ones.**

> **And the commonest deficiency is not imprecise testing but INSUFFICIENT DEPTH OR COVERAGE — a soft layer, a buried channel, an old fill or a cavity missed entirely because no borehole went there.**

> **A missed stratum cannot be compensated for by careful testing of the strata that were found.**

**The number and spacing of boreholes, since depth is only one dimension of coverage:**

| Project | Guidance |
|---|---|
| **Small building** | **At least THREE boreholes, so that a plane can be fitted through the strata** ← |
| **Large or important building** | **A grid at 15-30 m spacing; closer where the ground is variable** |
| **Roads** | **Every 150-300 m, closer at structures and cuttings** |
| **Bridges** | **At least one at EVERY pier and abutment — no exceptions** ← |
| **Dams** | Along the axis and at the abutments, closely spaced |

> **The BRIDGE requirement is absolute for a good reason: piers carry very large concentrated loads, they are founded in a river bed where the geology is most variable and least visible, and a foundation failure at one pier is a total loss of the structure.**

> **Interpolating between boreholes at two abutments to found a pier in the middle is a gamble against a buried channel or a rock ledge, and it has been lost often enough to make the rule inflexible.**

> **The THREE-BOREHOLE minimum for a small building has a neat geometrical justification: two boreholes define a line and tell you nothing about variation across it, while three define a PLANE and reveal whether the strata are dipping.**

> **So three is not a bureaucratic minimum but the smallest number that yields information about the ground's structure rather than merely its composition.**

**The methods of exploration, briefly, since the depth determines which is practicable:**

| Method | Depth reached | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Trial PITS** | **Up to 3-4 m** | **The best — the soil can be SEEN and sampled in place** ← |
| **Auger boring (hand)** | **Up to 6-10 m in soft soil above the water table** | Cheap |
| **Auger boring (mechanical)** | 30 m and more | — |
| **WASH boring** | Considerable depth | **Cheap and fast, but the wash water DESTROYS the sample's identity — for boring, not sampling** |
| **Percussion / rotary drilling** | **Great depth; the only option in rock** | Rotary gives core samples |
| **Geophysical (seismic, resistivity)** | **Large areas rapidly** | **Indirect — must be CALIBRATED against boreholes; never a substitute for them** ← |

> **The TRIAL PIT deserves its place at the top: nothing else lets an engineer look at the soil in place, see the strata boundaries, note the seepage, and take a genuinely undisturbed sample from a chosen point.**

> **Its limitation is depth and the water table — below about 4 m or below groundwater it becomes impracticable and unsafe without support.**

> **And GEOPHYSICAL methods deserve the caution attached: they cover ground quickly and cheaply and they measure a PROXY — seismic velocity, resistivity — not the soil itself.**

> **They are excellent for INTERPOLATING between boreholes and for finding anomalies worth drilling, and they cannot replace the boreholes that calibrate them.**

examTip.trick: **1.5 to 2 times the width of the LOADED AREA below the base** — the depth at which the imposed stress falls to about 10 % of the applied pressure.
examTip.trap: **Closely spaced footings have OVERLAPPING stress bulbs and act as ONE loaded area** — so a 20 m building on 2 m footings needs 30 m of exploration, not 3 m. Missing a soft layer at depth this way is a documented failure mode.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three boreholes minimum for a small building — two define a line, THREE define a PLANE** and reveal dipping strata. And at least one at EVERY bridge pier, without exception.

questions.stem: A retaining wall retains a cohesive backfill with c = 20 kPa, γ = 18 kN/m³ and φ = 30°. The depth of the tension crack that will form behind the wall is:
questions.solution:
**3.85 m.**

**The active pressure distribution in a c-φ soil:**

> **p_a = K_a γ z − 2c √K_a**

> **The first term grows with depth; the SECOND is a CONSTANT NEGATIVE (tensile) contribution from the cohesion.**

> **So near the surface the computed pressure is NEGATIVE — the soil is in tension — and soil cannot sustain tension.**

> **It CRACKS instead, and the crack extends to the depth at which p_a = 0.**

**Setting p_a = 0:**

> **K_a γ z₀ = 2c √K_a**

> **z₀ = 2c / (γ √K_a)**

**The computation:**

> **For φ = 30°:  K_a = (1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°) = 1/3, so √K_a = 0.5774**

> **z₀ = (2 × 20) / (18 × 0.5774) = 40 / 10.39 = 3.85 m** ✓

> **Option (a) 1.28 m and option (d) 6.67 m arise from using K_a instead of √K_a in the denominator, in one direction or the other: 40/(18 × 1/3) = 6.67 and 40/(18 × 3) = 0.74.**

> **So the √K_a is the detail the question tests, and it is easy to lose.**

**Why the square root appears — worth understanding rather than memorising:**

> **Rankine's active pressure for a c-φ soil comes from the Mohr-Coulomb failure condition:**

> **σ₃ = σ₁ K_a − 2c √K_a**

> **The cohesion term carries √K_a because it enters through tan(45° − φ/2), whose square is K_a.**

> **So the friction contributes K_a = tan²(45° − φ/2) and the cohesion contributes √K_a = tan(45° − φ/2) — one power each, from the same angle.**

> **Noticing that the two terms carry DIFFERENT powers of the same quantity is what prevents the error.**

**The consequences of the tension crack — and they are considerable:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The wall receives NO PRESSURE over the top z₀ in theory** | Which appears to reduce the thrust |
| **But the crack FILLS WITH WATER in rain** | **Water in a 3.85 m crack exerts FULL HYDROSTATIC pressure — and that is far worse than the soil pressure it replaced** ← |
| **The crack admits water to the backfill generally** | Saturating it and raising the pressure everywhere |
| **The crack allows the soil surface to soften and slake** | Progressive deterioration |
| **Frost action in the crack (where applicable)** | Widening it |

> **The SECOND row is the critical one and it reverses the apparent benefit:**

> **Hydrostatic pressure at the base of a 3.85 m water-filled crack is 9.81 × 3.85 = 37.8 kPa.**

> **The soil pressure that would have acted there, had there been no cohesion, is K_a γ z = (1/3)(18)(3.85) = 23.1 kPa.**

> **So the water in the crack pushes HARDER than the soil it displaced — by more than 60 per cent.**

> **Which means the tension crack is not a relief but a HAZARD, and design practice reflects it:**

| Design practice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **NEGLECT the negative pressure zone and take the pressure as ZERO down to z₀** | **A conservative simplification — do not credit the cohesion with reducing the thrust** ← |
| **Alternatively, assume the crack is WATER FILLED and add hydrostatic pressure over that depth** | **The severe case, and the correct one for a wall exposed to rain** ← |
| **Do NOT rely on cohesion for long-term design at all** | See below |
| **Provide surface sealing and drainage behind the wall** | Prevent the crack filling |
| **Prefer a granular backfill** | No cohesion, no crack |

> **The THIRD row is the most important professional point in this topic and it deserves stating plainly:**

> **COHESION SHOULD NOT BE RELIED UPON IN THE LONG-TERM DESIGN OF A RETAINING WALL.**

> **The reasons are several and all real:**

| Why cohesion is unreliable | Note |
|---|---|
| **It FALLS as the soil takes up water** | **A clay's c is far lower saturated than at its as-placed moisture content** ← |
| **It falls further over the LONG TERM, toward the drained residual value** | c' is much smaller than c_u |
| **It is destroyed by weathering, wetting and drying cycles and root action** | Progressive |
| **It varies enormously across a fill** | Difficult to specify or verify |
| **Its benefit is greatest exactly where the crack forms** | Self-defeating |

> **So a wall designed on the cohesive backfill's full c will be adequate when built and progressively less so for years afterward, which is the worst possible pattern for a structure meant to last.**

> **The practical answer, and the one specifications enforce, is to use a GRANULAR (cohesionless) BACKFILL behind a retaining wall wherever it can be obtained:**

| Advantage of granular backfill | Note |
|---|---|
| **No cohesion to rely on or lose — the design is honest** | ← |
| **FREE DRAINING, so no water pressure builds up** | **The single greatest cause of retaining wall failure is water, and granular fill removes it** ← |
| **No tension crack** | — |
| **Predictable and verifiable properties** | Can be specified by grading and compaction |
| **No shrink-swell movement** | Clay backfill expands against the wall on wetting |

> **The last row is worth a note in its own right: an expansive clay backfill can exert SWELLING PRESSURE far exceeding any active earth pressure — pressures of 100 to 300 kPa are recorded — and walls have been pushed over by it.**

> **So the case against a cohesive backfill is not merely that its cohesion cannot be trusted, but that its expansiveness may be actively dangerous.**

> **Granular fill, a drainage layer, weep holes and a surface seal together cost a fraction of a wall and remove the failure modes that destroy most walls that fail.**

examTip.trick: **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a) = 40/(18 × 0.577) = 3.85 m.** Note the SQUARE ROOT — friction carries K_a, cohesion carries √K_a.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (d) use K_a instead of √K_a.** The two terms carry different powers of tan(45° − φ/2): the friction term squared, the cohesion term to the first power.
examTip.mnemonic: **The crack is a HAZARD, not a relief** — water filling a 3.85 m crack exerts 37.8 kPa against the 23.1 kPa of soil it displaced, over 60 % more. Which is why cohesion is never relied on long-term and why GRANULAR backfill is specified.

questions.stem: A foundation is conventionally classified as SHALLOW when:
options: Its depth of embedment is less than or equal to its width
It is founded below the water table
It carries only a light load
questions.solution:
**When its DEPTH OF EMBEDMENT is less than or equal to its WIDTH — that is, D_f / B ≤ 1.**

**The criterion:**

| Classification | Criterion | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| **SHALLOW foundation** | **D_f / B ≤ 1** ← | **Spread footings, strip footings, combined and strap footings, rafts** |
| **DEEP foundation** | **D_f / B > 1, and often very much greater** | **Piles, piers, well (caisson) foundations** |
| **Terzaghi's stricter form for a deep foundation** | **D_f / B > 4** | — |

> **So the classification rests on a RATIO, not on an absolute depth — which is the point of the question.**

> **A 20 m wide raft at 5 m depth is a SHALLOW foundation (D_f/B = 0.25), while a 0.5 m diameter pile at 5 m depth is a DEEP one (D_f/B = 10).**

> **The raft is four times deeper in absolute terms and still shallow by classification, which shows the ratio is doing real work rather than serving as a convention.**

**Why the RATIO is the right criterion — the mechanical reason:**

> **The distinction is about WHERE THE LOAD IS CARRIED and about whether the soil beside the foundation contributes:**

| | **SHALLOW foundation** | **DEEP foundation** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load carried by** | **END BEARING on the base alone** | **END BEARING plus SKIN FRICTION along the shaft** ← |
| **Shear resistance of the soil ALONGSIDE** | **NEGLIGIBLE — the embedment is too small to mobilise it** | **SIGNIFICANT, and often the larger part of the capacity** |
| **Failure surface** | **Reaches the GROUND SURFACE — a general shear wedge that heaves the ground beside the footing** ← | **CONFINED around the base; the ground surface is not disturbed** |
| **Overburden's role** | **A surcharge term γD_f in the bearing capacity equation** | Confining stress along the whole shaft |

> **The THIRD row is the physical heart of the distinction: a shallow foundation's failure mechanism BREAKS OUT AT THE SURFACE, and one can see the ground heave beside a failing footing.**

> **A deep foundation's failure is contained within the soil mass around its base, because there is too much soil above for a surface wedge to form.**

> **That difference is what makes the two require entirely different theories — Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation for the first, and skin-friction-plus-end-bearing analysis for the second.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a real but irrelevant circumstance:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Rests on rock** | **A footing on rock at 1 m depth is shallow; a PILE socketed into rock at 30 m is deep. The founding material is irrelevant to the classification** |
| **(c) Below the water table** | **The water table affects the bearing capacity (through the effective unit weight) and the construction method, but not the classification** ← |
| **(d) Carries a light load** | **A heavily loaded raft is shallow; a lightly loaded pile is deep. The load is irrelevant** |

> **Option (c) is worth the note it gets, because the water table DOES matter — just not for this.**

> **A water table at or above the foundation level reduces the effective unit weight from γ to γ' — roughly halving it — and hence reduces the surcharge and the γ-term contributions to bearing capacity substantially.**

> **So the water table is a major influence on the CAPACITY and no influence at all on the CLASSIFICATION, and keeping those separate is the discipline the option tests.**

**The types of shallow foundation, since the class covers several:**

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| **Isolated (spread) PAD footing** | **A single column on adequate soil — the commonest and cheapest** |
| **STRIP (continuous) footing** | **A load-bearing wall, or a row of closely spaced columns** |
| **COMBINED footing** | **TWO columns on one footing — where they are close together, or one is near a boundary** ← |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** | **Two footings joined by a beam — where a column is right on a boundary and its footing cannot be centred** ← |
| **Mat / RAFT** | **The whole building on one slab — weak or variable soil, or a basement** |
| **Inverted arch** | Traditional; between adjacent footings |

> **The COMBINED and STRAP footings both solve the BOUNDARY problem, and the distinction between them is worth understanding:**

> **A column at a site boundary cannot have a footing centred beneath it, because the footing would encroach on the neighbour.**

> **An ECCENTRIC footing under it alone would apply a moment to the soil and tilt.**

> **A COMBINED footing extends to include the next column, and is proportioned so that its centroid coincides with the RESULTANT of the two column loads — giving uniform pressure.**

> **A STRAP footing keeps the two footings separate but connects them with a rigid BEAM, so the beam carries the eccentric moment from the boundary footing back to the interior one.**

> **The strap footing is preferred where the columns are FAR APART, because a combined footing spanning a long distance becomes a heavy and expensive slab.**

> **And in both cases the object is the same: convert an eccentric load into a concentric one, so that the soil is loaded uniformly and the footing does not rotate.**

**The minimum depth of a shallow foundation, since it is not free to be as shallow as one likes:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Below the zone of SEASONAL MOISTURE CHANGE** | **An expansive clay swells and shrinks in the top 1-2 m and would lift the footing** ← |
| **Below the FROST line (where applicable)** | Frost heave |
| **Below topsoil, organic matter, roots and fill** | Compressible and variable |
| **Below the depth of possible SCOUR or erosion** | Rivers, drains, adjacent excavation |
| **At least 500 mm, and IS 1904 requires a minimum of 500 mm below ground** | A general minimum |
| **Rankine's minimum depth: D = (p/γ)[(1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ)]²** | **The theoretical minimum for the soil to provide the required pressure** |

> **The SEASONAL MOISTURE requirement is the one that governs most often in practice, and it is why founding depths in expansive clay areas are specified at 1.5 m or more regardless of what the bearing capacity would allow.**

> **A footing placed at 600 mm in a black cotton soil will be lifted and dropped by 30 to 50 mm each year as the clay wets and dries, and the building above will crack from that movement alone — while the soil's bearing capacity was never in question.**

> **Which is a good closing point for the topic: the depth of a shallow foundation is usually fixed by the SOIL'S BEHAVIOUR near the surface rather than by its strength, and a bearing capacity calculation alone will not tell you where to found.**

examTip.trick: **SHALLOW means D_f/B ≤ 1 — a RATIO, not an absolute depth.** A 20 m raft at 5 m is shallow; a 0.5 m pile at 5 m is deep.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is a real influence on CAPACITY and none on CLASSIFICATION** — the water table roughly halves the effective unit weight and so cuts the bearing capacity, but it does not make a footing deep.
examTip.mnemonic: **A shallow foundation's failure wedge BREAKS OUT at the ground surface; a deep one's is CONFINED** — which is why they need entirely different theories. And founding depth is usually fixed by seasonal moisture movement, not by bearing capacity.

questions.stem: A 4 m thick normally consolidated clay layer has a compression index of 0.30 and an initial void ratio of 0.90. If the effective vertical stress at its centre increases from 100 kPa to 200 kPa, the consolidation settlement is:
questions.solution:
**190 mm.**

**The consolidation settlement relation for a normally consolidated clay:**

> **Δ = (C_c H) / (1 + e₀) × log₁₀(σ'_f / σ'₀)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **C_c** | **COMPRESSION INDEX — the slope of the e-log σ' line** | **0.30** |
| **H** | **Thickness of the compressible layer** | **4 m** |
| **e₀** | **Initial void ratio** | **0.90** |
| **σ'₀** | **Initial effective stress at mid-depth** | **100 kPa** |
| **σ'_f** | **Final effective stress** | **200 kPa** |

**The computation:**

> **Δ = (0.30 × 4)/(1 + 0.90) × log₁₀(200/100)**

> **= (1.2/1.9) × log₁₀ 2**

> **= 0.6316 × 0.3010**

> **= 0.1901 m = 190 mm** ✓

> **The log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010 is worth knowing outright, since a doubling of stress is the commonest case in these problems.**

**Why the settlement is so large — and it is worth pausing on:**

> **190 mm of settlement is very substantial. The usual tolerable limit for a building is 25 to 40 mm.**

> **So a structure imposing this stress increase on this clay would settle far beyond what it could tolerate, and the design would have to change — a deeper or piled foundation, a lighter structure, ground improvement, or preloading.**

> **Recognising that the computed answer is UNACCEPTABLE rather than merely large is the engineering content of the calculation, and it is what the number is for.**

> **Note also the sensitivity: doubling the stress gave 190 mm, but adding only 50 kPa would give (0.6316)(log 1.5) = 0.6316 × 0.176 = 111 mm.**

> **The LOGARITHMIC form means the settlement depends on the RATIO of the stresses, not their difference — so the same 100 kPa increase applied to a clay already under 400 kPa would give only 0.6316 × log(1.25) = 61 mm.**

> **Which has an important practical implication: a given load causes FAR MORE settlement on a lightly stressed (shallow, young) clay than on a heavily stressed (deep, old) one.**

> **And it is why loading a deep clay layer beneath an existing building matters less than loading a shallow one — the ratio, not the increment, governs.**

**The OVERCONSOLIDATED case, since the stem specifies NORMALLY consolidated:**

> **A clay that has in the past carried a greater stress than it does now is OVERCONSOLIDATED, and it behaves quite differently:**

| Condition | Relation | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMALLY consolidated (σ'₀ = σ'_c)** | **Δ = (C_c H/(1+e₀)) log(σ'_f/σ'₀)** | **LARGE** ← as here |
| **OVERCONSOLIDATED, and σ'_f stays BELOW the preconsolidation pressure σ'_c** | **Δ = (C_r H/(1+e₀)) log(σ'_f/σ'₀)**, using the RECOMPRESSION index | **SMALL — C_r is typically 1/5 to 1/10 of C_c** ← |
| **Overconsolidated, and σ'_f EXCEEDS σ'_c** | **BOTH terms: recompression to σ'_c, then virgin compression beyond** | Intermediate |

> **The middle row is the most consequential fact in settlement analysis:**

> **Loading an overconsolidated clay WITHIN its preconsolidation pressure produces only about a fifth to a tenth of the settlement, because the soil is merely retracing a path it has already been down.**

> **So determining the PRECONSOLIDATION PRESSURE σ'_c is often the single most valuable output of a consolidation test — it determines whether the settlement will be 20 mm or 200 mm.**

> **And it explains why a building on a clay that once carried a glacier, or a thick eroded overburden, settles far less than the same building on a recently deposited clay of identical index properties.**

> **CASAGRANDE'S CONSTRUCTION on the e-log σ' curve is how σ'_c is found: locate the point of maximum curvature, draw the horizontal and the tangent there, bisect the angle between them, and intersect that bisector with the extended virgin compression line.**

**The TIME for the settlement to occur, which the magnitude calculation does not address:**

> **t = T_v d² / c_v**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T_v** | **TIME FACTOR — a dimensionless number depending on the degree of consolidation (0.197 for 50 %, 0.848 for 90 %)** |
| **d** | **The longest DRAINAGE PATH** |
| **c_v** | **Coefficient of consolidation** |

> **The DRAINAGE PATH is the detail that matters most and is easiest to get wrong:**

| Drainage condition | d |
|---|---|
| **Drainage at BOTH faces (sand above and below)** | **H/2 = 2 m here** ← |
| **Drainage at ONE face only (impervious rock beneath)** | **H = 4 m** |

> **And since t goes as d², SINGLE drainage takes FOUR TIMES as long as double drainage for the same layer.**

> **For this 4 m layer with c_v = 3 m²/year, drained both faces:**

> **t₉₀ = 0.848 × 2²/3 = 1.13 years**

> **Drained one face only:  t₉₀ = 0.848 × 4²/3 = 4.5 years** — four times as long.

> **So establishing whether the clay is drained on one face or two is worth as much as measuring c_v accurately, and it is determined by the site investigation rather than by any test.**

**And the practical measures where the settlement is unacceptable, since that is the case here:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **PRELOADING (surcharging)** | **Load the ground with fill BEFORE building, let it consolidate, then remove the fill and build — the settlement happens before the structure exists** ← |
| **Preloading with SAND DRAINS or PVDs (wick drains)** | **Vertical drains shorten the drainage path DRASTICALLY, so the same consolidation happens in months instead of years** ← |
| **Piled foundation to a firm stratum** | Bypass the clay |
| **Reduce the net pressure — a compensated (floating) raft** | Excavate a weight of soil equal to the building's weight |
| **Lighten the structure or the fill** | Lightweight fill materials |
| **Stone columns, deep soil mixing** | Ground improvement |

> **The VERTICAL DRAIN measure is the elegant one and follows directly from the t ∝ d² relation: installing drains at 1.5 m spacing reduces the drainage path from 2 m to about 0.75 m radially, and since the time goes as the square, the consolidation period collapses from years to weeks.**

> **The drains do not reduce the TOTAL settlement at all — they only make it happen sooner, which is precisely what is wanted if it can be made to happen before the structure is built.**

> **That distinction — accelerating settlement rather than preventing it — is the key to understanding the whole family of preloading techniques.**

examTip.trap: **The logarithm means the RATIO governs, not the increment** — the same 100 kPa added to a clay already at 400 kPa gives only 61 mm. So a shallow, lightly stressed clay settles far more than a deep one.
examTip.mnemonic: **190 mm is UNACCEPTABLE (tolerable is 25-40 mm)** — recognising that is the point of the calculation. And an OVERCONSOLIDATED clay loaded within σ'_c settles only a fifth to a tenth as much, which is why finding σ'_c is the most valuable output of a consolidation test.

questions.stem: The capillary rise of water in a clean glass tube of 1 mm internal diameter, taking the surface tension as 0.073 N/m and the contact angle as zero, is:
questions.solution:
**About 29.8 mm.**

**The capillary rise relation:**

> **h = 4 σ cos θ / (ρ g d)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **σ** | **Surface tension** | **0.073 N/m** |
| **θ** | **Contact angle** | **0°, so cos θ = 1** |
| **ρ** | **Density of water** | **1000 kg/m³** |
| **d** | **DIAMETER of the tube** | **0.001 m** |

**The computation:**

> **h = (4 × 0.073 × 1) / (1000 × 9.81 × 0.001)**

> **= 0.292 / 9.81**

> **= 0.0298 m = 29.8 mm** ✓

**The DIAMETER against RADIUS form — where the factor-of-two errors come from:**

> **h = 4σ cos θ/(ρ g d)   is the same as   h = 2σ cos θ/(ρ g r)**

> **Both are correct; using 4 with the RADIUS or 2 with the DIAMETER is not.**

> **Option (b) 14.9 mm is exactly HALF the answer — the result of using 2σ/(ρgd), that is the radius coefficient with the diameter.**

> **Option (d) 59.6 mm is exactly DOUBLE — the diameter coefficient applied to the radius.**

> **So the option set punishes precisely that confusion, and the safeguard is to write down which length is being used before substituting.**

**Where the formula comes from — the force balance, which takes two lines:**

> **The surface tension acts around the CIRCUMFERENCE of the meniscus, pulling upward with a vertical component σ cos θ per unit length:**

> **Upward force = σ cos θ × π d**

> **The weight of the raised column of water:**

> **Downward force = ρ g h × (π d²/4)**

> **Equating them:  σ cos θ π d = ρ g h π d²/4**

> **h = 4 σ cos θ / (ρ g d)** ✓

> **Deriving it means the coefficient can never be misremembered: the 4 comes from the ratio of the tube's CIRCUMFERENCE (πd) to its AREA (πd²/4).**

**The 1/d dependence, which is the important physical content:**

| Tube diameter | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| **10 mm** | **3.0 mm** |
| **1 mm** | **29.8 mm** ← |
| **0.1 mm** | **298 mm** |
| **0.01 mm (a fine soil pore)** | **2.98 m** ← |

> **The rise is INVERSELY proportional to the diameter, so a fine pore lifts water enormously higher than a coarse one.**

> **That is why capillary rise matters so much in soils and hardly at all in pipes:**

| Soil | Typical capillary rise |
|---|---|
| **Coarse gravel** | **Negligible** |
| **Coarse sand** | **0.1-0.15 m** |
| **Fine sand** | **0.3-1.0 m** |
| **SILT** | **1-10 m** ← |
| **CLAY** | **10-30 m in principle, though very slow** |

> **SILT is the material with the most troublesome combination: pores fine enough to lift water metres, and permeability high enough for the water to actually arrive at a useful rate.**

> **Clay's pores are finer still but its permeability is so low that the water moves very slowly, and coarse sand's water moves freely but rises hardly at all.**

> **So SILT IS THE FROST-SUSCEPTIBLE AND WATERLOGGING-PRONE SOIL — the worst of both properties — and that single fact explains a great deal:**

| Consequence in silt | Note |
|---|---|
| **FROST HEAVE** | **Capillary water is drawn continuously to the freezing front, forming ICE LENSES that lift the pavement** ← |
| **Waterlogging of the root zone** | Water reaches it from a water table well below |
| **Pavement subgrade softening** | Capillary water saturates the layer beneath the pavement |
| **Difficult excavation and trafficking** | Silt becomes a slurry when wet and disturbed |

> **The FROST HEAVE mechanism deserves the emphasis because it is often misunderstood: the heave is NOT the expansion of the water already in the soil (which would be only 9 per cent of the water volume).**

> **It is the growth of ICE LENSES fed by capillary water drawn from below, continuously, for as long as the freezing front persists — and it can lift a pavement by 100 mm or more, far beyond anything the in-situ water could explain.**

> **The remedies follow directly from the mechanism: BREAK THE CAPILLARY PATH with a coarse granular layer, LOWER the water table by drainage, or REPLACE the frost-susceptible soil.**

**Why the CONTACT ANGLE matters and can reverse the effect:**

| Liquid and surface | Contact angle | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Water on clean glass** | **≈ 0°** | **Full capillary RISE — the liquid WETS the surface** ← |
| **Water on a waxed or oily surface** | **> 90°** | **Capillary DEPRESSION — the liquid is pushed DOWN** |
| **MERCURY on glass** | **≈ 130-140°** | **DEPRESSION — mercury in a glass tube stands BELOW the free surface** ← |

> **The MERCURY case is the one to remember, because it explains a real reading correction: in a mercury manometer the meniscus is CONVEX and the level is DEPRESSED, so the reading is taken at the TOP of the meniscus.**

> **In a water manometer the meniscus is CONCAVE and elevated, so the reading is taken at the BOTTOM.**

> **Reading a mercury manometer at the bottom of its meniscus, out of habit from water, is a genuine and repeated laboratory error.**

> **And the WATER-REPELLENT case has a practical use: treating a surface or a soil to make its contact angle exceed 90° REVERSES the capillary effect, pushing water out rather than drawing it in.**

> **That is exactly the principle of a chemical injection damp proof course — a silicone or siloxane injected into masonry makes the pore walls water-repellent, so capillary rise stops without any physical barrier being inserted.**

> **A remedy that works by changing the sign of cos θ rather than by blocking the path — which is an elegant application of the formula used here.**

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(ρgd) = 0.292/9.81 = 29.8 mm.** The 4 goes with the DIAMETER; use 2 with the RADIUS.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) are exactly half and double** — the radius coefficient used with the diameter and vice versa. Derive it: the 4 is the ratio of circumference (πd) to area (πd²/4).
examTip.mnemonic: **h ∝ 1/d, so SILT is the worst soil** — pores fine enough to lift water metres and permeability high enough for it to arrive. Hence frost heave by ICE LENSES fed from below, not by the in-situ water expanding. Break the capillary path with a granular layer.

questions.stem: With an increase in temperature, the dynamic viscosity of a LIQUID and that of a GAS behave as follows:
options: The liquid's decreases while the gas's increases
The liquid's increases while the gas's decreases
questions.solution:
**The LIQUID'S viscosity DECREASES while the GAS'S viscosity INCREASES.**

**Why they behave oppositely — the mechanisms are entirely different:**

> **In a LIQUID, viscosity arises from the COHESIVE FORCES between closely packed molecules.**

> **The molecules are in contact, and shearing the liquid requires them to slide past one another against their mutual attraction.**

> **HEATING increases the molecules' thermal energy, which WEAKENS the effect of those cohesive bonds and lets the molecules slip past more easily.**

> **So a liquid's viscosity FALLS with temperature — which everyone has observed: honey, oil and bitumen all thin when warmed.**

> **In a GAS, the molecules are FAR APART and cohesive forces are negligible. Viscosity arises instead from the TRANSFER OF MOMENTUM by molecules moving BETWEEN the layers of flow.**

> **A molecule crossing from a fast layer into a slow one carries its momentum with it, and the resulting exchange is what resists the shear.**

> **HEATING makes the molecules move FASTER, so MORE momentum is carried across per unit time.**

> **So a gas's viscosity RISES with temperature.**

> **The two mechanisms — COHESION in liquids, MOMENTUM TRANSFER in gases — are so different that the opposite behaviour follows naturally rather than being a curiosity to be memorised.**

**The magnitudes, to show the effect is not small:**

| Fluid | At 0 °C | At 20 °C | At 100 °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WATER (× 10⁻³ Pa·s)** | **1.79** | **1.00** | **0.28** |
| **AIR (× 10⁻⁵ Pa·s)** | **1.71** | **1.81** | **2.18** |

> **Water's viscosity falls by a factor of SIX between 0 and 100 °C — a very large change.**

> **Air's rises by about 27 per cent over the same range — a real but much smaller change.**

> **So for water, temperature is a significant variable and must be accounted for; for air it is usually a secondary correction.**

**Where the liquid behaviour matters in civil engineering — the cases worth knowing:**

| Application | Consequence of the temperature dependence |
|---|---|
| **BITUMEN in road construction** | **The whole basis of hot-mix asphalt: bitumen is far too viscous to mix or place at ambient temperature, and heating to 150-165 °C makes it fluid enough to coat the aggregate** ← |
| **Soil PERMEABILITY tests** | **k depends on the water's viscosity, so results are CORRECTED to a standard 27 °C** ← |
| **Viscosity grading of bitumen (VG10 to VG40)** | Graded by viscosity at 60 °C, near a hot pavement's temperature |
| **Pipe flow head loss in winter against summer** | Colder water is more viscous, giving a higher Reynolds-number-dependent friction factor |
| **Lubrication of machinery** | Oil grade chosen for the operating temperature |
| **Grouting** | Grout viscosity governs penetration |

> **The BITUMEN case is the most consequential in civil engineering and it is worth stating fully:**

> **Bitumen at 25 °C is effectively a solid — its penetration test measures how far a needle sinks in five seconds, in tenths of a millimetre.**

> **At 160 °C it flows freely enough to coat every aggregate particle with a film a few microns thick.**

> **The whole hot-mix process exploits that enormous viscosity change: heat it to mix and place, then let it cool to become a stiff binder that holds the pavement together.**

> **And the temperature limits are strict at BOTH ends: too cold and the mix cannot be compacted before it stiffens; too hot and the bitumen OXIDISES and hardens permanently, losing its ductility.**

> **Which is why a mixing plant's temperature is monitored and why a load of asphalt that has cooled below the specified laying temperature must be rejected rather than laid.**

> **The PERMEABILITY CORRECTION deserves its note because it is a required step often skipped:**

> **k_27 = k_T × (μ_T / μ_27)**

> **A permeability measured with water at 20 °C must be multiplied by about 1.11 to give the value at 27 °C, since the warmer water is less viscous and flows more readily.**

> **Ignoring the correction introduces an error of 10 per cent or more — small against the order-of-magnitude uncertainties in permeability generally, but easy to avoid.**

**The kinematic viscosity, since it combines both effects:**

> **ν = μ/ρ, and BOTH μ and ρ change with temperature.**

| Fluid | Effect on ν of heating |
|---|---|
| **LIQUID** | **μ falls sharply, ρ falls slightly → ν FALLS** |
| **GAS** | **μ rises, and ρ falls SUBSTANTIALLY (a gas expands) → ν RISES STRONGLY** ← |

> **For a gas the kinematic viscosity rises much more steeply than the dynamic viscosity, because the density falls at the same time as the viscosity rises.**

> **Air's kinematic viscosity roughly DOUBLES between 0 and 100 °C, against a 27 per cent rise in its dynamic viscosity.**

> **That matters for any Reynolds number computed in air over a temperature range — a wind tunnel test, a chimney flow, a ventilation calculation — since Re = VD/ν.**

**And the IDEAL FLUID, for completeness, since it is the useful idealisation:**

| Fluid model | Viscosity | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **IDEAL (inviscid, perfect) fluid** | **ZERO** | **Potential flow theory, flow nets, lift theory — where viscosity's effects are confined to a thin boundary layer** ← |
| **REAL fluid** | Finite | Everything else |

> **The ideal fluid is not a fiction but a very good approximation OUTSIDE the boundary layer, and it is what makes flow nets and potential flow theory work.**

> **Its famous failure is D'ALEMBERT'S PARADOX: an ideal fluid predicts ZERO DRAG on a body moving through it, which is plainly wrong.**

> **The resolution is that drag arises entirely within the boundary layer and from its separation — the very region the ideal model excludes.**

> **So the ideal fluid gives the pressure distribution and the lift correctly and the drag not at all, which is a precise statement of when it may be relied upon.**

examTip.trick: **LIQUID viscosity FALLS with temperature (cohesion weakens); GAS viscosity RISES (faster molecules carry more momentum across the layers).** The mechanisms are entirely different, so the opposite behaviour follows naturally.
examTip.trap: **The effect is large for liquids** — water's viscosity falls SIXFOLD from 0 to 100 °C, against a 27 % rise for air. So temperature is a primary variable for water and a secondary one for air.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hot-mix asphalt exists entirely because of this: bitumen is a solid at 25 °C and fluid at 160 °C.** And permeability results must be corrected to 27 °C, since k depends on the water's viscosity.

questions.stem: A simple U-tube manometer connected to a pipe carrying water shows a mercury difference of 200 mm. Taking the specific gravity of mercury as 13.6, the gauge pressure at the point of connection (neglecting the water column) is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 26.7 kPa.**

**The computation:**

> **p = ρ_mercury g h = (13.6 × 1000) × 9.81 × 0.200**

> **= 13,600 × 9.81 × 0.2**

> **= 26,683 Pa = 26.7 kPa** ✓

> **Equivalently: p = S γ_w h = 13.6 × 9.81 × 0.2 = 26.68 kPa**, working in kN/m³ directly.

**Why the manometric fluid must be denser than the fluid measured:**

> **Option (b) 1.96 kPa is the pressure of a 200 mm column of WATER (9.81 × 0.2 = 1.96 kPa) — the answer with the mercury's specific gravity omitted.**

> **That comparison shows why mercury is used: the SAME pressure that raises mercury 200 mm would raise water 13.6 times as far — 2.72 metres.**

| Manometric fluid | Column length for 26.7 kPa |
|---|---|
| **MERCURY (S = 13.6)** | **200 mm** ← |
| **Carbon tetrachloride (S = 1.6)** | **1.70 m** |
| **Water (S = 1.0)** | **2.72 m** |
| **Oil (S = 0.8)** | **3.40 m** |

> **So a DENSE manometric fluid keeps the instrument SHORT and manageable, at the cost of resolution — each millimetre of mercury is 13.6 mm of water equivalent.**

> **And that trade-off is exactly what determines the choice of manometer:**

| Pressure to be measured | Suitable manometer |
|---|---|
| **LARGE pressures** | **MERCURY U-tube — compact** |
| **SMALL pressures** | **A LIGHT fluid, and a magnified reading — see below** ← |

**The manometers designed for SMALL pressure differences, since that is where the ingenuity lies:**

| Type | Device | Magnification |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple U-tube** | Two vertical limbs | **1 ×** |
| **INCLINED (single column) manometer** | **The reading limb is INCLINED at angle α, so the length read is h/sin α** | **1/sin α — a 10° incline magnifies by about 5.8 ×** ← |
| **Single column (well type)** | One large reservoir, one narrow tube; only one reading needed | Convenience rather than magnification |
| **INVERTED U-tube** | **The manometric fluid is LIGHTER than the fluid measured, and sits at the top** | **Suits small differences between two liquid pressures** |
| **MICROMANOMETER (two-fluid)** | **Two immiscible fluids of nearly EQUAL density in enlarged bulbs** | **VERY LARGE — the reading depends on the DIFFERENCE of the two densities** ← |

> **The TWO-FLUID MICROMANOMETER is worth understanding because its principle is genuinely clever:**

> **The reading depends on (ρ₁ − ρ₂), the DIFFERENCE between the two manometric fluids' densities.**

> **By choosing two fluids whose densities are nearly equal, that difference can be made very small — and since the deflection is inversely proportional to it, the deflection becomes very large.**

> **So an almost undetectable pressure difference produces a readable movement, and the instrument's sensitivity is set by how closely the two fluids' densities can be matched.**

> **The INCLINED manometer achieves the same end by geometry rather than by chemistry, and is far more practical: tilting the limb to 10 degrees multiplies the reading by 5.8, and the tilt is easily adjusted.**

**GAUGE against ABSOLUTE pressure, since the question specifies gauge:**

> **A manometer open to the atmosphere measures GAUGE pressure — the pressure ABOVE atmospheric — because the atmosphere presses equally on the open limb.**

> **p_absolute = p_gauge + p_atmospheric**

| Quantity | Value at sea level |
|---|---|
| **Atmospheric pressure** | **101.3 kPa = 10.3 m of water = 760 mm of mercury** |
| **This gauge reading** | **26.7 kPa** |
| **Absolute pressure** | **128.0 kPa** |

> **And a NEGATIVE gauge pressure — a vacuum — is a pressure below atmospheric, with an absolute limit of −101.3 kPa (a perfect vacuum) at sea level.**

> **That limit is why a SUCTION LIFT is bounded: a pump cannot lift water more than 10.3 m by suction even in principle, and in practice not more than about 6 to 7 m, because the pressure would fall to the water's vapour pressure and the water would boil — CAVITATION.**

> **So the theoretical limit of atmospheric pressure and the practical limit of vapour pressure together fix the maximum suction lift of any pump, and no amount of pump design can exceed it.**

> **A pump that must lift water from a deeper source must be PLACED LOWER, or a submersible or jet pump must be used — the water is pushed, not sucked.**

**A caution on the stem's simplification, worth stating:**

> **The stem says "neglecting the water column", and that is a deliberate simplification.**

> **In a real U-tube manometer connected to a water pipe, the water in the connecting limb also exerts pressure, and the full relation is:**

> **p_pipe + γ_w × h_water = γ_Hg × h_mercury**

> **so  p_pipe = γ_Hg h_Hg − γ_w h_water**

> **The water column's contribution is SUBTRACTED, because it acts in the opposite sense to the mercury.**

> **For a water limb of, say, 300 mm, the correction is 9.81 × 0.3 = 2.94 kPa — an 11 per cent reduction, giving 23.7 kPa rather than 26.7.**

> **So the simplification is significant and is made here only to isolate the mercury calculation.**

> **The general procedure for any manometer is worth stating because it never fails: START AT ONE END AT A KNOWN PRESSURE, then WORK THROUGH THE FLUID, ADDING γh when moving DOWN and SUBTRACTING γh when moving UP, until the other end is reached.**

> **That single rule handles every manometer configuration — U-tube, inverted, differential, multi-fluid — without any need to remember individual formulae.**

examTip.trick: **p = S γ_w h = 13.6 × 9.81 × 0.2 = 26.7 kPa.** Option (b) 1.96 kPa is the same column of WATER — the answer with the specific gravity left out.
examTip.trap: **The stem's "neglecting the water column" is a real simplification** — in practice the connecting water limb's pressure is SUBTRACTED, since it acts opposite to the mercury, and it can be a 10 % correction.
examTip.mnemonic: **One rule handles every manometer: start at a known pressure and ADD γh going DOWN, SUBTRACT γh going UP.** And atmospheric pressure (10.3 m of water) plus vapour pressure together limit any pump's suction lift to about 6-7 m in practice.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a floating vessel of total weight 1000 N, moving a 50 N weight through 0.3 m across the deck produces a heel of 2°. The metacentric height is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 0.43 m.**

**The experimental relation:**

> **GM = (w × x) / (W × tan θ)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **w** | **The weight MOVED** | **50 N** |
| **x** | **The distance it is moved ACROSS the deck** | **0.3 m** |
| **W** | **The TOTAL weight of the vessel (including w)** | **1000 N** |
| **θ** | **The angle of heel produced** | **2°** |

**The computation:**

> **tan 2° = 0.03492**

> **GM = (50 × 0.3) / (1000 × 0.03492)**

> **= 15 / 34.92**

> **= 0.4296 m ≈ 0.43 m** ✓

**Where the relation comes from — a moment balance:**

> **Moving the weight w through x creates a HEELING MOMENT:  M = w x**

> **The vessel heels until the RESTORING MOMENT balances it. For a small angle θ, the restoring moment is:**

> **M_restoring = W × GM × sin θ ≈ W × GM × tan θ** for small θ.

> **Equating:  w x = W GM tan θ, hence GM = w x/(W tan θ)** ✓

> **The approximation sin θ ≈ tan θ holds well for small angles — at 2° they differ by 0.06 per cent — which is why the experiment must be conducted at a SMALL heel.**

> **A large heel would invalidate the small-angle assumption, and it would also change the waterline shape enough that GM itself would alter.**

**Why the experiment is done at all — and it is done, on every ship:**

> **GM can be CALCULATED as  GM = I/V − BG**, where I is the second moment of the waterline area and V the displaced volume.

> **But that calculation requires the vessel's exact hull geometry AND the exact position of its centre of gravity G — and G depends on how the vessel is actually loaded, built and fitted out.**

> **The position of G is the difficult part: it depends on the distribution of every item of structure, machinery, fuel, cargo and ballast, and small errors accumulate.**

> **So an INCLINING EXPERIMENT is performed on the completed vessel: known weights are moved across the deck, the heel is measured with a long pendulum, and GM is obtained DIRECTLY — from which G's position follows, since I/V can be calculated reliably from the hull lines.**

> **That is the standard order of the reasoning: measure GM, calculate KM = I/V + KB from the geometry, and DEDUCE KG = KM − GM.**

> **So the experiment's real purpose is to locate the CENTRE OF GRAVITY — the one quantity that cannot be computed reliably — by measuring the one quantity that can be measured easily.**

**The stability criterion, since GM is what it is measured against:**

| Condition | Stability |
|---|---|
| **M ABOVE G (GM POSITIVE)** | **STABLE — a heel produces a RESTORING couple** ← |
| **M coincides with G (GM = 0)** | **NEUTRAL — the vessel stays wherever it is put** |
| **M BELOW G (GM NEGATIVE)** | **UNSTABLE — a heel produces an OVERTURNING couple, and the vessel capsizes** |

> **And the remarkable feature worth restating: a FLOATING body can be stable with G ABOVE B, which a fully submerged body cannot.**

> **The reason is that heeling CHANGES THE SHAPE of the displaced volume — the vessel takes on more water on the low side — which shifts B SIDEWAYS and creates the restoring lever.**

> **A submerged body's displaced volume cannot change shape, so no such shift occurs and it must have B above G to be stable.**

> **That is why a ship, with heavy superstructure and cargo well above its waterline, floats stably — and why a submarine must keep its ballast low.**

**Why a LARGE GM is not simply better — the trade-off:**

> **The ROLLING PERIOD of a vessel is:**

> **T = 2π √(k² / (g × GM))**, with k the radius of gyration about the roll axis.

| GM | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **LARGE GM** | **Very stable, but a SHORT, SNAPPY rolling period — violent motion, uncomfortable, and severe on the structure and the cargo lashings** ← |
| **Moderate GM** | **A comfortable, easy roll — the design target** |
| **Small positive GM** | Slow roll, little reserve of stability |
| **Zero or negative** | Unstable |

> **So a "stiff" vessel with a large GM rolls quickly and violently, and a "tender" one with a small GM rolls slowly and lazily.**

> **Neither extreme is wanted: excessive stiffness has caused cargo to break loose and deck fittings to fail, while tenderness leaves too little margin.**

> **Typical design values are 0.3 to 1.5 m for merchant ships, and the choice is a compromise — which makes stability one of the clearer engineering examples of a criterion that must be OPTIMISED rather than MAXIMISED.**

> **A GM of 0.43 m as measured here sits at the lower end of that range: a comfortable, somewhat tender vessel with a modest reserve.**

**Where this matters in civil engineering, since ships are not our subject:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAISSONS floated out and sunk into position** | **Stability during the float-out is a genuine design case, and caissons have been lost by capsizing** ← |
| **Pontoon bridges and floating jetties** | Must be checked with the design live load in the worst position |
| **Barges carrying plant, cranes or spoil** | The crane's load raises G as it lifts |
| **Floating dry docks** | — |
| **BUOYANCY of an empty basement box below the water table** | **The same principle: it will float, and it may float unevenly** ← |
| **Dredgers and floating pipelines** | — |

> **The CRANE ON A BARGE case is the one most often mishandled: as the crane lifts a load, the load's weight is effectively transferred to the crane's hook — high above the deck — which RAISES the combined centre of gravity G and REDUCES GM.**

> **So a barge that is perfectly stable at rest can become unstable while lifting, and the stability must be checked for the LIFTING condition with the load at its maximum radius, not merely for the loaded condition.**

> **That has caused overturnings, and it is why marine lifting operations require a stability calculation for every stage of the lift rather than for the start and finish alone.**

examTip.trick: **GM = w x/(W tan θ) = 15/(1000 × 0.0349) = 0.43 m.** W is the TOTAL weight including the moved weight.
examTip.trap: **The experiment must be at a SMALL heel** — the derivation uses sin θ ≈ tan θ, and a large heel would also change the waterline shape and hence GM itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **The experiment's real purpose is to locate G**, the one quantity that cannot be computed reliably: measure GM, calculate KM from the hull geometry, deduce KG. And a LARGE GM gives a violent snappy roll (T = 2π√(k²/g·GM)) — stability is optimised, not maximised.

questions.stem: A pitot tube inserted in a pipe carrying water registers a dynamic head of 0.80 m. Taking the coefficient as unity, the velocity of flow is:
questions.solution:
**3.96 m/s.**

**The pitot tube relation:**

> **V = C_v √(2 g h)**

> **With C_v = 1:**

> **V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.80) = √15.696 = 3.962 m/s ≈ 3.96 m/s** ✓

> **Option (d) 15.70 m/s is the quantity 2gh itself — the answer with the SQUARE ROOT omitted.**

> **Option (a) 7.92 m/s is exactly double, and option (c) 1.98 m/s exactly half — factor-of-two errors in the 2 or in h.**

> **The magnitude check that catches them: √(2gh) for h in metres is roughly 4.43√h, so a head of 0.8 m gives about 4.43 × 0.894 = 3.96 m/s.**

> **That coefficient 4.43 = √(2 × 9.81) is worth carrying, since it converts any head directly to a velocity: V ≈ 4.43√h.**

**How the pitot tube works — the principle:**

> **A pitot tube has an opening facing DIRECTLY INTO the flow.**

> **The fluid at that opening is brought to REST — a STAGNATION POINT — so its entire velocity head is converted into pressure head.**

> **By Bernoulli, along the streamline reaching the stagnation point:**

> **p_static/γ + V²/2g = p_stagnation/γ**

> **So the DIFFERENCE between the stagnation and static pressures is exactly the velocity head:**

> **h = (p_stagnation − p_static)/γ = V²/2g**

> **Hence V = √(2gh)** ✓

> **The instrument therefore measures a POINT velocity — the velocity at the tip — and not a mean velocity.**

**The distinction between the tube types, since the names are used loosely:**

| Instrument | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Simple PITOT tube** | **STAGNATION pressure only — a separate static tapping is needed** |
| **PITOT-STATIC tube (Prandtl tube)** | **BOTH stagnation and static pressure in one instrument, with the static holes on the side of the stem** ← |
| **Pitot tube with a manometer across both tappings** | Reads the difference directly |

> **The PITOT-STATIC tube is the practical instrument, and the placement of its static holes is a real design matter: they must be far enough back from the nose that the local flow disturbance has died away, and far enough forward of the stem that the stem's own disturbance has not begun.**

> **Getting that placement wrong makes the measured static pressure wrong, and the error appears directly in the velocity.**

**Measuring the MEAN velocity, since a point velocity is rarely what is wanted:**

> **A pitot tube gives the velocity at one point, and the velocity varies across the section.**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Traverse the section and integrate** | **The rigorous method — readings on a grid or on equal-area annuli** |
| **Measure at the point where V = V_mean** | **In a pipe, about 0.75 R from the axis for turbulent flow** |
| **Use the ONE-POINT or TWO-POINT method in an open channel** | **0.6 of the depth from the surface gives approximately the mean; or average the readings at 0.2 and 0.8 depth** ← |
| **Apply a known ratio V_mean/V_max** | About 0.8-0.85 for turbulent pipe flow |
