> **The OPEN CHANNEL 0.6-depth rule is worth knowing because it is used constantly in river gauging: a current meter lowered to 0.6 of the depth below the surface reads very nearly the mean velocity in that vertical.**

> **The reason is that the logarithmic velocity profile in an open channel happens to pass through its own mean at about that depth — so a single reading substitutes for a traverse.**

> **For deeper water the TWO-POINT method (averaging 0.2 and 0.8 depth) is more accurate, and for a full gauging the vertical is traversed at several points.**

**The COEFFICIENT C_v, since the stem sets it to unity:**

> **For a well-made pitot tube, C_v is between 0.98 and 1.00 — so taking it as unity introduces at most 2 per cent of error.**

> **That is unusually good for a flow-measuring device, and it is why the pitot tube is the reference instrument for point velocity.**

> **The reason is that the measurement involves NO CONTRACTION, no orifice and no separation — the fluid is simply brought to rest, which is a clean and nearly loss-free process.**

> **Compare the other flow meters:**

| Device | Coefficient | Head loss | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PITOT tube** | **C_v ≈ 0.98-1.00** | **NEGLIGIBLE** | **Point velocity; almost no obstruction** ← |
| **VENTURIMETER** | **C_d ≈ 0.95-0.99** | **LOW (10-20 % of the differential) — the gradual expansion recovers most of the pressure** ← | Expensive, long |
| **ORIFICE meter** | **C_d ≈ 0.60-0.65** | **HIGH (40-90 %) — the jet separates and the energy is lost in turbulence** | Cheap, compact |
| **NOZZLE meter** | C_d ≈ 0.95-0.98 | Intermediate | — |
| **Rotameter** | — | Moderate | Direct visual reading |

> **The VENTURI against ORIFICE comparison is the classic one and the reason for the difference is worth stating:**

> **A venturimeter's downstream cone expands GRADUALLY — typically at 5 to 7 degrees — so the flow follows the wall without separating, and most of the velocity head is converted back into pressure.**

> **An orifice plate is an abrupt hole: the jet issuing from it SEPARATES, forms a vena contracta, and then dissipates its energy in violent turbulence downstream.**

> **So the orifice meter's cheapness is paid for in permanent head loss — which, for a pumped system, is a permanent energy cost for the life of the installation.**

> **The economic conclusion follows directly: an orifice plate suits an occasional measurement or a gravity system with head to spare, and a venturimeter suits a permanent installation on a pumped main, where the head loss is paid for in electricity every hour.**

> **And the very low C_d of an orifice (0.62) against a venturi's (0.98) reflects the same physics: the coefficient measures how far the real flow departs from the ideal, and the orifice's contraction and separation account for the whole difference.**

examTip.trap: **Option (d) 15.70 is 2gh with the SQUARE ROOT omitted**, and the other two are factor-of-two slips. The 4.43√h check catches all three.
examTip.mnemonic: **A pitot tube reads a POINT velocity** — for the mean in an open channel, measure at 0.6 of the depth, or average 0.2 and 0.8. And note the head loss: pitot negligible, VENTURI low (gradual expansion recovers pressure), ORIFICE high (the jet separates).

questions.stem: For flow through an orifice, the coefficient of discharge is related to the coefficient of velocity and the coefficient of contraction by:
questions.solution:
**C_d = C_v × C_c.**

**The three coefficients defined:**

| Coefficient | Definition | Typical value for a sharp-edged orifice |
|---|---|---|
| **C_v, coefficient of VELOCITY** | **Actual velocity at the vena contracta / theoretical velocity √(2gh)** | **0.95-0.99** |
| **C_c, coefficient of CONTRACTION** | **Area of the VENA CONTRACTA / area of the orifice** | **0.61-0.69** |
| **C_d, coefficient of DISCHARGE** | **Actual discharge / theoretical discharge** | **0.60-0.65** ← |
| **C_r, coefficient of RESISTANCE** | Loss of head / head at the outlet | 0.06 or so |

**Why the relation is a PRODUCT — the derivation in two lines:**

> **Actual discharge = actual AREA × actual VELOCITY**

> **= (C_c × A) × (C_v × √(2gh))**

> **= C_c C_v × A √(2gh)**

> **= C_c C_v × theoretical discharge**

> **Therefore  C_d = C_c × C_v** ✓

> **The discharge is a product of an area and a velocity, so the two corrections MULTIPLY. That is the whole reasoning, and it makes the relation impossible to misremember.**

> **Checking the numbers: 0.62 (typical C_c) × 0.98 (typical C_v) = 0.61, which is the observed C_d** ✓

> **That numerical consistency is the confirmation: the three coefficients are not independent measurements but two independent ones and their product.**

**Which coefficient accounts for most of the reduction — worth noticing:**

> **C_v ≈ 0.98 — so the VELOCITY is nearly ideal, only 2 per cent low.**

> **C_c ≈ 0.62 — so the AREA is reduced by 38 per cent.**

> **So the orifice's low discharge coefficient is almost entirely a CONTRACTION effect, not a friction effect.**

> **That is a useful diagnosis: the water is not slowed much by the orifice, but the jet passes through an area far smaller than the hole.**

> **Which means the remedy, if a higher C_d is wanted, is to reduce the CONTRACTION rather than to smooth the surface — and that is exactly what a bell-mouthed or rounded orifice does:**

| Orifice type | C_c | C_d |
|---|---|---|
| **SHARP-EDGED** | **0.62** | **0.62** ← |
| **Rounded / bell-mouthed** | **≈ 1.00 — no contraction at all** | **0.95-0.98** |
| **Mouthpiece, running full** | — | **0.80 or so** |
| **Borda's mouthpiece, running free** | **0.5 (theoretically exact)** | **0.5** |

> **The BELL-MOUTHED entry shows the point plainly: rounding the entry so the streamlines are not required to turn sharply eliminates the contraction and raises C_d from 0.62 to nearly 0.98.**

> **So a bell-mouth is not a refinement but a 50 per cent increase in discharge for the same hole — which is why every well-designed intake, penstock entry and pump suction is bell-mouthed.**

**The VENA CONTRACTA, since C_c describes it:**

> **Water approaching a sharp-edged orifice arrives from all directions, including radially inward along the wall.**

> **The streamlines therefore cannot turn abruptly through 90° at the edge — they curve, and continue converging for a short distance BEYOND the orifice.**

> **The jet reaches its MINIMUM cross-section at about ONE HALF THE ORIFICE DIAMETER downstream — the VENA CONTRACTA — and only there is the flow parallel and the pressure atmospheric.**

> **That is why measurements and calculations refer to the vena contracta rather than to the orifice plane: at the orifice itself the streamlines are still converging and the pressure is not atmospheric.**

> **And it is why the contraction is a matter of the fluid's INERTIA rather than of viscosity — the streamlines overshoot because they cannot turn instantaneously, which is a purely inertial effect.**

> **Hence C_c is nearly independent of the Reynolds number for a sharp-edged orifice, while C_v (a friction effect) does vary with it.**

**How the coefficients are MEASURED, since each needs its own experiment:**

| Coefficient | Measurement |
|---|---|
| **C_d** | **Collect the discharge in a measured time; divide by A√(2gh)** — the easiest |
| **C_v** | **Measure the JET TRAJECTORY: from x and y coordinates of a point on the jet, C_v = x/√(4yh)** ← |
| **C_c** | **Obtained as C_d/C_v — since measuring the vena contracta's area directly is difficult** ← |

> **The TRAJECTORY method for C_v is worth knowing because it is elegant: the jet leaving a vertical orifice is a projectile, so its horizontal and vertical coordinates give its initial velocity by kinematics alone, with no flow measurement at all.**

> **Horizontally: x = V t. Vertically: y = ½ g t².**

> **Eliminating t:  V = x √(g/2y), and dividing by √(2gh) gives C_v = x/√(4yh)** ✓

> **And the last row is the practical point: C_c is almost never measured directly, because locating and measuring the vena contracta's area accurately is difficult.**

> **It is DEDUCED from the other two, using exactly the relation this question asks for — which is the relation's principal use.**

**Where orifice theory is applied in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Discharge through a SLUICE GATE or an outlet** | **Submerged orifice flow** |
| **Emptying and filling times of tanks and locks** | **Integrating the orifice equation as the head falls** ← |
| **Orifice METERS in pipelines** | Flow measurement |
| **Flow through a MODULE or an outlet in an irrigation canal** | Proportional distribution |
| **Leakage estimation through a crack or a hole** | Q = C_d A √(2gh) |
| **Flow from a reservoir through a low-level outlet** | — |

> **The TANK EMPTYING calculation is the commonest application and is worth setting out, since it requires integration:**

> **As the tank empties, the head h falls, so the discharge falls too — the flow is UNSTEADY.**

> **For a tank of constant plan area A_tank draining through an orifice of area a:**

> **T = (2 A_tank / (C_d a √(2g))) × (√H₁ − √H₂)**

> **Note the √H terms: the time depends on the SQUARE ROOTS of the initial and final heads, not on their difference.**

> **A consequence worth knowing: emptying a tank from full to half-full takes much LESS time than from half-full to empty, because the head — and hence the discharge — is greater during the first part.**

> **The last few centimetres take a disproportionate time, which anyone who has drained a tank has observed and which the √H form explains exactly.**

examTip.trick: **C_d = C_c × C_v, because discharge = AREA × VELOCITY and the two corrections MULTIPLY.** Check: 0.62 × 0.98 = 0.61 ✓.
examTip.trap: **The low C_d is almost entirely a CONTRACTION effect (C_c = 0.62), not friction (C_v = 0.98).** So the remedy is a BELL MOUTH, which removes the contraction and raises C_d to nearly 0.98 — a 50 % gain for the same hole.
examTip.mnemonic: **C_c is deduced as C_d/C_v, not measured** — the vena contracta's area is too hard to measure directly, and that deduction is this relation's main use. And tank emptying time goes as (√H₁ − √H₂), so the last centimetres take disproportionately long.

questions.stem: Water flows through a pipe that suddenly enlarges, the velocity falling from 3 m/s to 1 m/s. The head loss at the enlargement is:
questions.solution:
**0.204 m.**

**The head loss at a sudden enlargement:**

> **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)² / (2 g)**

**The computation:**

> **h_L = (3 − 1)² / (2 × 9.81) = 4 / 19.62 = 0.2039 m ≈ 0.204 m** ✓

> **Option (c) 0.102 m is half the answer, and option (b) 0.408 m is double — both from mishandling the 2g or the squaring.**

> **Option (d) 0.816 m is (V₁² − V₂²)/2g = (9 − 1)/19.62 = 0.408, doubled — or a related slip.**

> **The essential point is that the loss involves the SQUARE OF THE DIFFERENCE of the velocities, NOT the difference of the squares:**

> **(V₁ − V₂)² = (3 − 1)² = 4**

> **V₁² − V₂² = 9 − 1 = 8**

> **The two differ by a factor of two here, and confusing them is the commonest error in this calculation.**

**Where the formula comes from — and its derivation is unusually satisfying:**

> **This is one of very few loss coefficients derived THEORETICALLY rather than measured, and the derivation uses the MOMENTUM equation together with Bernoulli.**

> **Applying the momentum equation to the control volume across the enlargement:**

> **(p₁ − p₂) A₂ = ρ Q (V₂ − V₁)**

> **Applying Bernoulli with a loss term:**

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + h_L**

> **Eliminating (p₁ − p₂) between them and simplifying gives:**

> **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g** ✓

> **This is BORDA-CARNOT'S relation, and it is worth knowing that it agrees closely with experiment — which is a genuine confirmation that the loss mechanism is understood.**

**The PHYSICAL mechanism of the loss:**

> **The fluid leaving the small pipe cannot expand instantly to fill the large one.**

> **It continues as a JET into the larger pipe, and the annular region around that jet is filled with slow, RECIRCULATING EDDIES.**

> **The jet mixes with those eddies over a length of several pipe diameters, and the mixing is TURBULENT and DISSIPATIVE — the ordered kinetic energy of the jet is converted into turbulence and then into heat.**

> **So the loss is a MIXING loss, and it occurs DOWNSTREAM of the enlargement rather than at it.**

> **That mechanism explains the two limiting cases:**

| Case | h_L |
|---|---|
| **A gradual enlargement (a diffuser)** | **MUCH LESS — the flow follows the wall without separating, so there is no jet and no mixing** ← |
| **Discharge into a large tank or reservoir (V₂ → 0)** | **h_L = V₁²/2g — the ENTIRE velocity head is lost** ← |

> **The SECOND row is the important special case: a pipe discharging into a reservoir loses ALL of its velocity head, because the jet dissipates entirely into the still water.**

> **That is the origin of the EXIT LOSS coefficient K = 1.0, and it is why a pipe outlet is sometimes fitted with a diffuser or a flared end — to recover some of that head rather than throwing it away.**

> **For this pipe, if it discharged into a reservoir instead, the loss would be 3²/19.62 = 0.459 m — more than twice the loss at the enlargement, because the whole velocity head goes rather than only the part associated with the change.**

**The GRADUAL enlargement, since it is the practical remedy:**

| Cone angle | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Below about 7°** | **The flow follows the wall — NO separation, minimal loss. The efficient diffuser** ← |
| **7° to 40°** | **Progressive separation; the loss rises steeply and is worse than a sudden enlargement in part of this range** |
| **Above 40°** | Fully separated; behaves much like a sudden enlargement |

> **The middle row contains a counter-intuitive and genuinely useful fact: a MODERATELY tapered enlargement can lose MORE head than an abrupt one.**

> **The reason is that at intermediate angles the flow separates from the wall but the wall continues to diverge, so a large unstable separated region forms with vigorous mixing.**

> **An abrupt enlargement at least confines the mixing to a predictable annular region.**

> **So a diffuser is either designed properly — at 7 degrees or less, which makes it LONG — or not attempted at all.**

> **A short, steep cone is the worst of both, and it is a common piece of well-intentioned bad design.**

> **That is why a turbine draft tube's expansion is so gradual and so long, and why the elbow type accepts a real efficiency penalty to shorten it.**

**The minor loss coefficients, for context:**

| Fitting | K in h_L = K V²/2g |
|---|---|
| **SUDDEN ENLARGEMENT** | **(1 − A₁/A₂)², applied to V₁** ← |
| **EXIT into a reservoir** | **1.0** |
| **SUDDEN CONTRACTION** | **0.5 approximately, applied to the DOWNSTREAM velocity** |
| **Sharp-edged ENTRY from a reservoir** | **0.5** |
| **BELL-MOUTHED entry** | **0.04-0.05 — an order of magnitude better** ← |
| **90° elbow (standard)** | 0.9 |
| **90° bend, long radius** | 0.2-0.4 |
| **Gate valve, fully open** | 0.2 |
| **Globe valve, fully open** | 10 |

> **The ENTRY comparison in rows four and five makes the strongest practical point in the whole table: rounding a pipe entry reduces its loss coefficient from 0.5 to about 0.05 — a TENFOLD reduction — for the cost of a shaped inlet.**

> **That is the cheapest head saving available anywhere in a pipeline, and it is why bell-mouthed entries are universal in hydropower intakes, pump suctions and penstock inlets.**

> **And note the CONTRACTION against ENLARGEMENT asymmetry: a sudden contraction (K = 0.5) loses LESS than a sudden enlargement of the same ratio.**

> **The reason is that ACCELERATING flow is stable and does not separate — the streamlines converge willingly — while DECELERATING flow against a rising pressure separates readily.**

> **That asymmetry between accelerating and decelerating flow is one of the most general facts in fluid mechanics, and it explains why nozzles are efficient and diffusers are difficult.**

examTip.trick: **h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g = 4/19.62 = 0.204 m** — the SQUARE OF THE DIFFERENCE, not the difference of the squares (which would give 8/19.62 = 0.408).
examTip.trap: **A pipe discharging into a reservoir loses its ENTIRE velocity head (K = 1.0)** — here that would be 0.459 m, more than twice the enlargement loss.
examTip.mnemonic: **A MODERATELY tapered enlargement can lose MORE than an abrupt one** — so design a diffuser at 7° or less, or don't attempt one. And rounding a pipe ENTRY cuts K from 0.5 to 0.05, the cheapest head saving in any pipeline.

questions.stem: In a pipe flow, the hydraulic gradient line (HGL) and the total energy line (TEL) are related as follows:
options: The HGL lies above the TEL by the velocity head
The HGL lies below the TEL by the velocity head
questions.solution:
**The HGL lies BELOW the TEL by the VELOCITY HEAD.**

**The definitions:**

| Line | Plots | Represents |
|---|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC GRADIENT LINE (HGL)** | **z + p/γ** | **The level to which water would rise in a PIEZOMETER tapped into the pipe** ← |
| **TOTAL ENERGY LINE (TEL)** | **z + p/γ + V²/2g** | **The total head available — the level to which a PITOT tube would rise** |

> **So the TEL is above the HGL by exactly V²/2g everywhere, and the gap between them IS the velocity head.**

> **Since the velocity head cannot be negative, THE TEL IS NEVER BELOW THE HGL** — which makes option (b) impossible on principle, not merely wrong.

**The behaviour of the two lines — the properties worth knowing:**

| Property | TEL | HGL |
|---|---|---|
| **Always falls in the direction of flow?** | **YES — energy is always lost to friction, never gained (unless a PUMP adds it)** ← | **NO — it can RISE** |
| **Can it rise?** | **Only across a PUMP** | **YES — wherever the pipe ENLARGES, the velocity falls and the pressure head rises** ← |
| **Can it fall abruptly?** | **Yes — at a valve, a bend, a sudden change** | Yes |
| **Slope in a uniform pipe** | **The friction slope, h_f/L** | **PARALLEL to the TEL, since V is constant** |
| **Relation to the pipe axis** | Above it | **BELOW the pipe axis means NEGATIVE pressure** ← |

> **The SECOND row is the fact worth understanding: THE TEL CAN ONLY FALL, BUT THE HGL CAN RISE.**

> **The TEL falls because energy is dissipated — that is the second law of thermodynamics applied to a pipe, and it admits no exception except a pump.**

> **The HGL can rise because it represents PRESSURE, and pressure can be recovered from velocity: at an enlargement the flow slows, velocity head converts to pressure head, and the piezometric level rises even as the total energy falls.**

> **So a rising HGL is not an error but a diffuser at work — and a rising TEL in a computed profile IS an error, unless a pump is present.**

> **That is a useful check on any hydraulic gradient diagram: follow the TEL and confirm it only ever descends.**

**The most important practical use of the HGL — spotting NEGATIVE PRESSURE:**

> **Where the HGL falls BELOW the pipe's own axis, the pressure inside the pipe is BELOW ATMOSPHERIC.**

| Consequence of negative pressure | Note |
|---|---|
| **AIR is drawn in at every joint, valve gland and imperfect fitting** | **Air pockets collect at high points and reduce the pipe's effective area** ← |
| **Contaminated groundwater can be SUCKED IN through a leak** | **A public health hazard — the leak that normally leaks OUT now leaks IN** ← |
| **CAVITATION if the pressure approaches vapour pressure** | Damage and noise |
| **Column separation and subsequent water hammer** | The rejoining column slams |
| **A thin-walled pipe may COLLAPSE inward** | Buckling under external pressure |

> **The SECOND row is the most serious and the least obvious: a water main under negative pressure will draw in whatever surrounds it, and a main laid alongside a sewer in a trench that floods is then a direct route from the sewer to the consumer.**

> **Intermittent supply systems — common throughout South Asia — are particularly exposed, because when the supply is off the main is empty and the pressure is atmospheric or below, and contaminated water enters freely.**

> **That is a genuine and documented cause of waterborne disease outbreaks, and it is the strongest public-health argument for CONTINUOUS PRESSURISED SUPPLY: a main always under positive pressure leaks outward, and outward leakage wastes water while inward leakage spreads disease.**

> **So drawing the HGL and confirming it stays above the pipe throughout is not an academic exercise but a check on the safety of the supply.**

**A SIPHON, since it is the deliberate case of negative pressure:**

> **A siphon carries water OVER an obstruction higher than the HGL, so the pressure at its summit is necessarily negative.**

| Requirement for a working siphon | Note |
|---|---|
| **The summit must be BELOW the theoretical limit** | **The absolute pressure cannot fall below the vapour pressure — so the summit is limited to about 7-8 m above the upstream water surface in practice, against a theoretical 10.3 m** ← |
| **The pipe must be AIRTIGHT** | Any leak admits air and breaks the siphon |
| **An AIR VALVE or vacuum arrangement is needed at the summit** | To evacuate accumulated air |
| **It must be PRIMED to start** | The pipe filled before flow begins |

> **The practical limit of 7 to 8 m rather than the theoretical 10.3 m is worth knowing, and its cause is the same one that limits pump suction: as the pressure approaches vapour pressure the water begins to boil and release dissolved air, and the siphon breaks.**

> **So the theoretical limit is never approached, and a design that assumes it will fail.**

**Drawing the lines, since the exercise is the standard way of presenting a pipeline's hydraulics:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Draw the pipe PROFILE to scale, with the reservoir levels** |
| **2** | **Start the TEL at the upstream reservoir surface, LESS the entry loss** |
| **3** | **Deduct h_f progressively along each length, and each minor loss as a step** |
| **4** | **Add the pump head as a STEP UP where a pump occurs** |
| **5** | **Draw the HGL parallel to the TEL, below it by V²/2g in each length** |
| **6** | **CHECK: does the HGL stay above the pipe everywhere?** ← |
| **7** | **The TEL must end at the downstream reservoir surface, having lost the exit velocity head** |

> **Step 6 is the purpose of the whole exercise, and step 7 is the check that the arithmetic closes: the total of all the losses must equal the difference between the two reservoir levels.**

> **If it does not, a loss has been omitted or double-counted — so the diagram checks itself, which is why it remains worth drawing even when the computation is done by software.**

examTip.trick: **The gap between TEL and HGL IS the velocity head V²/2g, so the HGL is always BELOW.** Since V²/2g cannot be negative, option (b) is impossible on principle.
examTip.trap: **The TEL can only FALL (except across a pump), but the HGL can RISE** — wherever the pipe enlarges, velocity head converts to pressure head. A rising TEL in a computed profile is an error; a rising HGL is a diffuser working.
examTip.mnemonic: **Where the HGL falls BELOW the pipe axis, the pressure is negative — and a leaking main then sucks contaminated water IN.** That is a documented cause of disease outbreaks in intermittent supplies, and the strongest argument for continuous pressurised supply.

questions.stem: A hydraulic jump occurs in a rectangular channel with an upstream depth of 0.5 m and a downstream depth of 2.0 m. The energy loss in the jump is:
questions.solution:
**0.844 m.**

**The energy loss in a hydraulic jump:**

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂)**

**The computation:**

> **E_L = (2.0 − 0.5)³ / (4 × 0.5 × 2.0)**

> **= 1.5³ / 4.0**

> **= 3.375 / 4.0**

> **= 0.844 m** ✓

> **Note the CUBE in the numerator — the loss grows very rapidly with the height of the jump.**

> **Option (a) 0.422 m is half the answer and option (d) 0.211 m a quarter, both from mishandling the denominator.**

> **Option (c) 1.500 m is simply (y₂ − y₁), the height of the jump itself, offered as the energy loss.**

**Checking the answer against the specific energies — the direct confirmation:**

> **First, the discharge. The sequent depth relation gives the upstream Froude number:**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)**

> **4 = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1), so √(1 + 8Fr₁²) = 9, hence Fr₁² = 10 and Fr₁ = 3.162**

> **V₁ = Fr₁ √(g y₁) = 3.162 × √(9.81 × 0.5) = 3.162 × 2.215 = 7.00 m/s**

> **So q = V₁ y₁ = 7.00 × 0.5 = 3.5 m³/s per metre width, and V₂ = 3.5/2.0 = 1.75 m/s.**

> **Now the specific energies:**

| Section | Depth | Velocity | V²/2g | E = y + V²/2g |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Upstream (1)** | **0.50 m** | **7.00 m/s** | **2.498 m** | **2.998 m** |
| **Downstream (2)** | **2.00 m** | **1.75 m/s** | **0.156 m** | **2.156 m** |
| **LOSS** | — | — | — | **0.842 m** ✓ |

> **0.842 m against the formula's 0.844 m — agreement to rounding.**

> **That independent route is the best available check, and it also reveals how MUCH energy the jump destroys: 0.842 out of 2.998 m, or 28 per cent of the incoming specific energy.**

> **And it confirms the flow regimes: Fr₁ = 3.16 (supercritical) upstream and Fr₂ = 1.75/√(9.81 × 2) = 0.395 (subcritical) downstream — which is what a jump is.**

**What a hydraulic jump IS, and why it must be abrupt:**

> **A hydraulic jump is the transition from SUPERCRITICAL to SUBCRITICAL flow.**

> **It cannot happen smoothly, and the reason is instructive:**

> **On the specific energy curve, the supercritical and subcritical branches meet only at the critical point. To pass smoothly from one to the other, the flow would have to lose energy down to E_min and then GAIN it back — and it cannot gain energy.**

> **So the transition occurs as a violent, turbulent, DISSIPATIVE jump that loses energy while gaining depth, cutting across the curve rather than travelling along it.**

> **The MOMENTUM equation, not the energy equation, governs it — because the loss is unknown in advance and momentum is conserved while energy is not:**

> **The SPECIFIC FORCE (momentum function) is EQUAL on both sides:  y²/2 + q²/(g y) = constant**

> **The two depths satisfying that equation are the SEQUENT (conjugate) DEPTHS — 0.5 m and 2.0 m here.**

> **That is a crucial distinction worth stating: SEQUENT depths have equal SPECIFIC FORCE, while ALTERNATE depths have equal SPECIFIC ENERGY.**

| | **ALTERNATE depths** | **SEQUENT (conjugate) depths** |
|---|---|---|
| **Equal quantity** | **SPECIFIC ENERGY** | **SPECIFIC FORCE (momentum)** ← |
| **Occur in** | **A smooth transition with no loss** | **A HYDRAULIC JUMP, with loss** |
| **Related by** | The specific energy curve | **y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1+8Fr₁²) − 1)** |

> **Confusing the two is the commonest conceptual error in this topic, and using the energy equation to find the downstream depth of a jump is the error it produces.**

**The CLASSIFICATION of jumps by Froude number, since the type governs the design:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Character | Energy dissipation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1.0-1.7** | **UNDULAR** | **Standing waves; no real roller** | **< 5 %** |
| **1.7-2.5** | **WEAK** | **A series of small rollers; smooth surface beyond** | **5-15 %** |
| **2.5-4.5** | **OSCILLATING** | **The jet oscillates up and down erratically, generating LARGE WAVES that travel far downstream** | **15-45 %** ← the type to AVOID |
| **4.5-9.0** | **STEADY** | **Well-balanced, stable, the roller and the jet in equilibrium — the BEST for a stilling basin** ← | **45-70 %** |
| **> 9.0** | **STRONG (choppy)** | **Very rough and effective, but severe on the structure** | **70-85 %** |

> **This jump at Fr₁ = 3.16 falls in the OSCILLATING range — the one range that designers deliberately avoid.**

> **The reason is worth understanding: an oscillating jump's entering jet flips erratically between the bed and the surface, generating irregular waves that propagate a long way downstream.**

> **Those waves erode banks, damage boats and moorings, and make the tailwater unpredictable — and the jump's position also wanders, so it may leave the paved basin.**

> **So a stilling basin design that lands in the 2.5 to 4.5 range is usually altered — by changing the basin's level, adding baffle blocks, or narrowing the approach — to push Fr₁ into the STEADY range above 4.5.**

> **That is a real design decision made on exactly the number computed here, and it is why the Froude number is calculated before the basin is sized.**

**The uses of a hydraulic jump, since it is engineered deliberately:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **ENERGY DISSIPATION below a spillway, sluice or canal fall** | **The principal use — it destroys energy that would otherwise scour the bed** ← |
| **Raising the water level for downstream diversion or measurement** | — |
| **MIXING chemicals in water treatment** | **The intense turbulence gives rapid, complete mixing with no moving parts** ← |
| **Aeration — increasing dissolved oxygen** | Used in wastewater treatment |
| **Removing air pockets from a pipeline** | — |
| **Desalting or removing sediment** | — |

> **The MIXING application is worth noting because it is a genuinely elegant use of a phenomenon usually regarded as a nuisance: a hydraulic jump in a channel provides the violent turbulence that rapid mixing of a coagulant requires, with no power input and nothing to maintain.**

> **A PARSHALL FLUME or a simple weir-and-jump arrangement can therefore serve as both a flow meter AND a flash mixer in a water treatment works — two functions from one structure.**

examTip.trick: **E_L = (y₂−y₁)³/(4y₁y₂) = 3.375/4 = 0.844 m.** Note the CUBE — the loss grows rapidly with the jump height. Option (c) 1.5 m is just (y₂−y₁).
examTip.trap: **SEQUENT depths have equal SPECIFIC FORCE; ALTERNATE depths have equal SPECIFIC ENERGY.** Using the energy equation to find a jump's downstream depth is the error that confusion produces — momentum governs a jump, because the loss is unknown in advance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr₁ = 3.16 here, in the OSCILLATING range (2.5-4.5) that designers deliberately AVOID** — its erratic jet throws waves far downstream and the jump wanders. Basins are redesigned to reach the STEADY range above 4.5.

questions.stem: A catchment of 2 km² has a runoff coefficient of 0.6. For a rainfall intensity of 50 mm/hour, the peak runoff by the rational formula is:
questions.solution:
**16.67 m³/s.**

**The rational formula in the units used here:**

> **Q = C i A / 3.6**

| Symbol | Meaning | Units | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Q** | Peak runoff | **m³/s** | to find |
| **C** | **Runoff coefficient** | **dimensionless** | **0.6** |
| **i** | **Rainfall intensity** | **mm/hour** | **50** |
| **A** | **Catchment area** | **km²** | **2** |
| **3.6** | **The unit-conversion constant** | — | — |

**The computation:**

> **Q = 0.6 × 50 × 2 / 3.6 = 60/3.6 = 16.67 m³/s** ✓

> **Option (c) 30.0 m³/s is C i A without the /3.6, and option (a) 6.0 is roughly a factor-of-ten slip.**

**Where the 3.6 comes from — worth deriving so the formula need not be memorised:**

> **In consistent SI units the formula is simply Q = C i A, with i in m/s and A in m².**

> **Converting the practical units:**

> **i = 50 mm/h = 50 × 10⁻³ m / 3600 s = 1.389 × 10⁻⁵ m/s**

> **A = 2 km² = 2 × 10⁶ m²**

> **Q = 0.6 × 1.389 × 10⁻⁵ × 2 × 10⁶ = 16.67 m³/s** ✓

> **And the constant: (10⁻³/3600) × 10⁶ = 1000/3600 = 1/3.6** ✓

> **So the 3.6 is just 3600 seconds per hour divided by the 1000 mm per metre — which means it can be rebuilt in ten seconds if forgotten.**

> **Note the alternative form used where the area is in HECTARES: Q = C i A/360, with A in ha.** The constant differs by the factor of 100 between hectares and square kilometres.

> **Mixing the two constants is the commonest error in this formula, and checking which area unit the data use prevents it.**

**The critical assumption — the DURATION of the rainfall:**

> **The rational formula gives the PEAK runoff, and it assumes:**

> **THE RAINFALL LASTS AT LEAST AS LONG AS THE TIME OF CONCENTRATION.**

> **The TIME OF CONCENTRATION t_c is the time for runoff to travel from the HYDRAULICALLY MOST REMOTE point of the catchment to the outlet.**

> **The reasoning is important and is the whole basis of the method:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **Storm duration < t_c** | **The WHOLE catchment is not contributing at once, so the peak is LESS than C i A** |
| **Storm duration = t_c** | **The whole catchment contributes simultaneously for the first time — THE PEAK** ← |
| **Storm duration > t_c** | **The whole catchment still contributes, but the INTENSITY of a longer storm is LOWER, so the peak is lower** |

> **So the CRITICAL storm duration is EXACTLY the time of concentration — long enough for the whole catchment to contribute, and no longer, because intensity falls as duration rises.**

> **That is why the design intensity must be taken from an INTENSITY-DURATION-FREQUENCY curve at a duration equal to t_c, and not simply at any convenient value.**

> **Using a longer duration understates the intensity and the peak; using a shorter one overstates the intensity while the catchment cannot fully contribute.**

**Time of concentration, since it must be estimated:**

> **KIRPICH'S formula:  t_c = 0.0195 L^{0.77} S^{−0.385}** (t_c in minutes, L in metres, S the average slope)

> **Or in a common alternative form:  t_c = 0.01947 L^{0.77} / S^{0.385}**

| Catchment character | Time of concentration |
|---|---|
| **Small, steep, paved urban catchment** | **A few minutes to 20 minutes** |
| **Small rural catchment** | **30 minutes to a few hours** |
| **Large river basin** | **Many hours to days — and the rational formula is INAPPLICABLE** ← |

**The LIMITS of the rational formula, stated honestly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **AREA — valid only for SMALL catchments, up to about 50 ha (0.5 km²), or 25 km² at the very most** | **Because it assumes uniform rainfall over the whole area, which fails on a large catchment** ← |
| **Assumes UNIFORM intensity over the whole catchment and the whole duration** | Real storms are patchy and vary in time |
| **Assumes the runoff coefficient is CONSTANT** | **C actually rises during a storm as the ground saturates** ← |
| **Gives only the PEAK, not a hydrograph** | No volume, no shape, no timing |
| **Assumes the return period of the runoff equals that of the rainfall** | An approximation |
| **Ignores storage in the catchment and channel** | — |

> **The AREA limit is the one most often violated, and the 2 km² of this question is at the upper end of what is defensible.**

> **For anything larger, the unit hydrograph, a synthetic hydrograph or a full rainfall-runoff model is required — and applying the rational formula to a 500 km² basin, which does happen, produces a number with no meaning.**

> **The CONSTANT C assumption deserves its note too: at the start of a storm on dry ground, much rainfall infiltrates and C is low; as the ground saturates, C rises toward 1.**

> **So the tabulated C values are effectively average or design values for a saturated condition, and they understate the runoff from a prolonged storm and overstate it from a brief one on dry ground.**

**The RUNOFF COEFFICIENT values, since C is the parameter that matters most:**

| Surface | C |
|---|---|
| **Watertight roofs, concrete and asphalt paving** | **0.70-0.95** |
| **Closely built-up urban area** | **0.70-0.90** |
| **Residential area, moderate density** | **0.40-0.60** |
| **Parks, lawns and open ground** | **0.05-0.25** |
| **Cultivated land** | **0.20-0.40** |
| **Wooded and forested land** | **0.10-0.20** |
| **Steep, bare rock** | **0.80-0.90** |

> **C = 0.6 in this question therefore describes a moderately developed catchment — a mixed suburban area, or cultivated land on a steep slope.**

> **For a mixed catchment, a WEIGHTED C is computed as Σ(C_i A_i)/ΣA — which is the ordinary work of urban drainage design.**

> **And the values in that table explain why URBANISATION increases flood peaks so sharply: converting cultivated land (C ≈ 0.3) into a built-up area (C ≈ 0.8) nearly TRIPLES the peak runoff from the same rainfall, and shortens the time of concentration at the same time — so a higher peak arrives sooner.**

> **That combination is the reason urban flooding worsens as a catchment develops, even with no change in rainfall — and it is why modern drainage practice requires new development to attenuate its runoff to the pre-development rate rather than simply discharging it.**

examTip.trick: **Q = CiA/3.6 = 0.6 × 50 × 2/3.6 = 16.67 m³/s**, with i in mm/h and A in km². The 3.6 is just 3600 s/h ÷ 1000 mm/m.
examTip.trap: **With A in HECTARES the constant is 360, not 3.6** — mixing the two is the commonest error. Check which area unit the data use before substituting.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CRITICAL storm duration is exactly the TIME OF CONCENTRATION** — shorter and the whole catchment cannot contribute, longer and the intensity is lower. And the formula is valid only for SMALL catchments (up to about 25 km² at most), because it assumes uniform rainfall throughout.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its LEFT HALF only. The maximum shear force is:
questions.solution:
**60 kN, at the LEFT support.**

**Step 1 — the reactions:**

> **Total load = 20 × 4 = 80 kN, acting at its centroid 2 m from the left support.**

> **Taking moments about the RIGHT support:  R_A × 8 = 80 × 6, so R_A = 60 kN**

> **And R_B = 80 − 60 = 20 kN**

> **Check: 60 + 20 = 80 ✓**

**Step 2 — the maximum shear force:**

> **For any beam, the maximum shear occurs AT A SUPPORT (or at a point load), and equals the larger reaction.**

> **V_max = R_A = 60 kN** ✓

> **Options (c) 40 kN and (d) 20 kN are wL/4 and the smaller reaction respectively, and option (b) 80 kN is the total load.**

**Why the reactions are so unequal — and the check that confirms them:**

> **The load's centroid is 2 m from A and 6 m from B, so A is THREE TIMES closer.**

> **A reaction is inversely proportional to its distance from the load, so R_A must be THREE TIMES R_B — and 60 : 20 is exactly 3 : 1** ✓

> **That inverse-distance check is worth making a habit of: it verifies the reactions in a glance without repeating the moment equation.**

**The shear force diagram, since its shape follows from the loading:**

| Position | Shear force |
|---|---|
| **Just right of A** | **+60 kN** |
| **Falling LINEARLY under the UDL** | dV/dx = −w = −20 kN/m |
| **At midspan (x = 4 m)** | **60 − 20 × 4 = −20 kN** |
| **CONSTANT at −20 kN over the unloaded right half** | No load, so no change |
| **Just left of B** | **−20 kN, jumping to zero at the reaction** |

> **The shear crosses ZERO where 60 − 20x = 0, that is at x = 3 m — and that is where the BENDING MOMENT is maximum:**

> **M_max = 60 × 3 − 20 × 3 × 1.5 = 180 − 90 = 90 kNm**

> **Note that the maximum moment is NOT at midspan for this unsymmetrical loading — it is at 3 m — which is exactly why the shear-crosses-zero rule is more useful than assuming midspan.**

> **For comparison, a UDL of 20 kN/m over the WHOLE span would give M_max = 20 × 64/8 = 160 kNm at midspan. So half the load in the same place gives 90/160 = 56 per cent of the moment — more than half, because it is concentrated nearer one support.**

**The general rules worth carrying:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maximum SHEAR occurs at a SUPPORT or at a point load** | **Equal to the larger reaction for a simply supported beam** ← |
| **Maximum MOMENT occurs where the SHEAR crosses zero** | Since dM/dx = V |
| **The shear diagram's slope is −w** | So no load means constant shear |
| **The area under the shear diagram between two points equals the CHANGE in moment** | A useful way to construct the moment diagram |
| **A point load causes a STEP in shear and a KINK in moment** | — |

> **The FOURTH rule is the most efficient method of drawing a bending moment diagram: rather than computing moments at many sections, compute the AREAS of the shear diagram and accumulate them.**

> **Here: the area from A to x = 3 m is ½ × 3 × 60 = 90, which IS the maximum moment ✓ — obtained by geometry with no moment equation at all.**

> **And continuing: the area from 3 m to 4 m is −½ × 1 × 20 = −10, so M at midspan = 90 − 10 = 80 kNm; and the area from 4 m to B is −20 × 4 = −80, bringing the moment to zero at B ✓**

> **The moment closing exactly to zero at the far support is the check that the whole diagram is right, and it is available for every simply supported beam.**

examTip.trick: **Maximum shear = the LARGER REACTION.** The load's centroid is 2 m from A and 6 m from B, so R_A : R_B = 3 : 1, giving 60 and 20 kN.
examTip.trap: **The maximum MOMENT is not at midspan for an unsymmetrical load** — it is where the shear crosses zero, here at 3 m, giving 90 kNm. Assuming midspan is the error.
examTip.mnemonic: **The AREA under the shear diagram is the CHANGE in moment** — so ½ × 3 × 60 = 90 kNm directly, with no moment equation. And the diagram must close to ZERO at the far support, which checks the whole construction.

questions.stem: A cantilever 3 m long carries a triangular load of zero intensity at the fixed end increasing to 12 kN/m at the free end. The bending moment at the fixed end is:
questions.solution:
**36 kNm.**

**The method — total load times the distance to its centroid:**

> **Step 1 — the TOTAL LOAD is the AREA of the load diagram:**

> **W = ½ × base × height = ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 kN**

> **Step 2 — locate its CENTROID. A triangle's centroid lies ONE THIRD OF THE BASE FROM ITS WIDE END.**

> **The wide end (maximum intensity, 12 kN/m) is at the FREE end, so the centroid is 1 m from the free end — that is 2 m from the fixed end.**

> **Step 3 — the fixing moment:**

> **M = 18 kN × 2 m = 36 kNm** ✓

> **The standard formula confirms it: M = wL²/3 = 12 × 9/3 = 36 kNm** ✓

**The two triangular-load cases, which must be kept apart:**

| Load arrangement | Total load | Centroid from the FIXED end | M at the fixed end |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Maximum at the FREE end, zero at the fixed end** | **wL/2** | **2L/3 = 2 m** | **wL²/3 = 36 kNm** ← this case |
| **Maximum at the FIXED end, zero at the free end** | **wL/2** | **L/3 = 1 m** | **wL²/6 = 18 kNm** |

> **The TOTAL LOAD is IDENTICAL in both — half the base times the height — and only the LEVER ARM differs, by a factor of two.**

> **So the two cases differ by exactly a factor of two in the fixing moment, and identifying WHICH END carries the maximum intensity is the entire task.**

> **Option (b) 18 kNm is wL²/6, the answer for the OTHER arrangement — and it is the well-made distractor, because that case arises far more often in practice (see below).**

> **Option (a) 54 kNm is wL²/2, the answer for a UNIFORM load of 12 kN/m over the whole length — a heavier load with a shorter lever arm.**

> **Option (c) 27 kNm is wL²/4, which corresponds to no standard case.**

> **So every distractor except (c) is the correct answer to a neighbouring loading, which makes the option set a test of reading the stem rather than of arithmetic.**

**The reliable procedure, which needs no formulae at all:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the TOTAL LOAD as the AREA of the load diagram** |
| **2** | **Locate its CENTROID — for a triangle, ONE THIRD OF THE BASE FROM THE WIDE END** ← |
| **3** | **M at the fixed end = total load × distance from the fixed end to that centroid** |
| **4** | **Check against the standard formula, if one is recalled** |

> **Stating step 2 as "one third from the WIDE end" removes the ambiguity that "L/3 or 2L/3" invites, and it is the step at which errors occur.**

> **The procedure also handles loads no formula covers — a trapezoidal load, a partial triangle, a load with a step — by splitting the diagram into simple areas and summing their moments.**

**The complete results for this cantilever:**

| Quantity | Expression | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Total load** | **wL/2** | **18 kN** |
| **Shear force at the fixed end** | **wL/2** | **18 kN** |
| **Bending moment at the fixed end** | **wL²/3** | **36 kNm** ← |
| **Shear force diagram** | **PARABOLIC (2nd degree)** | Zero at the free end |
| **Bending moment diagram** | **CUBIC (3rd degree)** | Zero at the free end |
| **Deflection at the free end** | **11 wL⁴/(120 EI)** | — |

> **The DIAGRAM DEGREES follow the integration rule: the load varies LINEARLY (1st degree), so the shear is PARABOLIC (2nd) and the moment is CUBIC (3rd).**

> **Each integration raises the degree by one, and checking a sketched diagram's degree against that rule catches most drawing errors at once.**

> **For comparison, a UNIFORM load gives a LINEAR shear diagram and a PARABOLIC moment diagram — one degree lower in each, which is the familiar case.**

**Where a triangular load actually arises, since the case is not artificial:**

| Situation | Which end carries the maximum |
|---|---|
| **HYDROSTATIC pressure on a wall or a gate** | **Maximum at the BASE — the FIXED end** ← |
| **ACTIVE EARTH PRESSURE on a retaining wall stem** | **Maximum at the BASE — the FIXED end** ← |
| **A cantilever retaining wall stem** | Same |
| **Snow or material heaped against a wall** | Maximum at the base |
| **A tapering load from a sloping surcharge** | Depends on the geometry |

> **Every common real case puts the MAXIMUM AT THE FIXED END, which is the wL²/6 form — not the case in this question.**

> **A cantilever wall stem of height H under active pressure has a fixing moment of K_a γ H³/6, and a gate or dam face under water has γH³/6.**

> **So the wL²/6 form is met constantly and the wL²/3 form of this question is the rarer one — which is exactly why option (b) is such a plausible distractor, and why the stem's wording must be read rather than the familiar case assumed.**

> **That is a genuine hazard in practice as well as in examinations: a load diagram sketched the wrong way round produces a fixing moment wrong by a factor of two, and in the unsafe direction if the true case is the wL²/3 one.**

examTip.trick: **Total load = area of the triangle = 18 kN; centroid ONE THIRD OF THE BASE FROM THE WIDE END, so 2 m from the fixed end. M = 18 × 2 = 36 kNm** (= wL²/3).
examTip.trap: **The two triangular cases differ by a factor of TWO: wL²/3 with the maximum at the FREE end, wL²/6 with it at the FIXED end.** The total load is identical; only the lever arm differs. Option (b) is that other case — and it is the one that arises in practice.
examTip.mnemonic: **Say "one third from the WIDE end" and the L/3-or-2L/3 ambiguity disappears.** Hydrostatic and earth pressure both put the maximum at the FIXED end (wL²/6), so this question's arrangement is the rarer one — read the stem, don't assume the familiar case.

questions.stem: At a point in a strained body, σ_x = 100 MPa (tensile), σ_y = 0 and the shear stress is 30 MPa. The major principal stress is:
questions.solution:
**108.3 MPa.**

**The principal stress relation:**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ²]**

**The computation:**

> **Mean stress = (100 + 0)/2 = 50 MPa**  ← the CENTRE of the Mohr circle

> **Radius = √[(50)² + (30)²] = √(2500 + 900) = √3400 = 58.31 MPa**

> **σ₁ = 50 + 58.31 = 108.31 MPa** ✓

> **σ₂ = 50 − 58.31 = −8.31 MPa** (compressive)

**The Mohr circle reading, which makes the arithmetic transparent:**

| Feature of the circle | Value here |
|---|---|
| **CENTRE** | **(σ_x + σ_y)/2 = 50 MPa on the σ axis** |
| **RADIUS** | **√[((σ_x−σ_y)/2)² + τ²] = 58.31 MPa** |
| **σ₁ (major principal stress)** | **Centre + radius = 108.31 MPa** ← |
| **σ₂ (minor principal stress)** | **Centre − radius = −8.31 MPa** |
| **MAXIMUM SHEAR STRESS** | **The RADIUS itself = 58.31 MPa** |

> **Option (c) 58.3 MPa is the RADIUS — that is, the maximum shear stress — offered as the major principal stress. A well-made distractor, since it is a real and important quantity from the same calculation.**

> **Option (b) 100 MPa is σ_x itself, the answer if the shear were zero.**

> **Option (d) 130 MPa is σ_x + τ, an incorrect direct addition.**

**Three results worth noticing in the answer:**

> **FIRST — σ₁ = 108.3 EXCEEDS σ_x = 100. The presence of shear RAISES the maximum normal stress above either applied normal stress.**

> **That is why a member under combined bending and torsion is more severely stressed than either action alone would suggest, and it is the whole reason principal stresses are computed rather than the applied stresses being used directly.**

> **SECOND — σ₂ is NEGATIVE (−8.31 MPa), that is COMPRESSIVE, even though neither applied normal stress is compressive.**

> **Shear alone produces tension on one diagonal and compression on the other, so a state with shear always has principal stresses of opposite tendency pushed apart from the mean.**

> **THIRD — τ_max = 58.31 MPa exceeds the applied shear of 30 MPa.**

> **The maximum shear stress occurs on planes at 45° to the principal planes, and it equals (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = (108.31 + 8.31)/2 = 58.31** ✓

> **So all three of the important quantities are LARGER than the applied values, which is the reason this transformation matters: the applied stresses on the chosen axes are not the worst the material experiences.**

**The ORIENTATION of the principal planes:**

> **tan 2θ = 2τ / (σ_x − σ_y) = 60/100 = 0.6**

> **2θ = 30.96°, so θ = 15.48°**

> **The major principal plane's normal is inclined at 15.5° to the x axis, and the other principal plane is at 90° to it (105.5°).**

> **And the planes of maximum shear are at 45° to those, that is at 60.5° and 150.5°.**

> **Note that on the Mohr circle the angle is 2θ — angles on the circle are DOUBLE the physical angles — which is the single most common source of error in reading a Mohr circle.**

**Why principal stresses matter — the failure theories that use them:**

| Theory | Failure criterion | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **RANKINE (maximum principal stress)** | **σ₁ reaches the yield stress** | **BRITTLE materials — cast iron, concrete, masonry** ← |
| **TRESCA (maximum shear stress)** | **τ_max = (σ₁−σ₂)/2 reaches half the yield stress** | **DUCTILE materials; simple and conservative** |
| **VON MISES (maximum distortion energy)** | **√(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) reaches the yield stress** | **DUCTILE metals — the most accurate, and standard in steel design** ← |
| **Saint-Venant (maximum principal strain)** | ε₁ reaches the yield strain | Little used |
| **Haigh (total strain energy)** | Total strain energy criterion | Superseded by von Mises |

> **Checking this stress state against the two principal theories, for a material of yield stress 250 MPa:**

> **TRESCA:  2 τ_max = 2 × 58.31 = 116.6 MPa against 250 — safe, with a factor of 2.14**

> **VON MISES:  √(108.31² − 108.31(−8.31) + (−8.31)²) = √(11731 + 900 + 69) = √12700 = 112.7 MPa against 250 — safe, factor 2.22**

> **The two agree closely here, and TRESCA gives the more conservative result — which it always does, being an inscribed hexagon within the von Mises ellipse.**

> **That is worth knowing as a general relation: TRESCA IS ALWAYS CONSERVATIVE RELATIVE TO VON MISES, by at most about 15 per cent (which occurs in pure shear).**

> **So using Tresca is never unsafe relative to von Mises, and it is simpler — which is why it survives in design codes despite von Mises being the better description of real ductile yielding.**

> **And the RANKINE theory's place in the table matters for civil engineering specifically: for CONCRETE and MASONRY, which fail in tension in a brittle manner, the maximum PRINCIPAL TENSILE STRESS is the relevant criterion — which is why diagonal tension governs shear failure in a concrete beam, and why the cracks appear perpendicular to σ₁.**

examTip.trick: **Centre = (σ_x+σ_y)/2 = 50; radius = √(50² + 30²) = 58.31; σ₁ = 50 + 58.31 = 108.3 MPa.** Read it as a circle and the arithmetic is transparent.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 58.3 is the RADIUS — the maximum SHEAR stress** — offered as the major principal stress. Both come from the same calculation, so read which is asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear RAISES σ₁ above either applied normal stress (108 > 100) and pushes σ₂ into COMPRESSION (−8.3), even with no compressive load applied.** That is why principal stresses are computed at all. And angles on the Mohr circle are DOUBLE the physical angles.

questions.stem: A steel bar is fully restrained at both ends and its temperature rises by 25 °C. Taking E = 200 GPa and α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, the thermal stress induced is:
questions.solution:
**60 MPa (compressive).**

**The relation:**

> **σ = E α ΔT**

**The computation:**

> **σ = 200,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 25**

> **= 200,000 × 3 × 10⁻⁴**

> **= 60 N/mm² = 60 MPa** ✓

> **Working in N and mm as always: E = 200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm².**

**The reasoning behind the formula — worth following, because it explains what is and is not present:**

> **If the bar were FREE, heating it would produce a strain with no stress at all:**

> **ε_free = α ΔT = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 3 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.03 %**

> **The bar is instead FULLY RESTRAINED, so that free expansion is entirely PREVENTED.**

> **Preventing a strain of 3 × 10⁻⁴ requires an equal and opposite MECHANICAL strain, which by Hooke's law demands a stress:**

> **σ = E ε = 200,000 × 3 × 10⁻⁴ = 60 MPa** ✓

> **The stress is COMPRESSIVE, because the bar wants to lengthen and the restraint pushes back.**

> **Note the two crucial features of the result:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The LENGTH of the bar does NOT appear** | **A 1 m bar and a 100 m bar develop the SAME thermal stress** ← |
| **The cross-sectional AREA does not appear either** | The stress is independent of the section |
| **Only E, α and ΔT matter** | Material properties and the temperature change |

> **The FIRST is the striking one and it has real consequences: a long member is no more susceptible to thermal STRESS than a short one, though its thermal MOVEMENT is proportionally greater.**

> **So a long bridge deck does not develop higher thermal stress than a short one — it develops a larger MOVEMENT, which is why long structures need expansion joints rather than thicker sections.**

**Why 60 MPa is a significant stress:**

> **For Fe 415 steel with a design yield of 0.87 × 415 = 361 MPa, 60 MPa is about 17 per cent of the capacity — consumed by a 25 °C temperature change alone, with no load applied.**

> **And 25 °C is a modest range: a steel member exposed to the sun can vary by 40 to 50 °C over a day, giving 96 to 120 MPa.**

> **So thermal stress in a fully restrained member is comparable with the stress from the working loads, and it cannot be neglected.**

> **That is why the ordinary practice is NOT to restrain members but to allow them to move:**

| Provision | Application |
|---|---|
| **EXPANSION JOINTS in a structure** | **IS 456 requires them at intervals not exceeding 45 m in a concrete building** ← |
| **Bridge BEARINGS — one fixed, the others sliding** | **Only ONE end is restrained; the rest are free to move** ← |
| **Rail EXPANSION gaps (in jointed track)** | Classical practice |
| **Expansion joints and loops in pipelines** | Between anchor blocks |
| **Sliding joints in long walls and pavements** | Contraction joints in concrete pavement |

> **The BRIDGE BEARING arrangement is the clearest illustration of the principle: a bridge deck is restrained at ONE pier only, and every other support carries a sliding or elastomeric bearing.**

> **So the deck is free to expand and contract, developing NO thermal stress — and the horizontal thermal FORCE that a full restraint would generate is avoided entirely.**

> **If every pier were fixed, the deck would push the piers apart with the enormous force σ × A, and either the deck would buckle or the piers would fail.**

> **Which is exactly what happens to CONTINUOUSLY WELDED RAIL in extreme heat: the rail is fully restrained by the sleepers and ballast, the compressive stress builds, and when it exceeds the track's lateral resistance the rail BUCKLES sideways — a "sun kink", and a derailment hazard.**

> **The remedy there is to lay the rail at a controlled STRESS-FREE TEMPERATURE near the middle of the expected range, so that neither the summer compression nor the winter tension reaches a dangerous value.**

**The PARTIALLY restrained case, since full restraint is an idealisation:**

> **If the supports yield by an amount δ, the prevented strain is reduced:**

> **σ = E (α ΔT L − δ)/L = E α ΔT − E δ/L**

> **So even a small yielding of the restraint relieves a great deal of stress.**

> **For this bar, if it were 2 m long and the supports yielded 0.2 mm:**

> **Free expansion = 3 × 10⁻⁴ × 2000 = 0.6 mm; prevented = 0.6 − 0.2 = 0.4 mm**

> **σ = 200,000 × 0.4/2000 = 40 MPa** — a third less than the fully restrained value.

> **That sensitivity is worth understanding because it cuts both ways: a nominally "fixed" support that yields slightly gives useful relief, and a design that assumes such relief must be sure the yielding will actually occur.**

> **And it explains why thermal stresses in real structures are usually LOWER than a fully restrained calculation predicts — real supports, joints and connections all yield a little — while remaining large enough to matter.**

**The coefficients of thermal expansion worth having:**

| Material | α (per °C) |
|---|---|
| **STEEL** | **12 × 10⁻⁶** |
| **CONCRETE** | **10-14 × 10⁻⁶** ← |
| **Aluminium** | **23 × 10⁻⁶** |
| **Brick masonry** | **5-7 × 10⁻⁶** |
| **Timber (along the grain)** | **3-5 × 10⁻⁶** |
| **Glass** | **9 × 10⁻⁶** |

> **The CONCRETE and STEEL match — both about 12 × 10⁻⁶ — is one of the fortunate accidents on which reinforced concrete depends.**

> **Because the two materials expand and contract almost equally, a temperature change produces almost no differential movement between them, and hence almost no stress at the bond.**

> **Had the coefficients differed substantially, every temperature cycle would work the bond loose and reinforced concrete would be impossible as a composite material.**

> **That coincidence, together with concrete's alkalinity protecting the steel from corrosion, is why the combination works at all — and both are worth appreciating rather than taking for granted.**

examTip.trick: **σ = EαΔT = 200,000 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 25 = 60 MPa**, compressive. Work in N and mm.
examTip.trap: **Neither the LENGTH nor the AREA appears** — a 1 m bar and a 100 m bar develop the SAME thermal stress. A long structure needs expansion JOINTS, not a thicker section.
examTip.mnemonic: **60 MPa is 17 % of Fe 415's design capacity from a 25 °C change alone** — which is why bridges are fixed at ONE pier only and every other bearing slides. Fully restrained rail buckles in heat: the "sun kink".

questions.stem: In a rectangular beam section subjected to transverse shear, the maximum shear stress is:
options: Equal to the average shear stress
questions.solution:
**1.5 times the average shear stress, and it occurs at the NEUTRAL AXIS.**

**The shear stress distribution:**

> **τ = V A ȳ / (I b)**

> **For a rectangular section of width b and depth d, evaluating at a distance y from the neutral axis gives:**

> **τ = (6V/(bd³)) × (d²/4 − y²)**

> **which is a PARABOLA in y:**

| Position | Shear stress |
|---|---|
| **At the NEUTRAL AXIS (y = 0)** | **τ_max = 3V/(2bd) = 1.5 × V/(bd)** ← |
| **At the extreme fibres (y = ±d/2)** | **ZERO** |
| **Average over the section** | **V/(bd)** |

> **So τ_max / τ_avg = 1.5** ✓

**Why the shear stress is ZERO at the extreme fibres — the reason is worth knowing:**

> **The top and bottom surfaces of a beam are FREE surfaces, carrying no applied shear.**

> **By the complementary shear stress principle, a shear stress on one plane requires an equal shear stress on the perpendicular plane.**

> **Since there is no shear on the horizontal free surface, there can be none on the vertical plane at that level either.**

> **So the shear stress MUST vanish at the top and bottom, and it is maximum where the bending stress is zero — at the neutral axis.**

> **The two stresses are therefore in COMPLEMENTARY distribution:**

| At the section | BENDING stress | SHEAR stress |
|---|---|---|
| **Extreme fibres** | **MAXIMUM** | **ZERO** |
| **Neutral axis** | **ZERO** | **MAXIMUM** ← |

> **Which is a fortunate arrangement: neither location suffers both stresses at once, so a simple check of each separately is usually adequate.**

> **It is at INTERMEDIATE levels that both act together, and where a principal-stress check would be needed if the two were of comparable magnitude — which in a slender beam they are not.**

**The shape factors for other sections, since 1.5 is one of a family:**

| Section | τ_max / τ_avg | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE** | **1.5** ← |
| **CIRCLE (solid)** | **4/3 = 1.333** | Option (d) — a real value for a different shape |
| **Thin-walled circular TUBE** | **2.0** | Option (c) — likewise |
| **Triangle** | **1.5** | Same as a rectangle |
| **I-SECTION** | **Roughly 1.1-1.2 based on the WEB area** | **Nearly uniform in the web** ← |
| **Diamond (square on its diagonal)** | 1.125 | — |

> **Every distractor in this question is a genuine shape factor for a different section, which makes the option set well formed.**

> **The I-SECTION entry is the practically important one: because the web is thin and the flanges are far from the neutral axis, the shear is carried almost entirely by the WEB and is nearly UNIFORM across it.**

> **That is why steel design simply takes τ = V/(web area) for an I-section, with no shape factor — the approximation is close enough and it is conservative in the right places.**

> **And it is why the FLANGES carry almost no shear while carrying nearly all the bending: the I-section separates the two functions, web for shear and flanges for moment, which is the whole logic of its shape.**

**Why the shear check rarely governs a beam's design — with an important exception:**

> **For a slender beam the bending stress dominates. Consider a rectangular beam of span L carrying a UDL w:**

> **σ_max = (wL²/8)/(bd²/6) = 0.75 wL²/(bd²)**

> **τ_max = 1.5 × (wL/2)/(bd) = 0.75 wL/(bd)**

> **Ratio σ/τ = L/d**

> **So for a beam of span-to-depth ratio 15 — an ordinary beam — the bending stress is FIFTEEN TIMES the shear stress.**

> **That is why bending governs slender beams and why the shear check is usually a formality.**

> **But the ratio is L/d, so for a DEEP or SHORT-SPAN member the shear stress becomes comparable:**

| L/d | σ/τ | Governing action |
|---|---|---|
| **20** | **20** | **Bending, decisively** |
| **10** | **10** | Bending |
| **4** | **4** | Shear becoming significant |
| **2 or less** | **2** | **SHEAR governs; the member is a DEEP BEAM and ordinary flexure theory no longer applies** ← |

> **So the exception matters: a DEEP BEAM, a CORBEL, a PILE CAP or a short SHEAR WALL is governed by shear, and its behaviour is not described by the flexure formula at all.**

> **Such members are designed by STRUT-AND-TIE modelling, in which the load path is idealised as a truss of concrete compression struts and steel ties — a quite different method, and the correct one when the member is too deep for beam theory.**

**And the practical consequence for TIMBER, where shear does govern:**

> **Timber's shear strength PARALLEL TO THE GRAIN is very low — perhaps 1/15 to 1/20 of its bending strength along the grain.**

> **So for timber the ratio of allowable stresses works against it, and HORIZONTAL SHEAR frequently governs a timber beam's design where it would not govern a steel or concrete one.**

> **The failure appears as a longitudinal split along the grain at the neutral axis near the supports — which is exactly where this analysis predicts the maximum shear stress to be.**

> **That is a satisfying confirmation of the theory from a failure mode that can be seen, and it is why timber beams are checked for shear as a matter of course rather than as a formality.**

examTip.trick: **Rectangular section: τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg, at the NEUTRAL AXIS.** The distribution is parabolic, zero at the extreme fibres.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor is a real shape factor: 4/3 for a solid circle, 2.0 for a thin tube, 1.0 for none of them.** Match the section named in the stem.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ/τ = L/d for a UDL, so bending governs a slender beam by a factor of 15 or more** — but SHEAR governs a DEEP beam (L/d ≤ 2), which needs strut-and-tie modelling, not flexure theory. And shear governs TIMBER beams routinely, splitting them along the grain.

questions.stem: A column 3 m long is hinged at both ends and has E = 200 GPa and I = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Its Euler crippling load is:
questions.solution:
**About 877 kN.**

**Euler's formula:**

> **P_cr = π² E I / L_e²**

> **For a column HINGED AT BOTH ENDS, L_e = L = 3000 mm.**

**The computation, in N and mm:**

> **P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 4 × 10⁶ / 3000²**

> **= 9.8696 × 8 × 10¹¹ / 9 × 10⁶**

> **= 7.8957 × 10¹² / 9 × 10⁶**

> **= 877,300 N = 877 kN** ✓

> **The intermediate EI = 200,000 × 4 × 10⁶ = 8 × 10¹¹ N·mm² is worth writing down as its own step, since it is the quantity the formula actually needs.**

**Why the distractors are placed as they are — each is another end condition:**

| Option | Corresponds to |
|---|---|
| **(a) 219 kN** | **P_cr/4 — the FIXED-FREE case, L_e = 2L** |
| **(b) 439 kN** | **P_cr/2 — roughly the FIXED-HINGED case, L_e = 0.707L, which actually gives 2P_cr; 439 is P_cr/2** |
| **(c) 877 kN** | ✓ **HINGED-HINGED, L_e = L** |
| **(d) 1755 kN** | **2 P_cr — near the FIXED-HINGED value of 1755 kN** |

> **So the option set spans the range of end conditions, and reading "hinged at both ends" is what selects the answer.**

> **The full set for this column:**

| End condition | L_e | P_cr |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L = 1500 mm** | **3509 kN** |
| **Fixed-hinged** | **0.707 L = 2121 mm** | **1755 kN** |
| **Both ends HINGED** | **L = 3000 mm** | **877 kN** ← |
| **Fixed-free** | **2 L = 6000 mm** | **219 kN** |

> **The range is 16 to 1 across the four cases, which is the point made earlier about end restraint being the cheapest improvement available to a compression member.**

**The essential caution — IS EULER'S FORMULA EVEN APPLICABLE HERE?**

> **Euler's formula describes ELASTIC buckling and is valid only for a SLENDER column. It must be checked.**

> **The check is on the slenderness ratio, so the radius of gyration is needed. Taking a section with A = 2000 mm² for illustration:**

> **r = √(I/A) = √(4 × 10⁶/2000) = √2000 = 44.7 mm**

> **λ = L_e/r = 3000/44.7 = 67**

> **And the Euler stress: σ_cr = P_cr/A = 877,300/2000 = 439 MPa**

> **That EXCEEDS the yield stress of ordinary steel (250 MPa) — which means the column would YIELD before it buckled elastically, and Euler's formula does NOT apply.**

> **That is a genuinely important check and it is the commonest omission in this class of problem:**

| Condition | Governing behaviour |
|---|---|
| **σ_cr (Euler) < yield stress** | **ELASTIC buckling — Euler's formula is valid** |
| **σ_cr (Euler) > yield stress** | **The column YIELDS first — Euler's formula gives a meaningless answer, larger than the section can carry** ← |

> **The boundary is the CRITICAL SLENDERNESS RATIO, at which the Euler stress equals the yield stress:**

> **λ_critical = π √(E/σ_y) = π √(200,000/250) = π × 28.3 = 88.9**

> **So for mild steel, Euler's formula applies only for λ > about 89, and this column at λ = 67 is in the INTERMEDIATE range where neither pure yielding nor pure elastic buckling governs.**

> **The question asks for the EULER crippling load, so 877 kN is the correct answer to the question posed — and it is worth knowing that the column's actual capacity would be less, governed by inelastic buckling.**

**The formulae for the intermediate range, since that is where real columns mostly sit:**

| Formula | Expression | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **EULER** | **π²EI/L_e²** | **Valid only for λ above the critical value** |
| **RANKINE-GORDON** | **P = σ_c A/(1 + a λ²)** | **Empirical; approaches the crushing load for short columns and Euler's for long ones — covers the WHOLE range** ← |
| **PERRY-ROBERTSON** | Based on an assumed initial curvature | **The basis of IS 800 and BS design curves** |
| **Johnson's parabolic** | A parabola fitted below the Euler curve | Used in some codes |
| **Straight line (Tetmajer)** | A straight line in the intermediate range | Simple |

> **The RANKINE-GORDON formula's structure is worth understanding, because it is elegantly constructed to work at both extremes:**

> **1/P_Rankine = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler**

> **For a SHORT column, P_Euler is enormous so its reciprocal vanishes, and P_Rankine → P_crushing.**

> **For a LONG column, P_crushing is the larger, so P_Rankine → P_Euler.**

> **And in between it gives a smooth transition, always BELOW both — which is physically right, since a real column suffers from both effects at once.**

> **That reciprocal-addition structure is a general device for combining two limiting behaviours, and it appears elsewhere in engineering for the same reason.**

**And the honest limitations of Euler's formula, all of which matter:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **The column is PERFECTLY STRAIGHT** | **Real columns have an initial bow, which starts the bending immediately** ← |
| **The load is applied EXACTLY at the centroid** | **Real loads are eccentric; codes require a MINIMUM eccentricity to be assumed** ← |
| **The material is homogeneous and perfectly elastic** | Residual stresses from rolling and welding exist |
| **The section is uniform** | Often true |
| **The end conditions are ideal** | Never exactly |

> **The first two are why real column capacities fall BELOW the Euler value even when λ is large, and why the PERRY-ROBERTSON approach — which builds an assumed initial curvature into the analysis — became the basis of modern design curves.**

> **So Euler's formula is the theoretical anchor of column design and not the design equation itself, which is a useful thing to be clear about: it tells you the mechanism and the code tells you the capacity.**

examTip.trick: **P_cr = π²EI/L_e² with L_e = L for hinged-hinged: π² × 8×10¹¹/9×10⁶ = 877 kN.** Write EI = 8 × 10¹¹ N·mm² as its own step.
examTip.trap: **Every distractor corresponds to another end condition** — 219 kN fixed-free, 1755 kN fixed-hinged, 3509 kN fixed-fixed. Reading the end condition selects the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always check whether Euler even APPLIES: λ_critical = π√(E/σ_y) = 89 for mild steel.** Below that the column yields first and Euler's answer exceeds what the section can carry. Rankine-Gordon covers the whole range: 1/P = 1/P_crush + 1/P_Euler.

questions.stem: At an UNLOADED joint of a pin-jointed truss where only TWO non-collinear members meet, the forces in those members are:
options: Equal and opposite in the two members
Each equal to the nearest support reaction
questions.solution:
**ZERO in both members.**

**The proof, in two lines:**

> **At a pin joint the member forces are CONCURRENT, so two equations of equilibrium apply: ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.**

> **Resolve PERPENDICULAR to one member. Only the OTHER member has a component in that direction — and since the members are NOT collinear, that component is non-zero.**

> **So that member's force must be ZERO.**

> **Now resolve along the first member: only it remains, so its force must be zero too.**

> **Both forces are zero.** ✓

> **The NON-COLLINEAR condition is essential: if the two members were in a straight line, resolving perpendicular to them would give 0 = 0 and prove nothing — the two forces would simply be equal and opposite, which is option (b) and is the correct answer for the COLLINEAR case.**

**The ZERO-FORCE MEMBER rules, which this is the first of:**

| Situation | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| **TWO non-collinear members at an UNLOADED joint** | **BOTH are zero-force members** ← |
| **THREE members at an unloaded joint, TWO of them COLLINEAR** | **The THIRD (non-collinear) member is a zero-force member; the two collinear ones carry equal forces** ← |
| **Two members at an unloaded joint, COLLINEAR** | **Equal and opposite forces — NOT zero** |
| **A joint with a load acting ALONG one member** | That member carries the load; the rule may still apply to others |

> **The SECOND rule is the one most used in practice, and it is worth stating with its proof: at a joint with three members, two of them in a straight line, resolve PERPENDICULAR to the collinear pair.**

> **The collinear members have no component in that direction, so the third member's force must be zero.**

> **Those two rules together can eliminate a surprising number of members from a truss before any calculation begins — often a third of them in a typical roof truss.**

**Why zero-force members exist at all, since they appear to be useless:**

> **A member carrying no force under a given loading is not pointless, and the reasons are worth knowing:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It carries force under a DIFFERENT load case** | **A member zero under symmetric load may be heavily loaded under wind on one side, or under unsymmetrical live load** ← |
| **It provides LATERAL SUPPORT, reducing another member's effective length** | **A long compression chord braced at intervals by "zero-force" members has a much higher buckling capacity** ← |
| **It maintains the truss's GEOMETRY and stability** | Without it the truss may be a mechanism |
| **It carries the member's own self-weight and any local load** | — |
| **It is needed for the determinacy count** | m + r = 2j |

> **The SECOND reason is the most important in practice and the most often overlooked: a member with no axial force still holds the joint it connects to in position.**

> **A top chord in compression, braced at midlength by a vertical carrying zero force, has its effective length HALVED — and hence FOUR TIMES the buckling capacity.**

> **So removing a zero-force member from a truss because "it carries nothing" can cause the truss to fail by buckling of a member that had been relying on it.**

> **That is a documented error and a good illustration of the difference between an axial force analysis and a real structure: the analysis reports the member's force, not its function.**

**The METHOD OF JOINTS, since this rule is part of it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Find the SUPPORT REACTIONS from overall equilibrium** |
| **2** | **Identify ZERO-FORCE members by inspection, using the rules above** ← |
| **3** | **Start at a joint with NOT MORE THAN TWO unknown member forces** |
| **4** | **Apply ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 at that joint — two equations, two unknowns** |
| **5** | **Move to the next joint that now has only two unknowns, and repeat** |
| **6** | **Check at the last joint: its equations should be satisfied automatically** ← |

> **Step 3 is the practical constraint: the method can only start where two unknowns remain, so the ORDER of joints is dictated by the truss's geometry rather than chosen freely.**

> **And step 6 is the check that validates the whole solution: by the time the last joint is reached, all its member forces are known, so its two equilibrium equations must balance of their own accord.**

> **If they do not, an error has been made earlier — and the check costs nothing.**

**The METHOD OF SECTIONS, for contrast, since the two are complementary:**

| | **Method of JOINTS** | **Method of SECTIONS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cuts** | **Around one joint at a time** | **Right THROUGH the truss, dividing it in two** |
| **Equations available** | **TWO per joint (concurrent forces)** | **THREE for the whole free body (ΣF_x, ΣF_y, ΣM)** ← |
| **Unknowns solvable at once** | **Two** | **THREE** |
| **Best for** | **ALL member forces** | **A FEW SPECIFIC members, deep inside the truss** ← |
| **Requires working through the truss?** | **YES, joint by joint from an end** | **NO — a single cut reaches any member directly** ← |

> **The last row is the decisive advantage of the method of sections: to find the force in one diagonal at the middle of a large truss, the method of joints requires working through every joint from an end, while a single section reaches it immediately.**

> **And the MOMENT equation is what makes it powerful: taking moments about the point where two of the three cut members intersect eliminates both of them, giving the third directly in ONE equation.**

> **Choosing that moment centre well is the whole skill of the method, and it turns a three-unknown problem into a one-line calculation.**

> **So the practical approach to any truss is to use both: sections to reach a particular member quickly, and joints to sweep through the whole truss systematically — with the zero-force rules applied first to reduce the work in either case.**

examTip.trick: **Resolve PERPENDICULAR to one member: only the other has a component there, so it must be zero — then the first follows.** Both are zero-force members.
examTip.trap: **The NON-COLLINEAR condition is essential.** If the two members were in a straight line, the forces would be EQUAL AND OPPOSITE, not zero — which is option (b), correct for that case.
examTip.mnemonic: **A zero-force member is not useless: it BRACES the compression chord.** Removing one because "it carries nothing" doubles the effective length of the member relying on it and quarters its buckling capacity — a documented error.

questions.stem: A three-hinged SEMICIRCULAR arch of radius R carries a point load of 100 kN at its crown. The horizontal thrust at each support is:
questions.solution:
**50 kN.**

**Step 1 — the vertical reactions, by symmetry:**

> **V_A = V_B = W/2 = 100/2 = 50 kN**

**Step 2 — take moments about the CROWN HINGE for the LEFT half:**

> **For a SEMICIRCULAR arch, the span L = 2R and the central rise h = R.**

> **The left support is a horizontal distance R from the crown and a vertical distance R below it.**

| Force on the left half | Lever arm about the crown | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **V_A = 50 kN (upward at A)** | **R (horizontal)** | **50 R** |
| **H (horizontal at A)** | **R (vertical)** | **H × R** |
| **The 100 kN load** | **Applied AT the crown, so ZERO lever arm** | **0** ← |

> **ΣM_crown = 0:  50 R − H R = 0**

> **H = 50 kN** ✓

**Why the load contributes nothing to the moment equation:**

> **The load acts AT the crown, which is the point about which moments are being taken — so its lever arm is zero.**

> **That is what makes this problem a one-liner, and it is the same feature exploited in the internal-hinge beam problem: a force acting THROUGH the moment centre drops out.**

> **So the equation reduces to V_A × R = H × R, and since the two lever arms are EQUAL for a semicircular arch (both R), the result is simply H = V_A = W/2.**

> **That equality of lever arms is specific to the SEMICIRCULAR case, where the rise equals the half-span — and it is why the answer comes out so neatly.**

**The general result, for comparison:**

> **For a three-hinged arch of span L and rise h with a point load W at the crown:**

> **H = W L / (4 h)**

> **For a semicircular arch, L = 2R and h = R, so H = W(2R)/(4R) = W/2** ✓

> **And the general form shows the dependence: H is INVERSELY proportional to the rise, as always.**

| Arch shape | L/h | H for W = 100 kN |
|---|---|---|
| **Semicircular** | **2** | **50 kN** ← |
| **Rise = quarter span** | **4** | **100 kN** |
