| **Rise = one eighth of span** | **8** | **200 kN** |
| **Rise = span/16** | **16** | **400 kN** |

> **Options (a) 100 kN and (c) 200 kN are the answers for rise-to-span ratios of 1/4 and 1/8 — flatter arches — so the option set punishes a misread geometry.**

> **And the pattern confirms the general rule: a FLAT arch generates a LARGE thrust, and a semicircular arch — the tallest practical shape — generates the smallest.**

**Why a semicircular arch is NOT structurally ideal, despite its low thrust:**

> **The semicircle is the classical Roman form and it has a low thrust, which seems entirely favourable.**

> **But the circle is NOT the FUNICULAR shape for any common loading, so a semicircular arch carries BENDING MOMENT as well as thrust:**

| Arch shape | Funicular for | Bending under that load |
|---|---|---|
| **PARABOLA** | **A UNIFORM load per unit HORIZONTAL length** | **ZERO** ← |
| **CATENARY** | **A uniform load per unit length ALONG THE ARCH — that is, self-weight** | **ZERO** ← |
| **CIRCLE (semicircular)** | **A radial pressure load, which rarely occurs** | **Real bending under gravity load** |

> **So a semicircular arch under its own weight or a deck load develops bending moments, and it needs a section deep enough to carry them.**

> **The CATENARY is the shape a hanging chain takes under its own weight, and inverted it carries its own weight in pure compression — which is why it is the ideal form for a self-weight-dominated masonry arch.**

> **And the PARABOLA suits a load uniform per horizontal metre, such as a deck with fill above it — which is why parabolic arches are used for bridges.**

> **The practical distinction: for a THIN arch where self-weight dominates, use a catenary; for an arch carrying a level deck on fill, a parabola.**

> **The semicircle persists because it is easy to set out with a compass and because a masonry arch of adequate thickness can accommodate the bending — the thickness being what Roman arches have in abundance.**

**The LINE OF THRUST, which is the concept unifying all of this:**

> **The LINE OF THRUST is the locus of the points through which the resultant compressive force passes at each section of the arch.**

| Condition | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The line of thrust COINCIDES with the arch axis** | **PURE COMPRESSION, no bending — the funicular condition** ← |
| **The line of thrust departs from the axis by e** | **A bending moment M = H × e is generated** |
| **The line of thrust leaves the arch's THICKNESS entirely** | **A HINGE forms at that section — the arch cracks** ← |
| **Enough hinges form to make a mechanism (usually four)** | **COLLAPSE** |

> **The THIRD row is the criterion for a MASONRY arch, and it is the basis of the classical middle-third rule and of modern limit analysis:**

> **Masonry cannot carry tension, so the arch remains sound as long as the line of thrust stays WITHIN the masonry.**

> **HEYMAN'S SAFE THEOREM states it precisely: if ANY line of thrust can be found that lies entirely within the arch and is in equilibrium with the loads, the arch is SAFE.**

> **That is a remarkably useful result, because it means an arch need not be analysed exactly — it suffices to demonstrate that ONE admissible thrust line exists.**

> **And it explains why old masonry arches, cracked and deformed as they often are, continue to stand: the cracking has merely relocated the thrust line into a position the arch can accommodate, and the structure has found its own equilibrium.**

> **Which is a genuinely reassuring piece of theory, and it is why masonry arch bridges built for horse traffic still carry lorries.**

examTip.trick: **Take moments about the CROWN HINGE for one half. The load acts AT the crown, so its lever arm is ZERO** — leaving 50R = HR, hence H = 50 kN. For a semicircle the two lever arms are both R.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (c) are the answers for FLATTER arches (rise = L/4 and L/8).** H = WL/(4h) is inversely proportional to the rise, so a misread geometry is a large error.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CIRCLE is not the funicular shape for gravity load, so a semicircular arch carries real BENDING** — a CATENARY suits self-weight, a PARABOLA suits a uniform horizontal load. And Heyman's safe theorem: if ANY thrust line fits inside the masonry, the arch is safe.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam of span L traversed by a single concentrated rolling load W, the absolute maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**W L / 4, occurring when the load is at MIDSPAN.**

**The reasoning:**

> **For a single point load W at a distance x from the left support of a simply supported span L, the bending moment UNDER THE LOAD is:**

> **M = W x (L − x) / L**

> **That expression is maximised when x(L − x) is maximised, which occurs at x = L/2:**

> **M_max = W (L/2)(L/2)/L = W L/4** ✓

> **So the absolute maximum moment occurs with the load at midspan, and equals WL/4 — the familiar static result.**

**Why the answer is so simple for a SINGLE load, and why it is not for several:**

> **With ONE load, the critical position is obvious by symmetry, and the maximum moment is the same as for a statically placed central load.**

> **With TWO OR MORE loads the problem becomes genuinely interesting, because the loads cannot all be at midspan at once:**

| Load system | Absolute maximum moment position |
|---|---|
| **A single load W** | **At MIDSPAN; M = WL/4** ← |
| **A UDL longer than the span** | **Load covering the whole span; M = wL²/8 at midspan** |
| **A UDL shorter than the span** | **Positioned so the section divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span** |
| **TWO or more point loads** | **When the resultant of the loads on the span is at a specific position — see the rule below** ← |
| **A train of loads** | Determined by trial, using the criterion below |

> **The rule for a SYSTEM of point loads is worth knowing, because it is not obvious:**

> **THE ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM MOMENT OCCURS UNDER ONE OF THE LOADS, AT A SECTION SUCH THAT THE LOAD AND THE RESULTANT OF ALL LOADS ON THE SPAN ARE EQUIDISTANT FROM MIDSPAN.**

> **Equivalently: place the system so that the midspan bisects the distance between the chosen load and the resultant.**

> **Which load to choose is settled by trial — usually the heaviest, or the one nearest the resultant — and the criterion for whether a load should be on the span at all is:**

> **THE MAXIMUM MOMENT OCCURS WHEN THE AVERAGE LOAD TO THE LEFT OF THE SECTION EQUALS THE AVERAGE LOAD TO THE RIGHT.**

> **That is the general criterion for maximum bending moment under a rolling load system, and it reduces to "load at midspan" for a single load.**

**The related maxima, since a rolling load produces several:**

| Quantity | Critical position of a single load W | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute maximum BENDING MOMENT** | **At MIDSPAN** | **WL/4** ← |
| **Absolute maximum SHEAR FORCE** | **At a SUPPORT (as close to it as possible)** | **W** ← |
| **Maximum moment at a GIVEN section x** | **Load AT that section** | **Wx(L−x)/L** |
| **Maximum shear at a given section x** | **Load just at the section, on the side giving the larger reaction** | **W(L−x)/L** |

> **The SHEAR result is worth noting: the maximum shear from a rolling load is the FULL LOAD W, occurring when the load sits directly over a support.**

> **And note the important distinction between the last two rows and the first two: the maximum at a GIVEN SECTION is a different question from the ABSOLUTE maximum anywhere on the beam, and a design must consider both.**

> **A beam is designed for the ABSOLUTE maximum moment at the critical section, but the reinforcement or the flange plates are CURTAILED according to the ENVELOPE of maximum moments at every section — which is a different and larger curve than the moment diagram for any single load position.**

**The INFLUENCE LINE, which is the systematic tool for all of this:**

> **An INFLUENCE LINE shows how a particular RESPONSE (a reaction, a shear, a moment at one chosen section) varies as a UNIT LOAD moves across the structure.**

> **The crucial distinction, and the one most often confused:**

| | **BENDING MOMENT DIAGRAM** | **INFLUENCE LINE for moment** |
|---|---|---|
| **Shows** | **The moment at EVERY section, for a FIXED load position** | **The moment at ONE section, for EVERY load position** ← |
| **Horizontal axis** | **Position along the beam** | **Position of the LOAD** |
| **Used for** | Designing a beam under known static loads | **Finding the WORST position of a moving load** ← |

> **The two diagrams can look identical — for a simply supported beam both are triangular — which is precisely why they are confused.**

> **The influence line for the moment at midspan of a simply supported span is a triangle with an ordinate of L/4 at midspan, and reading it gives WL/4 directly for a unit load times W** ✓

> **The great advantage of an influence line is that once drawn, it answers the question for ANY load system:**

| Load system | Response from the influence line |
|---|---|
| **A single load W at a point** | **W × (the ordinate at that point)** |
| **Several point loads** | **Σ(W_i × ordinate_i)** |
| **A UDL of intensity w over a length** | **w × (the AREA under the influence line over that length)** ← |

> **The UDL rule is the most useful: the response is the load intensity times the AREA of the influence line, so placing a UDL to maximise a response means covering the region of LARGEST AREA — and for shear, covering only the part of the influence line with ONE SIGN.**

> **That last point is worth stating: to maximise the SHEAR at a section, a UDL should cover only the portion of the span where the influence line is POSITIVE (or only the negative portion, for the opposite sign) — because loading both would partly cancel.**

> **Which is why a bridge's design live load is applied in PATTERNS rather than over the whole structure, and why a continuous beam's design moments come from several different loading arrangements rather than one.**

examTip.trick: **M = Wx(L−x)/L is maximised at x = L/2, giving WL/4** — the same as a statically placed central load.
examTip.trap: **Maximum SHEAR from a rolling load is the FULL LOAD W, with the load over a support** — a different critical position from the moment. Both must be considered.
examTip.mnemonic: **An INFLUENCE LINE gives one response for EVERY load position; a moment DIAGRAM gives every response for ONE load position.** They look identical for a simple span, which is why they are confused. For a UDL, the response is w × the AREA under the influence line.

questions.stem: A beam of span 6 m, fixed at both ends, carries a central point load of 40 kN. The bending moment at each fixed end is:
questions.solution:
**30 kNm.**

**The standard result:**

> **For a beam fixed at both ends with a central point load W:**

> **M at each fixed end = W L / 8**

> **= 40 × 6/8 = 30 kNm** ✓

**The complete set of results for this case:**

| Quantity | Expression | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at each support** | **W/2** | **20 kN** |
| **Moment at each FIXED END (hogging)** | **W L/8** | **30 kNm** ← |
| **Moment at MIDSPAN (sagging)** | **W L/8** | **30 kNm** |
| **Points of CONTRAFLEXURE** | **At L/4 from each end** | **1.5 m from each support** |
| **Maximum deflection (at midspan)** | **W L³/(192 EI)** | — |

> **The remarkable feature is that the SUPPORT moment and the MIDSPAN moment are EQUAL in magnitude — both WL/8 — and opposite in sign.**

> **So a fixed-ended beam under a central point load is loaded equally at three sections, and none of them governs over the others.**

> **That is the ideal condition for a symmetrically reinforced or symmetrically shaped member, and it is one reason the case is so often used as a teaching example.**

**Comparison with the simply supported case — the value of fixity:**

| Beam, central point load W | Maximum moment | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **W L/4 = 60 kNm** | **W L³/(48 EI)** |
| **FIXED both ends** | **W L/8 = 30 kNm** | **W L³/(192 EI)** ← |
| **Ratio** | **HALF the moment** | **A QUARTER of the deflection** |

> **So fixing both ends HALVES the maximum moment and reduces the deflection to a QUARTER.**

> **Option (d) 60 kNm is the simply supported value WL/4, which is the designed trap: it is the answer for the same beam without fixity.**

> **And the improvement is obtained purely by RESTRAINING ROTATION at the ends — no extra material in the span, no change of section.**

> **That is why moment connections are worth detailing, and why a continuous frame is so much more efficient than a series of simply supported spans.**

**How the fixing moments arise — the compatibility argument:**

> **The beam has 6 reaction components (3 at each fixed end) and 3 equations of equilibrium, so D_s = 3.**

> **For a symmetric beam under symmetric load, two of those reduce by symmetry, leaving effectively one unknown to solve by compatibility.**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Take the beam as simply supported and apply the load: the ends ROTATE by θ = WL²/16EI** |
| **2** | **The real beam's ends CANNOT rotate — that is what "fixed" means** |
| **3** | **Apply end moments M large enough to rotate the ends BACK by the same amount** |
| **4** | **For equal end moments M, the end rotation is ML/2EI** |
| **5** | **Setting ML/2EI = WL²/16EI gives M = WL/8** ✓ |

> **That is the METHOD OF SUPERPOSITION applied to a fixed beam, and it is the clearest derivation of the result.**

> **The essential idea is the one common to all indeterminate analysis: equilibrium alone is insufficient, and the extra condition is a statement about DEFORMATION — here, that the ends do not rotate.**

**The related fixed-beam results, since they come as a family:**

| Loading on a fixed-ended beam of span L | Support moment | Midspan moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Central point load W** | **W L/8** | **W L/8** ← |
| **UDL of intensity w** | **w L²/12** | **w L²/24** |
| **Point load W at distance a from one end (b from the other)** | **W a b²/L² and W a² b/L²** | — |
| **Two point loads at the third points** | **2 W L/9** | **W L/9** |
| **Triangular load, maximum at midspan** | **5wL²/96** | — |

> **The UDL case is the most used and deserves noting: the support moment (wL²/12) is TWICE the midspan moment (wL²/24).**

> **So a fixed beam under a UDL is MORE heavily stressed at the SUPPORTS than at midspan — the reverse of a simply supported beam, and the reason continuous beams need their heaviest reinforcement over the supports.**

> **And note the comparison with the point-load case, where the two are equal: the distribution of the moment between support and span depends on the LOADING as well as on the restraint.**

**Why TRUE fixity is rarely achieved — the practical caution:**

> **A "fixed" end requires a support of INFINITE rotational stiffness, which nothing provides.**

| Real support | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **A beam framing into a very stiff column or wall** | **Nearly fixed** |
| **A beam framing into a slender column** | **PARTIALLY restrained — the column rotates with the beam** ← |
| **A beam on a masonry wall** | **Nearly simply supported, whatever the detail suggests** |
| **A bolted end-plate connection** | Partial, depending on the detail |
| **A welded moment connection to a stiff column** | Close to fixed |

> **The consequence of partial fixity is that the real moments lie BETWEEN the fixed and simply supported values:**

> **Support moment somewhere between 0 and WL/8; midspan moment between WL/8 and WL/4.**

> **Which produces a genuine design dilemma: designing for full fixity underestimates the MIDSPAN moment, while designing as simply supported underestimates the SUPPORT moment.**

> **The conservative and common answer is to design the SPAN for the simply supported moment AND provide the support reinforcement for the fixed-end moment — accepting a small excess of material in exchange for safety under either behaviour.**

> **That is not elegant, and it is what a careful designer does when the actual degree of restraint is uncertain — which it usually is.**

examTip.trick: **Fixed both ends, central point load: M = WL/8 = 30 kNm at the ends AND at midspan — equal in magnitude, opposite in sign.**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 60 kNm is the SIMPLY SUPPORTED value WL/4.** Fixing both ends HALVES the moment and reduces deflection to a QUARTER, from restraint alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under a UDL the fixed-end moment (wL²/12) is TWICE the midspan moment (wL²/24)** — which is why continuous beams need their heaviest steel over the supports. And real fixity is always partial, so design the span as simply supported AND the support as fixed.

questions.stem: As per IS 875 (Part 3), the design wind pressure at a height z is obtained from the design wind speed V_z as:
questions.solution:
**p_z = 0.6 V_z²**, giving the pressure in N/m² when V_z is in m/s.

**Where the 0.6 comes from — it is not arbitrary:**

> **The dynamic (stagnation) pressure of a moving fluid brought to rest is:**

> **p = ½ ρ V²**

> **For air at standard conditions, ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³:**

> **p = ½ × 1.2 × V² = 0.6 V²** ✓

> **So the 0.6 is simply HALF THE DENSITY OF AIR, and the formula is nothing more than Bernoulli's dynamic pressure term.**

> **Option (d) 0.5 V_z² is the coefficient with the density omitted — that is, ½ρV² with ρ taken as 1 — and option (c) 1.2 V_z² is ρV² without the ½.**

> **Option (a) is dimensionally impossible: a pressure must go as the SQUARE of a velocity, and any expression linear in V can be rejected without recall.**

**Building up to V_z — the chain of factors:**

> **V_z = V_b × k₁ × k₂ × k₃ × k₄**

| Factor | Represents | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **V_b** | **BASIC wind speed — from the wind map, a 3-second gust at 10 m in open terrain with a 50-year return period** | **33-55 m/s in India; Nepal is mapped in its own code** |
| **k₁** | **RISK (probability) factor** | **0.71-1.08, by design life and importance** |
| **k₂** | **TERRAIN, HEIGHT and STRUCTURE SIZE factor** | **0.67-1.27** ← the one that varies most |
| **k₃** | **TOPOGRAPHY factor** | **1.0-1.36 — for hills, ridges and escarpments** ← |
| **k₄** | **IMPORTANCE factor for CYCLONIC regions** | **1.0-1.30** |

> **The k₂ factor is the one that does most of the work, and it contains two opposing influences:**

> **WIND SPEED INCREASES WITH HEIGHT, because the ground's friction retards the lower air — the boundary layer of the atmosphere.**

> **And it DECREASES with the ROUGHNESS of the terrain, because a built-up or wooded surface retards it more than open water.**

| Terrain category | Character | k₂ at 10 m |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Open terrain, few obstructions — coastal, desert, open water** | **1.05** |
| **2** | **Open terrain with scattered obstructions up to 10 m** | **1.00** |
| **3** | **Terrain with numerous closely spaced obstructions — towns, industrial areas** | **0.91** |
| **4** | **Terrain with numerous large, tall, closely spaced obstructions — city centres** | **0.80** |

> **So a building in a city centre experiences a wind speed some 24 per cent lower at 10 m than one on an open coast — and since the pressure goes as V², that is a 42 per cent reduction in pressure.**

> **The V² dependence is what makes wind design so sensitive: a 20 per cent error in the speed is a 44 per cent error in the pressure.**

**The TOPOGRAPHY factor k₃, which matters greatly in Nepal:**

> **Wind ACCELERATES over a hill, a ridge or an escarpment, because the flow is compressed between the ground and the undisturbed air above.**

> **k₃ can reach 1.36 near the crest of a steep hill — a 36 per cent increase in speed and hence an 85 PER CENT INCREASE IN PRESSURE.**

> **For a country whose settlements sit on ridges and hilltops, that is a first-order effect rather than a refinement, and neglecting k₃ in a hill location understates the wind load severely.**

> **The factor depends on the upwind slope and on the position relative to the crest, and it decays with distance downwind of it.**

**From pressure to FORCE — the shape and pressure coefficients:**

> **The design wind pressure p_z is not the force on the structure. The force requires the coefficients:**

> **F = (C_pe − C_pi) A p_z**  for a cladding element, or  **F = C_f A_e p_z**  for the structure as a whole.

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C_pe** | **EXTERNAL pressure coefficient — positive for windward pressure, NEGATIVE for suction** |
| **C_pi** | **INTERNAL pressure coefficient, depending on the building's PERMEABILITY** ← |
| **C_f** | Force (drag) coefficient for the whole structure |

> **The INTERNAL pressure coefficient is the one most often decisive for cladding and roofs, and its behaviour is worth understanding:**

| Building permeability | C_pi |
|---|---|
| **Effectively sealed (openings below 5 % of the wall area)** | **±0.2** |
| **Normal permeability (5-20 % openings)** | **±0.5** |
| **LARGE openings (above 20 %) — or a door or window that FAILS or is left open** | **±0.7, and up to +0.7 on the windward side** ← |

> **The last row explains the commonest form of wind damage: a windward door or window BREAKS or is left open, the building's interior is pressurised to nearly the full stagnation pressure, and that internal pressure ADDS to the external SUCTION on the roof.**

> **The roof is then lifted by the sum of the two, which can be twice what the design assumed for a sealed building — and roofs are lost this way in almost every severe windstorm.**

> **Which is why the code requires the large-opening case to be considered where a dominant opening can occur, and why securing windward openings is a genuine wind-mitigation measure rather than housekeeping.**

**And the SUCTION point, which is the most under-appreciated in wind design:**

> **The largest wind pressures on a building are usually SUCTIONS, not pressures:**

| Location | Typical C_pe |
|---|---|
| **Windward wall** | **+0.7 (pressure)** |
| **Leeward wall** | **−0.25 to −0.5 (suction)** |
| **Side walls** | **−0.5 to −0.7 (suction)** |
| **ROOF, general** | **−0.5 to −0.8 (suction)** |
| **ROOF EDGES, RIDGES and CORNERS (local)** | **−1.5 to −2.0, and −2.5 at some corners** ← |

> **So the local suction at a roof corner can be THREE TIMES the windward wall pressure — and it is a suction, acting outward, which the structure's self-weight does not resist.**

> **That is why roof sheeting fixings are specified more closely at eaves, ridges and corners than in the field of the roof, and why lightweight roofs need HOLDING DOWN rather than merely supporting.**

> **A roof of corrugated sheeting weighing 0.1 kN/m² under a suction of 1.5 kN/m² has a net uplift of 1.4 kN/m², and every fixing and every purlin connection down to the foundation must carry it in TENSION — a load path that a gravity-only design never provides.**

> **Which is the practical heart of wind design in light construction: the structure must be tied together AGAINST UPLIFT, continuously from the sheeting to the foundation, and the weakest link in that chain is what fails.**

examTip.trick: **p_z = 0.6 V_z² N/m², and the 0.6 is just ½ρ for air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³)** — Bernoulli's dynamic pressure. Option (a) is dimensionally impossible: pressure goes as V².
examTip.trap: **The V² dependence makes wind design very sensitive** — a 20 % error in speed is a 44 % error in pressure. And in Nepal the TOPOGRAPHY factor k₃ reaches 1.36 on a ridge crest, which is an 85 % increase in pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **The largest wind loads are SUCTIONS: −1.5 to −2.5 at roof corners against +0.7 on the windward wall.** A light roof needs HOLDING DOWN, continuously to the foundation. And a broken windward window pressurises the interior, adding to the roof suction — the commonest cause of roof loss.

questions.stem: In the limit state method, the partial safety factor applied to the strength of CONCRETE and of REINFORCING STEEL respectively are:
questions.solution:
**1.5 for CONCRETE and 1.15 for STEEL.**

**The IS 456 partial safety factors for material strength:**

| Material | Partial safety factor γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **CONCRETE** | **1.5** | **0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck** ← |
| **REINFORCING STEEL** | **1.15** | **f_y / 1.15 = 0.87 f_y** ← |

> **The familiar coefficients 0.446 and 0.87 come directly from those factors, which is worth recognising:**

> **0.87 = 1/1.15 exactly — so wherever 0.87 f_y appears, it is the design yield strength after the material factor.**

> **And 0.446 f_ck = 0.67 f_ck/1.5, where the additional 0.67 accounts for the difference between the CUBE strength and the strength of concrete in a FLEXURAL member under sustained load.**

> **Option (a) 1.5 and 1.5 applies the concrete factor to both, and option (b) has them the wrong way round — which is the designed trap, since the two numbers are so easily transposed.**

**Why CONCRETE carries the LARGER factor — the reasoning is the substance of the question:**

| Reason | Concrete | Steel |
|---|---|---|
| **Where it is made** | **ON SITE, in variable conditions** | **In a FACTORY, under controlled conditions** ← |
| **Variability of strength** | **HIGH — standard deviation 4-5 N/mm² on 25-40 N/mm²** | **LOW — closely controlled and tested** |
| **Sensitivity to workmanship** | **VERY HIGH — mixing, placing, compaction and curing all affect it** ← | **None, once delivered** |
| **Relation of the test specimen to the structure** | **A 150 mm cube, cured in water, is NOT the concrete in the member** | **A tensile test on the bar itself** |
| **Failure mode** | **BRITTLE in compression** | **DUCTILE** |
| **Certainty of the actual strength in place** | **LOW** | **HIGH** |

> **So the factor is larger for concrete because THE UNCERTAINTY IS LARGER, and a partial safety factor is precisely a measure of uncertainty rather than of importance.**

> **That is the general principle of the limit state method and it is worth stating clearly: EACH SOURCE OF UNCERTAINTY GETS ITS OWN FACTOR, sized to that uncertainty.**

> **The older WORKING STRESS method used a single global factor of safety on the material strength, which lumped every uncertainty together and could not distinguish a well-controlled steel from a variable concrete, or a dead load from a live one.**

> **Partial factors separate them, which is why the method gives a more uniform reliability across different structures and load combinations.**

**The load factors, for the other half of the method:**

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| **DL + LL + WL/EL** | **1.2 (DL + LL ± EL)** |
| **DL + WL/EL** | **1.5 (DL ± EL)** |
| **DL opposing the lateral load (uplift, overturning)** | **0.9 DL ± 1.5 EL** ← |

> **And the LOAD factors for the limit state of SERVICEABILITY are quite different:**

| Combination | Serviceability factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** |
| **DL + LL + WL** | **1.0 DL + 0.8 LL + 0.8 WL** |
| **DL + WL** | **1.0 DL + 1.0 WL** |

> **And the MATERIAL factors for serviceability are 1.0 for both concrete and steel.**

> **That is the point worth understanding: at SERVICEABILITY the structure is being checked under its ACTUAL expected loads with its ACTUAL expected material properties, because the question is how it will BEHAVE — how much it will deflect and crack — not whether it will collapse.**

> **Applying collapse-level factors to a deflection calculation would predict a deflection the structure will never experience, which is why the two limit states use different factors throughout.**

**The two limit states compared, since the whole method is built on their distinction:**

| | **Limit state of COLLAPSE** | **Limit state of SERVICEABILITY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Question asked** | **Will it FAIL?** | **Will it be USABLE?** |
| **Consequence of exceeding** | **Collapse — loss of life** | **Discomfort, damage to finishes, loss of function** |
| **Load factors** | **1.5, 1.2, 0.9** | **1.0, 0.8** |
| **Material factors** | **1.5 concrete, 1.15 steel** | **1.0 both** ← |
| **Checks** | **Flexure, shear, torsion, compression, bond** | **DEFLECTION, CRACK WIDTH, vibration** |
| **Acceptable probability of exceedance** | **VERY LOW — perhaps 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ per year** | **HIGHER — an occasional exceedance is tolerable** ← |

> **The last row is the philosophical basis of the whole method: the two limit states are assigned DIFFERENT ACCEPTABLE PROBABILITIES, because their consequences differ enormously.**

> **A structure that deflects visibly once a decade is a nuisance; a structure that collapses once a decade is intolerable.**

> **So the factors are calibrated to give a very small probability of collapse and a modest probability of a serviceability exceedance — and that deliberate asymmetry is what makes limit state design more rational than a single global factor of safety.**

**And the additional 0.67 on the concrete, since it is often asked separately:**

> **The 150 mm cube gives a HIGHER apparent strength than the same concrete in a real member, for two reasons:**

| Reason | Effect |
|---|---|
| **PLATEN RESTRAINT in the cube test** | **The testing machine's platens confine the cube laterally, raising its apparent strength** ← |
| **SUSTAINED loading in a real structure** | **Concrete under sustained load fails at about 0.85 of its short-term strength — creep-induced microcracking** ← |
| **Size effect** | A large member is weaker than a small specimen |

> **Combining those effects gives about 0.67 f_ck as the usable strength in a flexural member, and dividing by γ_m = 1.5 gives the 0.446 f_ck in the stress block.**

> **So the coefficient 0.446 encodes three separate physical facts — platen restraint, sustained-load strength reduction, and the material safety factor — and knowing that makes it intelligible rather than a number to be memorised.**

examTip.trick: **Concrete 1.5, steel 1.15.** Recognise them in the familiar coefficients: 0.87 f_y = f_y/1.15, and 0.446 f_ck = 0.67 f_ck/1.5.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) has them transposed** — the two numbers are easily swapped. Concrete gets the LARGER factor because its uncertainty is larger: made on site, workmanship-sensitive, brittle, and the cube is not the member.
examTip.mnemonic: **At SERVICEABILITY both material factors are 1.0 and the load factors are 1.0/0.8** — because the question is how the structure will BEHAVE, not whether it will collapse. The two limit states carry deliberately different acceptable probabilities.

questions.stem: The 7-day compressive strength of ordinary Portland cement concrete is generally about what percentage of its 28-day strength?
questions.solution:
**About 65 per cent (commonly quoted as 65 to 70 per cent).**

**The strength development of OPC concrete:**

| Age | Percentage of the 28-day strength |
|---|---|
| **1 day** | **About 16 %** |
| **3 days** | **About 40 %** |
| **7 days** | **About 65 %** ← |
| **14 days** | **About 90 %** |
| **28 days** | **100 % — the reference age** |
| **3 months** | **About 110-115 %** |
| **1 year** | **About 120 %** |

> **Two features of that table matter more than the individual figures.**

> **FIRST — the gain is RAPID EARLY and SLOW LATE. Two thirds of the strength arrives in the first quarter of the 28 days.**

> **SECOND — the strength CONTINUES TO RISE beyond 28 days, indefinitely and at a diminishing rate, as long as moisture is available.**

> **The 28-day figure is therefore a CONVENTION, not a final value — chosen because it is a practical waiting period at which most of the strength has developed and the remaining gain is slow enough to be ignored.**

> **That is worth being clear about: there is nothing physically special about 28 days.**

**Why the 7-day test is used at all, since 28 days is the specified age:**

> **A 7-day result gives EARLY WARNING.**

> **If a pour's 7-day strength is well below 65 per cent of the target, the 28-day result will very probably fail — and knowing that at 7 days rather than at 28 allows the problem to be found and corrected before three more weeks of concrete has been placed on the same mix.**

> **By 28 days, three weeks of potentially defective work has been built.**

| Situation | Value of the 7-day test |
|---|---|
| **7-day strength well above 65 % of the target** | **Reassurance; work continues** |
| **7-day strength around 65 %** | On track |
| **7-day strength well BELOW 65 %** | **INVESTIGATE NOW — mix proportions, cement, water content, curing** ← |

> **So the 7-day cube is a PROCESS CONTROL measure and the 28-day cube is the ACCEPTANCE measure, and the two serve quite different purposes.**

> **The same logic as monitoring filtered-water turbidity continuously while relying on a bacteriological test for compliance: the fast, imperfect measurement controls the process and the slow, definitive one judges it.**

**How the ratio varies with the cement type — an important qualification:**

| Cement | 7-day strength as a percentage of its own 28-day strength |
|---|---|
| **OPC 33 grade** | **About 65 %** |
| **OPC 43 grade** | **About 70 %** |
| **OPC 53 grade** | **About 75 %** |
| **RAPID HARDENING cement** | **About 85-90 %** ← |
| **PPC (Portland pozzolana cement)** | **About 55-60 % — SLOWER early gain** ← |
| **PSC (Portland slag cement)** | **About 55 % — slower still** |
| **LOW HEAT cement** | **About 40-50 % — much slower** |

> **The PPC and PSC entries are practically important, because BLENDED CEMENTS now dominate the market in India and Nepal:**

> **Fly ash and slag react POZZOLANICALLY — they require the calcium hydroxide released by the cement's own hydration before they can react at all, so their contribution comes LATE.**

> **So a PPC concrete gains strength more slowly early and CONTINUES GAINING LONGER, often overtaking an equivalent OPC concrete by 90 days.**

> **The consequences are real:**

| Consequence of using PPC or PSC | Note |
|---|---|
| **Formwork must stay LONGER** | **The striking times based on OPC are unsafe for a blended cement** ← |
| **CURING must continue longer** | **The pozzolanic reaction needs moisture for far longer — 14 days minimum against 7** ← |
| **A 7-day cube result looks alarming and may be perfectly satisfactory** | **Judge it against the right benchmark for that cement** |
| **Long-term strength and durability are BETTER** | **Lower permeability, better sulphate and chloride resistance, less heat** ← |
| **Lower heat of hydration** | Suits mass concrete |

> **The last two rows are why blended cements are preferred despite their slow start: the pozzolanic reaction refines the pore structure, giving a markedly LESS PERMEABLE concrete — and permeability is the master variable for durability.**

> **So PPC gives a better long-term concrete AND uses an industrial waste product, at the price of patience during construction.**

> **The error that follows from ignorance of it is common and serious: applying OPC formwork-striking and curing periods to a PPC concrete produces a structure that was loaded before it had strength and cured for half the necessary time.**

**CURING — since the whole strength development depends on it:**

> **Hydration requires WATER. If the concrete dries, hydration STOPS and the strength gain stops with it — permanently, since re-wetting resumes it only partially.**

| Curing period | IS 456 requirement |
|---|---|
| **OPC** | **At least 7 days** |
| **Blended cements (PPC, PSC), and in hot weather** | **At least 10-14 days** ← |
| **Mass concrete** | Longer still |

> **The strength loss from inadequate curing is large and irrecoverable:**

| Curing | Approximate 28-day strength achieved |
|---|---|
| **Continuously moist for 28 days** | **100 %** |
| **Moist 7 days, then in air** | **About 85 %** |
| **Moist 3 days, then in air** | **About 75 %** |
| **No curing — in air from the start** | **About 50-60 %** ← |

> **So poor curing can halve the strength of a concrete whose mix design, materials and workmanship were all correct — which makes it the cheapest way to ruin a structure and the cheapest way to protect one.**

> **And it is invisible: the concrete looks identical, and only a cube test or a later failure reveals it.**

> **That is why curing is specified, inspected and paid for as a distinct operation rather than left to the gang who placed the concrete.**

examTip.trick: **7 days ≈ 65 % of the 28-day strength for OPC.** The pattern: 1 day 16 %, 3 days 40 %, 7 days 65 %, 14 days 90 %, 28 days 100 % — and it keeps rising beyond, reaching about 120 % at a year.
examTip.trap: **PPC and PSC reach only about 55-60 % at 7 days** — the pozzolanic reaction needs the cement's own hydration products first. Applying OPC striking and curing periods to a blended cement is a real and serious error.
examTip.mnemonic: **28 days is a CONVENTION, not a physical milestone.** The 7-day cube is PROCESS CONTROL (early warning); the 28-day cube is ACCEPTANCE. And no curing halves the strength — invisibly, and irrecoverably.

questions.stem: The purpose of adding an AIR-ENTRAINING admixture to concrete is principally to:
options: Improve resistance to freeze-thaw damage and improve workability
questions.solution:
**To improve resistance to FREEZE-THAW damage, and incidentally to improve workability.**

**How entrained air resists freeze-thaw damage — the mechanism:**

> **Water expands about 9 per cent on freezing.**

> **Water held in the fine capillary pores of hardened concrete, on freezing, generates enormous hydraulic pressure as the ice expands and forces the remaining unfrozen water through the pore network.**

> **That pressure cracks the paste, and repeated cycles progressively disintegrate the surface and then the body of the concrete.**

> **ENTRAINED AIR provides millions of tiny, DISCRETE, closely spaced bubbles — typically 10 to 100 μm across, spaced about 0.2 mm apart.**

> **Those bubbles act as PRESSURE RELIEF CHAMBERS: the expanding water is pushed into the nearest bubble instead of stressing the paste.**

> **The critical parameter is therefore the SPACING FACTOR — the distance water must travel to reach a bubble — and not merely the total air content.**

| Requirement for effective air entrainment | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bubbles must be SMALL** | **10-100 μm — large voids do not help** |
| **They must be CLOSELY SPACED** | **Spacing factor below about 0.2 mm** ← the governing criterion |
| **They must be DISCRETE and not interconnected** | **Interconnected voids would conduct water rather than relieve it** ← |
| **Total air typically 4-7 % by volume** | Depending on the maximum aggregate size |

> **The DISCRETE requirement is what distinguishes ENTRAINED air from ENTRAPPED air, and the distinction is essential:**

| | **ENTRAINED air** | **ENTRAPPED air** |
|---|---|---|
| **Introduced by** | **DELIBERATELY, by an admixture** | **ACCIDENTALLY, during mixing and placing** |
| **Bubble size** | **10-100 μm — very small** | **Large, irregular, often mm-scale** |
| **Distribution** | **Uniform and closely spaced** | **Random and sparse** |
| **Effect on freeze-thaw resistance** | **GREATLY IMPROVED** ← | **NONE** |
| **Effect on strength** | **A modest reduction (see below)** | **A large reduction** |
| **Removed by vibration?** | **NO — the bubbles are stable** | **YES — that is what vibration is for** ← |

> **The last row is the practically important one: vibration expels ENTRAPPED air, which is desirable, and does NOT remove ENTRAINED air, which must be retained.**

> **So air entrainment and proper compaction are compatible, and an air-entrained concrete is compacted normally.**

> **Over-vibration will eventually drive out some entrained air, which is one more reason not to over-vibrate.**

**The COST of air entrainment, which must be acknowledged:**

> **Air is a void, and voids reduce strength.**

> **The rule of thumb: EACH 1 PER CENT OF AIR COSTS ABOUT 5 PER CENT OF COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH.**

> **So 5 per cent entrained air costs roughly 25 per cent of the strength — which is substantial.**

> **But part of that is recovered, because entrained air markedly improves WORKABILITY:**

> **The bubbles act as a lubricant, behaving like a fine, frictionless aggregate — so the same workability can be achieved with LESS WATER.**

> **And less water means higher strength, which offsets part of the void penalty.**

> **The net effect is a strength reduction of perhaps 10 to 15 per cent rather than 25, which is the price paid for freeze-thaw durability.**

> **Option (a) is therefore precisely wrong: air entrainment REDUCES strength, and knowing which direction the effect runs is the point.**

**The other benefits of entrained air, since they are real:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **FREEZE-THAW resistance** | **The principal purpose** ← |
| **Improved WORKABILITY and cohesion** | **The bubbles lubricate; a harsh mix becomes workable** |
| **Reduced BLEEDING and SEGREGATION** | **The bubbles hold the mix together and impede water rising** ← |
| **Improved resistance to DE-ICING SALTS** | Related to freeze-thaw scaling |
| **Reduced permeability in some cases** | Because less water is needed |
| **Better pumpability** | The mix flows more readily |

> **The BLEEDING and SEGREGATION benefit makes air entrainment useful even where freezing never occurs — a lean or harsh mix, a pumped mix, or a mix with poorly graded sand can all be improved by it.**

> **So in Nepal's Terai, where freezing does not occur, air entrainment may still be specified for workability and cohesion — while in the high hills it is specified for its primary purpose.**

**The admixture families, for context, since three of the options name other types:**

| Admixture | Function | Typical chemical |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTICISER (water reducer)** | **Same workability with 5-10 % LESS water, or more workability at the same water** | Lignosulphonates, hydroxycarboxylic acids |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER (high-range water reducer)** | **15-30 % less water — makes high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible** ← | Sulphonated melamine or naphthalene formaldehyde, polycarboxylate ethers |
| **ACCELERATOR** | **Faster set and early strength — for cold weather and urgent work** | **Calcium chloride (NEVER in reinforced concrete — it corrodes the steel), calcium formate** ← |
| **RETARDER** | **Delays setting — for hot weather, long hauls, large pours** | Sugars, gypsum, lignosulphonates |
| **AIR-ENTRAINING agent** | **Freeze-thaw resistance and workability** ← | Vinsol resin, fatty acid salts |
| **Waterproofing / integral water repellent** | Reduces permeability | Stearates, silicates |
| **Corrosion inhibitor** | Protects the reinforcement | Calcium nitrite |

> **Option (c) describes a PLASTICISER or SUPERPLASTICISER, and option (b) an ACCELERATOR — both real admixtures serving different ends, which is what makes the option set well formed.**

> **The CALCIUM CHLORIDE warning in the accelerator row deserves emphasis because the error is still made: calcium chloride is a cheap and effective accelerator and it introduces CHLORIDE IONS, which destroy the passive film on the reinforcement and cause pitting corrosion.**

> **IS 456 therefore prohibits it in reinforced and prestressed concrete, and limits total chloride content strictly.**

> **An accelerator that gains a day on the programme and shortens the structure's life by decades is a poor bargain, and it is the clearest illustration of why admixtures must be selected on their whole effect rather than on the one property wanted.**

examTip.trick: **Entrained air gives millions of tiny DISCRETE bubbles that act as pressure relief chambers when pore water freezes.** The governing parameter is the SPACING FACTOR (below ~0.2 mm), not the total air content.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is precisely backwards — air entrainment REDUCES strength, about 5 % per 1 % of air.** Part is recovered because the bubbles improve workability and so allow less water. Options (b) and (c) describe accelerators and plasticisers.
examTip.mnemonic: **ENTRAINED air is deliberate, tiny and stable to vibration; ENTRAPPED air is accidental, large, and is what vibration expels.** And never use calcium chloride as an accelerator in reinforced concrete — the chloride corrodes the steel.

questions.stem: A singly reinforced rectangular beam of Fe 415 steel has b = 300 mm and an effective depth of 450 mm. Its limiting moment of resistance in M20 concrete is:
questions.solution:
**About 168 kNm.**

**The limiting moment of resistance:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.138 f_ck b d²**  for Fe 415 steel

**The computation:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.138 × 20 × 300 × 450²**

> **= 0.138 × 20 × 300 × 202,500**

> **= 0.138 × 20 × 6.075 × 10⁷**

> **= 1.677 × 10⁸ N·mm = 167.7 kNm ≈ 168 kNm** ✓

**The coefficients by steel grade, which is the fact to hold:**

| Steel grade | x_u,max/d | **M_u,lim / (f_ck b d²)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** | **0.148** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** | **0.138** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** | **0.133** |

> **Option (c) 205 kNm corresponds to a coefficient of about 0.169 and option (a) 112 kNm to about 0.092 — neither a standard value.**

> **Option (d) 251 kNm is roughly 0.207 f_ck b d², well above any grade's limit.**

> **So the option set requires the correct coefficient, and the three real values differ by only 10 per cent across the grades — which means an approximate recall will not discriminate.**

**Where the coefficient comes from — the derivation, so it can be rebuilt:**

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b x_u,max (d − 0.42 x_u,max)**

> **With x_u,max = 0.48 d for Fe 415:**

> **= 0.36 f_ck b (0.48 d)(d − 0.42 × 0.48 d)**

> **= 0.36 × 0.48 × (1 − 0.2016) f_ck b d²**

> **= 0.1728 × 0.7984 f_ck b d²**

> **= 0.138 f_ck b d²** ✓

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.36 f_ck** | **The AVERAGE stress in the equivalent rectangular compression block** |
| **0.42 x_u** | **The depth of the compression centroid below the extreme fibre** |
| **(d − 0.42 x_u)** | **The LEVER ARM between the compression and tension resultants** |

> **The 0.36 and 0.42 come from integrating the code's parabolic-plus-rectangular stress block, and they are the SAME for every steel grade — only x_u,max changes.**

> **So all three coefficients in the table above are generated by the same two constants and three neutral-axis depths, which makes them recoverable rather than three separate facts.**

**What the answer MEANS — the decision it governs:**

> **M_u,lim = 168 kNm is the MAXIMUM moment this section can carry AS A SINGLY REINFORCED SECTION.**

| If the applied M_u is | Then |
|---|---|
| **Less than 168 kNm** | **Design as SINGLY reinforced (under-reinforced); compute A_st from the moment** ← |
| **Equal to 168 kNm** | **The balanced limiting section** |
| **Greater than 168 kNm** | **The section CANNOT be singly reinforced. Either make it DEEPER, or make it DOUBLY REINFORCED with compression steel** ← |

> **So this calculation is the first step in any beam design: compute M_u,lim for the section available, and compare it with the applied moment.**

> **That comparison determines the whole subsequent design route, which is why the value is computed before any reinforcement is worked out.**

**The steel area required, to complete the picture:**

> **At the limiting condition, equating the compression and tension forces:**

> **0.36 f_ck b x_u,max = 0.87 f_y A_st**

> **A_st = 0.36 × 20 × 300 × (0.48 × 450) / (0.87 × 415)**

> **= 0.36 × 20 × 300 × 216 / 361**

> **= 466,560/361 = 1292 mm²**

> **which is about 0.96 per cent of bd — and note that this is the MAXIMUM steel for a singly reinforced section, the balanced percentage.**

| Steel grade | Limiting (balanced) steel percentage, p_t,lim, in M20 |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **1.76 %** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.96 %** ← |
| **Fe 500** | **0.76 %** |

> **Note that a HIGHER grade of steel gives a LOWER limiting percentage — because each square millimetre carries more force, so less area balances the same concrete compression.**

> **And note the practical consequence: a beam reinforced beyond about 1 per cent with Fe 415 is over-reinforced and requires either a deeper section or compression steel.**

> **In practice beams are usually designed at 0.4 to 0.8 per cent, comfortably below the limit — both to stay well under-reinforced and to keep the deflection acceptable.**

**DOUBLY REINFORCED sections, since that is the route when M_u exceeds the limit:**

> **Compression steel is added near the compression face, and the section's capacity becomes:**

> **M_u = M_u,lim + A_sc (f_sc − 0.45 f_ck)(d − d')**

> **The additional moment is carried by a couple between the compression steel and an equal additional area of tension steel.**

| Aspect of doubly reinforced design | Note |
|---|---|
| **f_sc depends on the STRAIN at the compression steel's level** | **Read from the stress-strain curve; for Fe 415 at d'/d = 0.1, f_sc ≈ 353 MPa, LESS than 0.87f_y** ← |
| **The 0.45 f_ck deduction** | **Allows for the concrete DISPLACED by the compression steel, which would have carried stress anyway** |
| **Compression steel must be RESTRAINED against buckling** | **Stirrups at not more than 16 × the bar diameter — the same rule as for a column** ← |
| **It substantially improves DUCTILITY and reduces long-term deflection** | **A real benefit beyond the strength gain** ← |

> **The last row is worth knowing because it is the reason compression steel is sometimes provided even when not needed for strength: it restrains CREEP and SHRINKAGE deflection, and it greatly improves the section's rotation capacity, which matters for seismic design.**

> **So IS 13920 requires a minimum of half the tension steel to be provided as compression steel in a beam of a ductile frame — a requirement about ductility, not about moment capacity.**

examTip.trap: **The three coefficients differ by only 10 %**, so approximate recall will not discriminate. Rebuild them from 0.36 f_ck b x_u,max (d − 0.42 x_u,max) with the right x_u,max/d.
examTip.mnemonic: **This value decides the whole design route: below it design singly reinforced, above it go DEEPER or DOUBLY reinforced.** And the balanced steel percentage is 0.96 % for Fe 415 in M20 — beams are normally designed at 0.4-0.8 %.

questions.stem: In a reinforced concrete beam, the shear reinforcement is provided principally to resist:
options: The horizontal shear stress at the neutral axis
The diagonal tension resulting from the combination of shear and flexural stresses
The compressive stress in the web
The bond stress between the concrete and the steel
questions.solution:
**The DIAGONAL TENSION resulting from the combination of shear and flexural stresses.**

**Why concrete fails in "shear" by cracking in TENSION — the essential idea:**

> **Concrete is strong in compression and WEAK IN TENSION — its tensile strength is only about a tenth of its compressive strength.**

> **A shear stress does not act alone. At any point, a shear stress τ combined with a flexural stress produces PRINCIPAL STRESSES, and one of them is TENSILE:**

> **At the NEUTRAL AXIS, where the flexural stress is zero and only τ acts, the principal stresses are ±τ at 45° — so there is a tensile stress of magnitude τ acting on a plane at 45°.**

> **The concrete cracks on the plane PERPENDICULAR to that principal tension — that is, at 45° to the beam's axis.**

> **So what is called a "shear failure" is in reality a DIAGONAL TENSION failure, and the shear reinforcement's job is to carry that tension across the crack.**

> **Option (a) is therefore describing the applied stress rather than the failure mechanism: the horizontal shear stress is real, but the concrete does not fail in shear — it fails in the tension that the shear produces.**

**Why the reinforcement is arranged as it is — following from the mechanism:**

| Reinforcement type | Orientation | Effectiveness |
|---|---|---|
| **VERTICAL STIRRUPS** | **Perpendicular to the axis** | **The standard: they cross a 45° crack at 45°, which is adequate and they are easy to fix** ← |
| **INCLINED stirrups at 45°** | **Perpendicular to the crack** | **THEORETICALLY THE MOST EFFICIENT — directly along the tension** ← |
| **BENT-UP (cranked) bars** | **Tension bars bent up at 45° near the supports** | **Efficient, and they use bars no longer needed for moment there** |
| **A combination of bent-up bars and stirrups** | — | **IS 456 limits bent-up bars to carrying at most HALF the shear** |

> **The INCLINED stirrup is the most efficient and is rarely used, and the reason is purely practical: bending and fixing stirrups at 45° is laborious, and a vertical stirrup can be dropped over the bars.**

> **And a vertical stirrup still crosses the crack, just at a less favourable angle — so the modest loss of efficiency is accepted for a large gain in buildability.**

> **The BENT-UP BAR is an elegant device worth understanding: the tension steel required at midspan is NOT required near the support, where the moment is small.**

> **So those bars can be bent up at 45° and used to carry shear instead — which is exactly where the shear is largest.**

> **The two requirements are complementary in their distribution along the span: moment is greatest at midspan and shear at the supports, so the same steel serves both if it is bent at the right place.**

> **The code's limit — bent-up bars may carry at most half the shear — exists because they act only over a limited length and do not confine the concrete as stirrups do.**

**The TRUSS ANALOGY, which is how the design equations are understood:**

> **A cracked reinforced concrete beam behaves like a TRUSS:**

| Truss element | Beam element |
|---|---|
| **Top chord (compression)** | **The concrete compression zone** |
| **Bottom chord (tension)** | **The longitudinal tension steel** |
| **Diagonal compression struts** | **The concrete between the diagonal cracks** ← |
| **Vertical (or diagonal) ties** | **The STIRRUPS** ← |

> **That model explains the design provisions and their limits:**

> **The stirrups act as TIES, carrying the tension across the cracks — which is what V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d/s_v expresses.**

> **The concrete between the cracks acts as COMPRESSION STRUTS, and those struts can CRUSH if the shear is too high — which is why IS 456 sets a MAXIMUM shear stress τ_c,max that no amount of stirrups can exceed.**

| Concrete grade | τ_c,max (N/mm²) |
|---|---|
| **M20** | **2.8** |
| **M25** | **3.1** |
| **M30** | **3.5** |
| **M35** | **3.7** |
| **M40 and above** | **4.0** |

> **The existence of that ceiling is the practically important consequence of the truss model, and it is often misunderstood:**

> **IF τ_v EXCEEDS τ_c,max, ADDING MORE STIRRUPS DOES NOT HELP.**

> **The failure mode has changed from diagonal tension to WEB CRUSHING, and the remedy is to increase the SECTION or the CONCRETE GRADE — nothing else works.**

> **A designer who responds to a high shear stress by packing in more stirrups has misdiagnosed the problem, and the beam will crush its web at a load the stirrup calculation says it can carry.**

**The design procedure, for completeness:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute the nominal shear stress τ_v = V_u/(b d)** |
| **2** | **Compare with τ_c,max. If τ_v > τ_c,max, REDESIGN the section** ← |
| **3** | **Find τ_c, the concrete's own shear capacity, from IS 456 Table 19 (depends on the grade AND on the tension steel percentage)** |
| **4** | **If τ_v ≤ τ_c, provide MINIMUM shear reinforcement only** |
| **5** | **If τ_v > τ_c, design stirrups for the EXCESS: V_us = V_u − τ_c b d** ← |
| **6** | **Check the spacing limits: not more than 0.75d, nor 300 mm, nor the value from the minimum-steel rule** |

> **Step 3 contains a point worth noting: the concrete's shear capacity τ_c INCREASES with the percentage of TENSION steel.**

> **That seems odd until the mechanism is considered: more tension steel means a stiffer tension chord, narrower cracks, and hence better aggregate interlock across the crack — and aggregate interlock is a substantial part of the concrete's shear resistance.**

> **So the longitudinal steel contributes to shear capacity indirectly, by controlling the crack width.**

> **And step 5 embodies the code's approach of ADDING the concrete's contribution to the steel's, rather than requiring the steel to carry everything — which is a reasonable model of a cracked beam in which both mechanisms act together.**

**The MINIMUM shear reinforcement, since it applies even where no shear demands it:**

> **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)**

> **Its purposes are worth knowing, since a beam with τ_v below τ_c apparently needs none:**

| Purpose of minimum stirrups | Note |
|---|---|
| **Guard against an unexpected or accidental shear** | Load positions not considered |
| **Resist SHRINKAGE and TEMPERATURE stresses in the web** | — |
| **Hold the longitudinal bars in position during concreting** | **A practical necessity — without stirrups the cage collapses** ← |
| **Provide some CONFINEMENT to the compression zone** | Improves ductility |
| **Prevent a SUDDEN brittle diagonal tension failure** | **The most important: a beam with no stirrups fails abruptly when the diagonal crack forms** ← |

> **The last row is the safety argument, and it parallels the minimum tension steel rule: a beam with no shear reinforcement fails the instant a diagonal crack develops, with no warning and no reserve.**

> **Minimum stirrups convert that abrupt failure into a gradual one in which the cracks widen visibly first — which is the same reasoning, and the same purpose, as every other minimum-reinforcement clause in the code.**

examTip.trick: **A "shear failure" in concrete is really a DIAGONAL TENSION failure** — shear produces principal tension at 45°, and concrete's tensile strength is a tenth of its compressive strength. Stirrups carry that tension across the crack.
examTip.trap: **If τ_v exceeds τ_c,max (2.8 N/mm² for M20), MORE STIRRUPS DO NOT HELP** — the failure mode has become WEB CRUSHING of the concrete struts. Increase the section or the grade.
examTip.mnemonic: **Think of the cracked beam as a TRUSS: concrete compression chord, steel tension chord, concrete diagonal STRUTS, stirrups as TIES.** That model explains both the stirrup equation and the τ_c,max ceiling. And τ_c rises with the TENSION steel percentage, through aggregate interlock.

questions.stem: In the design of an isolated square footing, the critical section for ONE-WAY SHEAR is taken at a distance from the face of the column equal to:
options: The effective depth of the footing
The face of the column itself
questions.solution:
**At a distance equal to the EFFECTIVE DEPTH d from the face of the column.**

**The three critical sections in a footing, which must be kept distinct:**

| Check | Critical section located at |
|---|---|
| **BENDING (flexure)** | **The FACE of the column** ← |
| **ONE-WAY SHEAR (beam shear)** | **A distance d from the face of the column** ← |
| **TWO-WAY SHEAR (PUNCHING shear)** | **A perimeter at a distance d/2 from the face of the column, all round** ← |
| **Development length** | Measured from the face of the column |

> **All three distances — d, d/2 and the face itself — appear as options here, so the specific check named in the stem must be matched.**

> **Option (b) d/2 is the PUNCHING shear perimeter, and option (d) the face is the BENDING section — both real locations for other checks.**

**Why each section is where it is — the reasoning:**

> **BENDING at the COLUMN FACE: the footing acts as a cantilever projecting from the column, so its maximum moment is at the root of that cantilever — the column face.**

> **The moment is computed from the soil pressure acting on the projection beyond that face, times the distance to its centroid.**

> **ONE-WAY SHEAR at DISTANCE d: a diagonal tension crack in a slab or footing forms at roughly 45°, so it originates at the column face and reaches the tension face a distance d away.**

> **A section closer than d to the support is crossed by the compression fan spreading from the support and is not the critical plane — so the code takes the section at d, where the crack actually intersects the reinforcement.**

> **PUNCHING at d/2 ALL ROUND: the column tends to punch THROUGH the footing, pushing out a truncated pyramid of concrete.**

> **The failure surface slopes outward from the column, and the code idealises it as a vertical perimeter at d/2 from the face — a simplification of the sloping surface that gives the right answer with a simple calculation.**

**Why PUNCHING SHEAR usually governs an isolated footing:**

> **The punching perimeter is short and the whole column load must cross it, so the shear stress there is high:**

> **τ_v = V_u / (perimeter × d)**, with the perimeter being 4(c + d) for a square column of side c.

> **And the permissible punching shear stress is:**

> **τ_c = k_s × 0.25 √f_ck**, where k_s = (0.5 + β_c) ≤ 1, with β_c the ratio of the column's short side to its long side.

> **For a SQUARE column, β_c = 1 so k_s = 1, and for M20 concrete:**

> **τ_c = 0.25 √20 = 1.12 N/mm²**

> **That is a low permissible stress applied over a short perimeter, which is why punching commonly determines the footing's THICKNESS.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Punching shear usually fixes the DEPTH of an isolated footing** | **Not bending, and not one-way shear** ← |
| **The depth cannot be reduced by adding reinforcement** | **Shear reinforcement in a footing is awkward and often impractical** |
| **A footing is therefore made THICK enough to pass punching without shear steel** | **The normal practice** ← |
| **Where the depth would be excessive, a PEDESTAL or a column capital is used** | Increasing the punching perimeter |

> **The third row is the practical rule: an isolated footing is designed thick enough that the punching check passes on the concrete alone, and shear reinforcement is avoided.**

> **The reason is buildability rather than theory — placing and supporting shear links in a shallow footing is difficult, and their effectiveness depends on anchorage that is hard to achieve in a thin slab.**

> **So the design converges on "make it thicker" as the answer to a punching failure, which is why footings look heavier than a bending calculation alone would suggest.**

**The PUNCHING failure mode itself, since it is the one to visualise:**

> **The column pushes a plug of concrete DOWN and OUT through the footing, in the shape of a truncated pyramid or cone.**

> **It is a BRITTLE failure — sudden, with no warning — and the footing's flexural reinforcement does almost nothing to prevent it, because the failure surface is inclined and the bars cross it at an unhelpful angle.**

> **That brittleness is why punching is treated so conservatively, and it is the same class of hazard as web crushing in a beam: a failure mode that additional reinforcement in the usual place does not address.**

> **The most notorious cases are FLAT SLAB structures, where a punching failure at one column can drop the slab onto the floor below and initiate a PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE through the building.**

> **Which is why flat slabs receive drop panels, column capitals, or purpose-made shear reinforcement (shear studs, shear heads), and why the punching check is the governing calculation in flat slab design.**

**The complete footing design sequence, since these checks come in an order:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Size the PLAN AREA from the SERVICE load and the safe bearing capacity: A = (load + footing weight)/SBC** ← note: SERVICE load, unfactored |
| **2** | **Compute the net upward SOIL PRESSURE from the FACTORED load** ← factored, for the structural design |
| **3** | **Check PUNCHING shear at d/2 and fix the DEPTH** ← usually governs |
| **4** | **Check ONE-WAY shear at d from the face** |
| **5** | **Compute the BENDING moment at the column face and the reinforcement** |
| **6** | **Check the DEVELOPMENT LENGTH available from the column face to the footing edge** |
| **7** | **Check bearing pressure on the concrete at the column base, and design the dowels** |

> **Step 1 against step 2 contains the point most often got wrong: THE PLAN AREA IS FIXED BY THE SERVICE LOAD AND THE STRUCTURAL DESIGN BY THE FACTORED LOAD.**

> **The soil's safe bearing capacity is already a working-stress value with its own factor of safety of 2.5 or 3, so applying a load factor to it as well would double-count the safety and give an absurdly large footing.**

> **But the concrete and steel must be designed by the limit state method, which requires factored loads.**

> **So the two steps use different loads for good reasons, and mixing them produces either a wasteful footing or an unsafe one.**

> **Step 6 is the one most often forgotten and it does occasionally govern: a small footing under a large column may not have enough projection to develop the reinforcement, and the bars must then be bent up at the edges or the footing widened.**

examTip.trick: **Bending at the column FACE; one-way shear at distance d; punching shear on a perimeter at d/2 all round.** All three distances appear as options, so match the check named.
examTip.trap: **PUNCHING shear usually fixes the footing's DEPTH** — not bending, not one-way shear. And it cannot be solved by adding reinforcement in practice, so footings are simply made thick enough.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plan AREA from the SERVICE load and the SBC; structural design from the FACTORED load.** The SBC already carries a factor of 2.5-3, so factoring it again double-counts the safety. Mixing the two gives a wasteful or unsafe footing.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the minimum eccentricity to be assumed in the design of a short column is the GREATER of 20 mm and:
questions.solution:
**L/500 + D/30**, where L is the unsupported length and D the lateral dimension in the plane considered.

**The clause:**

> **e_min = GREATER of  [ L/500 + D/30 ]  and  20 mm**

> **For a column 3 m high and 400 mm square:**

> **e_min = 3000/500 + 400/30 = 6.0 + 13.3 = 19.3 mm**

> **Since that is less than 20 mm, the governing value is 20 mm** — which is very often the case for ordinary columns, and is why the 20 mm floor exists.

> **For a taller or larger column: L = 6 m, D = 600 mm gives 12 + 20 = 32 mm, and the formula then governs.**

**Why a MINIMUM eccentricity is required at all — the reasoning:**

> **A column is designed as if the load acts at its centroid, giving pure axial compression.**

> **THAT NEVER HAPPENS. Real columns and real loads depart from the ideal in several ways:**

| Source of unintended eccentricity | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONSTRUCTION tolerance — the column is not exactly where the drawing says** | **Setting-out and formwork errors** ← |
| **The column is not exactly PLUMB** | Erection tolerance |
| **The reinforcement is not exactly centred** | Fixing tolerance |
| **The beam reactions are not exactly balanced** | **Unequal spans, unequal loading, pattern loading** ← |
| **Initial curvature of the member** | Casting and shrinkage |
| **Variation in the concrete's properties across the section** | — |

> **So a nominally axially loaded column always carries SOME moment, and the code requires a minimum to be designed for rather than allowing the ideal case to be assumed.**

> **That is the same reasoning as the minimum reinforcement clauses: the code refuses to permit a design that depends on a perfection construction cannot deliver.**

> **And it means that in IS 456 there is NO SUCH THING as a purely axially loaded column: every column is designed for combined axial load and a moment of at least P × e_min.**

**The consequence for the design equation:**

> **If the eccentricity does not exceed 0.05 D, IS 456 permits the simplified formula for a SHORT AXIALLY LOADED column:**

> **P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc**

| Coefficient | Note |
|---|---|
| **0.4 f_ck** | **The concrete's design compressive strength, reduced from 0.446 to allow for the minimum eccentricity** ← |
| **0.67 f_y** | **The steel's contribution — note 0.67, not 0.87** |
| **A_c** | **The NET concrete area, that is the gross area MINUS the steel area** |

> **The 0.4 rather than 0.446 is precisely where the minimum eccentricity is accounted for: the formula looks like a pure axial capacity but has the minimum moment already built into its coefficient.**

> **So a designer using P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc has satisfied the minimum eccentricity requirement without computing it — provided the ACTUAL eccentricity does not exceed 0.05D.**

> **Where it does, the column must be designed for combined axial load and bending, using an INTERACTION DIAGRAM.**

**Why the steel coefficient is 0.67 f_y and not 0.87 f_y — a point worth understanding:**

> **In a BEAM the steel is in TENSION and reaches its design yield 0.87 f_y, because the section is under-reinforced and the steel yields before the concrete crushes.**

> **In a COLUMN the steel is in COMPRESSION, and it is limited by the CONCRETE'S crushing strain rather than by its own yield strain.**

> **The concrete crushes at a strain of 0.002 in pure compression (not 0.0035, which applies in bending).**

> **At a strain of 0.002, Fe 415 steel has reached a stress of about 342 MPa — which is 0.82 f_y, not 0.87 f_y.**

> **Applying the material factor and rounding, the code takes 0.67 f_y ≈ 0.75 × 0.87 f_y as a conservative design value.**

> **So the steel in a column cannot be worked as hard as in a beam, because the CONCRETE fails first and limits the strain the steel can reach.**

> **That is a genuinely instructive constraint: in a composite section, the LESS DUCTILE material governs how far the other can be exploited.**

**SHORT against SLENDER columns, since the clause specifies short:**

| Classification | Criterion | Design |
|---|---|---|
| **SHORT column** | **Both l_ex/D and l_ey/b LESS than 12** | **The simplified formula applies; failure by CRUSHING** ← |
| **SLENDER column** | **Either ratio 12 or more** | **ADDITIONAL MOMENTS from buckling must be included** |

> **For a slender column, IS 456 requires ADDITIONAL MOMENTS to be added:**

> **M_ax = P_u D (l_ex/D)² / 2000**   and similarly for the other axis.

> **Note the SQUARE: the additional moment grows as the square of the slenderness, so it rises steeply.**

> **For l_ex/D = 12 (the threshold) the additional moment is P_u D × 144/2000 = 0.072 P_u D — that is, an additional eccentricity of 0.072 D, about 29 mm for a 400 mm column.**

> **Which already exceeds the minimum eccentricity of 20 mm — so at the very threshold of slenderness the buckling effect has become the larger of the two, and beyond it, it dominates entirely.**

> **The maximum permitted slenderness ratio is 60 (or 100 D²/b where one end is unrestrained), beyond which a column may not be designed at all — the additional moments become so large that the section is uneconomic and the behaviour unreliable.**

**And the practical detailing consequence, since it follows from all of this:**

> **Because every column carries a moment, the reinforcement must be able to resist it in ANY direction — which is why:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bars are distributed around the PERIMETER, not clustered** | **To resist bending about either axis** ← |
| **At least 4 bars (rectangular) or 6 (circular)** | One near each corner or spread round |
| **Maximum spacing 300 mm along the face** | Distribution |
| **Ties at not more than 16 × the smallest bar diameter** | **To prevent the compression bars BUCKLING between ties** ← |

> **The TIE SPACING rule is the one whose violation is most visible in earthquake damage: widely spaced ties allow the longitudinal bars to buckle outward, the cover spalls, and the column loses both its steel and its confinement at once.**

> **That failure is a direct consequence of the compression steel being a slender strut in its own right — which is why its effective length must be controlled, exactly as the column's own is.**

examTip.trick: **e_min = GREATER of (L/500 + D/30) and 20 mm.** For ordinary columns the 20 mm floor usually governs — a 3 m, 400 mm column gives only 19.3 mm.
examTip.trap: **The minimum eccentricity is already built into P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc** — the 0.4 rather than 0.446 is where it sits. So using that formula satisfies the clause, provided the actual eccentricity stays under 0.05 D.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.67 f_y, not 0.87 f_y, because the CONCRETE crushes at 0.002 strain and limits how far the compression steel can be worked.** In a composite section the less ductile material governs. And additional moments for slender columns grow as the SQUARE of the slenderness.

questions.stem: In a bolted connection, the bearing capacity of a bolt refers to the strength governed by:
options: The shear on the bolt's cross-section
The tension in the bolt shank
The crushing of the connected PLATE material against the bolt shank
The friction between the connected plates
questions.solution:
**The CRUSHING of the connected PLATE material against the bolt shank.**

**The failure modes of a bolted connection, which the options survey:**

| Failure mode | What fails | Design check |
|---|---|---|
| **BOLT SHEAR** | **The bolt is cut across its shank** | **V_dsb = (f_ub/√3)(n_n A_nb + n_s A_sb)/γ_mb** |
| **BEARING (crushing)** | **The PLATE is crushed and elongated by the bolt pressing into it** ← | **V_dpb = 2.5 k_b d t f_u/γ_mb** |
| **BOLT TENSION** | The bolt is pulled apart | For bolts in tension |
| **PLATE TENSION rupture** | The plate tears across the net section | Net section check |
| **PLATE SHEAR-OUT / block shear** | A block of plate tears out beyond the bolt | Block shear check |
| **SLIP** | **The plates slide relative to one another — relevant only for HSFG bolts** | Slip resistance |

> **Each of the four options names one of those modes, so the option set is a survey of the connection's failure possibilities and requires the specific term to be matched.**

> **The essential point is that BEARING IS A PLATE FAILURE, NOT A BOLT FAILURE — the bolt survives and the hole becomes an elongated slot.**

**Why bearing depends on the PLATE, and what that implies:**

> **The bearing capacity formula contains the PLATE'S properties:**

> **V_dpb = 2.5 k_b d t f_u / γ_mb**

| Symbol | Belongs to |
|---|---|
| **d** | **The bolt's diameter** |
| **t** | **The PLATE'S thickness** ← |
| **f_u** | **The PLATE'S ultimate tensile strength** ← |
| **k_b** | **The EDGE DISTANCE and PITCH, and the bolt/plate strength ratio** ← |

> **So a connection can be strengthened against bearing by using a THICKER or STRONGER PLATE, or by increasing the EDGE DISTANCE — and NOT by using a stronger bolt.**

> **That is a practically useful diagnosis: if bearing governs, changing the bolt grade achieves nothing.**

> **And the k_b factor is where the geometry enters:**

> **k_b is the LEAST of:  e/(3d₀),  p/(3d₀) − 0.25,  f_ub/f_u,  and 1.0**

> **where e is the end distance, p the pitch and d₀ the hole diameter.**

> **The first two terms mean that a bolt too CLOSE TO THE EDGE has a reduced bearing capacity — because the plate material behind it is insufficient to resist being pushed out.**

> **Which is why MINIMUM EDGE DISTANCES are specified, and why they are not merely a fabrication nicety:**

| Edge condition | Minimum edge/end distance |
|---|---|
| **A SHEARED or hand-flame-cut edge** | **1.7 × the hole diameter** |
| **A ROLLED, machine-flame-cut, sawn or planed edge** | **1.5 × the hole diameter** |
| **Maximum edge distance** | **12 t ε, or 40 mm + 4t in a corrosive environment** ← |

> **The SHEARED edge requires a LARGER distance because the shearing process work-hardens and micro-cracks the edge, leaving it weaker than a rolled or sawn one.**

> **And the MAXIMUM edge distance exists for a different reason entirely: if the bolt is too far from the edge, the plates can separate and gape between the bolt and the edge, admitting moisture and causing corrosion — so the limit is a DURABILITY requirement, not a strength one.**

**Which mode governs — and it depends on the geometry:**

> **For a connection in single shear with an M20 bolt of grade 4.6 in 10 mm plates of Fe 410:**

| Check | Computation | Capacity |
|---|---|---|
| **Bolt SHEAR (single, threads in the plane)** | **(400/√3) × 245 / 1.25** | **45.3 kN** |
| **BEARING (k_b = 1)** | **2.5 × 1.0 × 20 × 10 × 410 / 1.25** | **164 kN** |
| **GOVERNING** | **The LESSER** | **45.3 kN — bolt shear** ← |

> **So for thin plates and a low-grade bolt in single shear, SHEAR usually governs.**

> **But the balance shifts:**

| Situation | Likely governing mode |
|---|---|
| **THIN plates** | **BEARING — little plate material to resist crushing** ← |
| **THICK plates, single shear** | **BOLT SHEAR** |
| **DOUBLE shear** | **Bearing more likely, since the bolt's shear capacity is DOUBLED but the bearing is not** ← |
| **High-grade bolt in mild plate** | **BEARING** |
| **Small edge distance** | **BEARING, with k_b reduced** |

> **The DOUBLE SHEAR row is worth noting: putting a bolt in double shear doubles its shear capacity but does NOT double its bearing capacity, because the bearing is still limited by the thickness of the plate that bears on it.**

> **So a double-shear connection is more likely to be governed by bearing — and the design must always check BOTH and take the lesser.**

**BEARING-TYPE against FRICTION-TYPE (HSFG) connections, since option (d) names friction:**

| | **BEARING-type (ordinary bolts)** | **FRICTION-type (HSFG bolts)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transferred by** | **BEARING and SHEAR — the plates slip until the bolts bear** | **FRICTION between the plates, from the bolt's PRETENSION** ← |
| **Slip** | **OCCURS — up to the hole clearance** | **NONE, until the friction is overcome** |
| **Bolt** | Grade 4.6, 8.8; snug-tightened | **High-strength (8.8, 10.9), TENSIONED to a specified value** |
| **Suits** | **Static loads; most building connections** | **FATIGUE loading, reversible loads, connections where slip is unacceptable** ← |
| **Surface preparation** | Not critical | **CRITICAL — the slip factor depends on the faying surfaces being clean and untreated** ← |
| **Cost** | Lower | Higher — tensioning must be controlled and verified |

> **The FATIGUE argument is the decisive one for HSFG bolts: in a bearing-type connection under reversing load, the plates slip back and forth within the hole clearance, and that repeated movement wears the hole and initiates fatigue cracks.**

> **A friction-type connection does not slip at all, so there is no relative movement and no wear — which is why bridges, crane girders and machinery supports use HSFG bolts.**

> **The SURFACE PREPARATION row is the practical trap: the slip factor μ depends entirely on the condition of the contact faces, and a painted, oiled or galvanised surface has a much lower μ than a clean, wire-brushed one.**

> **So a friction-grip connection whose faying surfaces were painted before assembly may have a fraction of its design capacity — and the defect is invisible once the joint is made.**

> **Which is why the specification excludes paint from the faying surfaces and why that exclusion must be shown on the drawings and observed on site.**

examTip.trick: **BEARING is a PLATE failure, not a bolt failure** — the hole elongates into a slot. Its formula 2.5 k_b d t f_u/γ_mb contains the PLATE'S thickness and strength, so a stronger BOLT does not help.
