> **So options (c) and (d) are quantities describing the whole season's water use, while the question asks about one particular watering — which makes them the designed distractors.**

> **And option (b) PALEO is the watering at the OTHER end of the sequence, before sowing rather than after germination.**

**Why the kor watering matters so much — and why the canal is sized on it:**

> **The kor watering is the MOST CRITICAL of a crop's waterings, for two reasons:**

> **FIRST — the young plant is at its most vulnerable. A delay at this stage can lose the crop outright, whereas a delay later merely reduces the yield.**

> **SECOND — the whole command area needs it AT ROUGHLY THE SAME TIME, because sowing is concentrated into a short season.**

> **So the kor watering produces the PEAK DEMAND on the canal system, and the canal's FULL SUPPLY DISCHARGE is determined by it:**

> **Q_design = (Area × kor depth) / (kor period)**

| Crop | Kor depth | Kor period |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE** | **190 mm** | **2-4 weeks** |
| **WHEAT** | **135 mm** | **3-4 weeks** |
| **Sugarcane** | **165 mm** | **4 weeks** |
| **Cotton** | **100 mm** | **— ** |

> **So the canal is sized not for the AVERAGE seasonal demand but for the SHORT PEAK of the kor watering — which is a much larger figure.**

> **That is the same principle as sizing a water distribution main for the peak hourly demand rather than the daily average, and for the same reason: the system must deliver when the demand actually occurs.**

**The OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR, which follows from the kor:**

> **The duty computed at the kor period is called the OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR — the duty of water at the head of a watercourse.**

> **It is the figure used to size the outlet and the distributary, because it corresponds to the peak condition rather than to the seasonal average.**

> **For wheat with a kor depth of 135 mm over a kor period of 4 weeks (28 days):**

> **Duty = 8.64 × B/Δ = 8.64 × 28/0.135 = 1792 ha/cumec**

> **So one cumec at the outlet serves about 1790 hectares during the kor watering — and that is the number the distributary's capacity is based on.**

**The other irrigation terms worth having, since this family recurs:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CROP PERIOD** | **Sowing to harvest** |
| **BASE PERIOD** | **First watering to last watering — slightly shorter** |
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **Total depth of water for the whole base period** |
| **DUTY (D)** | **Hectares per cumec over the base period** |
| **KOR watering, depth, period** | **The critical first watering and its parameters** ← |
| **PALEO irrigation** | **Pre-sowing watering** |
| **INTENSITY of irrigation** | Percentage of the CCA irrigated in a season |
| **TIME FACTOR** | **Days the canal actually runs ÷ days in the irrigation period** |
| **CAPACITY FACTOR** | **Average discharge carried ÷ the canal's full supply discharge** |
| **FULL SUPPLY COEFFICIENT** | Same as the outlet discharge factor |
| **CONSUMPTIVE USE (evapotranspiration)** | Water consumed by the crop plus that evaporated from the soil |
| **EFFECTIVE RAINFALL** | The part of the rainfall usefully available to the crop |

> **The TIME FACTOR and CAPACITY FACTOR pair is worth understanding, since both describe how fully a canal is used and they differ:**

> **TIME FACTOR concerns the PROPORTION OF DAYS the canal runs — a canal closed for maintenance or rotation has a time factor below 1.**

> **CAPACITY FACTOR concerns the PROPORTION OF ITS CAPACITY carried while it does run.**

> **A canal running every day at half capacity has a time factor of 1 and a capacity factor of 0.5; one running every other day at full capacity has a time factor of 0.5 and a capacity factor of 1.**

> **The two multiply to give the overall utilisation, and they have different implications: a low time factor means the canal is idle (and possibly silting), while a low capacity factor means it was built too large.**

**And the CONSUMPTIVE USE concept, since it is what all of this is ultimately serving:**

> **CONSUMPTIVE USE (evapotranspiration, ET) is the water actually consumed — transpired by the plants plus evaporated from the soil surface.**

> **It is the crop's real requirement, and the irrigation requirement is derived from it:**

> **NET irrigation requirement = Consumptive use − Effective rainfall − Contribution from groundwater and soil moisture storage**

> **GROSS irrigation requirement = Net requirement / (overall irrigation efficiency)**

| Method of estimating consumptive use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Direct measurement — lysimeters, field experiments** | **The most reliable and the most laborious** |
| **BLANEY-CRIDDLE formula** | **Temperature and daylight hours; simple, widely used in India and Nepal** ← |
| **PENMAN and PENMAN-MONTEITH** | **Energy balance plus aerodynamic terms — the most rigorous, and it needs radiation, humidity and wind data** ← |
| **Modified Penman (FAO)** | The international standard |
| **Pan evaporation with a crop coefficient** | Practical where a pan record exists |
| **Hargreaves, Thornthwaite** | Temperature-based approximations |

> **The choice among them is governed by DATA AVAILABILITY rather than by preference, and that is the honest position: Penman-Monteith is the best method and requires radiation, humidity and wind records that most Nepali stations do not have.**

> **So Blaney-Criddle or a pan-based method is used in practice, with the understanding that it is an approximation — and the resulting uncertainty is one reason irrigation systems are designed with the generous efficiencies and factors discussed earlier.**

examTip.trick: **KOR watering is the FIRST watering after the plants are a few centimetres high** — the most critical one. PALEO is the pre-sowing watering; DELTA and DUTY describe the whole season.
examTip.trap: **The canal is sized on the KOR watering, not the seasonal average** — the whole command needs it at once, so it produces the peak demand. Q = (area × kor depth)/kor period.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kor depths: rice 190 mm, wheat 135 mm, sugarcane 165 mm, over a 2-4 week kor period.** And the TIME factor (days running) differs from the CAPACITY factor (fraction of capacity carried) — a low time factor means idle, a low capacity factor means oversized.

questions.stem: The duty of water at the head of a watercourse, computed for the kor period, is known as the:
questions.solution:
**The OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR**, also called the full supply coefficient.

**The definition:**

> **The OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR is the DUTY of water at the head of a watercourse — that is, the number of hectares that one cumec delivered at the outlet will irrigate.**

> **It is computed for the KOR PERIOD, because that is when the demand peaks and therefore when the outlet's capacity is determined.**

> **Δ = 8.64 B/D, so rearranged:  D = 8.64 B/Δ**, with B the kor period in days and Δ the kor depth in metres.

**A worked example, since the factor is a computed quantity:**

> **For wheat: kor depth 135 mm, kor period 4 weeks = 28 days.**

> **Outlet discharge factor = 8.64 × 28 / 0.135 = 241.9/0.135 = 1792 ha/cumec**

> **So one cumec at the outlet commands about 1790 hectares during the kor watering.**

> **For rice: kor depth 190 mm, kor period 3 weeks = 21 days.**

> **Factor = 8.64 × 21/0.190 = 181.4/0.190 = 955 ha/cumec**

> **Rice's factor is about half wheat's — one cumec commands only half the area — which is the same statement as rice needing roughly twice the water, expressed the other way round.**

**Why the factor is defined AT THE OUTLET specifically:**

> **The duty depends on WHERE it is measured, because conveyance losses intervene:**

| Point of measurement | Duty | Why it differs |
|---|---|---|
| **At the FIELD (nakka)** | **HIGHEST** | Counts only the water the crop receives |
| **At the OUTLET (head of the watercourse)** | **Lower** ← the outlet discharge factor | **Includes the watercourse losses** |
| **At the head of the DISTRIBUTARY** | Lower still | Plus distributary losses |
| **At the CANAL HEAD** | **LOWEST** | Plus all the main canal losses |

> **So a duty figure without its point of reference is incomplete data, and the OUTLET is chosen as the standard reference because that is where the system's responsibility ends and the farmers' begins.**

> **The outlet is the point at which water passes from the government's canal system to the cultivators' own watercourse — so it is the natural place to define a delivery obligation, and hence the natural place to define the duty.**

> **That is an administrative reason as much as a hydraulic one, and it is why the factor is named for the outlet.**

**The OUTLET itself, since the factor sizes it — the three classes:**

| Class | Discharge depends on | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR outlet** | **The levels in BOTH the distributary AND the watercourse** | **A simple pipe or open cut — cheapest, and the discharge varies with everything** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULE (flexible module)** | **The DISTRIBUTARY level only — INDEPENDENT of the watercourse level** | **The practical compromise, and the most used** ← |
| **RIGID MODULE** | **NEITHER — a constant discharge within working limits** | **The fairest, and the most complex and costly** |

> **The SEMI-MODULE is the type used in practice, and the reason is worth understanding:**

> **A non-modular outlet lets a cultivator increase his own supply by lowering his watercourse level — by deepening it, or by drawing water away quickly — which is manifestly unfair to those downstream.**

> **A semi-module cannot be influenced from the watercourse side at all, so the cultivator gets what the distributary level entitles him to and no more.**

> **That removes the principal avenue for tampering, which in an irrigation system serving many independent farmers is the central administrative problem.**

> **The RIGID MODULE goes further and delivers a constant discharge regardless of the distributary level too — which sounds ideal and has a real drawback: when the distributary is running below its full supply level, a rigid module continues to take its full share, so the shortage falls entirely on the outlets that are NOT rigid.**

> **So a rigid module is fair only if ALL outlets are rigid, and a mixture of rigid and semi-modular outlets on one distributary distributes a shortage very unfairly.**

> **That is a genuinely instructive point about equity in a shared system: a device that guarantees one user's supply necessarily transfers the variability onto everyone else.**

**The requirements of a good outlet, since these govern the choice:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **It should be SIMPLE, cheap and robust** | It is replicated thousands of times |
| **It should draw its FAIR SHARE OF SILT** | **CRITICAL — see below** ← |
| **It should be TAMPER-PROOF, with no moving parts** | **No gates the cultivator can adjust** ← |
| **It should work over the expected range of levels** | — |
| **Its discharge should be readily measurable or predictable** | For accountability |
| **It should not be liable to blockage** | — |

> **The SILT-DRAWING requirement is the one that surprises people and it is important:**

> **An outlet that draws LESS than its fair share of silt leaves the excess in the distributary, which then SILTS UP progressively.**

> **An outlet that draws MORE than its share silts up the cultivator's watercourse and his fields.**

> **So the objective is proportionality — each outlet taking silt in the same proportion as it takes water — and an outlet is characterised by its SILT CONDUCTING FACTOR, the ratio of its silt-drawing to its water-drawing capacity.**

> **An outlet drawing from near the BED of the distributary takes silt-rich water; one drawing from higher up takes cleaner water.**

> **Hence the setting of the outlet's sill level is not merely a hydraulic matter but determines whether the distributary or the watercourse silts up — and getting it wrong produces a maintenance liability at one end or the other for the system's whole life.**

> **That is a good illustration of why irrigation engineering is so much concerned with sediment: the water is the product, and the silt it carries determines whether the works remain usable.**

examTip.trick: **The OUTLET DISCHARGE FACTOR is the duty at the head of the watercourse, computed for the KOR period: D = 8.64 B/Δ.** For wheat that is about 1790 ha/cumec; for rice about 955.
examTip.trap: **A duty figure is incomplete without its POINT OF REFERENCE** — field, outlet, distributary head or canal head all differ, because conveyance losses intervene. The outlet is the standard because that is where the system's responsibility ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **NON-MODULAR depends on both levels; SEMI-MODULE on the distributary only (the practical choice, tamper-proof from the watercourse side); RIGID MODULE on neither** — and a rigid module is fair only if ALL outlets are rigid, or it pushes the shortage onto everyone else.

questions.stem: The principal benefit of lining an irrigation canal is:
options: Reduction of seepage losses and the prevention of waterlogging
An increase in the canal's bed slope
An increase in the canal's silt-carrying capacity
A reduction in the canal's command area
questions.solution:
**Reduction of SEEPAGE losses, and hence the prevention of WATERLOGGING.**

**The magnitude of the benefit — why it is the principal one:**

> **Seepage from unlined canals is the LARGEST single loss in most irrigation systems, and commonly the largest source of the recharge that causes waterlogging.**

| Canal condition | Typical seepage loss |
|---|---|
| **Unlined canal in coarse sand or gravel** | **Very high — up to 6 m³/s per million m² of wetted area** |
| **Unlined canal in loam** | **Moderate** |
| **Unlined canal in clay** | **Lower** |
| **LINED canal** | **A fraction — often 10-20 % of the unlined value** ← |

> **Conveyance efficiencies of 60 to 70 per cent are typical for unlined systems and 85 to 95 per cent for lined ones — so lining recovers something like a quarter of the water diverted.**

> **And that recovered water is available WITHOUT building a new headworks, a new reservoir or a new canal — which makes lining one of the cheapest sources of irrigation water available.**

**The DOUBLE benefit, which is the point worth grasping:**

> **Seepage causes harm at BOTH ENDS:**

> **THE WATER IS LOST — it never reaches a crop, so the command area is smaller than the diversion would allow.**

> **AND THE SEEPED WATER CAUSES DAMAGE — it raises the water table alongside the canal, waterlogging the land and bringing salts to the surface.**

> **So lining a canal simultaneously RECOVERS a resource and REMOVES a hazard, and the two benefits are counted together in its justification.**

> **That is unusual: most engineering measures buy one benefit at a cost, and lining buys two.**

**The full list of benefits, since several are substantial:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduced SEEPAGE — more water delivered** | **The principal benefit** ← |
| **Prevention of WATERLOGGING and SALINITY alongside the canal** | **Equally important, and often the greater in the long run** ← |
| **Higher permissible VELOCITY, so a SMALLER section carries the same flow** | **A lined channel cannot scour, so 2 m/s or more is permissible against 0.7-1.0 in earth** ← |
| **Reduced LAND acquisition, since the section is smaller** | Follows from the above |
| **Elimination of WEED GROWTH** | **Weeds increase roughness and reduce capacity substantially** ← |
| **Reduced MAINTENANCE — no silt clearance or bank repair** | A recurring saving |
| **Elimination of the risk of BREACH by burrowing animals** | A real cause of failure in earth banks |
| **Freedom from the regime constraints — no silting or scouring** | Designed by Manning's equation alone |

> **The HIGHER VELOCITY benefit is the one that is easy to overlook and produces a direct capital saving:**

> **An unlined canal's velocity is limited by scour to perhaps 0.7 to 1.0 m/s. A lined canal can carry 2 m/s or more.**

> **So a lined canal carrying the same discharge needs roughly HALF the cross-sectional area — a much smaller excavation, less land, and shorter structures where it crosses obstacles.**

> **And a smaller section on a given slope means less earthwork, which offsets part of the lining's own cost.**

> **The WEED benefit is more significant than it sounds: a weed-grown earth channel can have its Manning's n doubled, from 0.025 to 0.04 or worse, which cuts its capacity by a third — so weed growth alone can make a canal fail to deliver its design flow.**

**Why the other options are wrong — and each is instructive:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(b) Increase the bed slope** | **Lining does NOT change the slope, which is fixed by the topography and the command requirement. It allows a smaller SECTION at the same slope, or the same section at a flatter one** |
| **(c) Increase the silt-carrying capacity** | **Partly true and NOT the purpose. A lined canal's higher velocity does carry more silt through — but the object is to exclude silt at the headworks, not to transport it** ← |
| **(d) Reduce the command area** | **The OPPOSITE: by saving water, lining INCREASES the area that can be commanded from the same diversion** ← |

> **Option (d) is worth its note because it states the benefit backwards, and the correct statement is one of lining's strongest arguments: the water saved extends the command.**

> **A system with 65 per cent conveyance efficiency raised to 90 per cent delivers 38 per cent more water to the fields from the same diversion — which can irrigate a substantially larger area, or irrigate the existing area more reliably in the dry season.**

**The lining types, since the choice is a real one:**

| Lining | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cast in-situ CONCRETE** | **The most durable and most expensive; 75-100 mm thick, with contraction joints** ← |
| **Shotcrete / guniting** | Applied by spray; good for repairs and irregular surfaces |
| **PRECAST concrete slabs** | Quicker; joints are the weakness |
| **BRICK or tile lining** | **Labour-intensive and material-cheap — suits Nepal and India where bricks are local and labour available** ← |
| **Stone (rubble) masonry** | Where stone is local |
| **COMPACTED EARTH / clay puddle lining** | **Cheapest; reduces seepage without eliminating it; needs a clay source** |
| **Boulder lining, soil-cement** | Intermediate |
| **PLASTIC / geomembrane (LDPE, HDPE) with a soil cover** | **Very low seepage, cheap, and VULNERABLE to puncture and to exposure** ← |

> **The GEOMEMBRANE option deserves its note because it is transforming the economics of lining: a polythene sheet costs a fraction of concrete and stops seepage almost completely.**

> **Its weaknesses are entirely practical — it must be protected by a cover of soil or concrete against sunlight, livestock, cultivation and vandalism, and a single puncture leaks.**

> **So the sheet is cheap and the PROTECTION is the cost, and a membrane lining laid without adequate cover fails quickly.**

**And the honest limitation of lining, which must be stated:**

| Drawback | Note |
|---|---|
| **HIGH capital cost** | **Often the reason it is not done, or is done only on the main canal** ← |
| **The canal must be taken out of service to line it** | A season's supply lost, or work confined to the closure period |
| **CRACKING from settlement, uplift and temperature** | **A cracked lining can leak nearly as much as no lining** ← |
| **UPLIFT failure where the outside water table is high** | **The lining can be lifted and burst when the canal is empty — pressure relief valves or weep holes are needed** ← |
| **Loss of the groundwater recharge that the seepage provided** | **Where farmers pump that groundwater, lining removes their source** ← |
| **Maintenance requires different skills and materials** | — |

> **The last drawback is a genuine and under-appreciated one: in some systems the canal's seepage has become the RECHARGE for a shallow aquifer that farmers pump from, and lining the canal dries up their wells.**

> **So the water "saved" was not wholly lost — part of it was being used, just not through the canal — and a lining project's benefit must be assessed net of that.**

> **That is a good instance of a general lesson in water resources: a "loss" from one part of a system is frequently an input to another, and improving efficiency in isolation can transfer a problem rather than solve one.**

examTip.trick: **Lining buys TWO benefits at once: it RECOVERS the seeped water and REMOVES the waterlogging it caused.** Conveyance efficiency rises from 60-70 % to 85-95 %.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) states the benefit backwards** — saving water INCREASES the command area. And lining does not change the SLOPE; it permits a smaller SECTION, because a lined channel tolerates 2 m/s against 0.7-1.0 in earth.
examTip.mnemonic: **A canal's seepage may be the RECHARGE that farmers pump from** — so lining can dry up their wells, and the benefit must be assessed net of that. A "loss" in one part of a water system is often an input to another.

questions.stem: The ratio of the number of days a canal actually runs to the number of days in the irrigation period is called the:
questions.solution:
**The TIME FACTOR.**

**The two utilisation factors, which must be kept apart:**

| Factor | Definition | Describes |
|---|---|---|
| **TIME factor** | **Days the canal ACTUALLY RUNS ÷ days in the irrigation period** ← | **HOW OFTEN it runs** |
| **CAPACITY factor** | **Average discharge carried ÷ the canal's FULL SUPPLY DISCHARGE** | **HOW FULL it runs when it does** |

> **Option (a) is therefore the other member of the pair, and the two are constantly interchanged.**

> **The distinction is best fixed by an example:**

| Canal operation | Time factor | Capacity factor |
|---|---|---|
| **Runs every day at FULL supply** | **1.0** | **1.0** |
| **Runs every day at HALF supply** | **1.0** | **0.5** |
| **Runs every OTHER day at full supply** | **0.5** | **1.0** |
| **Runs 3 days in 4, at 80 % of capacity** | **0.75** | **0.8** |

> **So the two are independent: one describes the TIMING of the operation and the other its INTENSITY.**

> **And their PRODUCT gives the overall utilisation of the canal's capacity over the period.**

**Why a canal does NOT run continuously — the reasons the time factor exists:**

| Reason for closure | Note |
|---|---|
| **ROTATIONAL water supply (warabandi)** | **The canal is run to different branches in turn, so each runs part of the time** ← |
| **Annual maintenance CLOSURE** | **Silt clearance, bank repair, structure maintenance — impossible with water flowing** ← |
| **Insufficient water in the river** | The supply itself fails in the dry season |
| **Demand below the canal's capacity** | Early or late in the season |
| **Repairs after a breach or a flood** | Unplanned |

> **The ROTATIONAL SUPPLY reason is the most significant and is a deliberate operating strategy worth understanding:**

> **When the available water is less than the full demand, there are two ways to distribute the shortage:**

| Strategy | Method | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Run all channels CONTINUOUSLY at reduced discharge** | Everyone gets less all the time | **The discharge falls BELOW the self-cleansing velocity, and the channels SILT UP** ← |
| **ROTATION — run each channel at FULL supply for part of the time** | **Each area gets its full share, in turn** | **Self-cleansing velocity maintained; and the supply to each area is adequate while it lasts** ← |

> **The second is far better, and for two distinct reasons.**

> **HYDRAULICALLY, running at full supply keeps the velocity self-cleansing, so the channels do not silt — whereas continuous reduced running silts every channel in the system at once.**

> **AGRONOMICALLY, a full watering at intervals is more use to a crop than a continuous trickle: the soil is wetted to root depth and then allowed to dry, which is exactly the pattern irrigation aims for.**

> **A continuous small flow wets only the surface, evaporates, and does not reach the roots.**

> **So ROTATION is the correct response to a shortage, and it is why a canal system is designed with a time factor below 1 and operated in rotation as a matter of course rather than as an emergency measure.**

**WARABANDI, since it is the formal system of rotation:**

> **WARABANDI is a fixed roster of turns: each cultivator on a watercourse receives the WHOLE flow of the outlet for a stated number of hours, on a stated day of the week, in a fixed sequence.**

| Feature of warabandi | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each turn's DURATION is proportional to the holding's area** | **Equity by area** ← |
| **The roster is FIXED and published** | **Predictability — the farmer knows when his turn comes** ← |
| **The whole outlet flow goes to one field at a time** | **Adequate depth of watering, and no division losses** |
| **The sequence rotates through the week** | So no one always gets the least convenient time |
| **Enforced by the community and the irrigation department** | — |

> **The PREDICTABILITY is what makes the system work socially, and it is the feature most often lost when a system is poorly managed: a farmer who knows his turn is Thursday at 6 am can plan his cultivation, and one who does not know when water will come cannot.**

> **So the reliability of the schedule matters as much as the quantity of water, and an unreliable system is used inefficiently even when it delivers enough — because farmers over-irrigate when water is available, not knowing when it will next appear.**

> **That is a genuine and important observation about irrigation management: UNRELIABILITY CAUSES WASTE, and improving the reliability of a supply can raise its effective productivity without delivering a drop more water.**

**Where the time factor enters the DESIGN, since it is a design parameter:**

> **The canal's capacity is computed from the peak demand and the time factor:**

> **Q_design = (Area × kor depth) / (kor period × time factor)**

> **A time factor of 0.75, meaning the canal runs 3 days in 4, requires the canal to be 1/0.75 = 1.33 TIMES LARGER than one running continuously.**

> **So a low time factor buys operational flexibility and silt control at the price of a larger canal, and choosing it is a genuine design trade-off:**

| Time factor | Canal size | Operation |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0** | **Smallest** | **Continuous running; no closure possible without loss of supply** |
| **0.8** | **25 % larger** | **Room for rotation and maintenance** ← the usual choice |
| **0.5** | **DOUBLE** | Very flexible, and expensive |

> **The usual practice is a time factor of about 0.8, which provides for a rotational schedule and an annual maintenance closure at a modest increase in capacity.**

> **And note that the time factor must be decided BEFORE the canal is sized, because it directly scales the design discharge — so an operational policy decision determines a capital cost, which is a good example of design and operation being inseparable.**

examTip.trick: **TIME factor = days the canal RUNS ÷ days in the period (how OFTEN). CAPACITY factor = average discharge ÷ full supply (how FULL).** Option (a) is the other member of the pair.
examTip.trap: **ROTATION is the correct response to a shortage, not continuous reduced running** — reduced flow drops below the self-cleansing velocity and silts every channel, and a trickle never reaches the roots.
examTip.mnemonic: **A time factor of 0.8 means the canal must be 25 % LARGER** — Q = (area × kor depth)/(kor period × time factor). So an operating policy fixes a capital cost, and the factor must be chosen before the canal is sized.

questions.stem: A FISH LADDER at a diversion headworks is provided:
options: To pass surplus flood water safely
To enable fish to migrate past the barrier
To exclude silt from the canal head
To measure the discharge passing the weir
questions.solution:
**To enable FISH to migrate past the barrier.**

**Why a fish ladder is needed:**

> **Many fish species MIGRATE along a river — upstream to spawn and downstream as juveniles — and a weir or barrage BLOCKS that migration completely.**

> **The consequence is not merely a reduction in fish numbers but the loss of the species from the whole reach above the barrier, since it cannot reach its spawning grounds.**

> **That is an ecological loss and, in a country where river fisheries support livelihoods and nutrition, an economic and social one.**

> **A FISH LADDER (fish pass, fishway) provides a route past the structure that a fish can negotiate.**

**How it works — the design principle:**

> **The total fall across the weir is DIVIDED INTO SMALL STEPS, each of which a fish can ascend.**

| Design parameter | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Velocity in the ladder** | **NOT MORE than about 3-3.5 m/s — a fish cannot swim against more** ← |
| **Drop between successive pools** | **Small enough for the fish to leap or swim — typically 150-300 mm** ← |
| **Pool size** | **Large enough for the fish to REST between efforts** ← |
| **A continuous flow of ATTRACTION water** | **So the fish can FIND the entrance** ← critical |
| **Entrance located where fish naturally congregate** | **At the downstream face, near the main flow** |
| **Operation at ALL river stages** | The fish migrate when they migrate, not when convenient |

> **The two requirements that make or break a fish ladder are the VELOCITY LIMIT and the ATTRACTION FLOW.**

> **The velocity limit is a biological constraint: a fish's sustained swimming speed is limited, and a ladder with too steep a slope simply cannot be ascended however well built.**

> **So the ladder must be LONG, and a high weir needs a very long fishway — which is why fish passes at large barrages are substantial structures rather than appurtenances.**

> **The ATTRACTION FLOW is the requirement most often neglected and the commonest cause of a fish ladder that does not work: a fish arriving at the foot of a weir searches for a way through, and it follows the FLOW.**

> **If the ladder's discharge is small compared with the weir's, the fish never finds the entrance — and a perfectly designed ladder passes no fish because nothing enters it.**

> **So the ladder must discharge enough water, and be located where the fish will encounter it, and a ladder tucked into a convenient corner of the structure is likely to be useless.**

**The types of fish pass, since several exist:**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **POOL AND WEIR (stepped pools)** | **A series of pools separated by small weirs — the classic and simplest form** ← |
| **DENIL fishway** | Baffles in a steep chute dissipate energy, allowing a steeper slope |
| **VERTICAL SLOT fishway** | **Slots in successive baffles; works over a wide range of water levels** ← |
| **Fish LOCK** | A chamber operated like a navigation lock |
| **Fish LIFT (elevator)** | **Fish are trapped and physically lifted — for very high dams** ← |
| **Bypass channel (nature-like fishway)** | **A gently sloping artificial stream around the structure — the most effective, and needs the most room** ← |
| **Trap and truck** | Fish are caught and transported by road |

> **The NATURE-LIKE BYPASS CHANNEL is now widely regarded as the most effective, and the reason is instructive: rather than requiring the fish to negotiate an engineered structure, it provides a low-gradient artificial stream that resembles a natural channel, which a much wider range of species and sizes can use.**

> **An engineered ladder is typically designed around one target species' swimming ability, and it may be impassable to smaller fish, to bottom-dwelling species, and to invertebrates.**

> **A bypass channel with a natural bed passes almost everything, and it also provides habitat in its own right — but it requires land and a long gentle gradient, which a confined site cannot give.**

> **The FISH LIFT exists for the case where no ladder is possible: a dam 100 m high cannot have a fishway of acceptable slope, so the fish are collected and lifted mechanically.**

> **Which raises a point worth stating plainly: for a HIGH DAM there is no satisfactory solution to fish passage, and the loss of migratory fish is a genuine and largely unmitigated impact of high dams.**

> **That is the honest position rather than the comfortable one, and it belongs in an environmental assessment as such.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real component of the headworks:**

| Option | The component that does it |
|---|---|
| **(a) Pass surplus flood water** | **The WEIR or BARRAGE itself, with its under-sluices and spillway** |
| **(c) Exclude silt from the canal head** | **The SILT EXCLUDER, the divide wall and the still pond arrangement** |
| **(d) Measure the discharge** | A meter flume or a gauged section |

> **So the option set surveys the headworks' components and requires the ecological one to be identified — which is appropriate, since the fish ladder is the only component present for a reason other than water management.**

**The wider environmental provisions at a diversion, since the fish ladder is one of several:**

| Provision | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FISH LADDER or bypass** | **Upstream and downstream fish passage** ← |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL (minimum) FLOW release** | **Maintain the river's habitat downstream — in Nepal, at least 10 % of the minimum monthly average flow** ← |
| **Fish screens at the canal intake** | **Prevent fish being drawn into the canal, where they are lost** ← |
| **Sediment sluicing to maintain the downstream sediment regime** | A starved river degrades its bed |
| **Provision for downstream passage of juveniles** | Often harder than upstream passage |

> **The FISH SCREEN at the intake is the complement to the ladder and is frequently forgotten: a ladder lets fish past the weir, and an unscreened canal intake then draws them into the irrigation system, where they die.**

> **So passage and screening must be provided together, or the ladder merely delivers fish into a trap.**

> **And the ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW is the provision on which all the others depend: a fish ladder is useless if the river below the weir is dry, and a minimum flow release is what keeps the downstream reach habitable at all.**

> **Which is why the environmental flow requirement, though it costs generation or irrigation water, is the foundation of the whole set of mitigation measures rather than one item among them.**

examTip.trick: **A fish ladder divides the fall into small steps a fish can ascend** — velocity not more than about 3-3.5 m/s, drops of 150-300 mm, and pools large enough to REST in.
examTip.trap: **The ATTRACTION FLOW is the requirement most often neglected** — a fish follows the flow to find the entrance, so a ladder with too small a discharge or a badly placed entrance passes no fish however well built.
examTip.mnemonic: **A ladder without an intake FISH SCREEN merely delivers fish into a trap** — the canal draws them in and they are lost. And for a HIGH dam there is no satisfactory passage solution; that impact is largely unmitigated, and should be stated as such.

questions.stem: By Bligh's creep theory, the total creep length for a hydraulic structure with a floor length of 40 m, an upstream cut-off 4 m deep and a downstream cut-off 6 m deep is:
questions.solution:
**60 m.**

**Bligh's creep length:**

> **L = floor length + 2(d₁ + d₂)**

> **Bligh's theory treats HORIZONTAL and VERTICAL creep as EQUALLY effective — the whole distinction that Lane later introduced does not exist here.**

**The computation:**

> **L = 40 + 2(4 + 6) = 40 + 20 = 60 m** ✓

> **Option (a) 40 m is the floor length alone, with the cut-offs omitted.**

> **Option (b) 50 m omits the FACTOR OF 2 on the cut-offs: 40 + (4 + 6) = 50.**

> **Option (c) 53.3 m is LANE'S weighted creep length: 40/3 + 2(10) = 13.3 + 20 = 33.3 — no; recomputing, Lane gives 13.33 + 20 = 33.3 m. The 53.3 m figure corresponds to weighting differently, and is offered as a plausible near value.**

> **So the two errors the option set punishes are omitting the cut-offs entirely and omitting the factor of two on them.**

**Why the factor of 2 appears — the physical picture:**

> **Water seeping beneath the structure travels DOWN one face of a cut-off and UP the other.**

> **So a cut-off of depth d contributes 2d to the creep path, not d.**

> **The check is to trace the path with a finger: from the upstream water, DOWN the upstream cut-off, ALONG the floor, DOWN and UP the downstream cut-off, and out — each cut-off traversed twice.**

> **Forgetting it halves the vertical contribution and gives option (b).**

**BLIGH against LANE — the comparison the option set invites:**

| | **BLIGH'S creep theory** | **LANE'S weighted creep theory** |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal creep** | **Counted at FULL value** | **Weighted at ONE THIRD** ← |
| **Vertical creep** | **Counted at full value** | **Counted at full value** |
| **Creep length here** | **40 + 20 = 60 m** ← | **40/3 + 20 = 33.3 m** |
| **Basis** | **Empirical; head lost uniformly along the path** | **Empirical, with an observational correction** |
| **Coefficient** | **Bligh's coefficient C** | **Lane's weighted creep coefficient C** |

> **LANE'S refinement came from the observation that VERTICAL cut-offs are FAR more effective at destroying seepage head than an equal length of horizontal floor.**

> **Bligh's equal treatment therefore OVERSTATES the value of a long floor, and a structure designed on Bligh's theory with a long floor and shallow cut-offs may be less safe than the creep length suggests.**

> **Which is exactly the error Khosla's later work identified and quantified — and it explains the change in weir design practice from long floors to deep end cut-offs.**

**How the creep length is USED — safety against piping:**

> **The criterion:  L ≥ C × H**, where H is the seepage head and C the creep coefficient for the soil.

> **Bligh's coefficients:**

| Soil | Bligh's C |
|---|---|
| **Fine micaceous sand (Indo-Gangetic alluvium)** | **15** |
| **Coarse-grained sand** | **12** |
| **Sand mixed with boulders and gravel; loam** | **5-9** |
| **Light sand and mud** | **8** |

> **So for this structure with L = 60 m in fine sand (C = 15), the permissible seepage head is:**

> **H = L/C = 60/15 = 4 m**

> **That is a very modest head for a 40 m floor, which illustrates why creep-theory designs produced such long floors — and why they were expensive.**

> **The pattern in the coefficients is the same as in every seepage criterion: the FINER the soil, the LARGER the coefficient required, because fine particles are lifted at a gentler gradient.**

**The other use of the creep length — UPLIFT and floor thickness:**

> **Bligh's theory assumes the head is lost UNIFORMLY along the creep path, so at any point the residual head is:**

> **h = H (1 − L_travelled / L_total)**

> **That residual head acts UPWARD on the floor, and the floor must be thick enough that its own submerged weight holds it down:**

> **t = h / (G − 1)**, with G ≈ 2.24 for concrete

> **So a residual head of 2 m requires a floor thickness of 2/1.24 = 1.61 m — a substantial slab.**

> **And a factor of safety of about 4/3 is usually applied, giving t = 4h/(3(G−1)).**

> **Note that the floor is thickest where the residual head is greatest — that is, at the UPSTREAM end of the downstream floor, just below the crest — and it tapers downstream as the head is dissipated.**

> **Which is why weir floors are drawn as tapering slabs rather than uniform ones, and it follows directly from the uniform-loss assumption.**

**And the honest assessment of these theories, which is worth stating:**

| | **Creep theories (Bligh, Lane)** | **KHOSLA'S theory** |
|---|---|---|
| **Basis** | **EMPIRICAL — an assumed uniform loss along a path** | **MATHEMATICAL — the actual potential flow, by conformal mapping** |
| **Uniform head loss assumption** | **Central to the method, and NOT TRUE** ← | Not needed |
| **Intermediate sheet piles** | **Credited at full value** | **Shown to be nearly USELESS** ← |
| **Output** | A creep length to compare with the head | **Uplift pressures at defined points, and the EXIT GRADIENT** |
| **Status** | **Superseded; retained for its simplicity and for older designs** | **Standard practice** |

> **The UNIFORM LOSS assumption is the theories' central weakness: the real head loss is NOT uniform along the path — it is concentrated near the cut-offs and near the exit, which is precisely why the exit gradient can be dangerous while the average gradient looks safe.**

> **So Bligh's theory can pass a structure that Khosla's analysis would condemn, and the difference is not a refinement but a change in the failure mode considered.**

> **The creep theories remain on the syllabus because they are quick, because they give a first check, and because a great many existing structures were designed by them — which is a good reason to understand them and not a reason to use them for new work.**

examTip.trick: **Bligh: L = floor length + 2(d₁ + d₂) = 40 + 20 = 60 m.** Horizontal and vertical creep count EQUALLY, unlike Lane's.
examTip.trap: **Each cut-off contributes 2d, not d** — the water goes DOWN one face and UP the other. Trace it with a finger. Option (b) 50 m omits that factor of two.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh's central assumption — UNIFORM head loss along the path — is not true**, and the loss is really concentrated at the cut-offs and the exit. That is why Bligh can pass a structure Khosla would condemn, and why the exit gradient is the criterion that matters.

questions.stem: GUIDE BANKS at a bridge or barrage are provided principally:
options: To guide the river through the waterway and prevent it outflanking the structure
To increase the river's discharge capacity
To trap sediment upstream of the structure
To provide an embankment for the approach road
questions.solution:
**To GUIDE the river through the waterway and to prevent it OUTFLANKING the structure.**

**The problem guide banks solve:**

> **A large alluvial river does not stay where it is put. It MEANDERS, shifts its course, and can move its channel by hundreds of metres in a single flood season.**

> **A bridge or barrage, however, is fixed — and its waterway is much NARROWER than the river's flood plain.**

> **So two dangers arise:**

| Danger | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The river approaches the structure OBLIQUELY** | **The flow attacks one abutment, scours it, and the approach is uneven** ← |
| **The river OUTFLANKS the structure entirely** | **It cuts a new channel AROUND the end of the works, leaving the bridge spanning dry land** ← catastrophic |

> **The second is the failure guide banks primarily exist to prevent, and it has happened: a bridge left standing over a dry bed while the river flows round it through the approach embankment.**

> **GUIDE BANKS (also called BELL'S BUNDS, after their originator) are earthen embankments, armoured with stone pitching, that extend UPSTREAM and DOWNSTREAM of the structure on both sides, converging on the waterway.**

> **They confine the river to an approach corridor and deliver it to the waterway CENTRALLY and AXIALLY.**

**The standard dimensions, since they are asked:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM length** | **1.0 to 1.25 times the waterway length L** ← |
| **DOWNSTREAM length** | **0.2 to 0.4 L** |
| **Total length** | **About 1.25 to 1.5 L** |
| **Shape in plan** | **Straight, with a CURVED (upstream) head — a mole head** ← |
| **Radius of the upstream curved head** | **0.4 to 0.5 L, sweeping through 120-145°** |
| **Radius of the downstream curved tail** | **0.3 to 0.5 of the upstream radius, through 45-60°** |
| **Side slopes** | **2:1 or flatter, with stone pitching** |
| **Top width** | 3-6 m, often carrying a road |
| **Free board above the design HFL** | 1.0-1.5 m |

> **The UPSTREAM length being greater than the downstream is the feature worth understanding: the upstream bank must reach far enough up to intercept the river's approach and turn it, while the downstream bank need only prevent the emerging flow from attacking the embankment as it expands again.**

> **And the CURVED HEAD is essential rather than decorative: a straight-ended bank presents a blunt obstruction that the flow attacks fiercely, while a curved head turns the flow gradually and reduces the scour at the nose.**

**The critical design element — SCOUR AT THE NOSE:**

> **The upstream curved head, the "mole head", is where the flow is turned most sharply, and it suffers the most severe scour of any part of the works:**

| Location | Design scour depth |
|---|---|
| **Nose of the upstream guide bank head** | **2.0 to 2.5 R (Lacey's normal scour depth)** ← |
| **Along the straight shank of the guide bank** | **1.5 R** |
| **Downstream tail** | 1.25 to 1.5 R |
| **At the bridge piers** | 2.0 R |

> **So the guide bank nose is designed for the DEEPEST scour anywhere in the scheme — deeper than the piers — and it receives the heaviest protection.**

> **The protection is a LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone laid on the bed around the nose: as the scour hole forms, the stone slides down and armours the slope, building its own protection to whatever depth the river scours.**

> **The apron's stone QUANTITY is the critical design figure, computed for the launched slope down to the anticipated scour depth — and its failure mode is simply running out of stone.**

> **A guide bank nose whose apron exhausts itself is undermined and breached, and the breach then admits the river behind the bank — which is the outflanking failure the bank existed to prevent.**

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(b) Increase the discharge capacity** | **Guide banks CONFINE the river, which if anything RESTRICTS the waterway. They do not increase capacity — they make the available waterway work properly** ← |
| **(c) Trap sediment upstream** | **Not their purpose. The confinement actually increases the velocity, so sediment is carried THROUGH rather than deposited** |
| **(d) Approach road embankment** | **The approach embankment is a separate structure. A guide bank's top may carry a road incidentally, and that is not why it is built** |

> **Option (b) contains a misconception worth naming: confining a river between guide banks does not increase the flood it can pass, and the AFFLUX — the rise in upstream water level caused by the constriction — is a cost of the works that must be computed and provided for in the approach embankment levels and the land acquisition.**

> **So guide banks make a constricted waterway WORK; they do not remove the constriction.**

**The other river training works, since guide banks are one of a family:**

| Work | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **GUIDE BANKS (Bell's bunds)** | **Guide the river to a structure's waterway; prevent outflanking** ← |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS / flood embankments** | **Confine the flood and protect land from inundation** |
| **GROYNES / spurs** | **Protect a bank and rebuild a bank line** |
| **REVETMENT / pitching** | Armour a bank face directly |
| **Artificial CUT-OFF** | Shorten the course through a severe meander |
| **Bed bars, sills** | Control the bed level |
| **Bio-engineering** | Low-cost bank protection |

> **The MARGINAL BUND deserves a note because it is often confused with a guide bank and serves a different purpose:**

> **A GUIDE BANK guides the river TO a structure and is short — a fraction of the waterway length.**

> **A MARGINAL BUND runs for KILOMETRES along the river to keep the flood off the land, and it has nothing to do with any structure.**

> **And marginal bunds carry their own risk, worth stating: confining a river between embankments raises its flood level, accelerates the deposition of sediment WITHIN the confined channel, and progressively RAISES THE BED — so the embankments must be raised in turn, and the river ends up flowing above the surrounding land.**

> **When such an embankment eventually breaches, the flood is far more destructive than an unconfined one would have been, because the water falls from a perched channel onto land that has been developed in the belief that it was protected.**

> **That is the well-documented history of the embanked rivers of the Terai and north Bihar, and it is a genuine caution about a measure that appears straightforwardly beneficial.**

examTip.trick: **Guide banks confine an alluvial river to deliver it CENTRALLY and AXIALLY to the waterway, and prevent it OUTFLANKING the structure** — cutting a new channel round the end of the works.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is a misconception: guide banks do not increase capacity** — they make a constricted waterway work. The AFFLUX from the constriction is a cost to be computed, not removed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Upstream length 1.0-1.25 L, downstream 0.2-0.4 L, with a CURVED mole head** whose nose is designed for 2.0-2.5 R scour — deeper than the piers. Its launching apron's failure mode is running out of stone, and that breach admits the river behind the bank.

questions.stem: A river is generally classified as MEANDERING when its sinuosity (the ratio of the channel length to the direct axial length) exceeds about:
questions.solution:
**About 1.5.**

**The definition and the classification:**

> **SINUOSITY = (length measured ALONG the channel) / (direct AXIAL length between the same two points)**

> **It is therefore always at least 1, and equals 1 only for a perfectly straight channel.**

| Sinuosity | Classification |
|---|---|
| **1.0 to about 1.05** | **STRAIGHT — and note that a truly straight natural alluvial river is very rare** |
| **1.05 to 1.5** | **SINUOUS (transitional)** |
| **Above 1.5** | **MEANDERING** ← |
| **Above 2.5-3.0** | **Tortuous — a highly developed meander pattern** |

> **So options (a) and (b) are within the sinuous range and option (d) describes a tortuous river, which makes the option set a test of where the meandering threshold falls.**

**Why rivers meander at all — the mechanism:**

> **A straight alluvial channel is UNSTABLE. Any small disturbance — a local obstruction, a variation in bank material, a bar — deflects the flow slightly toward one bank.**

> **That deflection sets up a self-reinforcing process:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **The flow is deflected against one bank** |
| **2** | **The velocity is HIGHER on that (outer) bank, so it ERODES** ← |
| **3** | **A HELICOIDAL (spiral) secondary current develops: surface water moves outward, bed water inward** ← |
| **4** | **The inward bed current carries eroded material to the INNER bank, where it DEPOSITS as a point bar** |
| **5** | **The bend therefore grows: eroding outside, building inside** |
| **6** | **The flow is thrown across to the opposite bank downstream, and the process repeats in the other direction** |

> **The HELICOIDAL CURRENT in step 3 is the mechanism that makes a meander grow rather than merely persist, and it is worth understanding:**

> **At a bend, centrifugal effects push the faster SURFACE water toward the OUTER bank, raising the water surface there (superelevation).**

> **That surface slope drives a return flow along the BED, inward toward the inner bank.**

> **The bed current carries the sediment it has picked up from the scoured outer bank and deposits it on the inner bank — so material is transferred ACROSS the channel, deepening the outside and building the inside.**

> **The result is the characteristic asymmetric bend section: DEEP on the outside (the pool), SHALLOW on the inside (the point bar).**

> **And it explains why the deep channel — the thalweg — swings from side to side, crossing at the inflection points between bends where a shallow RIFFLE or crossing forms.**

**The consequences for engineering, which are the reason this matters:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The OUTER bank erodes — continuously and predictably** | **Land is lost; structures on the outer bank are attacked** ← |
| **The meander MIGRATES downstream and grows outward** | **A bridge or intake fixed in position finds the river moving away from or against it** ← |
| **Maximum SCOUR at the outer bank of a bend** | **1.5 R for a moderate bend, 1.75 R for a severe one, 2.0 R for a right-angled bend** ← |
| **The inner bank builds up, so the channel may become too shallow for an intake** | A common cause of intake failure |
| **Eventually a CUT-OFF forms, abandoning the loop as an oxbow lake** | **A sudden and complete change of course** ← |

> **The CUT-OFF is the event that most often destroys works: as a meander loop grows, its neck narrows, until a flood cuts across it and the river abandons the loop entirely — instantaneously shortening its course and steepening its slope.**

> **A structure built on the loop is left on a backwater, and the new steepened reach scours vigorously.**

> **So a bridge or an intake should NOT be sited on a meander loop, and predicting where the river will be in fifty years is part of siting it — which is why old maps, satellite imagery and the flood-plain geomorphology are studied before a site is chosen.**

> **That is one of the clearest instances in civil engineering where reading the LANDFORM tells you more than any calculation: the abandoned channels, oxbows and scroll bars on the flood plain record where the river has been, and they indicate where it can go again.**

**Where to site works on a meandering river, since the mechanism gives the answer:**

| Location | Suitability |
|---|---|
| **At a NODAL POINT — where the river is confined by rock or high ground and cannot shift** | **THE BEST site; the position is stable** ← |
| **On a STRAIGHT reach between bends** | Reasonable, with training works |
| **On the OUTER bank of a bend** | **Deep water (good for an intake) and severe erosion (bad for everything)** ← |
| **On the INNER bank of a bend** | **Shallow and silting — an intake here will be left dry** ← |
| **On a meander LOOP liable to cut off** | **The worst — the river may leave altogether** |

> **The NODAL POINT is what a river engineer looks for first, and it is why so many bridges and headworks in the Himalayan foothills sit exactly where the river emerges from a gorge or passes a rock outcrop.**

> **At such a point the river's position is fixed by geology rather than by training works, and the structure needs far less protection.**

> **The OUTER-BANK entry contains the classic dilemma of intake siting: the outer bank of a bend has the DEEP water an intake needs and the EROSION that will destroy it.**

> **The usual resolution is to site the intake on the outer bank of a bend that is CONFINED — by rock, or by substantial protection works — so the depth is available and the erosion is controlled.**

> **And the inner bank is avoided absolutely for an intake, because the point bar builds progressively and the intake is left above the water within a few seasons — which is a documented and repeated failure in Nepali and Indian irrigation intakes.**

**The meander geometry relations, since they are asked:**

| Relation | Approximate form |
|---|---|
| **Meander LENGTH (wavelength)** | **About 10-14 times the channel width; or 54.7 Q^{0.5} in metres** |
| **Meander BELT width** | **About 17-18 times the channel width** |
| **Radius of curvature** | **About 2-3 times the channel width** |
| **Meander length / meander belt width** | About 0.6-0.8 |

> **The striking feature of those relations is that meander geometry SCALES WITH THE CHANNEL WIDTH, and hence with the discharge — so a meander pattern looks the same on a small stream and a great river, differing only in scale.**

> **That self-similarity is one of the more elegant facts in river engineering, and it means the geometry can be predicted for an ungauged river from its width alone — which is useful precisely where data are lacking.**

examTip.trick: **Sinuosity above about 1.5 means MEANDERING.** Below 1.05 straight, 1.05-1.5 sinuous, above 2.5-3 tortuous.
examTip.trap: **Meanders GROW by a HELICOIDAL current** — surface water outward, bed water inward — which carries material from the scoured outer bank to the inner bank. That is why bends deepen outside and build inside.
examTip.mnemonic: **Site works at a NODAL POINT where rock confines the river.** Never site an intake on the INNER bank — the point bar builds and leaves it dry within a few seasons. And meander geometry scales with the channel WIDTH, so it can be predicted for an ungauged river.

questions.stem: An irrigation outlet that delivers a constant discharge irrespective of the water levels in BOTH the distributary and the watercourse, within working limits, is called:
questions.solution:
**A RIGID MODULE.**

**The three classes of outlet, defined by what their discharge depends on:**

| Class | Discharge depends on | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** | **The levels in BOTH the distributary AND the watercourse** | **A simple pipe outlet, an open sluice** ← |
| **SEMI-MODULE (flexible module)** | **The DISTRIBUTARY level ONLY — independent of the watercourse** | **Kennedy's gauge outlet, open flume, orifice semi-module** |
| **RIGID MODULE** | **NEITHER — constant within working limits** ← | **Gibb's module, Khanna's module** |

> **Option (d) "pipe outlet" is a specific example of a NON-MODULAR outlet, which makes it a well-made distractor: it names a real device belonging to the wrong class.**

**How a rigid module achieves a constant discharge — the mechanism:**

> **GIBB'S MODULE is the classic design and its principle is worth understanding:**

> **Water enters an inlet pipe and passes into a RISING SPIRAL (helical) channel.**

> **In that spiral, the water develops a FREE VORTEX motion, in which the velocity is higher at the inner radius than at the outer.**

> **A series of BAFFLES projects into the spiral from its roof.**

> **When the head RISES, the water level in the spiral rises, strikes MORE baffles, and loses MORE energy in turbulence — so the discharge does not increase.**

> **The excess head is DELIBERATELY DESTROYED rather than being allowed to increase the flow.**

> **That is the essential idea of every rigid module: the extra energy from a higher head is DISSIPATED, so the discharge remains constant.**

> **It is an entirely mechanical, self-regulating device with no moving parts — which is what makes it suitable for an irrigation system where thousands of outlets must operate unattended and untampered.**

**Why rigid modules are nevertheless UNCOMMON — the honest assessment:**

| Drawback | Note |
|---|---|
| **COMPLEX and expensive to build** | **A spiral channel with baffles, against a length of pipe** ← |
| **Bulky, needing a substantial structure** | Space at the distributary bank |
| **Requires a MINIMUM WORKING HEAD to function** | Cannot be used where the head is small |
| **Liable to blockage by weeds and debris** | The baffles catch material |
| **It DESTROYS head deliberately** | **Head is a scarce resource in a flat command area** ← |
| **The equity problem — see below** | **The decisive objection** ← |

> **The EQUITY problem is the one that governs practice and it is worth setting out fully:**

> **When a distributary runs BELOW its full supply level — which happens whenever the river is short — a rigid module CONTINUES TO DRAW ITS FULL DISCHARGE.**

> **So the shortage is not shared: it falls entirely on the outlets that are NOT rigid.**

> **A distributary with a mixture of rigid and semi-modular outlets therefore distributes a shortage very unfairly, and the rigid outlets' owners are insulated from a scarcity everyone else bears.**

> **A rigid module is thus fair ONLY IF EVERY outlet on the distributary is rigid — and converting a whole system is rarely practicable.**

> **The SEMI-MODULE is the practical answer: its discharge falls proportionally as the distributary level falls, so a shortage is shared automatically among all the outlets — and it is independent of the watercourse, so a cultivator cannot increase his own share by working on his channel.**

> **That combination — PROPORTIONAL in shortage, TAMPER-PROOF from below — is why the semi-module dominates in practice despite the rigid module being technically superior at a single outlet.**

> **It is a clear case of a SYSTEM-LEVEL requirement (equitable distribution) overriding a COMPONENT-LEVEL virtue (constant discharge), and that is a distinction worth carrying beyond irrigation.**

**The requirements of a good outlet, which explain the ranking:**

| Requirement | Non-modular | Semi-module | Rigid module |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Simple and cheap** | **BEST** | Good | Poor |
| **Tamper-proof from the watercourse** | **POOR — a cultivator can lower his channel and take more** ← | **GOOD** | **GOOD** |
| **Proportional sharing of a shortage** | Partly | **GOOD** ← | **POOR** ← |
| **Constant supply to the cultivator** | Poor | Fair | **BEST** |
| **Works with a small head** | **BEST** | Good | Poor |
| **Draws a fair share of SILT** | Variable | **Designed for** | Variable |

> **The TAMPER-PROOF row is the reason non-modular outlets are avoided despite their simplicity: a cultivator who deepens his watercourse, or draws the water away rapidly, lowers the level on the downstream side of his outlet and increases his own discharge at everyone else's expense.**

> **That is not a hypothetical abuse but the ordinary behaviour of a system in which water is scarce and the means of taking more is available — so removing the opportunity is more effective than policing it.**

> **Which is a general principle in the design of shared infrastructure: a device that CANNOT be tampered with is worth more than one that merely should not be.**

**And the SILT-DRAWING requirement, since it is the other half of an outlet's job:**

> **An outlet must draw silt in the SAME PROPORTION as it draws water, or one side of the system silts up:**

| Outlet behaviour | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Draws LESS than its share of silt** | **The excess stays in the distributary, which SILTS UP progressively** ← |
| **Draws MORE than its share** | **The cultivator's watercourse and fields silt up** |
| **Draws its FAIR share** | **The objective — the system stays in balance** |

> **The controlling factor is the SILL LEVEL: an outlet drawing from near the distributary's BED takes silt-rich water, and one drawing higher up takes cleaner water.**

> **Since sediment concentration is greatest near the bed, the sill level directly determines the silt drawn — and setting it is therefore not merely a hydraulic decision but one that determines whether the distributary or the watercourse accumulates the sediment for the system's whole life.**

> **An outlet's SILT CONDUCTING FACTOR expresses that ratio, and a well-designed system has outlets whose factors are close to unity throughout — which keeps the sediment moving to the fields where, in moderation, it is beneficial.**

examTip.trick: **RIGID module: independent of BOTH levels. SEMI-MODULE: independent of the WATERCOURSE only. NON-MODULAR: depends on both.** Option (d), a pipe outlet, is a non-modular example.
examTip.trap: **A rigid module creates an EQUITY problem: when the distributary runs low it keeps taking its full share, so the shortage falls entirely on the non-rigid outlets.** It is fair only if ALL outlets are rigid.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gibb's module destroys the excess head deliberately** — a rising level strikes more baffles and loses more energy, so the discharge stays constant. And the SEMI-MODULE wins in practice because it shares shortages proportionally AND cannot be tampered with from the watercourse.

questions.stem: For satisfactory crop growth, the water table should generally be maintained at a depth below the ground surface of at least:
questions.solution:
**1.0 to 1.5 m below the ground surface.**

**Why that depth — the two requirements it satisfies:**

> **FIRST — THE ROOT ZONE MUST BE AERATED.**

> **Most crops root to 0.5 to 1.0 m, and those roots require AIR as well as water. A water table within the root zone saturates it and the roots suffocate.**

> **SECOND — CAPILLARY RISE MUST NOT REACH THE ROOT ZONE OR THE SURFACE.**

> **Water rises above the water table by capillarity, and in a silty soil that rise can be 1 to 3 m.**

> **If capillary water reaches the SURFACE, it evaporates there and leaves its dissolved SALTS behind — the salinisation mechanism.**

> **So the water table must be deep enough that neither the roots are drowned nor the surface is fed by capillary rise, and 1.0 to 1.5 m is the conventional criterion.**

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) are all shallower than the root depth of most crops, and a water table at any of those depths constitutes WATERLOGGING.**

**The critical depth by soil type, since capillary rise governs it:**

| Soil | Capillary rise | Required water table depth |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse sand and gravel** | **Negligible to 0.15 m** | **1.0 m is ample** |
| **Fine sand** | **0.3 to 1.0 m** | **1.0-1.5 m** |
| **SILT and silty loam** | **1 to 3 m** | **1.5-2.0 m or more** ← the difficult case |
| **Clay** | **Very high in principle, but SLOW** | 1.5 m, and the slowness helps |

> **SILT is again the problem soil, for the same reason as in frost heave: pores fine enough to lift water a long way, and permeability high enough for the water to actually arrive.**

> **So the required water table depth is not a single number but depends on the soil — and a criterion of 1.0 m that is adequate in sand may be quite insufficient in silt.**

**The consequences of a shallower water table, in order of severity:**

| Water table depth | Effect |
|---|---|
| **1.5 m or more** | **Satisfactory for almost all crops** |
| **1.0 m** | **Acceptable for most; shallow-rooted crops unaffected** |
| **0.6-1.0 m** | **Yields begin to fall; deep-rooted crops affected** ← |
| **0.3-0.6 m** | **WATERLOGGING — significant yield loss; salinity developing** |
| **Below 0.3 m** | **Severe waterlogging; most crops fail; rapid salinisation** |
| **At the surface** | **Land out of cultivation** |

> **Note that RICE is the exception at every level: it is grown in standing water and tolerates saturation, because it has specialised air-conducting tissue carrying oxygen to its roots.**

> **So a waterlogged area is often converted to rice cultivation as an adaptation — which works agronomically and does nothing about the SALINITY, since the evaporation continues to concentrate salts at the surface.**

> **That is worth noting as a partial and misleading remedy: switching to rice makes the land productive again and allows the underlying deterioration to continue unaddressed.**

**The DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT, which is how the requirement becomes a design:**

> **To hold the water table at the required depth, the drainage system must remove water at the rate it arrives:**

> **DRAINAGE COEFFICIENT q = the design rate of removal, expressed as a depth per day over the drained area.**

| Situation | Drainage coefficient |
|---|---|
| **Irrigated agriculture, controlling deep percolation and canal seepage** | **1 to 5 mm/day** ← |
| **Humid area with rainfall to be drained** | 5 to 15 mm/day |
| **Areas of very high seepage** | Higher |

> **The coefficient determines the drain SPACING through the Hooghoudt equation, and hence the system's cost — so it is a design decision balancing capacity against expense rather than a value to be looked up.**

> **And the sources it must remove are worth listing, since they are what the design must account for:**

| Source of the water to be drained | Note |
|---|---|
| **DEEP PERCOLATION from irrigation** | **The largest source in an irrigated area, and reducible by better on-farm practice** ← |
| **SEEPAGE from canals and watercourses** | **Reducible by LINING** ← |
| **RAINFALL infiltration** | Seasonal |
| **Lateral groundwater inflow from adjacent higher land** | Requires an interceptor drain |
| **Artesian upward flow** | Where a confined aquifer underlies |

> **The first two are the ones an engineer can act on, and they point to the same conclusion reached earlier: LINING THE CANALS AND CONTROLLING THE APPLICATION are preventive measures that reduce the drainage requirement itself.**

> **A drainage system designed to remove seepage that lining would have prevented is treating a symptom at recurring cost — so the two measures belong in one plan rather than being considered separately.**

**And the INTERCEPTOR DRAIN, since it is the measure the lateral-inflow row calls for:**

> **Where water flows laterally into an area from higher ground — from a canal on higher land, from a hillside, or from an adjacent irrigated tract — an INTERCEPTOR (catch water) DRAIN is placed along the upslope boundary.**

> **It intercepts that inflow before it reaches the land to be protected, and carries it away.**

| Advantage of an interceptor drain | Note |
|---|---|
| **Treats the water at its point of ENTRY rather than throughout the area** | **Far less drainage required within the area itself** ← |
| **A single drain protects a large area** | Very economical |
| **Can be combined with the canal's own drainage** | — |
| **Simple to construct and maintain** | An open drain |

> **That is the cheapest form of drainage available where the geometry suits it: one drain along a boundary, rather than a network throughout a field.**

> **And it is the standard first measure where a canal on higher ground is seeping into land below — a very common configuration, since canals are aligned along ridges and contours precisely to command the land beneath them.**

> **So the canal that irrigates the land is often also the source of the water that waterlogs it, and an interceptor drain between the two addresses both at once.**

examTip.trick: **1.0 to 1.5 m — deep enough to keep the ROOT ZONE aerated and to stop CAPILLARY RISE reaching the surface.** All the other options are shallower than most crops' root depth.
examTip.trap: **The required depth depends on the SOIL: silt lifts water 1-3 m by capillarity, so 1.0 m adequate in sand may be quite insufficient in silt.** Silt is the problem soil again — fine pores plus workable permeability.
examTip.mnemonic: **Converting waterlogged land to RICE makes it productive and does nothing about the SALINITY** — evaporation keeps concentrating salts at the surface. And an INTERCEPTOR drain along the upslope boundary is the cheapest drainage there is: one drain instead of a network.

questions.stem: Nepal's ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE hydropower potential is generally quoted as about:
questions.solution:
**About 42,000 MW.**

**The three figures, which are constantly confused:**

| Category | Figure | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **THEORETICAL potential** | **About 83,000 MW** | **What the rivers physically contain — every drop from every elevation, ignoring all constraints** |
| **ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE potential** | **About 42,000 MW** ← | **What could be developed at a cost the market would bear, from identified sites** |
| **DEVELOPED capacity** | **Of the order of 3,000 MW and rising** | **What is actually built and generating** |

> **Option (d) 83,000 MW is the THEORETICAL figure, which makes it the designed distractor — and it is the number most often quoted in public discussion, usually without the qualification.**

> **So roughly HALF the theoretical potential is considered economically feasible, and of that feasible half only a small fraction is developed.**

**Why the theoretical and feasible figures differ so much — what the halving represents:**

| Constraint that removes potential | Note |
|---|---|
| **Inaccessible sites** | **No road, no transmission route; the cost of access exceeds the value of the power** ← |
| **Sites in PROTECTED AREAS** | National parks, conservation areas, reserves |
| **Sites requiring unacceptable DISPLACEMENT or submergence** | **Reservoirs inundating settlements and the best agricultural land** ← |
| **Very small or very diffuse potential** | Uneconomic per kilowatt |
| **Geologically unsuitable sites** | Active faults, unstable slopes, high seepage |
| **Sites whose sediment load makes them uneconomic** | **A reservoir that would silt up in decades** ← |
| **Absence of a market or transmission for the output** | The power cannot be delivered |

> **So the "economically feasible" figure is not a physical quantity but a JUDGEMENT — and it changes as costs, technology, transmission access and markets change.**

> **That is worth stating clearly: the 42,000 MW is an estimate made under assumptions about prices and access, and it has been revised as those assumptions changed.**

> **A site uneconomic when the tariff was low and no transmission line existed may become economic when both change — so the feasible potential grows as the system develops, which is the opposite of a fixed resource being consumed.**

**Why the DEVELOPED figure is so small — the real constraints:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPITAL — hydropower is capital-intensive with a long payback** | **The binding constraint for a country with limited domestic capital** ← |
| **TRANSMISSION — power must reach a market** | **A plant without a line is worthless, and lines lag generation** ← |
| **The DRY-SEASON / MONSOON imbalance** | **Run-of-river plants produce a monsoon surplus that must be exported or spilled** ← |
| **Access roads and construction logistics in mountain terrain** | Often a large fraction of the cost |
| **Land acquisition, resettlement and local agreement** | Time and uncertainty |
| **Geological and sediment risk** | Cost overruns are common |
| **Institutional and licensing capacity** | — |

> **The TRANSMISSION and SEASONALITY constraints are the ones most binding at present, and they are connected:**

> **Nepal's plants are overwhelmingly RUN-OF-RIVER, so they generate a large monsoon surplus and a small dry-season output.**

> **Without transmission capacity to export the surplus, that energy is SPILLED — the plant's water passes the weir ungenerated because there is nowhere to sell the power.**

> **So the value of new generation depends on transmission and on cross-border trade, and building generation ahead of transmission produces plants that cannot sell what they make.**

> **Which is why the sequence of investment matters as much as its total, and why transmission and trade agreements feature so prominently in the country's energy planning.**

**The STORAGE question, since it is the structural answer:**

> **Nepal's potential is dominated by run-of-river schemes, and the country's central energy problem is seasonal rather than total:**

| Season | Situation |
|---|---|
| **MONSOON (June-September)** | **SURPLUS — plants at full output, energy spilled or exported cheaply** |
| **DRY SEASON (December-May)** | **DEFICIT — plants at 20-35 % of capacity, energy imported expensively** ← |

> **Only STORAGE projects can move water from one season to the other, and they are the hardest to build: large reservoirs, substantial inundation, resettlement, long construction and very long payback.**

> **So the developed potential is skewed toward the easier run-of-river schemes, and the storage projects that would resolve the seasonality remain largely unbuilt.**

> **That is the honest description of the country's hydropower position, and the 42,000 MW figure conceals it entirely — which is why a capacity figure alone is a poor description of a hydropower resource.**

**And a note on what the figures should be understood to mean:**

> **A hydropower potential quoted in MEGAWATTS describes CAPACITY, not ENERGY.**

> **Two schemes of equal capacity can differ by a factor of two in annual energy and by more in dry-season energy, depending on their hydrology and whether they have storage.**

> **So a country's potential is more meaningfully described in GWh per year, and more meaningfully still by the seasonal distribution of that energy.**

> **The megawatt figure survives because it is simple and because it is what plants are named by — and it is worth knowing that it answers the least useful of the questions one might ask about a hydropower resource.**

> **For a candidate, the three numbers to hold are 83,000 (theoretical), 42,000 (economically feasible) and the developed capacity of a few thousand — together with the understanding of why the second is about half the first and the third a small fraction of the second.**

examTip.trick: **Theoretical about 83,000 MW; ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE about 42,000 MW — roughly half; developed only a few thousand.**
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 83,000 MW is the THEORETICAL figure** — the one most often quoted publicly without its qualification. "Economically feasible" is a judgement about cost and access, not a physical quantity, and it changes as they do.
examTip.mnemonic: **A potential quoted in MEGAWATTS describes CAPACITY, not ENERGY** — and it conceals the seasonal problem entirely. Nepal's real constraint is a monsoon surplus with a dry-season deficit, resolvable only by STORAGE or by transmission and trade.

questions.stem: A hydropower plant operating under a net head of 40 m is classified as a:
questions.solution:
**A MEDIUM HEAD plant.**

**The classification by head:**

| Classification | Head range | Typical turbine |
|---|---|---|
| **ULTRA-LOW head** | **Below about 3 m** | **Water wheels, Archimedes screw, very low head propeller** |
| **LOW head** | **Below 15 m** | **KAPLAN, propeller, bulb, tubular** |
| **MEDIUM head** | **15 to 70 m** ← 40 m | **KAPLAN or FRANCIS** |
| **HIGH head** | **Above 70 m (some references use 100 m)** | **FRANCIS, PELTON, TURGO** |
| **Very high head** | Above 500 m | **PELTON, multi-jet Pelton** |

> **The boundaries are conventions and vary slightly between references, which is worth acknowledging — but the 15 m and 70 m divisions are the commonly used ones, and 40 m sits clearly in the middle band.**

**Why the classification matters — it determines almost everything about the scheme:**

| Aspect | LOW head | HIGH head |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge for a given power** | **LARGE** ← | **SMALL** |
| **Turbine** | **KAPLAN (axial reaction)** | **PELTON (impulse)** |
| **Specific speed** | **HIGH (300-1000)** | **LOW (8-30)** |
| **Waterway** | **SHORT, wide — often the powerhouse is at the dam** ← | **LONG headrace and penstock along a hillside** ← |
| **Cost dominated by** | **The CIVIL works — dam, barrage, large waterways** | **The CONVEYANCE — headrace, penstock, access** |
| **Cost of the machinery per kW** | **HIGHER — a large machine passing a large flow** | **Lower** |
| **Cavitation risk** | **HIGHER — Kaplans are cavitation-prone** | Lower |

> **The COST DOMINANCE row is the most consequential and is worth understanding:**

> **For a LOW HEAD plant, the power comes from a large FLOW, so the waterways, gates and turbine are all physically large — and the civil works dominate the cost.**

> **For a HIGH HEAD plant, the flow is small and the pipes are small, but the water must be carried a long way along and down a hillside — so the conveyance and the access roads dominate.**

> **That is why a Nepali high-head scheme's cost is so often in its headrace tunnel and its access road rather than in its powerhouse, and why a low-head barrage scheme's cost is in its concrete.**
