> **And it explains the general observation that HIGH HEAD IS CHEAPER PER KILOWATT: a small flow through a small pipe from a great height produces the same power as a large flow through vast structures from a small one, and small pipes are cheap.**

> **Which is why Nepal's steep topography is a genuine economic advantage — the country's hydropower is cheap because its heads are high, not merely because its rivers are large.**

**The turbine selection at 40 m, since it is a boundary case:**

> **At 40 m head, BOTH a Kaplan and a Francis turbine are viable, and the choice depends on other factors:**

| Consideration | Favours |
|---|---|
| **A LARGE flow relative to the head** | **KAPLAN — higher specific speed suits high flow** |
| **A SMALL flow relative to the head** | **FRANCIS** |
| **FLOW VARYING widely through the year** | **KAPLAN — its double regulation gives a FLAT efficiency curve from about 40 % load** ← |
| **Steady flow near the design value** | **FRANCIS — higher peak efficiency** |
| **Lowest machine cost** | Francis is generally simpler and cheaper |
| **Cavitation and setting depth** | **Francis is less cavitation-prone, so it can be set higher above tailwater** ← |

> **The FLOW VARIATION consideration usually decides it for a Nepali scheme: the flow varies enormously through the year, so a machine with a flat part-load efficiency curve generates far more annual energy than one with a peaky curve.**

> **A Kaplan's double regulation — adjustable runner blades AND adjustable guide vanes, moved together on a cam — is what gives it that flat curve, and it is worth the extra mechanical complexity where the flow varies.**

> **The alternative approach, common in Nepal, is to install SEVERAL SMALLER FRANCIS OR PELTON UNITS rather than one large one: at low flow, some units are shut down and the rest run near their design point.**

> **That achieves a flat overall efficiency curve using simple machines, at the price of more units to install and maintain — and it also provides redundancy, since one unit can be overhauled while the others generate.**

> **So there are two solutions to the same problem — one machine that works well at part load, or several machines run at full load in combination — and the choice is a genuine engineering trade-off rather than a matter of preference.**

**The other classifications of hydropower plants, for completeness:**

| Basis | Categories |
|---|---|
| **HEAD** | **Ultra-low, low, medium, high, very high** ← |
| **STORAGE and operation** | **Run-of-river, peaking run-of-river (PROR), storage, pumped storage** |
| **CAPACITY (Nepal's own definitions)** | **Micro (<100 kW), mini (100-1000 kW), small (1-25 MW), medium (25-100 MW), large (>100 MW)** |
| **LOAD served** | Base load, peaking |
| **Interconnection** | Isolated, grid-connected |
| **Location of powerhouse** | Surface, semi-underground, underground |

> **The CAPACITY bands are Nepal-specific and matter administratively: the licensing regime, the royalty rates and the approval process all depend on which band a project falls into.**

> **A scheme below 1 MW faces a materially lighter approval process than one above it, and that threshold has a real influence on how small schemes are designed — which is a case of a regulatory boundary shaping engineering decisions.**

> **The UNDERGROUND POWERHOUSE option deserves a note for Nepal specifically: in a narrow gorge there may be no site for a surface powerhouse, or a surface structure may be exposed to rockfall, landslide and flood.**

> **An underground powerhouse excavated into the valley side is protected from all of those, and its cost premium is often justified by the hazard avoided rather than by any operational advantage.**

examTip.trick: **Low head below 15 m, MEDIUM 15-70 m, high above 70 m.** At 40 m the plant is medium head, and both Kaplan and Francis turbines are viable.
examTip.trap: **HIGH HEAD IS CHEAPER PER KILOWATT** — a small flow through small pipes from a great height replaces a large flow through vast structures. That is why Nepal's steep topography is an economic advantage.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a widely varying flow there are two solutions: ONE Kaplan with double regulation (flat curve to 40 % load), or SEVERAL smaller units run at full load in combination.** The second also gives redundancy for overhaul.

questions.stem: The curve obtained by arranging the loads on a system in DESCENDING ORDER of magnitude against the time for which they are equalled or exceeded is called the:
questions.solution:
**The LOAD DURATION CURVE.**

**The two load curves, which are the same data presented differently:**

| Curve | Horizontal axis | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| **CHRONOLOGICAL LOAD CURVE (load curve)** | **TIME OF DAY, in order** | **WHEN the load occurs — the shape of the daily demand** ← |
| **LOAD DURATION CURVE** | **DURATION for which the load is equalled or exceeded** | **HOW LONG each load level persists** ← |

> **They contain EXACTLY THE SAME INFORMATION rearranged, and each answers a different question:**

> **The CHRONOLOGICAL curve tells you the load at 7 pm — which matters for scheduling generation and for understanding consumer behaviour.**

> **The DURATION curve tells you for how many hours the load exceeds 400 MW — which matters for deciding how much BASE LOAD capacity to build and how much PEAKING capacity.**

> **Note that the AREA under both curves is the same and equals the TOTAL ENERGY over the period, since energy is load integrated over time.**

> **That equality of areas is a useful check and a neat confirmation that the two are the same data.**

**How the duration curve is constructed:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Take the load readings over the period — a day, a month or a year** |
| **2** | **RANK them from HIGHEST to LOWEST** |
| **3** | **Plot each against the CUMULATIVE time for which that load is equalled or exceeded** |
| **4** | **The result descends monotonically from the peak load to the minimum** |

> **So the curve starts at the PEAK LOAD (exceeded for a moment) and ends at the MINIMUM or BASE LOAD (exceeded for the whole period).**

> **And it is monotonically decreasing by construction, which distinguishes it at a glance from a chronological curve with its morning and evening humps.**

**What the duration curve is USED for — the capacity mix:**

> **This is the curve's real purpose and it is worth setting out, because it is how a generating system is planned:**

| Region of the curve | Duration | Should be met by |
|---|---|---|
| **The BASE — load present all the time** | **100 % of the hours** | **BASE LOAD plant: high capital cost, LOW running cost — run continuously (storage hydro, large thermal, nuclear)** ← |
| **The INTERMEDIATE region** | **A substantial part of the time** | **Mid-merit plant** |
| **The PEAK — the topmost sliver** | **A few hours a year** | **PEAKING plant: LOW capital cost, high running cost — cheap to build, expensive to run (gas turbine, PROR hydro)** ← |

> **The economic logic is the whole point and it is genuinely elegant:**

> **A plant that will run 8,000 hours a year should be chosen for LOW RUNNING COST, because the fuel or water cost is incurred 8,000 times and the capital cost once.**

> **A plant that will run 200 hours a year should be chosen for LOW CAPITAL COST, because its capital is paid for whether it runs or not while its running cost is incurred only 200 times.**

> **So the load duration curve, read from the bottom up, tells a planner exactly what kind of plant to build for each slice of the demand — and the optimum mix falls out of the curve's shape.**

> **Building the wrong kind is expensive in a specific way: an expensive-to-build, cheap-to-run plant used for peaking has its capital idle most of the year, and a cheap-to-build, expensive-to-run plant used for base load burns money continuously.**

**The FLOW DURATION CURVE — option (d), and its exact analogy:**

| | **LOAD duration curve** | **FLOW duration curve** |
|---|---|---|
| **Quantity ranked** | **Electrical LOAD** | **River DISCHARGE** |
| **Axis** | **Duration equalled or exceeded** | **Percentage of time equalled or exceeded** |
| **Read for** | **Capacity mix; base and peak plant** | **Design discharge (Q40), firm power (Q95)** |
| **Both are** | **Ranked, monotonically descending, area = total quantity** | ← |

> **The two curves are constructed identically and used identically, which is worth noticing: one describes the DEMAND for energy and the other the SUPPLY of water, and a hydropower plan requires both.**

> **In fact the design of a hydropower plant is precisely the matching of the two: the flow duration curve says what water is available and when, the load duration curve says what power is wanted and when, and the plant's design flow and capacity are chosen where the two are best reconciled.**

> **That is why option (d) is such a well-made distractor — it is the same curve for a different quantity, and both belong to this chapter.**

**The MASS CURVE — option (c), which is a different construction entirely:**

| | **DURATION curve** | **MASS CURVE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Plots** | **Ranked magnitudes against duration** | **CUMULATIVE quantity against TIME, in chronological order** ← |
| **Monotonic?** | **Descending** | **Always RISING (cumulative)** |
| **Order preserved?** | **NO — the data are ranked** | **YES — chronological** |
| **Used for** | Capacity mix; design flow | **RESERVOIR CAPACITY — the storage needed to meet a demand from a variable supply** ← |

> **The MASS CURVE (Rippl diagram) is the tool for sizing a RESERVOIR, and its method is worth knowing:**

> **Plot the cumulative INFLOW against time, and the cumulative DEMAND as a line of constant slope.**

> **Where the demand line is STEEPER than the inflow curve, the reservoir is being DRAWN DOWN; where it is flatter, the reservoir is FILLING.**

> **The required STORAGE is the maximum VERTICAL DISTANCE between a tangent to a peak of the mass curve and the following trough — the largest accumulated deficit.**

> **So the mass curve preserves the CHRONOLOGICAL SEQUENCE, and it must: the storage needed depends on how long the dry period lasts and when it occurs, which ranking the data would destroy.**

> **That is the essential distinction between the two constructions: a DURATION curve discards the sequence and answers questions about how much and how often, while a MASS CURVE preserves it and answers questions about storage.**

> **And it explains why reservoir sizing cannot be done from a flow duration curve: the curve says the river was low for 30 per cent of the time and not whether those days were consecutive — and a reservoir's size depends entirely on whether they were.**

examTip.trick: **A LOAD DURATION CURVE ranks the loads in descending order against the time each is equalled or exceeded** — the same data as the chronological curve, rearranged, with the same area (total energy).
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is the identical construction for river DISCHARGE**, and both belong to this chapter — a hydropower design matches the two curves against each other.
examTip.mnemonic: **A DURATION curve DISCARDS the sequence (how much, how often); a MASS CURVE PRESERVES it (how much storage).** Which is why reservoir sizing needs a mass curve: a flow duration curve cannot say whether the low days were consecutive.

questions.stem: The energy a hydropower plant can generate in EXCESS of its firm power, available only when the river flow is high, is called:
questions.solution:
**SECONDARY energy**, also called surplus or seasonal energy.

**The classification of a plant's output:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) energy** | **Energy available with a high degree of reliability, based on the MINIMUM flow — commonly Q95** |
| **SECONDARY (surplus) energy** | **Energy available only PART of the year, when the flow exceeds the firm value** ← |
| **Total energy** | Firm plus secondary |

> **Option (a) is therefore the complementary term, and options (b) and (d) describe positions on the LOAD curve rather than on the SUPPLY side — peak and base energy are about when the demand occurs.**

> **That distinction between SUPPLY-side and DEMAND-side terms is worth keeping clear: firm and secondary describe what the RIVER can deliver; base and peak describe what the SYSTEM wants.**

**Why secondary energy is worth so much LESS than firm energy:**

| | **FIRM energy** | **SECONDARY energy** |
|---|---|---|
| **Available** | **Always** | **Only in the wet season** |
| **Can the system RELY on it?** | **YES — it counts toward dependable capacity** ← | **NO — other capacity is needed for when it is absent** |
| **When it is available** | Continuously | **When EVERY OTHER hydro plant also has a surplus** ← |
| **Market value** | **HIGH — a capacity payment plus energy** | **LOW — energy only, at a reduced rate, often curtailable** |
| **Contractual treatment** | Guaranteed offtake | May be sold on an as-available basis |

> **The THIRD row is the decisive one and it is worth dwelling on: secondary energy arrives in the MONSOON, which is precisely when every other run-of-river plant in the country also has surplus.**

> **So the market is glutted at exactly the moment the energy appears, and its price collapses — or there is no market at all and the water is spilled.**

> **That is the fundamental economics of run-of-river hydropower in a monsoon climate: the energy is abundant when it is worth least and scarce when it is worth most.**

> **And it explains why the FIRM component dominates a plant's value even though it may be a minority of its annual energy: a plant producing 100 GWh of which 30 is firm may earn more from that 30 than from the other 70.**

**The ways secondary energy can be made valuable, since it is otherwise wasted:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **EXPORT to a system with a different seasonal pattern** | **Nepal's monsoon surplus against India's summer demand — the largest opportunity** ← |
| **STORAGE — carry it into the dry season** | **The fundamental answer, and the most expensive** |
| **PUMPED STORAGE — use it to pump water uphill for later generation** | **Converts worthless wet-season energy into valuable dry-season energy, at a 20-30 % round-trip loss** ← |
| **Energy-intensive INDUSTRY operated seasonally** | **Cement, ferro-alloys, fertiliser — plants that can run hard in the monsoon** ← |
| **Displace imported fuel — electric cooking, electric transport, industrial boilers** | Domestic substitution |
| **Interruptible tariffs for large consumers** | Sell it cheaply on an as-available basis |

> **The PUMPED STORAGE option is the most elegant and deserves explanation: pumped storage is a net energy CONSUMER, which normally counts against it — but if the energy it consumes is otherwise WORTHLESS and the energy it returns is valuable, the economics reverse entirely.**

> **A pumped storage scheme in Nepal charged on spilled monsoon energy and discharging in the dry-season evening peak converts energy worth nothing into energy worth a great deal, and the 25 per cent round-trip loss is irrelevant when the input was going to be spilled.**
> **So a technology that looks wasteful in a system with expensive base-load energy is highly attractive in one with a seasonal surplus — which is a good illustration of why a technology's merit depends on the system it sits in.**

> **The SEASONAL INDUSTRY option is the least discussed and potentially significant: an industry whose product can be stockpiled — cement, ferro-alloys, fertiliser — can run hard on cheap monsoon power and idle in the dry season, monetising energy that would otherwise be spilled.**

> **It requires an industry willing to accept a seasonal operating pattern and a tariff that makes it worthwhile, which is a matter of policy design rather than engineering.**

**How firm energy is INCREASED, since that is what a designer can influence:**

| Measure | Effect on firm energy |
|---|---|
| **STORAGE — even a modest reservoir** | **The most effective: carries wet-season water into the dry season** ← |
| **PONDAGE for daily peaking (PROR)** | **Does NOT increase firm ENERGY; it increases the CAPACITY VALUE by placing the same energy at the peak hour** ← |
| **A larger catchment, or an INTER-BASIN TRANSFER** | More dry-season flow |
| **CASCADE development — a storage plant upstream of run-of-river plants** | **The upstream reservoir regulates the flow for every plant below it** ← |
| **Reducing the design flow (a smaller plant)** | Raises the plant factor and the firm fraction, and lowers total energy |

> **The CASCADE arrangement is the most valuable and the most under-exploited: a single storage reservoir high in a basin regulates the flow for EVERY run-of-river plant downstream, converting their secondary energy into firm energy without any reservoir of their own.**

> **So one storage project can raise the firm output of a whole cascade — which means its benefits accrue to plants other than itself, and that creates a genuine problem of who should pay for it.**

> **That is a real institutional obstacle to storage development: the reservoir's cost falls on one project and its benefits are spread across many, so no single developer has an incentive to build it.**

> **Resolving it requires either public investment or a mechanism for downstream beneficiaries to contribute — which is a matter of institutional design, and it is why storage projects in such basins are typically undertaken by the state rather than by private developers.**

examTip.trick: **FIRM energy is reliably available (from the minimum flow); SECONDARY energy comes only when the flow is high.** Options (b) and (d) are DEMAND-side terms (base and peak), not supply-side ones.
examTip.trap: **Secondary energy arrives in the monsoon, when EVERY other run-of-river plant also has surplus** — so the market is glutted exactly when the energy appears. A plant may earn more from 30 GWh of firm energy than from 70 GWh of secondary.
examTip.mnemonic: **PUMPED STORAGE reverses its own economics here: a 25 % round-trip loss is irrelevant if the input was going to be SPILLED.** And one CASCADE reservoir firms up every plant downstream — which is why no single developer will pay for it.

questions.stem: The ratio of the sediment retained in a reservoir to the total sediment flowing into it is called the:
questions.solution:
**TRAP EFFICIENCY.**

**The definition:**

> **TRAP EFFICIENCY = (sediment RETAINED in the reservoir) / (total sediment INFLOW) × 100**

> **It expresses what proportion of the incoming sediment the reservoir keeps, the remainder passing through to the river below.**

**What it depends on — chiefly one ratio:**

> **The dominant variable is the CAPACITY-INFLOW RATIO — the reservoir's capacity divided by the mean annual inflow volume:**

| Capacity / annual inflow | Trap efficiency |
|---|---|
| **0.001 (a very small pondage)** | **About 20-30 %** |
| **0.01** | **About 65-75 %** |
| **0.1** | **About 90-95 %** ← |
| **0.5 and above** | **95-100 % — almost everything is trapped** |

> **The relation is highly non-linear: a reservoir holding a tenth of the annual inflow traps over 90 per cent of the sediment, and one holding half traps essentially all of it.**

> **The physical reason is simple: a large reservoir gives the water a long RESIDENCE TIME, and given enough time even fine particles settle.**

> **A small pondage passes its water through in hours, so only the coarse fraction settles and the silt and clay go through.**

> **BRUNE'S CURVE is the standard empirical relation between the capacity-inflow ratio and the trap efficiency, and it is what a sedimentation study uses.**

**Why the other options are wrong — each is a real and different quantity:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SEDIMENT DELIVERY RATIO** | **The ratio of the sediment DELIVERED to a point in the river to the total EROSION in the catchment** — a catchment property, always well below 1, since most eroded material is deposited before reaching the river ← |
| **TRAP EFFICIENCY** | ✓ **A RESERVOIR property** |
| **SEDIMENT YIELD** | **The total sediment delivered per unit catchment area per year — tonnes per km² per year** |
| **Reservoir life index** | Not a standard term |

> **The SEDIMENT DELIVERY RATIO is the most instructive distractor because it is the mirror image of trap efficiency: both are ratios of sediment retained to sediment supplied, but for different systems.**

> **The delivery ratio describes how much of the CATCHMENT'S erosion reaches the river; the trap efficiency describes how much of the RIVER'S sediment stays in the reservoir.**

> **And the delivery ratio is typically small — 10 to 30 per cent for a large catchment — because most eroded soil is deposited on slopes, in field boundaries and in valley floors before it ever reaches a channel.**

> **That is why catchment treatment can be effective: much of the erosion is already being trapped naturally, and increasing that trapping is easier than removing sediment from a reservoir.**

**How trap efficiency is USED — computing the reservoir's LIFE:**

> **The sequence is:**

| Step | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **1** | **SEDIMENT YIELD of the catchment (t/km²/yr) × catchment area = annual sediment inflow in tonnes** |
| **2** | **× TRAP EFFICIENCY = tonnes retained per year** ← |
| **3** | **÷ the deposited DENSITY (typically 1.2-1.6 t/m³) = volume deposited per year** |
| **4** | **Dead storage ÷ annual deposition = years until the dead storage fills** |
| **5** | **Total storage ÷ annual deposition = the reservoir's nominal total life** |

> **A worked illustration for a Himalayan reservoir:**

> **Catchment 3,000 km², sediment yield 2,000 t/km²/yr, trap efficiency 90 per cent, deposited density 1.4 t/m³:**

> **Sediment inflow = 3,000 × 2,000 = 6 million t/yr**

> **Retained = 0.9 × 6 = 5.4 million t/yr**

> **Volume = 5.4/1.4 = 3.86 million m³ per year**

> **So a reservoir with 100 million m³ of dead storage would have it filled in about 26 years.**

> **That figure is the point of the whole calculation, and it is sobering: a substantial dead storage provision is consumed within a working generation in a high-yield Himalayan catchment.**

**Why this matters so much in Nepal — the honest position:**

| Region | Typical sediment yield (t/km²/yr) |
|---|---|
| **World average** | **About 150-200** |
| **Stable temperate catchments** | **50-150** |
| **HIMALAYAN catchments** | **1,000-5,000, and locally far higher** ← |

> **So Himalayan sediment yields are an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE above the world average, for reasons that are structural and unalterable:**

> **Young, rapidly rising mountains; very steep slopes; intense monsoon rainfall; widespread landsliding; and weak, highly fractured rock.**

> **The consequence is that a Himalayan reservoir's ECONOMIC LIFE is frequently governed by SEDIMENTATION rather than by the durability of its structure — a dam that will stand for two centuries may lose its useful storage in sixty years.**

> **That is a first-order design consideration rather than a detail, and it shapes the whole approach to storage in Nepal.**

**The measures, in order of how fundamental they are:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **CATCHMENT TREATMENT — afforestation, check dams, gully control, terracing** | **Reduces the yield at SOURCE; slow, permanent, and it addresses the cause** ← |
| **DEAD STORAGE allowance** | **The passive provision — accept the sediment and provide room** |
| **SLUICING — pass sediment-laden monsoon flows THROUGH low-level outlets while still in suspension** | **Effective, and it requires the outlets to be designed in from the start** ← |
| **DRAWDOWN FLUSHING — empty the reservoir and let the river scour it out** | **The most effective removal, and it costs the stored water** ← |
| **Density current venting** | Draw off the turbid underflow before it settles |
| **Dredging** | Very expensive per cubic metre; a last resort |
| **Bypass tunnel for sediment-laden flows** | Effective where the topography allows |

> **The DRAWDOWN FLUSHING option is the most effective and it works in Nepal specifically because the monsoon reliably REFILLS the reservoir afterward.**

> **So the reservoir is drawn down at the end of the dry season — when it is nearly empty anyway and its water is least valuable — the river scours out the deposits, and the monsoon refills it.**

> **In a climate without a reliable refilling season that strategy would be unavailable, which is why it is a Himalayan solution to a Himalayan problem.**

> **The critical requirement is that the LOW-LEVEL OUTLETS must be large enough and low enough, and they must be designed in at the outset: retrofitting an outlet near the bed of an existing dam is practically impossible.**

> **So a decision made at the design stage determines whether the reservoir can be maintained for a century or fills up in sixty years — which makes it one of the most consequential choices in the whole project.**

examTip.trick: **TRAP EFFICIENCY = sediment retained ÷ sediment inflow**, and it depends chiefly on the CAPACITY-INFLOW ratio (Brune's curve): 0.1 traps over 90 %, 0.5 traps essentially all.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) SEDIMENT DELIVERY RATIO is the mirror image for the CATCHMENT** — how much of its erosion reaches the river, typically only 10-30 %. Trap efficiency is a reservoir property; delivery ratio a catchment one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Himalayan yields of 1,000-5,000 t/km²/yr are an ORDER above the world average**, so a Nepali reservoir's economic life is set by SEDIMENT, not by the dam. Low-level FLUSHING outlets must be designed in from the start — they cannot be retrofitted.

questions.stem: The type of dam that transfers most of the water thrust to the valley sides by arch action is the:
questions.solution:
**The ARCH dam.**

**How each dam type resists the water thrust:**

| Dam type | Resists the thrust by | Requires |
|---|---|---|
| **GRAVITY dam** | **Its OWN WEIGHT, transferred to the FOUNDATION** | **A sound foundation able to carry a very heavy structure** |
| **ARCH dam** | **ARCH ACTION, transferring the thrust HORIZONTALLY to the ABUTMENTS (valley sides)** ← | **A NARROW valley with STRONG rock abutments** ← |
| **BUTTRESS dam** | **A sloping upstream deck carrying the load to buttresses, thence to the foundation** | Less concrete than gravity; more formwork and skilled work |
| **EMBANKMENT (earth/rockfill) dam** | **Its own weight and the shear strength of its fill** | **A wide base; suits almost any foundation** ← |
| **Arch-gravity (thick arch)** | **BOTH weight and arch action** | An intermediate case |

> **The essential distinction is the DIRECTION in which the load is delivered:**

> **A GRAVITY dam sends the thrust DOWNWARD into the foundation.**

> **An ARCH dam sends it SIDEWAYS into the abutments.**

> **That single difference determines everything about where each can be built.**

**Why an arch dam needs a narrow valley with strong abutments:**

> **The arch's whole action depends on the valley sides being able to receive an enormous horizontal thrust.**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **A NARROW valley — a gorge** | **The arch must span it; a wide valley requires an impossibly thick arch** ← |
| **STRONG, SOUND rock abutments** | **They must carry the entire horizontal thrust without yielding** ← |
| **The rock must not be jointed in a direction that permits sliding** | A wedge of rock could be pushed out |
| **A favourable ratio of crest length to height** | Generally below about 5 |

> **The ABUTMENT requirement is absolute and it is where arch dams fail:**

> **A gravity dam's foundation is beneath it, spread over a large area, and it fails gradually if the foundation is poor.**

> **An arch dam's thrust is concentrated into two abutments, and if either yields the arch loses its support entirely.**

> **The MALPASSET dam failure in France in 1959 is the case in point: a thin arch dam whose left abutment rock, a gneiss with an unfavourable joint set, was displaced by the thrust and by seepage pressure — and the dam failed completely and instantly, killing over 400 people.**

> **So an arch dam is the most material-efficient type and the least forgiving, and its site investigation must concentrate on the ABUTMENT GEOLOGY above everything else.**

**The comparison in material and cost, which is why arch dams are built at all:**

| Dam type | Concrete volume for the same height and site |
|---|---|
| **GRAVITY** | **1.0 (the reference) — very large** |
| **BUTTRESS** | **About 0.6-0.7** |
| **ARCH** | **About 0.2-0.3 — the most economical in material** ← |

> **So an arch dam uses perhaps a QUARTER of the concrete of a gravity dam of the same height — an enormous saving in a remote site where every tonne of cement must be hauled.**

> **And that saving is precisely what justifies the greater design sophistication, the more demanding site requirements and the higher risk.**

> **For a Himalayan gorge with sound rock, an arch dam can be dramatically cheaper than any alternative — and the same site with fractured or weathered abutment rock rules it out entirely.**

**The EMBANKMENT dam, for contrast, since it is the commonest type worldwide:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Built of EARTH or ROCKFILL, with an impervious core or membrane** | Local materials |
| **Suits ALMOST ANY foundation, including soil** | **Its low, spread loading tolerates weak foundations** ← |
| **Suits a WIDE valley** | No span limitation |
| **CANNOT be overtopped** | **Its spillway must be separate, in a flank or a saddle** ← |
| **Vulnerable to PIPING through the core or foundation** | **The principal failure mode** ← |
| **Very large volume of material, but locally won** | Low transport cost |
| **Slow to construct; sensitive to weather during placement** | — |

> **The two absolute rules for an embankment dam are worth stating because their violation causes the great majority of dam failures:**

> **IT MUST NEVER BE OVERTOPPED — flowing water erodes the downstream face and breaches it within hours.**

> **IT MUST NOT PIPE — seepage carrying soil particles out of the core or foundation progressively enlarges its own path until the dam is undermined.**

> **Together, OVERTOPPING and PIPING account for most embankment dam failures — which is why spillway capacity and internal filter design receive such attention.**

> **And it is why an embankment dam requires a graded FILTER between the core and the downstream shell: the filter must retain the core's fine particles while draining the seepage freely, which is the two-sided grading requirement met earlier.**

**Choosing a dam type at a given site — the decision sequence:**

| Site characteristic | Favours |
|---|---|
| **NARROW gorge, sound strong rock** | **ARCH — least material** ← |
| **Moderate valley, sound rock foundation** | **GRAVITY or arch-gravity** |
| **WIDE valley, any foundation** | **EMBANKMENT** ← |
| **Weak or soil foundation** | **EMBANKMENT — nothing else will do** |
| **Local earth and rock plentiful, cement expensive and remote** | **EMBANKMENT** ← |
| **A large spillway discharge required, with no flank site** | **GRAVITY — the spillway can go over the dam** ← |
| **Seismic region** | **Embankment (well designed) performs well; a thin arch is more sensitive** |

> **The SPILLWAY row is often decisive and is easy to overlook: if the flood to be passed is large and there is no saddle or flank in which to put a separate spillway, a CONCRETE dam becomes necessary simply because water can be passed over its crest.**

> **So the spillway requirement can select the dam type independently of the foundation — and a site that would otherwise suit an embankment dam may require a gravity dam for that reason alone.**

> **That is a good illustration of how a dam's components determine one another: the spillway is not chosen after the dam but with it, and in some sites it chooses the dam.**

examTip.trick: **A GRAVITY dam sends the thrust DOWN into its foundation; an ARCH dam sends it SIDEWAYS into the abutments.** That single difference decides where each can be built.
examTip.trap: **An arch dam uses only about a QUARTER of the concrete and is the LEAST FORGIVING** — its thrust is concentrated into two abutments, and if either yields the arch loses its support entirely (Malpasset, 1959).
examTip.mnemonic: **An EMBANKMENT dam must NEVER be overtopped and must not PIPE** — those two account for most dam failures. And the SPILLWAY requirement can select the dam type on its own: a large flood with no flank site forces a concrete dam.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme, the principal purpose of the DIVERSION WEIR is:
options: To raise the water level sufficiently to admit the design flow into the intake
To store water for peaking generation
To generate the head required by the turbine
To trap the whole of the river's sediment load
questions.solution:
**To RAISE THE WATER LEVEL sufficiently to admit the design flow into the intake.**

**What the weir does and does not do:**

| Does | Does NOT do |
|---|---|
| **RAISES the water level at the intake, so the design flow can be diverted** ← | **STORE any significant volume** ← |
| **Provides a stable, defined diversion point** | **Generate the head — that comes from the FALL along the conveyance** ← |
| **Rejects coarse bed load (with a trench weir or under-sluices)** | **Trap the sediment load — a weir traps almost nothing** |
| **Passes the flood flow safely** | Regulate the river |

> **Each of the three wrong options describes something the weir does not do, and each corresponds to a different element of the scheme — which makes the option set a test of what generates what.**

**Why the weir does NOT generate the head — the point most often confused:**

> **A run-of-river scheme's head comes from the RIVER'S OWN FALL along the reach that the conveyance short-circuits:**

| Element | Contribution to the head |
|---|---|
| **The DIVERSION WEIR** | **A metre or two at most — negligible** |
| **The HEADRACE, running at a gentle gradient along the hillside** | **NONE directly — but it carries the water forward while the RIVER falls steeply** ← |
| **The natural fall of the RIVER over that reach** | **ESSENTIALLY ALL OF IT** ← |
| **The PENSTOCK** | **Converts that accumulated elevation difference into pressure** |

> **So the mechanism is worth stating explicitly: the headrace carries the water NEARLY LEVEL along the valley side while the river below DROPS STEEPLY.**

> **After a few kilometres the headrace is high above the river, and that accumulated difference IS the head — delivered to the turbine through the penstock.**

> **The weir contributes almost nothing to it. Its only job is to lift the water surface enough to get the design flow through the intake opening.**

> **Which explains why run-of-river schemes in steep terrain have such low weirs — often only 2 to 4 m high — and such long headraces: the topography provides the head and the weir merely provides the diversion.**

> **And it explains why such a scheme is cheap: no large dam is needed, only a small weir and a long pipe or canal.**

**Why the weir does NOT store water — and what that means:**

> **A diversion weir creates a small pool, and its volume is trivial compared with the flow:**

> **A weir 3 m high across a 40 m wide river with a pool extending 300 m upstream impounds perhaps 20,000 m³.**

> **A plant taking 10 m³/s would empty that in 2,000 seconds — about half an hour.**

> **So the pool provides MINUTES of buffer, not hours, and the plant's output follows the river's flow almost exactly.**

> **That is precisely what "run-of-river" means, and option (b) describes a PONDAGE — a deliberately enlarged pool giving hours of storage, which converts the scheme into a PEAKING run-of-river (PROR) plant.**

> **The distinction is real and consequential: a PROR scheme requires a substantially larger impoundment, and therefore a higher weir or a dedicated pond, and it delivers energy at the peak hour rather than continuously.**

**What the weir must be designed for, since its function is modest but its loading is not:**

| Design requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pass the DESIGN FLOOD safely** | **Typically a 100-year flood for the weir, and a higher return period for the intake structures** ← |
| **Resist the flood's SCOUR at its toe and downstream** | **A stilling arrangement, cut-off and launching apron** ← |
| **Resist UPLIFT and PIPING beneath it** | Cut-offs, floor thickness — Khosla's method |
| **Withstand IMPACT from boulders and debris** | **In a Himalayan stream the weir is struck by metre-sized boulders** ← |
| **Provide for sediment passage or exclusion** | Under-sluices, or a trench weir arrangement |
| **Remain stable when the pool is silted up to the crest** | Which it will be |

> **The BOULDER IMPACT requirement is peculiar to steep mountain streams and is often decisive for the weir's form:**

> **A conventional ogee weir crest in a boulder-transporting stream is progressively chipped and eventually destroyed by impact and abrasion.**

> **So such weirs are built massively, with heavy concrete or a steel-armoured crest, or are designed as TRENCH WEIRS which are overtopped by the boulders rather than struck by them.**

> **And the last row is worth its emphasis: the weir's pool WILL fill with sediment, generally within a few seasons, and the weir must be stable in that condition — with sediment pressure against it rather than water, and with no scouring pool below.**

> **A weir designed only for the clear-water case is not designed for the condition it will spend most of its life in.**

**The complete function of the headworks, since the weir is one part:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **DIVERSION WEIR** | **Raise the level to admit the design flow** ← |
| **INTAKE with trash rack** | Admit the flow; exclude floating debris |
| **UNDER-SLUICE (or trench weir arrangement)** | **Reject and flush coarse bed load** |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | Remove gravel immediately after the intake |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | Remove sand down to about 0.2 mm |
| **Spillway / escape on the headrace** | Discharge surplus when the plant shuts down |
| **ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW release arrangement** | **Pass the mandated minimum flow downstream — in Nepal at least 10 % of the minimum monthly average** ← |

> **The ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW arrangement is a physical requirement of the weir and not merely an operating rule: there must be a notch, a pipe or an orifice that PASSES the required flow whatever the operators do.**

> **A release depending on a gate being opened will not be made reliably, whereas a fixed notch in the weir crest releases the flow automatically and can be verified by inspection.**

> **So the good practice is to build the environmental release into the structure rather than into the operating instructions — which is the same principle as preferring an ungated spillway or a tamper-proof irrigation outlet.**

> **A requirement embodied in the geometry is met; a requirement embodied in a procedure may not be.**

examTip.trick: **The weir only RAISES THE LEVEL enough to admit the design flow.** The HEAD comes from the river's own fall over the reach the conveyance short-circuits — the headrace runs nearly level while the river drops steeply.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes a PONDAGE (a PROR scheme).** A diversion weir's pool gives MINUTES of buffer, not hours — a 3 m weir on a 40 m river holds about half an hour of a 10 m³/s abstraction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design the weir for the SILTED condition it will spend most of its life in, and for BOULDER IMPACT** in a Himalayan stream. And build the ENVIRONMENTAL FLOW release into the geometry (a fixed notch), not into an operating instruction.

questions.stem: A minimum depth of water (submergence) is required above the mouth of a penstock or an intake principally:
options: To reduce the friction losses in the pipe
To increase the head available to the turbine
To prevent air being drawn in by vortex formation
To trap sediment before it enters the pipe
questions.solution:
**To prevent AIR being drawn in by VORTEX formation.**

**How the vortex forms and why it matters:**

> **Water approaching an intake mouth accelerates and, if the approach is asymmetric or the submergence is small, it develops a ROTATION.**

> **That rotation concentrates into a VORTEX above the intake — the same phenomenon as the swirl above a bath plug.**

> **If the submergence is insufficient, the vortex's core reaches down to the intake and DRAWS AIR into the pipe.**

> **The consequences are all bad:**

| Consequence of air entrainment | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of DISCHARGE and hence of output** | **The air occupies part of the pipe's cross-section** ← |
| **SURGING and unsteady flow** | The air pocket moves and collapses erratically |
| **VIBRATION and noise in the penstock and the machine** | Can be severe |
| **PRESSURE TRANSIENTS when an air pocket collapses** | **Comparable to water hammer** ← |
| **Damage to the turbine — air striking the runner** | Erosion and unbalanced loading |
| **Loss of prime, in a pumping installation** | The pump stops delivering |

> **The PRESSURE TRANSIENT effect is the most damaging: a pocket of air carried down a penstock and compressed, then suddenly released or collapsed, generates a pressure spike of the same character as water hammer — and the penstock was not designed for an extra one.**

**The required submergence — the design criterion:**

> **Various empirical relations exist; a commonly used form is:**

> **S ≥ 0.5 D + 0.3 V √D**  or, more simply,  **S ≥ 1.5 to 2.0 D**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | **SUBMERGENCE — depth of water above the top of the intake mouth** |
| **D** | **Diameter (or height) of the intake opening** |
| **V** | **Velocity at the intake** |

> **So a 2 m diameter penstock mouth needs roughly 3 to 4 m of water above it — a substantial depth, and one that must be provided in the forebay's design.**

> **Note that the requirement grows with the VELOCITY: a higher intake velocity generates a stronger swirl, so a fast intake needs more submergence than a slow one of the same size.**

> **Which gives the designer two levers: increase the depth, or enlarge the mouth to reduce the velocity — and the second is often cheaper, since a bell mouth costs less than deepening a forebay.**

**The ANTI-VORTEX measures, where submergence alone is insufficient:**

| Measure | How it works |
|---|---|
| **A BELL-MOUTHED (flared) intake** | **Reduces the entry velocity and smooths the approach — and it also cuts the entry loss from K = 0.5 to about 0.05** ← |
| **A SYMMETRICAL, straight approach to the intake** | **Asymmetric approach flow is the principal CAUSE of the swirl** ← |
| **ANTI-VORTEX plates, grids or a floating raft above the intake** | Physically break up the rotation |
| **A vertical splitter wall or a curtain wall** | Suppresses surface rotation |
| **Increasing the submergence** | The direct remedy |
| **A slotted or perforated approach screen** | Straightens the flow |

> **The SYMMETRICAL APPROACH is the most important and the cheapest, because asymmetry is the CAUSE rather than the submergence being the cure:**

> **Water arriving at an intake from one side has angular momentum about the intake axis, and that momentum must go somewhere — it concentrates into a vortex.**

> **Water arriving symmetrically from all sides has no net angular momentum, and no vortex forms even at modest submergence.**

> **So a forebay designed with the penstock centrally placed and the approach straight and symmetrical needs far less submergence than one where the pipe is tucked into a corner or fed from a side channel.**

> **Which means the vortex problem is best solved in the LAYOUT rather than in the depth — and a physical or numerical model study is often used for a large intake precisely to check the approach flow.**

**Why the other options are wrong — and one is nearly right:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **(a) Reduce friction losses** | **Submergence does not affect pipe friction, which depends on the velocity, diameter, length and roughness** |
| **(b) Increase the head** | **The head is the elevation difference between the water surface and the tailwater. Raising the water level DOES raise the head — but that is not why a MINIMUM SUBMERGENCE is specified** ← |
| **(d) Trap sediment** | **A SETTLING BASIN or gravel trap does that. Greater submergence may even draw MORE sediment, since the intake is then further below the surface** |

> **Option (b) deserves its note because it contains a true statement used to answer the wrong question: a deeper forebay does mean a slightly higher water surface and hence a marginally greater head.**

> **But the submergence requirement is not about head — it is a MINIMUM below which the intake malfunctions, and it must be satisfied even at the LOWEST operating water level.**

> **That last point is the practical form of the criterion: the submergence must be adequate at the MINIMUM DRAWDOWN LEVEL, not at the normal one — because that is when the vortex will form.**

> **A forebay or reservoir intake with adequate submergence at full supply and inadequate submergence when drawn down will entrain air precisely when the plant is most needed, in the dry season.**

> **So the intake's SETTING LEVEL is determined by the minimum operating level minus the required submergence — which frequently forces the intake lower than the sediment considerations would prefer, and that tension between air entrainment and sediment entry is a genuine design conflict.**

> **Its usual resolution is to set the intake as high as the submergence permits at minimum drawdown, and to accept the sediment that follows — dealing with it downstream in a settling basin rather than by lowering the intake and risking air.**

examTip.trick: **Insufficient submergence lets a VORTEX draw AIR into the penstock** — costing discharge, causing surging and vibration, and producing water-hammer-like transients when the pocket collapses. Roughly S ≥ 1.5-2.0 D.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is a true statement answering the wrong question** — a deeper forebay does raise the head slightly, but submergence is a MINIMUM below which the intake malfunctions, and it must hold at the LOWEST operating level.
examTip.mnemonic: **ASYMMETRIC approach flow is the CAUSE; submergence is only the cure.** Water arriving from one side carries angular momentum that concentrates into a vortex — so solve it in the LAYOUT, with a central, symmetrical, bell-mouthed intake.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river scheme, the structure that carries water at a gentle gradient along the hillside from the settling basin to the forebay is the:
questions.solution:
**The HEADRACE.**

**The conveyance elements in order, since the option set surveys them:**

| Element | Position | Function | Flow condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HEADRACE (power canal, headrace tunnel or pipe)** | **From the settling basin to the forebay** | **Carry the water forward at a GENTLE gradient while the river falls steeply, accumulating head** ← | **Free surface (canal) or pressurised (tunnel)** |
| **FOREBAY** | **At the end of the headrace** | Transition to pressurised flow; small pondage; final settling | Free surface |
| **PENSTOCK** | **From the forebay to the powerhouse** | **Carry the water DOWN the steep drop under PRESSURE** ← | **Pressurised** |
| **DRAFT TUBE** | **From the turbine runner to the tailrace** | **Recover the exit kinetic energy; allow the machine to be set above tailwater** | Pressurised, submerged |
| **TAILRACE** | **From the draft tube back to the river** | **Return the water to the river** ← | Free surface |

> **So the four options are four consecutive elements of the same waterway, and the question is one of sequence and function.**

> **The key distinction is between the HEADRACE and the PENSTOCK:**

> **The HEADRACE runs NEARLY LEVEL — a gradient of perhaps 1 in 500 to 1 in 2000 — along the hillside.**

> **The PENSTOCK runs STEEPLY DOWN, converting the accumulated elevation into pressure.**

> **The headrace GAINS the head (relative to the falling river); the penstock DELIVERS it.**

**Why the headrace is the element that creates the scheme — and its cost:**

> **A run-of-river plant's head comes entirely from the river's own fall over the reach the headrace bypasses.**

> **So the LONGER the headrace, the GREATER the head — and the greater the power from the same flow.**

| Headrace length | River's fall over that reach at 5 % slope | Gross head gained |
|---|---|---|
| **1 km** | **50 m** | **About 50 m** |
| **3 km** | **150 m** | **About 150 m** |
| **6 km** | **300 m** | **About 300 m** ← |

> **So extending the headrace buys head, and hence power, directly — which is why Nepali schemes have such long headraces, often several kilometres.**

> **And it is why the headrace is frequently the LARGEST single cost item in a run-of-river scheme: kilometres of canal, pipe or tunnel cut into a steep, unstable hillside.**

> **The optimisation is therefore a genuine one: each additional kilometre of headrace costs money and buys head, and the optimum length is where the marginal cost of headrace equals the marginal value of the energy it delivers.**

**The choice among headrace types, which is a real decision:**

| Type | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| **Open CANAL (lined)** | **Cheapest to build where the ground allows; simple; easy to inspect** | **Vulnerable to LANDSLIDE, rockfall and hillside drainage crossing it; evaporation and seepage; needs many cross-drainage works** ← |
| **Buried PIPE** | **Protected from rockfall; no cross-drainage works needed; no evaporation** | Costlier; harder to inspect and repair |
| **TUNNEL** | **Immune to landslide, rockfall and weather; shortest route; no land acquisition** ← | **Most expensive per metre; geological risk; needs a surge tank if pressurised** ← |
| **Flume or aqueduct on supports** | Crosses gullies and unstable ground | Expensive; exposed |

> **The TUNNEL option deserves emphasis for Nepal: a canal cut along an unstable Himalayan hillside crosses every gully and is exposed to every landslide, and its maintenance burden over decades can exceed the capital saved.**

> **A tunnel takes the direct line inside the mountain, is immune to surface hazards, requires no cross-drainage works, and needs almost no maintenance.**

> **Its costs are the excavation itself and the GEOLOGICAL RISK — a tunnel through fractured, water-bearing or squeezing rock can cost several times its estimate and take years longer.**

> **So the choice between canal and tunnel is a choice between a KNOWN higher capital cost with low risk and maintenance, and a LOWER capital cost with high exposure to hazard.**

> **In Nepal that judgement has increasingly favoured tunnels for schemes of any size, and the experience of canals destroyed by landslides is the reason.**

**The SURGE TANK requirement, since it depends on the headrace type:**

| Headrace type | Surge tank needed? |
|---|---|
| **Open canal or free-surface tunnel, ending in a forebay** | **NO — the forebay's free surface absorbs the transient** ← |
| **PRESSURISED tunnel or pipe** | **YES — a surge tank at the junction with the penstock** ← |
| **Short penstock direct from the intake** | Generally not, if L/H is below about 5 |

> **The reason is worth understanding: a free-surface headrace ending in a forebay has an open water surface at the top of the penstock, so a pressure wave travelling up the penstock is REFLECTED and released there — the forebay acts as the surge relief.**

> **A pressurised tunnel has no free surface, so the wave would travel the tunnel's whole length — and a surge tank must be provided at the junction to give it somewhere to go.**

> **So the surge tank is not a universal requirement but a consequence of choosing a pressurised conveyance, and a scheme with a canal and a forebay does not need one.**

> **That is a genuine cost consideration in the canal-versus-tunnel decision, and it slightly favours the canal option — a pressurised tunnel brings a surge tank with it.**

**And the TAILRACE, since it completes the sequence and is often neglected:**

| Requirement of the tailrace | Note |
|---|---|
| **Return the water to the river without erosion** | Protection at the outfall |
| **Its water level determines the TAILWATER, and hence the NET HEAD** | **A tailrace that silts up or backs up RAISES the tailwater and REDUCES the head** ← |
| **It must not be flooded by the river in a flood** | **A high river level drowns the draft tube and cuts the output — or floods the powerhouse** ← |
| **Sufficient submergence over the draft tube exit at all times** | Prevents air entering the draft tube |

> **The FLOOD row is the one that catches schemes out: a powerhouse set low to gain head is exposed to the river's flood level, and a plant flooded in the monsoon loses its output at the moment its energy is most abundant — or loses its machinery entirely.**

> **So the powerhouse floor level is set above the design flood level, and that requirement can cost several metres of head — a direct and permanent reduction in output accepted in exchange for not being flooded.**

> **That trade between head and flood safety is one of the sharper decisions in a run-of-river layout, and it is resolved firmly in favour of safety: a few per cent of output is a small price for a powerhouse that survives.**

examTip.trick: **The HEADRACE runs nearly LEVEL along the hillside and GAINS head as the river falls beneath it; the PENSTOCK runs steeply DOWN and DELIVERS that head.** All four options are consecutive elements of the same waterway.
examTip.trap: **A longer headrace buys more head and more power** — which is why it is often the largest cost item, and why its length is a genuine optimisation rather than a layout detail.
examTip.mnemonic: **A free-surface headrace ending in a FOREBAY needs no surge tank** — the forebay reflects the pressure wave. A PRESSURISED tunnel does. And the powerhouse floor must clear the design flood, which costs head and is worth it.

questions.stem: The device that regulates a turbine's speed by adjusting the water flow in response to changes in the electrical load is the:
questions.solution:
**The GOVERNOR.**

**Why speed regulation is essential — and it is not a refinement:**

> **A generator's output FREQUENCY is directly proportional to its rotational speed:**

> **f = N p / 120**, where N is the speed in rpm and p the number of poles.

> **So the frequency is fixed ONLY IF the speed is held constant — and the grid requires 50 Hz within a very narrow tolerance.**

> **The problem is that the turbine's speed depends on the BALANCE between the water power supplied and the electrical load taken:**

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| **Water power = electrical load** | **Speed CONSTANT — the desired state** |
| **Load DROPS (a consumer switches off, or the line trips)** | **The water power is now excess, and the machine ACCELERATES** ← |
| **Load RISES** | **The water power is insufficient, and the machine DECELERATES** |

> **So any change of load changes the speed, and hence the frequency, unless the water flow is adjusted to match.**

> **THAT ADJUSTMENT IS THE GOVERNOR'S JOB, and it must be made automatically and within seconds.**

**The RUNAWAY danger, which is why the governor is a safety device:**

> **If the load is lost COMPLETELY — the transmission line trips, or the breaker opens — and the water flow continues, the machine accelerates toward its RUNAWAY SPEED:**

| Turbine | Runaway speed as a multiple of the rated speed |
|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **1.8 to 1.9 ×** |
| **FRANCIS** | **1.8 to 2.2 ×** |
| **KAPLAN** | **2.0 to 3.2 ×** ← the highest |

> **At two or three times the rated speed the CENTRIFUGAL forces are four to nine times the design values, and the runner or the generator rotor can DISINTEGRATE.**

> **So the machine must be designed to WITHSTAND its runaway speed — every rotating part is checked for it — and the governor must shut the flow down before the speed rise causes damage or an unacceptable frequency excursion.**

> **The Kaplan's high runaway multiple is worth noting: an axial machine, having no centrifugal head to oppose the flow at high speed, accelerates further than a Francis or a Pelton.**

**How a governor works — the essential elements:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **SPEED SENSOR (mechanical flyball, or electronic pickup)** | **Detects the deviation from the set speed** |
| **AMPLIFIER / pilot valve** | **A small signal controls a large force** |
| **SERVOMOTOR (oil-hydraulic)** | **Moves the guide vanes or the spear valve — a very large force is required** ← |
| **OIL PRESSURE unit with an ACCUMULATOR** | **Stores energy so the governor can act even if the station's power fails** ← |
| **DASHPOT / damping and permanent-droop arrangement** | **Prevents HUNTING — oscillation about the set point** ← |
| **Feedback linkage** | Closes the control loop |

> **The ACCUMULATOR deserves emphasis because it is a safety-critical detail: the governor must be able to CLOSE the machine down at the moment the station loses its electrical supply, which is exactly when a load rejection occurs.**

> **So the operating energy is stored in a pressurised oil accumulator, sufficient for several full strokes without any power input — and its pressure is monitored and alarmed.**

> **A governor that cannot act without station power would fail precisely when it is needed.**

> **The DAMPING requirement addresses the opposite fault: a governor that responds too vigorously overshoots, corrects, overshoots again, and the machine HUNTS — oscillating in speed continuously.**

> **A hunting machine is unusable on a grid, and the cure is a deliberate PERMANENT DROOP: the governor is arranged so that a small speed drop is accepted at higher load, rather than the speed being held exactly.**

> **That droop is what allows several machines to SHARE a load stably: each takes more load as the frequency falls slightly, and the sharing is determined by their droop settings.**

> **Machines with zero droop — isochronous governors — cannot share load at all, because each would fight to set the frequency itself. So only ONE machine in an isolated system can be isochronous, and the rest must have droop.**

> **That is a genuinely important operating principle and it is not obvious: stability in a multi-machine system requires each machine to accept a small frequency error rather than to insist on perfection.**

**The conflict between the governor and WATER HAMMER — the central design tension:**

> **The governor's job is to close the flow QUICKLY when the load drops, to limit the speed rise.**

> **But closing quickly generates WATER HAMMER in the penstock — and the faster the closure, the higher the pressure rise.**

| Closure | Speed rise | Pressure rise |
|---|---|---|
| **FAST** | **SMALL — good** | **LARGE — dangerous** ← |
| **SLOW** | **LARGE — dangerous** | **Small — good** |

> **So the two requirements are in DIRECT OPPOSITION, and the closure time is chosen as a compromise between an acceptable speed rise and an acceptable pressure rise.**

> **The devices that relieve the conflict are worth knowing, because they are what allow a satisfactory compromise:**

| Device | How it helps |
|---|---|
| **SURGE TANK** | **Confines the water hammer to the penstock, so the pressure rise is computed over a much shorter length** ← |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF VALVE** | **Opens as the gates close, so the total flow changes slowly while the flow to the turbine stops quickly** ← |
| **FLYWHEEL effect (increased rotating inertia)** | **A heavier rotor accelerates more slowly, so a slower closure is tolerable** ← |
| **DEFLECTOR on a Pelton** | **Deflects the jet away from the buckets INSTANTLY, then the needle closes slowly** ← |

> **The PELTON DEFLECTOR is the most elegant of these and deserves explanation: the jet is deflected off the runner in a fraction of a second, removing the driving force at once — while the needle valve then closes over many seconds, so the flow in the penstock changes slowly and no water hammer is generated.**

> **The speed rise is arrested immediately AND the pressure rise is avoided, which resolves the conflict entirely rather than compromising between its horns.**

> **That is available only for an impulse turbine, because only an impulse machine's driving force can be removed without stopping the flow — which is one of the underappreciated advantages of the Pelton.**

> **For a reaction turbine the pressure relief valve performs the analogous function: it dumps water to waste as the gates close, so the penstock's flow changes gradually while the turbine's does not.**

> **The cost is the water wasted during each load rejection, which is trivial in occurrence and entirely acceptable against the alternative.**

examTip.trick: **Frequency is proportional to speed (f = Np/120), so holding the frequency means holding the speed — and that means matching the WATER FLOW to the electrical load.** That is the governor's job.
examTip.trap: **Runaway speed is 1.8-2.2 × rated for Pelton and Francis but up to 3.2 × for a KAPLAN** — and centrifugal forces go as the square, so up to nine times the design values. Every rotating part is checked for it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fast closure limits the SPEED rise and worsens WATER HAMMER — the two requirements are in direct opposition.** A Pelton DEFLECTOR resolves it entirely: remove the jet instantly, close the needle slowly. And a governor needs PERMANENT DROOP, or machines cannot share load.

questions.stem: As per IRC, the normal RIGHT OF WAY (land width) for a National or State Highway in plain and rolling terrain is:
questions.solution:
**45 m.**

**The IRC land width recommendations for plain and rolling terrain:**

| Road class | NORMAL right of way | Range (minimum to exceptional) |
|---|---|---|
| **National and State Highways** | **45 m** ← | **30-60 m** |
| **Major District Roads** | **25 m** | **25-30 m** |
| **Other District Roads** | **15 m** | **15-25 m** |
| **Village Roads** | **12 m** | **12-18 m** |

> **And in MOUNTAINOUS and STEEP terrain the widths are much smaller, because acquiring and cutting a wide corridor into a hillside is prohibitively expensive:**

| Road class | Right of way in mountainous terrain |
|---|---|
| **NH and SH** | **24 m** |
| **MDR** | **18 m** |
| **ODR and VR** | **15 m** |

> **Option (c) 24 m is the mountainous-terrain figure for a highway, and option (d) 15 m the village road figure — both real values, offered for the wrong case.**

> **So the option set requires both the road CLASS and the TERRAIN to be matched, which is the substance of this topic.**

**Why so much more land than the carriageway needs — what the 45 m is for:**

> **A two-lane highway's carriageway is only 7 m wide. The remaining 38 m serves other purposes:**

| Use of the land width | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shoulders and side drains** | 2.5 m of shoulder each side, plus drains |
| **CUT AND FILL SLOPES** | **A cutting or embankment of any height occupies a great width at 2:1 slopes** ← |
| **FUTURE WIDENING to four or six lanes** | **The most important reason — land acquired now is far cheaper than land acquired later** ← |
| **Utilities — water, power, telecommunications, gas** | **A highway corridor carries the country's services** |
| **Service roads and slip roads** | Where access must be controlled |
| **Roadside plantation** | Shade, stabilisation, appearance |
| **A margin against encroachment** | **See below** ← |

> **The FUTURE WIDENING reason is the decisive one and it is worth stating plainly: land is the one component of a road that cannot be manufactured, and its cost rises as development follows the road.**

> **Acquiring 45 m at the outset, when the corridor is agricultural, costs a fraction of acquiring an additional 20 m later when the frontage has been built up.**

> **So the generous right of way is an investment in the road's future capacity, and economising on it at the start is one of the more expensive false economies available in infrastructure planning.**

**The ENCROACHMENT problem, which is the practical reality:**

> **A right of way is legally acquired and physically empty, and it does not stay empty:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **A tea stall, a repair shop or a stack of materials appears on the margin** |
| **2** | **It becomes semi-permanent; then permanent** |
| **3** | **A row of frontage development follows, each with its own access** ← |
| **4** | **The road's MOBILITY function is destroyed — this is RIBBON DEVELOPMENT** ← |
| **5** | **Widening later requires the removal of established livelihoods, which is politically almost impossible** |

> **So the right of way must be DEMARCATED, RECORDED and PROTECTED, not merely acquired — and the failure to do so is why so many highways in the region are lined with development that both slows the traffic and prevents the widening the corridor was reserved for.**

> **The practical measures are boundary stones or pillars at intervals, a recorded and published alignment, and BUILDING LINE and CONTROL LINE setbacks enforced by the planning authority.**

**The BUILDING LINE and CONTROL LINE, since they extend beyond the right of way:**

| Line | Definition | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **RIGHT OF WAY (land width)** | **The land actually ACQUIRED and owned by the road authority** | The road and its future |
| **BUILDING LINE** | **A line beyond the right of way, within which NO BUILDING may be erected** ← | **Sight distance, future widening, and a setback from the traffic** |
| **CONTROL LINE** | **A further line, within which building is CONTROLLED and requires permission** | Longer-term protection of the corridor |

> **The typical setbacks for a highway in open country are a building line about 80 m apart overall and a control line about 150 m apart — considerably more than the 45 m acquired.**

> **So the corridor is protected in three concentric bands: land OWNED, land where building is FORBIDDEN, and land where building is CONTROLLED.**

> **That layered arrangement lets the authority protect a wide corridor without the cost of acquiring it, which is an economical piece of regulation — and it works only if the planning authority enforces it, which is where it usually fails.**

**And the CARRIAGEWAY widths, since they are asked alongside:**

| Carriageway | Width |
|---|---|
| **Single lane** | **3.75 m** |
| **Two lanes, without raised kerbs** | **7.0 m** ← |
| **Two lanes, with raised kerbs** | **7.5 m** |
| **Intermediate carriageway** | **5.5 m** |
| **Multi-lane, per lane** | **3.5 m** |

> **The INTERMEDIATE carriageway of 5.5 m deserves a note because it is a genuinely bad width and is nevertheless common:**

> **It is too narrow for two vehicles to pass comfortably and too wide for drivers to treat it as single lane — so drivers attempt to pass and both move onto the shoulders, damaging them.**

> **IRC accordingly discourages it, and a road is better built either as a proper single lane with passing places or as a full two-lane 7 m carriageway.**

> **That is a case where an intermediate solution is worse than either extreme, which is unusual and worth remembering — the accident rate on 5.5 m carriageways is disproportionately high for exactly that reason.**

examTip.trick: **NH/SH in plain terrain: 45 m normal right of way** (range 30-60 m). In MOUNTAINOUS terrain it falls to 24 m. MDR 25 m, ODR 15 m, VR 12 m.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) are real values for the wrong case** — 24 m is a highway in mountainous terrain, 15 m a village road. Match both the CLASS and the TERRAIN.
examTip.mnemonic: **The width is mostly for FUTURE WIDENING — land acquired now is far cheaper than land acquired after the frontage is built up.** And three concentric bands protect the corridor: land OWNED (right of way), building FORBIDDEN (building line), building CONTROLLED (control line).

questions.stem: As per IRC, the RULING GRADIENT for a road in MOUNTAINOUS terrain is:
questions.solution:
**1 in 20, that is 5 per cent.**

**The IRC gradients by terrain:**

| Terrain | RULING gradient | LIMITING gradient | EXCEPTIONAL gradient |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** | **1 in 30 (3.3 %)** | **1 in 20 (5 %)** | **1 in 15 (6.7 %)** |
| **MOUNTAINOUS, and steep with elevation above 3000 m** | **1 in 20 (5 %)** ← | **1 in 16.7 (6 %)** | **1 in 14.3 (7 %)** |
| **Steep terrain up to 3000 m** | **1 in 16.7 (6 %)** | **1 in 14.3 (7 %)** | **1 in 12.5 (8 %)** |

> **Note that EVERY option offered is a real IRC gradient from that table — 1 in 30 is the plain-terrain ruling gradient, 1 in 15 the plain-terrain exceptional gradient, and 1 in 12 close to the steep-terrain exceptional value.**

> **So the option set requires both the TERRAIN and the CLASS OF GRADIENT to be matched, and an approximate recall will not discriminate.**

**The three classes of gradient, and how each is used:**

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **RULING (design) gradient** | **The gradient the designer ADOPTS as a matter of course, and which governs the alignment** ← |
| **LIMITING gradient** | **Used where the ruling gradient would involve excessive cost — over SHORT lengths only** ← |
| **EXCEPTIONAL gradient** | **Used only in VERY DIFFICULT situations, over lengths not exceeding about 100 m at a stretch** ← |

> **The essential discipline is that the steeper gradients are permitted only over SHORT LENGTHS and must be separated by gentler stretches — not used continuously.**

> **A road built at the exceptional gradient throughout would comply with no part of the intent of the table.**

> **And IRC further requires that exceptional gradients should not be used for more than about 100 m at a time, with a minimum length of gentler gradient between successive steep stretches.**

**Why the gradient is limited at all — the two constraints:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **A loaded truck's CLIMBING ABILITY** | **A heavy vehicle slows drastically on a steep gradient; at 6 % a loaded truck may fall to 15-20 km/h** ← |
| **DESCENDING safety — brake fade** | **A long steep descent overheats the brakes; this is the more dangerous direction** ← |
| **Vehicle operating cost — fuel consumption rises steeply** | An economic cost for the road's life |
| **Capacity — slow vehicles hold up the stream** | **The truck's effective PCU rises above 5 on a steep upgrade** |
| **Surface deterioration from tractive effort** | Bituminous surfaces shove and rut on steep grades |

> **The DESCENDING case is worth emphasising because it is less obvious and more lethal: a loaded truck descending a long steep gradient must dissipate its potential energy through its brakes, and prolonged braking causes BRAKE FADE — the brakes lose effectiveness as they overheat.**

> **A vehicle that loses its brakes on a mountain descent has no means of stopping, and such accidents are among the most severe on Himalayan roads.**

> **So the gradient limits protect the descent as much as the climb, and the provision of ESCAPE LANES or arrester beds at the foot of long descents is the corresponding safety measure.**

**The RESISTING LENGTH concept, which controls the total climb:**

> **Limiting the gradient is not enough: a road at 5 per cent for twenty kilometres climbs a kilometre, and a loaded truck cannot sustain that.**

> **So the concept of RESISTING LENGTH is used: the length of road, measured as an equivalent level length, that a vehicle must overcome — combining the actual length with the extra effort of the rise.**

> **The practice is to insert LEVEL or GENTLE stretches at intervals in a long climb, allowing engines to cool and vehicles to recover speed — and in Nepal's hill roads those stretches are also where overtaking becomes possible.**

**GRADE COMPENSATION on curves, since it modifies the gradient:**

> **On a horizontal curve, a vehicle must overcome the curve resistance IN ADDITION to the gradient — so the effective effort is greater than the gradient alone suggests.**

> **IRC therefore requires the gradient to be EASED on sharp curves:**

> **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R per cent, subject to a maximum of 75/R per cent**

| Radius R | Compensation |
|---|---|
| **50 m** | **(30+50)/50 = 1.6 %, but capped at 75/50 = 1.5 %** ← |
| **100 m** | **(30+100)/100 = 1.3 %, cap 0.75 % — so 0.75 %** |
| **200 m** | 0.375 % |

> **And crucially: GRADE COMPENSATION IS NOT APPLIED WHERE THE GRADIENT IS FLATTER THAN 4 PER CENT.**

> **The reason is practical: on a gentle gradient the curve resistance is not the limiting factor, and easing an already gentle grade would require unnecessary earthwork.**

> **So compensation applies where it matters — on the steep, sharp curves of a hill road — and that combination is exactly the hairpin bend, where both the gradient and the curvature are at their limits.**

> **Which is why a properly designed hairpin bend is on a NEARLY LEVEL section: the gradient is eased through the bend and the climbing is done on the straights between them.**

> **A hairpin built on the full ruling gradient combines maximum curve resistance with maximum grade resistance, and a loaded truck may be unable to negotiate it at all — which is a documented failure of hill road design and the reason the compensation rule exists.**

**And the MINIMUM gradient, which is the other end of the requirement:**

| Situation | Minimum gradient for drainage |
|---|---|
| **A road in cutting, with side drains** | **1 in 200 (0.5 %) at least, and 1 in 100 preferred** ← |
| **On an embankment, where water can shed sideways** | **A level grade is acceptable** |

> **A road in CUTTING must have a longitudinal gradient, because its side drains need a fall to carry water away — and a level drain in a cutting ponds, saturates the subgrade and destroys the pavement from below.**

> **So the gradient has a permitted range rather than a maximum, and the drainage requirement at the flat end is as real as the traction requirement at the steep end.**

examTip.trick: **Mountainous terrain: ruling 1 in 20 (5 %), limiting 1 in 16.7 (6 %), exceptional 1 in 14.3 (7 %).** In plain terrain: 1 in 30, 1 in 20, 1 in 15.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real IRC gradient for a different terrain or class** — so match both. And the steeper gradients are for SHORT lengths only (about 100 m), separated by gentler stretches.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grade compensation = (30+R)/R %, capped at 75/R, and NOT applied below 4 % gradient** — which is why a hairpin bend must be on a nearly level section. And the DESCENT is the more dangerous direction: brake fade on a long steep grade.

questions.stem: The length of a transition curve is computed by three separate criteria. The value adopted for design is:
options: The largest of the three computed values
The value from the rate of change of centrifugal acceleration only
questions.solution:
**The LARGEST of the three computed values.**

**The three criteria:**

| Criterion | Expression | What it ensures |
|---|---|---|
| **RATE OF CHANGE of centrifugal acceleration** | **L = 0.0215 V³/(C R)**, with C = 80/(75+V), between 0.5 and 0.8 | **COMFORT — the sideways force builds up gradually** ← |
| **RATE OF ATTAINMENT of superelevation** | **L = e N (W + W_e)** for rotation about the centre line, or 2.7 V²/R (IRC empirical) | **The pavement is not warped too abruptly** ← |
| **IRC EMPIRICAL formula** | **L = 2.7 V²/R (plain and rolling); L = V²/R (mountainous and steep)** | **A minimum from experience** |

> **Each criterion protects a DIFFERENT requirement, so the design must satisfy ALL THREE — and satisfying all three means adopting the LARGEST value.**

> **That is the general principle whenever several independent criteria govern one dimension, and it is worth stating as such: TAKE THE MOST DEMANDING, because a value satisfying the largest satisfies the others automatically.**

> **Option (b) the smallest would violate two of the three criteria, and option (c) the average would violate at least one — so both are wrong by the same reasoning.**

> **And option (d) is the error of applying only the comfort criterion, which for a sharp curve at low speed is frequently NOT the governing one.**

**What a transition curve does — its three simultaneous functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Introduce the CURVATURE gradually** | **From infinity on the straight to R on the circular curve, so the driver need not turn the wheel suddenly** ← |
| **Attain the SUPERELEVATION gradually** | **The cross-slope is developed over the transition's length, not at a point** ← |
| **Develop the EXTRA WIDENING gradually** | **The carriageway widens over the same length** ← |

> **All three developments happen over the SAME length, which is what makes the transition curve such an economical element: one length of road accomplishes three changes that would each otherwise be abrupt.**

> **And it is why a curve without a transition is so uncomfortable even when its radius is generous: the curvature, the banking and the width all change suddenly at the tangent point, and the driver must respond to all three at once.**

**The SPIRAL (clothoid) shape, since the curve's form is not arbitrary:**

> **The ideal transition has its CURVATURE increasing LINEARLY with the distance travelled along it:**

> **1/R ∝ L, or  R L = constant**

> **That is the definition of the CLOTHOID or SPIRAL, and it is the ideal because a driver turning the steering wheel at a CONSTANT RATE traces exactly that path.**

> **So the clothoid is the curve a vehicle naturally follows, and a road built to it requires no correction from the driver.**

| Transition type | Note |
|---|---|
| **SPIRAL (clothoid)** | **THE IDEAL — curvature proportional to length; IRC recommends it** ← |
| **Cubic parabola** | A close approximation, easier to set out; used historically |
| **Lemniscate** | Used for very large deflection angles |

> **The SPIRAL is now standard because setting it out is no harder than any other curve with modern instruments, and the historical reasons for the approximations have gone.**

**Where the criteria come from — worth understanding rather than recalling:**

> **THE COMFORT criterion: a passenger experiences the centrifugal force building from zero to V²/R over the transition's length.**

> **The RATE at which it builds — the rate of change of centrifugal acceleration C, in m/s³ — is what determines comfort, and it is limited to between 0.5 and 0.8 m/s³.**

> **A higher rate is felt as a lurch; a lower one requires an impractically long transition.**

> **THE SUPERELEVATION criterion: the pavement's outer edge must be raised relative to the centre line, and the RATE at which it rises — the longitudinal slope of the edge relative to the centre — is limited.**

> **IRC limits it to 1 in 150 for plain and rolling terrain and 1 in 60 for mountainous terrain (where a longer transition would be prohibitively expensive).**

> **A steeper rate produces a visibly and perceptibly WARPED pavement, and it also creates a drainage problem where the cross-slope passes through zero.**

> **THE EMPIRICAL criterion is simply a minimum from experience, and it usually governs at low speeds and sharp radii — which is exactly the Nepali hill road case.**

**Which criterion governs, since that determines what matters in practice:**
