| Situation | Usually governing criterion |
|---|---|
| **HIGH speed, LARGE radius (a highway curve)** | **The COMFORT (rate of change of acceleration) criterion — because V³ dominates** ← |
| **LOW speed, SHARP radius (a hill road curve)** | **The EMPIRICAL or the SUPERELEVATION criterion** ← |
| **Where the superelevation is large** | **The superelevation attainment criterion** |

> **The V³ dependence of the comfort criterion is why it dominates at high speed: doubling the design speed multiplies that required length by EIGHT, while the empirical criterion's V² multiplies it by only four.**

> **So a high-speed road needs very long transitions, and the length of transition is one of the reasons a high design speed is expensive in earthwork.**

**The SHIFT, since it is the geometric consequence:**

> **Inserting a transition curve requires the circular curve to be SHIFTED inward, away from the tangent, by:**

> **S = L²/(24 R)**

> **The transition begins on the tangent and ends where the circular curve begins, and the circular curve's radius is unchanged — so the whole curve must move in to accommodate the transition.**

> **That shift is what makes retrofitting a transition to an existing curve difficult: the circular portion must be relocated, which means reconstructing the whole curve rather than adding a length at each end.**

> **Which is a good reason to provide transitions in the original design even where the traffic does not yet justify them — the geometry cannot be improved later without rebuilding the curve.**

> **And it is why IRC requires a transition on every curve of a road designed for 50 km/h or more, rather than leaving it to be added when the road is upgraded.**
tags: rate of change of centrifugal acceleration

examTip.trick: **Each criterion protects a DIFFERENT requirement, so all three must be satisfied — take the LARGEST.** That is the general rule whenever independent criteria govern one dimension.
examTip.trap: **The comfort criterion goes as V³, so it dominates at HIGH speed; the empirical one (V²) usually governs a sharp, low-speed hill curve.** Option (d) applies only one criterion and misses the governing case.
examTip.mnemonic: **One length does three jobs: introduces the CURVATURE, attains the SUPERELEVATION, develops the EXTRA WIDENING.** The ideal shape is the CLOTHOID (curvature ∝ length), the path a driver traces turning the wheel at a constant rate. And the shift L²/24R means a transition cannot be retrofitted without rebuilding the curve.

questions.stem: As per IRC, the recommended camber for a bituminous or cement concrete surface in an area of low rainfall is:
questions.solution:
**1 in 50, that is 2 per cent.**

**The IRC camber recommendations by surface type:**

| Surface type | Camber in LOW rainfall | Camber in HEAVY rainfall |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement concrete and high-type BITUMINOUS surface** | **1 in 50 (2.0 %)** ← | **1 in 50 (2.0 %)** |
| **Thin bituminous surface** | **1 in 50 (2.0 %)** | **1 in 40 (2.5 %)** |
| **Water bound macadam (WBM) and gravel** | **1 in 40 (2.5 %)** | **1 in 33 (3.0 %)** |
| **EARTH road** | **1 in 33 (3.0 %)** | **1 in 25 (4.0 %)** ← |

> **Every option offered is a real IRC camber value from that table, so the option set requires the SURFACE TYPE to be matched.**

> **And the pattern is the essential fact: THE MORE PERMEABLE THE SURFACE, THE STEEPER THE CAMBER REQUIRED.**

**Why the pattern runs that way — the reasoning:**

> **The camber's purpose is to shed rainwater from the surface QUICKLY, before it can infiltrate.**

| Surface | Behaviour | Camber needed |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement concrete, dense bituminous** | **Nearly IMPERVIOUS and SMOOTH — water runs off readily** | **Gentle (2 %) suffices** ← |
| **WBM, gravel** | **POROUS and ROUGH — water infiltrates and is retarded by the texture** | **Steeper (2.5-3 %)** |
| **EARTH** | **Very permeable, easily rutted; ruts channel water along the road** | **Steepest (3-4 %)** ← |

> **So the camber compensates for the surface's own inability to shed water, and the steeper values are needed precisely where the surface is worst at doing it.**

> **And the RAINFALL column adds the second variable: a heavy-rainfall area needs a steeper camber for the same surface, because more water must be shed faster.**

**Why water on the surface is so damaging — what the camber prevents:**

| Consequence of water remaining on or in the pavement | Note |
|---|---|
| **WEAKENING of the subgrade and the granular layers** | **A saturated subgrade's CBR can fall to a fraction of its soaked design value** ← |
| **STRIPPING of bitumen from the aggregate** | **Water displaces the binder from the stone; then traffic plucks the aggregate out** ← |
| **PUMPING of fines under traffic loading** | Water under pressure carries fines out, creating voids |
| **POTHOLE formation and accelerated ravelling** | The visible result |
| **HYDROPLANING — loss of tyre contact at speed** | **A SAFETY hazard, not merely a durability one** ← |
| **Reduced skid resistance; spray reducing visibility** | Safety |
| **Frost damage, where applicable** | Freeze-thaw of retained water |

> **The HYDROPLANING entry is worth emphasising because it makes camber a safety provision as well as a durability one: a film of water on the surface at speed can lift the tyre off the pavement entirely, and the vehicle becomes uncontrollable.**

> **So an inadequate camber, or a rutted surface that holds water in the wheel paths, is a direct accident risk — and ruts are dangerous chiefly because they hold water rather than because of their depth.**

> **That is why rut depth is a maintenance trigger and why a rutted road is resurfaced rather than merely watched.**

**The camber's own limits — why it is not made steeper still:**

| Problem with an excessive camber | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vehicles TEND TO SLIDE toward the edge** | **Especially a high-sided vehicle on a wet surface** ← |
| **Uncomfortable — the vehicle leans** | And drivers crowd the crown |
| **Traffic CONCENTRATES on the crown, rutting it** | **Which then holds water at the centre, defeating the camber** ← |
| **Difficult and uncomfortable to overtake** | The two vehicles lean opposite ways |
| **Increased tyre and suspension wear** | — |

> **The CROWN CONCENTRATION effect is the practical objection and it is self-defeating: drivers avoid the steeply sloping edges and drive along the crown, which then wears into a depression that holds water exactly where the camber was highest.**

> **So the camber has an optimum — steep enough to shed the water, gentle enough that traffic uses the full width — and the tabulated values sit at that optimum for each surface.**

**The SHAPES of camber, since the profile matters as well as the slope:**

| Shape | Note |
|---|---|
| **PARABOLIC (barrel)** | **A smooth curve; comfortable, and it sheds water faster near the edges where the flow is greatest** ← |
| **STRAIGHT LINE (two planes meeting at the crown)** | **Simple to construct and to check; a sharp crown that wears** |
| **COMBINATION — straight near the edges, parabolic at the crown** | **The practical compromise, and common practice** ← |

> **The PARABOLIC shape has a genuine hydraulic merit: the flow of water increases toward the edge as it collects from the width above, so a profile that STEEPENS toward the edge carries the increasing flow at a similar depth.**

> **A straight camber has a constant slope, so the water film DEEPENS toward the edge — which is where hydroplaning and spray originate.**

> **So the parabola sheds water at a more uniform depth across the width, which is why it is preferred for high-speed roads despite being harder to set out.**

> **And the combination shape is the working answer: a rounded crown that traffic does not wear into a ridge, with straight portions toward the edges that are easy to construct and check with a camber board.**

**And the relation to SUPERELEVATION, since the two interact:**

> **On a curve, the camber must be REMOVED from the outer half and replaced by superelevation — which is the "elimination of the crown" stage of the transition.**

> **The consequence is a length of road where the cross-slope passes through ZERO on the outer half, and at that point the water has no cross-fall to shed it.**

> **That length is a known drainage weak point, and it is handled by ensuring the LONGITUDINAL gradient is adequate there — so the water runs along the road rather than standing on it.**

> **A curve's transition on a level longitudinal gradient therefore creates a flat spot in both directions, which ponds water — and it is why the vertical and horizontal alignments must be coordinated rather than designed independently.**

examTip.trick: **Bituminous or cement concrete: 1 in 50 (2 %). WBM 2.5-3 %, EARTH 3-4 %.** The rule: the more PERMEABLE and rough the surface, the STEEPER the camber.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a real IRC camber for another surface type**, so match the surface. And a steeper camber is not simply safer — traffic then crowds the CROWN and ruts it, holding water exactly where the camber was highest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Camber is a SAFETY provision too — a water film causes HYDROPLANING**, which is why ruts are dangerous for holding water rather than for their depth. And where the camber passes through zero in a transition, the longitudinal gradient must shed the water instead.

questions.stem: The maximum permissible AGGREGATE IMPACT VALUE for aggregate used in a bituminous SURFACE COURSE is:
questions.solution:
**30 per cent.**

**The permissible aggregate impact values by pavement layer:**

| Application | Maximum aggregate impact value |
|---|---|
| **WEARING (surface) course — bituminous concrete, surface dressing** | **30 %** ← |
| **Bituminous macadam, base and binder courses** | **35 %** |
| **Water bound macadam (WBM) base course** | **40 %** |
| **WBM sub-base** | **50 %** |
| **Cement concrete pavement wearing surface** | **30 %** |

> **Every option offered is a real limit from that table, so the option set requires the LAYER to be matched.**

> **And the pattern is the same as for every other aggregate property: THE HIGHER THE LAYER, THE STRICTER THE REQUIREMENT.**

> **The reason is direct exposure: a surface-course aggregate receives the tyre loads and impacts directly, while a sub-base aggregate is protected by everything above it.**

**What the test measures and how:**

> **The AGGREGATE IMPACT TEST measures TOUGHNESS — the resistance to sudden SHOCK or impact, as distinct from a gradually applied load.**

| Test parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Aggregate size tested** | **Passing 12.5 mm and retained on 10 mm** |
| **Hammer mass** | **13.5 to 14 kg** |
| **Height of fall** | **380 mm** |
| **Number of blows** | **15** |
| **Sieve for the fines produced** | **2.36 mm** ← |
| **Result** | **(weight passing 2.36 mm / total weight) × 100** |

> **So the value is the PERCENTAGE OF FINES PRODUCED by the impact — a higher value means a weaker, more easily shattered aggregate.**

> **Note the 2.36 mm sieve, which distinguishes this test from the Los Angeles abrasion test's 1.7 mm sieve — a detail worth keeping straight, since the two tests are otherwise superficially similar.**

**The four principal aggregate mechanical tests, and what each measures:**

| Test | Measures | Property | Sieve for fines |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IMPACT value** | **Resistance to SUDDEN SHOCK** | **TOUGHNESS** ← | **2.36 mm** |
| **CRUSHING value** | **Resistance to a GRADUALLY applied compressive load** | **STRENGTH** | **2.36 mm** |
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION value** | **Resistance to WEAR by rubbing plus impact from steel spheres** | **HARDNESS** | **1.7 mm** |
| **SOUNDNESS (sulphate)** | **Resistance to accelerated WEATHERING cycles** | **DURABILITY** | — |

> **Four tests, four distinct properties — and it is worth being able to say which is which, because the option sets in this subject exploit the confusion.**

> **The IMPACT and CRUSHING tests are the most easily confused, and the distinction is the RATE of loading: impact is a sudden blow, crushing a gradual squeeze.**

> **Their limits are also similar (30 % for a surface course in both cases), which does not help — but the tests measure genuinely different things, and an aggregate can pass one and fail the other.**

> **A brittle rock, for instance, may resist a gradual load well and shatter under a blow.**

**Why the IMPACT test is often preferred to the CRUSHING test in practice:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The apparatus is SIMPLER and PORTABLE** | **A field-usable test, unlike the crushing test's compression machine** ← |
| **The test is quicker** | 15 blows against a slow load application |
| **Impact better represents the actual TRAFFIC action** | **A wheel load is applied and removed repeatedly and rapidly — closer to impact than to a static squeeze** ← |
| **Results correlate well with the crushing value** | So one can substitute for the other |

> **The PORTABILITY point is the decisive practical one: the impact test can be done at a quarry or on site with a simple apparatus, while the crushing test requires a laboratory compression machine.**

> **For routine acceptance of aggregate arriving at a road project, that difference determines which test is actually used.**

**The classification by impact value, since the number should be interpreted:**

| Impact value | Toughness classification |
|---|---|
| **Below 10 %** | **EXCEPTIONALLY strong** |
| **10-20 %** | **STRONG** |
| **20-30 %** | **SATISFACTORY for a surface course** ← |
| **30-35 %** | **Marginal — base courses only** |
| **Above 35 %** | **WEAK — unsuitable for a pavement surface** |

> **So a value of 30 per cent is at the BOUNDARY of acceptability for a surface course, and an aggregate testing at exactly 30 is only just satisfactory.**

> **Good practice specifies a margin: an aggregate at 20 to 25 per cent leaves room for the variability of a quarry's output, whereas one at 29 will fail some batches.**

> **That is a general point about specifying against a limit: the specification is the boundary of acceptability, and a material that only just meets it will not meet it consistently.**

**And the aggregate tests as a complete acceptance set, since a surface aggregate must pass several:**

| Requirement for a bituminous surface course aggregate | Typical limit |
|---|---|
| **Aggregate IMPACT value** | **30 % maximum** ← |
| **Los Angeles ABRASION value** | **30 % maximum** |
| **FLAKINESS and ELONGATION (combined index)** | **30 % maximum** |
| **WATER ABSORPTION** | **2 % maximum** |
| **SOUNDNESS (sodium/magnesium sulphate)** | **12 % / 18 % maximum loss** |
| **STRIPPING value / coating and stripping test** | **Retained coating minimum 95 %** ← |
| **POLISHED STONE value (for high-speed roads)** | **Minimum 55** ← |

> **The STRIPPING requirement is the one specific to bituminous work and it is essential: an aggregate that the bitumen will not adhere to in the presence of water will ravel however strong the stone is.**

> **Acidic siliceous aggregates — quartzite, some granites — are prone to it, and the remedies are an anti-stripping agent, hydrated lime in the mix, or a different aggregate.**

> **And the POLISHED STONE VALUE is the requirement most often omitted and specific to safety: an aggregate can be strong, tough, durable and still POLISH SMOOTH under traffic, becoming slippery when wet.**

> **Limestone is the classic offender — perfectly adequate on every strength test and unsuitable for a high-speed wearing course because it polishes.**

> **So a surface aggregate must satisfy STRENGTH, SHAPE, DURABILITY, ADHESION and POLISHING requirements, and passing the impact test alone establishes only one of the five.**

examTip.trick: **Surface course 30 %, bituminous macadam 35 %, WBM base 40 %, sub-base 50 %.** The higher the layer, the stricter — because it is directly exposed.
examTip.trap: **Four tests, four properties: IMPACT = toughness (sudden shock), CRUSHING = strength (gradual load), LOS ANGELES = hardness (wear), SOUNDNESS = durability.** Impact and crushing use a 2.36 mm sieve; Los Angeles uses 1.7 mm.
examTip.mnemonic: **A surface aggregate must pass FIVE kinds of requirement — strength, shape, durability, ADHESION (stripping) and POLISHING.** Limestone passes every strength test and polishes smooth, which is why it is barred from high-speed wearing courses.

questions.stem: The minimum MARSHALL STABILITY required for a bituminous concrete surface course carrying heavy traffic is about:
questions.solution:
**About 9 kN (900 kg).**

**What the Marshall test measures:**

> **A compacted cylindrical specimen of the bituminous mix — 101.6 mm diameter, 63.5 mm high — is brought to 60 °C and loaded diametrically at 50 mm per minute until it fails.**

| Quantity measured | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **MARSHALL STABILITY** | **The maximum LOAD the specimen carries, in kN — its resistance to deformation** ← |
| **FLOW value** | **The vertical DEFORMATION at that maximum load, in units of 0.25 mm** ← |

> **So the test gives a strength AND a deformation, and both are specified — because a mix can be strong and brittle, or soft and tough, and neither is wanted.**

**The specified requirements for a bituminous concrete surface course:**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Marshall STABILITY at 60 °C** | **Minimum 9 kN (900 kg)** ← |
| **FLOW value** | **2 to 4 mm (8 to 16 units of 0.25 mm)** |
| **Marshall QUOTIENT (stability/flow)** | **2 to 5 kN/mm** |
| **AIR VOIDS (Vv)** | **3 to 5 %** ← |
| **VOIDS IN MINERAL AGGREGATE (VMA)** | **Minimum 11-14 %, by nominal aggregate size** |
| **VOIDS FILLED WITH BITUMEN (VFB)** | **65 to 75 %** |
| **Compaction** | **75 blows on EACH face for heavy traffic (50 for medium)** ← |

> **The 60 °C test temperature is not arbitrary: it approximates the temperature of a bituminous pavement surface in hot weather, which is when the mix is softest and rutting occurs.**

> **So the test asks whether the mix will resist deformation at its WORST condition, which is the correct question.**

**Why the FLOW value is specified with limits at BOTH ends:**

| Flow | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Too LOW (below 2 mm)** | **The mix is BRITTLE — it will CRACK under traffic and thermal movement** ← |
| **2 to 4 mm** | **Satisfactory** |
| **Too HIGH (above 4 mm)** | **The mix is too PLASTIC — it will RUT and SHOVE under traffic** ← |

> **So the flow value has an optimum band, and the two failure modes at its extremes — cracking and rutting — are the two principal distresses of a bituminous pavement.**

> **That is why stability alone is insufficient: a very stiff, low-bitumen mix can have high stability and crack apart, and a rich mix can have adequate stability and rut.**

> **The MARSHALL QUOTIENT (stability divided by flow) combines the two into a single stiffness measure, and its limits catch mixes that satisfy each criterion separately and are unbalanced.**

**The AIR VOIDS requirement, which is the most consequential of the volumetric criteria:**

| Air void content | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Below about 3 %** | **The mix has no room for the bitumen to expand in hot weather, so it BLEEDS and RUTS. Also difficult to compact without over-compaction** ← |
| **3 to 5 %** | **The design target** |
| **Above about 7-8 %** | **The mix is PERMEABLE — water and air enter, causing STRIPPING and OXIDATION of the binder** ← |

> **Both extremes fail, and again for opposite reasons — which is the recurring structure of every mix design criterion in this subject.**

> **The LOW-VOID failure is the one that surprises people: a mix compacted to nearly zero voids has nowhere for the bitumen to go when it expands on a hot day, so it is squeezed to the surface (bleeding) and the mix deforms.**

> **And note that the pavement CONTINUES TO COMPACT under traffic after construction, so a mix designed with 3 per cent voids may reach 1 or 2 per cent in the wheel paths within a year — which is why the target is set toward the upper part of the band.**

> **The HIGH-VOID failure is the durability one: an open mix admits water and air, the water strips the binder from the aggregate and the air oxidises and hardens it, and the mix ravels and cracks.**

**How the OPTIMUM BINDER CONTENT is determined — the test's real purpose:**

> **The Marshall method is a MIX DESIGN procedure, not merely a test:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Prepare specimens at SEVERAL binder contents, typically five, at 0.5 % intervals** |
| **2** | **Test each for stability and flow, and compute the volumetric properties** |
| **3** | **PLOT each property against the binder content — six curves** |
| **4** | **Read the binder content at which EACH criterion is satisfied** ← |
| **5** | **The OPTIMUM binder content is the average of the values satisfying stability, unit weight and the median air void content** |
| **6** | **CHECK that all the criteria are simultaneously satisfied at that value** ← |

> **Step 6 is the essential check: the optimum is an average of three readings, and it must be verified that the resulting mix satisfies every requirement — flow, VMA, VFB and voids as well as stability.**

> **If it does not, the AGGREGATE GRADING must be changed rather than the binder content adjusted — because a grading that cannot satisfy all the criteria at any binder content is the wrong grading.**

> **That is the point most often missed: the Marshall method determines the binder content FOR A GIVEN GRADING, and if no binder content works, the grading is at fault.**

> **The commonest cause is inadequate VMA — a grading too dense to leave room for enough bitumen — and the remedy is a coarser or a gap-graded aggregate, not more binder.**

**And the honest limitations of the Marshall method, since it is being superseded:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The IMPACT compaction of the specimen does not reproduce the KNEADING action of a roller** | **So the laboratory density and orientation differ from the field's** ← |
| **It measures no FUNDAMENTAL material property** | **Stability is not a modulus or a strength in any transferable sense** ← |
| **It cannot predict rutting or fatigue performance directly** | Only correlate with it |
| **It tests at one temperature and one loading rate** | Real pavements see many |

> **The SUPERPAVE system, using a gyratory compactor that better reproduces field kneading and a suite of performance-related tests, was developed to address exactly those deficiencies.**

> **The Marshall method nevertheless remains in wide use in India and Nepal because it is simple, the apparatus is available and inexpensive, and decades of local experience are expressed in its criteria.**

> **Which is the same argument that keeps the SPT and the CBR in use: a crude method with a large body of accumulated experience frequently outlives a better method without one.**

examTip.trick: **Minimum Marshall stability 9 kN at 60 °C for a bituminous concrete surface, with a flow of 2-4 mm and air voids of 3-5 %.** The 60 °C is the pavement's hot-weather temperature — its worst condition.
examTip.trap: **FLOW is limited at BOTH ends: too low and the mix CRACKS (brittle), too high and it RUTS (plastic).** So stability alone is insufficient — a stiff lean mix can be strong and crack apart.
examTip.mnemonic: **Air voids fail at both extremes too: below 3 % the bitumen has nowhere to expand and BLEEDS; above 7 % the mix is PERMEABLE and STRIPS.** And if no binder content satisfies every criterion, the GRADING is wrong — usually insufficient VMA.

questions.stem: The ratio of the actual traffic volume on a road to its capacity, used to define the level of service, is the:
questions.solution:
**The VOLUME TO CAPACITY (V/C) ratio.**

**What it expresses:**

> **V/C = (actual traffic volume) / (the road's capacity), both in the same units, usually PCU per hour.**

> **It is a measure of how heavily the road is loaded relative to what it can carry — and it is the primary determinant of the LEVEL OF SERVICE.**

**The LEVELS OF SERVICE, which the ratio defines:**

| Level of service | V/C ratio | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Below 0.2** | **FREE FLOW — drivers choose their own speed; little interaction** |
| **B** | **0.2-0.4** | **Reasonably free flow; the presence of others is noticeable** |
| **C** | **0.4-0.6** | **STABLE flow; manoeuvring restricted; the usual DESIGN target for a rural highway** ← |
| **D** | **0.6-0.8** | **Approaching unstable; comfort and convenience decline sharply** |
| **E** | **0.8-1.0** | **UNSTABLE flow; the road is at CAPACITY; stop-and-go** ← |
| **F** | **Above 1.0** | **FORCED or BREAKDOWN flow — queuing; the demand exceeds the capacity** ← |

> **The bands are conventions and vary between references, and the pattern is what matters: A is excellent and F is breakdown.**

> **The DESIGN TARGET is usually level of service B or C — which means a road is designed to operate at roughly HALF its capacity in the design hour.**

> **That may look wasteful and is not: operating a road near its capacity means operating it at level E, where a small disturbance produces a breakdown and the throughput collapses.**

**The crucial non-intuitive point about level F — why capacity is not a target:**

> **As the flow approaches capacity, the traffic becomes UNSTABLE: any small disturbance — a vehicle braking, a lane change, a merging vehicle — propagates backward as a shock wave.**

> **Once breakdown occurs, the throughput does not merely stop rising — IT FALLS.**

| State | Flow achieved |
|---|---|
| **Just below capacity** | **The maximum, say 2000 PCU/h** |
| **BREAKDOWN (level F)** | **Substantially LESS — perhaps 1600-1800 PCU/h** ← |

> **So a congested road carries FEWER vehicles per hour than the same road just below capacity — which is the capacity drop phenomenon, and it is the reason ramp metering and flow control work.**

> **Deliberately restricting the entry of vehicles keeps the road below breakdown, and the total throughput is HIGHER than if everyone were admitted.**

> **That is genuinely counter-intuitive and it is well established: admitting fewer vehicles can move more vehicles.**

**The other options, since each is a real and distinct traffic quantity:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **VOLUME TO CAPACITY ratio** | ✓ **Volume ÷ capacity; defines the level of service** |
| **PEAK HOUR FACTOR (PHF)** | **Peak hour volume ÷ (4 × the peak 15-minute volume) — describes the peaking WITHIN an hour** ← |
| **PASSENGER CAR UNIT (PCU)** | **The factor converting a vehicle to its equivalent in cars — 3.0 for a truck** |
| **SATURATION FLOW** | **The maximum flow that can cross a SIGNALISED intersection's stop line while the signal is green — expressed in PCU per hour of green** ← |

> **The SATURATION FLOW deserves its note because it is the capacity concept specific to signalised intersections, and it is what signal timing is computed from:**

> **A signalised approach's capacity is the saturation flow times the proportion of the cycle that is green:**

> **Capacity = saturation flow × (effective green / cycle time)**

> **So an approach with a saturation flow of 1800 PCU/h of green and 30 seconds of green in a 90-second cycle has a capacity of 1800 × 30/90 = 600 PCU/h.**

> **And WEBSTER'S formula for the optimum cycle time follows from balancing the delay:**

> **C_o = (1.5 L + 5)/(1 − Y)**, where L is the total lost time per cycle and Y the sum of the critical flow ratios.

> **Note the (1 − Y) in the denominator: as Y approaches 1 — the intersection approaching saturation — the optimum cycle time approaches INFINITY.**

> **Which is the mathematical statement of a real phenomenon: a saturated intersection cannot be fixed by signal timing, because no cycle length will clear the queues.**

> **The remedy is then geometric or demand-side — more lanes, a flyover, or diverting the traffic — and a signal engineer who responds to a saturated junction by lengthening the cycle merely lengthens the queues.**

**How CAPACITY itself is determined, since the ratio needs it:**

| Road | Design capacity |
|---|---|
| **Single lane (3.75 m), two-way** | **About 2000 PCU/day** |
| **Two-lane (7.0 m), two-way** | **About 15,000 PCU/day** ← |
| **Four-lane divided** | **About 35,000 PCU/day** |
| **Two-lane, per hour, both directions** | **About 2000 PCU/hour** |

> **The capacity is reduced from those ideal values by a series of ADJUSTMENT FACTORS:**

| Factor reducing the capacity | Note |
|---|---|
| **Narrow lanes or restricted lateral clearance** | Drivers keep further apart |
| **Heavy vehicle proportion** | Accounted for by the PCU conversion |
| **GRADIENT** | **A sustained upgrade cuts the capacity substantially, since trucks slow** ← |
| **Restricted SIGHT DISTANCE, limiting overtaking** | **On a two-lane road, capacity depends heavily on the opportunity to overtake** ← |
| **Roadside friction — parking, pedestrians, frontage access** | **The dominant factor in South Asian conditions** ← |
| **Poor surface condition** | Reduces speeds |

> **The ROADSIDE FRICTION factor is the one that dominates in practice in the region and is least represented in the standard tables: a nominally two-lane road through a bazaar, with parked vehicles, pedestrians, animals, and frontage access every few metres, may carry a fraction of its tabulated capacity.**

> **So the capacity of a road in South Asian mixed-traffic conditions is often governed by roadside activity rather than by its width — and widening such a road achieves far less than the tables predict, while controlling the roadside achieves far more.**

> **That returns to the access-control point made earlier, and it is the practical reason it matters: access control is not merely a planning preference but the principal determinant of whether a road delivers the capacity it was built for.**

examTip.trick: **V/C defines the LEVEL OF SERVICE: A below 0.2 (free flow) to F above 1.0 (breakdown).** Roads are designed for level B or C — about half capacity in the design hour.
examTip.trap: **A congested road carries FEWER vehicles per hour than one just below capacity** — the capacity drop. So admitting fewer vehicles can move more, which is why ramp metering works.
examTip.mnemonic: **Webster's optimum cycle C_o = (1.5L+5)/(1−Y) goes to INFINITY as Y approaches 1** — a saturated junction cannot be fixed by signal timing. And in South Asian conditions ROADSIDE FRICTION governs capacity more than width does.

questions.stem: In accident studies, the diagram showing the physical features of an accident location — the road geometry, obstructions, sight distances and roadside development — is called the:
questions.solution:
**The CONDITION DIAGRAM.**

**The two accident-study diagrams, which are used together:**

| Diagram | Shows | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **CONDITION diagram** | **The PHYSICAL FEATURES of the site — geometry, widths, gradients, sight lines, obstructions, signs, markings, surface condition, roadside development, lighting** ← | **WHAT ABOUT THIS PLACE might cause accidents?** |
| **COLLISION diagram** | **The ACCIDENTS themselves — each drawn as arrows showing the vehicles' paths, with the date, time, weather, severity and type** ← | **WHAT KIND of accidents happen here, and in what pattern?** |

> **The two are prepared for the same location and read TOGETHER, and that combination is the substance of accident investigation:**

> **The COLLISION diagram reveals a PATTERN — for instance, that most accidents are rear-end collisions on the approach from the north, at night.**

> **The CONDITION diagram then supplies the EXPLANATION — that the approach from the north has a restricted sight distance to a queue caused by a hidden crest, and no lighting.**

> **Neither diagram alone identifies the remedy: a pattern without a physical cause suggests nothing to fix, and a physical deficiency without an accident pattern may be harmless.**

> **Together they point to a specific intervention — in that example, a warning sign, sight-line improvement or lighting — and that is how accident remedial work is actually done.**

**What a COLLISION diagram reveals — the patterns and their meanings:**

| Pattern in the collision diagram | Likely cause to look for in the condition diagram |
|---|---|
| **REAR-END collisions concentrated on one approach** | **Restricted sight distance to a queue; a hidden crest or curve; an unexpected stop** ← |
| **RIGHT-ANGLE collisions at an intersection** | **Obstructed sight triangle; inadequate control; a signal not visible** ← |
| **HEAD-ON collisions on a straight** | Overtaking with inadequate sight distance; no centre line |
| **SINGLE-VEHICLE run-off accidents on a curve** | **Inadequate superelevation, radius or advance warning; slippery surface** ← |
| **PEDESTRIAN accidents at one point** | **A desire line with no crossing provided** ← |
| **Accidents concentrated at NIGHT** | **Lighting, reflectivity of signs and markings, glare** ← |
| **Accidents concentrated in the WET** | **SKID RESISTANCE — a polished or bleeding surface, or ponding** ← |

> **The WET-WEATHER pattern is worth emphasising because its remedy is specific and effective: a location where accidents cluster in the wet almost always has a SKID RESISTANCE problem, and resurfacing with a high-PSV aggregate can eliminate them.**

> **That is one of the highest-return safety interventions available, and it is identified only by noticing the weather pattern in the collision diagram — which a summary accident count would conceal.**

> **Equally, a NIGHT pattern points to lighting or sign reflectivity rather than to geometry, and geometric improvements at such a site would achieve nothing.**

> **So the value of the collision diagram is that it DISCRIMINATES between causes, and the discrimination determines which remedy will work.**

**The complete accident study procedure, since the diagrams are two steps of it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Record accidents systematically — location, date, time, weather, vehicles, casualties, type** |
| **2** | **Identify BLACK SPOTS — locations with an accident frequency or rate significantly above normal** ← |
| **3** | **Prepare the COLLISION diagram for each black spot** |
| **4** | **Prepare the CONDITION diagram for the same location** |
| **5** | **Analyse the two together to identify the CONTRIBUTING factors** ← |
| **6** | **Design and implement remedial measures** |
| **7** | **MONITOR the accidents afterward to confirm the remedy worked** ← |

> **Step 7 is the one most often omitted and it matters: an intervention that does not reduce the accidents has not been established as effective, and the resources should go elsewhere.**

> **And it guards against a genuine statistical trap — REGRESSION TO THE MEAN.**

> **A location is identified as a black spot because it had an unusually high accident count in one period. Accident counts fluctuate randomly, so an unusually high count is likely to be followed by a lower one WHETHER OR NOT ANYTHING IS DONE.**

> **So a remedial measure at a black spot will appear to succeed even if it is useless — and attributing the reduction to the measure is a mistake.**

> **Proper evaluation therefore requires a longer before-and-after period, a control site, or a statistical method that allows for the regression effect.**

> **That is a real and important caution in road safety work, and it is why the reported effectiveness of some interventions has been revised downward on re-examination.**

**The ACCIDENT RATE measures, since step 2 requires one:**

| Measure | Expression | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Accident FREQUENCY** | **Accidents per km per year** | **Identifies locations with many accidents — but does not allow for the traffic volume** ← |
| **Accident RATE (involvement)** | **Accidents per 100 million vehicle-km** | **Allows for EXPOSURE — the fairer comparison** ← |
| **Accidents per 1000 vehicles registered** | — | A national statistic |
| **Severity index** | Fatal accidents as a proportion of the total | Weighting by outcome |

> **The distinction between FREQUENCY and RATE is the one that determines where money is spent:**

> **A busy urban junction will have MANY accidents simply because many vehicles pass — a high FREQUENCY and possibly a low RATE.**

> **A quiet rural bend may have few accidents in absolute terms and a very high RATE per vehicle passing — meaning it is genuinely dangerous.**

> **Ranking by FREQUENCY directs resources to busy places; ranking by RATE directs them to dangerous ones.**

> **Both have a claim: treating the busy junction saves more accidents in total, while treating the dangerous bend addresses the greater risk to each user.**

> **Practice generally uses both, treating high-frequency locations for the total benefit and high-rate locations because the risk to an individual traveller there is unacceptable — and being explicit about which criterion is being applied is part of doing the analysis honestly.**

examTip.trick: **CONDITION diagram = the PLACE (geometry, sight lines, obstructions). COLLISION diagram = the ACCIDENTS (paths, dates, weather, severity).** They are read together: one gives the pattern, the other the explanation.
examTip.trap: **A WET-weather cluster points to SKID RESISTANCE and a NIGHT cluster to lighting** — neither would be fixed by geometric improvement. The collision diagram's value is that it DISCRIMINATES between causes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Beware REGRESSION TO THE MEAN: a black spot's accident count will fall after treatment whether or not the treatment works**, because it was selected for being unusually high. Proper evaluation needs a control or a longer period.

questions.stem: For flexible pavement design in India and Nepal, the STANDARD AXLE LOAD is taken as:
questions.solution:
**80 kN (8160 kg, about 8.2 tonnes).**

**Why a standard axle is needed at all:**

> **A pavement carries axles of many different weights, and their damaging effects are NOT proportional to their loads.**

> **So the traffic must be converted into an EQUIVALENT NUMBER OF STANDARD AXLES before the pavement can be designed — and 80 kN is the standard chosen.**

> **The conversion uses the FOURTH POWER LAW:**

> **Equivalence factor = (axle load / 80)⁴**

**The fourth power law — the most consequential fact in pavement engineering:**

| Axle load | Equivalence factor (standard axles) |
|---|---|
| **20 kN (a car axle)** | **(20/80)⁴ = 0.004** |
| **40 kN** | **(40/80)⁴ = 0.0625** |
| **80 kN (the standard)** | **1.0** ← |
| **100 kN** | **(100/80)⁴ = 2.44** |
| **120 kN** | **(120/80)⁴ = 5.06** ← |
| **160 kN (a heavily overloaded axle)** | **(160/80)⁴ = 16.0** ← |

> **The implications are startling and worth stating plainly:**

> **ONE 160 kN axle does as much damage as SIXTEEN legal 80 kN axles.**

> **ONE 80 kN axle does as much damage as about 250 car axles at 20 kN.**

> **So a pavement is destroyed almost entirely by HEAVY VEHICLES, and cars are practically irrelevant to its structural design.**

> **A road carrying 10,000 cars and 100 trucks a day is damaged overwhelmingly by the 100 trucks.**

**Why OVERLOADING is so destructive — the practical consequence:**

> **A truck loaded 50 per cent above its legal axle limit — from 80 to 120 kN — does 5.06 TIMES the damage, not 1.5 times.**

> **And at double the legal load it does SIXTEEN times the damage.**

| Overload | Load | Damage relative to legal |
|---|---|---|
| **Legal** | **80 kN** | **1.0** |
| **+25 %** | **100 kN** | **2.44** |
| **+50 %** | **120 kN** | **5.06** ← |
| **+100 %** | **160 kN** | **16.0** |

> **So a small proportion of overloaded vehicles can consume a pavement's whole design life:**

> **If 10 per cent of the trucks are loaded to 120 kN, those 10 per cent do 5.06 × 0.10 = 0.51 standard axles per truck against the other 90 per cent's 0.90 — that is, a TENTH of the traffic does more than a third of the damage.**

> **That is why AXLE LOAD CONTROL — weighbridges and enforcement — is the single most cost-effective road preservation measure available, and why its absence destroys pavements built to a correct design.**

> **A road designed for 20 million standard axles and subjected to systematic overloading may reach that total in a fraction of its intended life, and the failure is then blamed on the design.**

> **So the fourth power law is not an academic curiosity but the reason road maintenance budgets are consumed, and it is the strongest technical argument that can be made for enforcement.**

**Where the fourth power comes from, briefly:**

> **It is EMPIRICAL, derived from the AASHO Road Test of the late 1950s — a full-scale experiment in which pavement sections were trafficked by controlled axle loads until they failed.**

> **The exponent is not exactly 4 and varies with the pavement type and the distress mode — values from about 3 to 5 are found, and rigid pavements show a higher exponent than flexible ones.**

> **But 4 is the conventional value and is used throughout Indian and Nepali practice, and its precise value matters less than the fact that it is LARGE.**

> **Any exponent above 1 produces the same qualitative conclusion — that heavy axles dominate — and an exponent of 4 makes that domination overwhelming.**

**The design traffic computation, since the standard axle feeds into it:**

> **N = 365 × A × [(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r × D × F**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **N** | **Cumulative standard axles over the design life — the design traffic in MSA (million standard axles)** ← |
| **A** | **Initial number of commercial vehicles per day (laden weight above 3 tonnes)** ← |
| **r** | **Annual growth rate of traffic** |
| **n** | **Design life in years — 15 years for a flexible pavement** |
| **D** | **Lane distribution factor** |
| **F** | **VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR — the average standard axles per commercial vehicle** ← |

> **Note that only COMMERCIAL VEHICLES enter the computation — cars and two-wheelers are ignored entirely, which follows directly from the fourth power law.**

> **And the VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR is the parameter that carries the overloading: it is measured by AXLE LOAD SURVEYS at the site, and its value ranges from about 1.5 on a lightly loaded road to 6 or more where overloading is prevalent.**

> **So an axle load survey is a required input to pavement design, and using a default VDF where overloading is common will underdesign the pavement by a factor of two or three.**

> **That is a real and common error, and its consequence is a pavement that fails in five years instead of fifteen.**

**And the LANE DISTRIBUTION factor, since it is easily mishandled:**

| Road | Lane distribution factor D |
|---|---|
| **Single lane** | **1.0 — all the traffic in one lane** |
| **Two-lane, single carriageway** | **0.5 of the total two-way commercial traffic in each direction** |
| **Four-lane divided** | **0.75 of the traffic in one direction, in the outer lane** ← |
| **Six-lane divided** | **0.60 of one direction's traffic in the outer lane** |

> **The four-lane figure of 0.75 is worth noting: the heavy vehicles CONCENTRATE in the outer (slow) lane, so that lane carries three quarters of the direction's commercial traffic rather than half.**

> **So the outer lane of a divided highway is loaded far more heavily than the inner one — and it is where the rutting and fatigue cracking appear first, which anyone who has driven such a road will have observed.**

> **Some designs accordingly provide a thicker pavement in the outer lane, and all designs must use the 0.75 factor rather than assuming an even distribution.**

examTip.trick: **80 kN is the standard axle, and the FOURTH POWER LAW converts others: factor = (load/80)⁴.**
examTip.trap: **A 50 % overload does FIVE times the damage, not 1.5 times; double the load does SIXTEEN times.** So a tenth of the traffic overloaded can do more than a third of the damage — which is why axle load control is the best road preservation measure there is.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only COMMERCIAL vehicles enter the design; cars are irrelevant** (one 80 kN axle equals about 250 car axles). And on a four-lane divided road the OUTER lane carries 0.75 of the direction's trucks, not half — which is where the rutting appears first.

questions.stem: The thin application of a low-viscosity bituminous material to an absorbent granular surface, before a bituminous course is laid over it, is called a:
questions.solution:
**A PRIME COAT.**

**The four bituminous applications distinguished:**

| Application | Applied to | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **PRIME COAT** | **An ABSORBENT, granular, NON-bituminous surface (WBM, WMM, granular base)** | **PENETRATE and seal the surface, bind the loose fines, and provide a bond for the bituminous layer above** ← |
| **TACK COAT** | **An EXISTING BITUMINOUS surface, or a primed surface, or concrete** | **Provide ADHESION between the existing layer and the new one — a bond, not a penetration** ← |
| **SEAL COAT** | **A newly laid OPEN-GRADED bituminous surface (a premix carpet or surface dressing)** | **SEAL the voids against water ingress, and improve the texture** ← |
| **SURFACE DRESSING** | **An existing surface needing a new wearing surface** | **A thin surfacing in its own right — bitumen sprayed and covered with chippings** |

> **The distinctions worth fixing are the SURFACE each is applied to and the FUNCTION each performs:**

> **PRIME goes on GRANULAR material and PENETRATES it.**

> **TACK goes on BITUMINOUS material and STICKS to it.**

> **SEAL goes on top of a NEW open surface and CLOSES it.**

**Why a prime coat must PENETRATE, and what that requires:**

> **A granular base is dusty, loose at its surface and porous. A bituminous layer laid directly on it bonds to the DUST rather than to the base — and the new layer then slips, shoves and ravels.**

> **The prime coat's job is to soak INTO the surface, binding the fines and creating a continuous surface for the layer above.**

> **That requires a LOW-VISCOSITY material, and the choice of material follows:**

| Material for priming | Note |
|---|---|
| **Low-viscosity CUTBACK bitumen (MC-30, MC-70)** | **Bitumen thinned with a solvent (kerosene) so it penetrates; the solvent then evaporates** ← |
| **Bitumen EMULSION (slow-setting, SS1)** | **Bitumen dispersed in water; penetrates, then the water separates — more environmentally acceptable** ← |
| **Rate of application** | **0.6 to 1.2 kg/m², depending on the base's porosity** |
| **Curing time before the next layer** | **24 hours or more, until the solvent or water has gone** ← |

> **The CURING requirement is the practical trap: laying the bituminous layer before the prime coat has cured traps the solvent or water beneath it.**

> **The trapped volatile then vaporises under the sun and forms BLISTERS, or it softens the layer above and causes it to shove.**

> **So the prime coat's curing is a real hold in the programme and cannot be shortened, which is why emulsion primes — which cure faster and release water rather than a solvent — are increasingly preferred.**

**Why a TACK COAT must NOT penetrate — the opposite requirement:**

> **A tack coat is applied to a surface that is already sealed — an existing bituminous layer or a cured prime coat — so there is nothing to penetrate.**

> **Its job is purely ADHESION, and it is applied VERY THINLY:**

| Surface being tacked | Rate of application |
|---|---|
| **A bituminous surface** | **0.20 to 0.30 kg/m²** ← very thin |
| **A granular or primed surface** | **0.25 to 0.30 kg/m²** |
| **A cement concrete surface** | **0.30 to 0.35 kg/m²** |

> **And an EXCESSIVE tack coat is a genuine defect, not merely a waste:**

> **Too much bitumen at the interface creates a SLIP PLANE — a layer of soft binder on which the new course can slide under braking and turning forces.**

> **The result is SHOVING and CORRUGATION of the new surface, particularly at junctions and on gradients where the horizontal forces are greatest.**

> **So more is definitely not better, and the rate is specified as a narrow band rather than a minimum.**

> **The tack coat must also be BROKEN (the emulsion's water separated, leaving the bitumen tacky) before the layer is laid — but not fully cured, since it must still be sticky.**

> **That gives a window: too soon and the emulsion is picked up by the paver's tyres; too late and it has lost its tack.**

**The SEAL COAT, since it completes the set:**

> **An open-graded surface such as a premix carpet or a surface dressing has interconnected voids, and water entering them reaches the layers beneath.**

| Type of seal coat | Description |
|---|---|
| **Type A — liquid seal** | **A layer of bitumen followed by stone chippings** |
| **Type B — premixed seal** | **A premixed thin layer of fine aggregate and bitumen** |
| **Type C — slurry seal** | **A mixture of fine aggregate, bitumen emulsion, filler and water, applied as a slurry** |

> **The seal coat's second function is to improve the SURFACE TEXTURE and hence the skid resistance — so it serves both durability and safety.**

> **And it is applied SOON after the carpet, not left: an unsealed premix carpet admits water from the first rain and ravels quickly.**

> **A carpet laid before the monsoon and not sealed until after it will not survive, which is a scheduling matter as much as a technical one.**

**The pavement construction sequence, since these applications sit within it:**

| Order | Layer or operation |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Prepare and compact the SUBGRADE** |
| **2** | **GRANULAR SUB-BASE (GSB)** |
| **3** | **Base course — WBM or WMM** |
| **4** | **PRIME COAT on the granular base** ← |
| **5** | **TACK COAT** ← |
| **6** | **Bituminous BASE / BINDER course (bituminous macadam, DBM)** |
| **7** | **TACK COAT again** |
| **8** | **Bituminous WEARING course (bituminous concrete, or a premix carpet)** |
| **9** | **SEAL COAT, if the wearing course is open-graded** ← |

> **Note that a TACK COAT appears TWICE — between every pair of bituminous layers — and that is the general rule: every interface between two bituminous layers gets a tack coat.**

> **Omitting it between the binder and the wearing course produces DELAMINATION: the wearing course separates and is stripped off in sheets under traffic, which is a spectacular and entirely avoidable failure.**

> **And it is a common defect, because the interface is invisible once the road is finished and the omission saves a day's work — so it is one of the details worth inspecting for rather than assuming.**

examTip.trick: **PRIME goes on GRANULAR material and PENETRATES it; TACK goes on BITUMINOUS material and STICKS to it; SEAL closes the voids of a new OPEN-GRADED surface.**
examTip.trap: **An EXCESSIVE tack coat is a defect, not a waste** — it creates a SLIP PLANE on which the new course shoves and corrugates. The rate (0.2-0.3 kg/m²) is a narrow band, not a minimum.
examTip.mnemonic: **A prime coat must CURE (24 hours) before the next layer, or trapped solvent blisters it.** And a TACK COAT belongs at EVERY bituminous interface — omitting it between binder and wearing course causes DELAMINATION, an invisible omission with a spectacular result.

questions.stem: In engineering drawing, a CENTRE LINE is represented by a:
questions.solution:
**A LONG-DASH SHORT-DASH (chain) THIN line.**

**The standard line types and their uses:**

| Line | Description | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous THICK** | **A solid heavy line** | **VISIBLE outlines and edges** ← |
| **Continuous THIN** | **A solid light line** | **Dimension lines, extension lines, leader lines, hatching, short centre lines** |
| **Continuous thin, WAVY or zig-zag** | — | **BREAK lines — a short break, or a long break** |
| **SHORT-DASHED thin (or medium)** | **Dashes of about 3 mm with 1 mm gaps** | **HIDDEN edges and outlines** ← |
| **LONG-DASH SHORT-DASH thin (chain thin)** | **A long dash, a short dash, alternating** | **CENTRE LINES, axes, lines of symmetry, pitch circles** ← |
| **Chain thin with THICK ENDS and at changes of direction** | — | **CUTTING PLANE lines (section planes)** ← |
| **Chain THICK** | — | **To indicate a surface requiring special treatment** |
| **Chain thin DOUBLE-DASHED** | — | Adjacent parts, alternative positions, centroidal lines |

> **Option (d) the short-dashed thin line is the HIDDEN LINE, which makes it the designed distractor — the two dashed types are the ones most often confused.**

> **The distinction is the PATTERN: a hidden line has UNIFORM short dashes, while a centre line ALTERNATES long and short.**

> **And they differ in weight in some conventions, with hidden lines drawn slightly heavier than centre lines.**

**Why line types matter — they carry information, not decoration:**

> **A drawing is a LANGUAGE, and the line types are part of its grammar. Each conveys a specific meaning that words would otherwise have to state:**

| The line tells the reader | Without needing a note |
|---|---|
| **This edge is VISIBLE from this direction** | Continuous thick |
| **This edge EXISTS but is CONCEALED behind material** | **Short-dashed — a genuinely important distinction for a fabricator** ← |
| **This is an AXIS, not an edge — there is no material here** | **Chain thin — and mistaking a centre line for an edge would produce a wrong part** ← |
| **The view beyond is a SECTION taken on this plane** | Cutting plane line |
| **This is a MEASUREMENT, not part of the object** | Continuous thin |

> **The third row is the one whose misreading is most consequential: a CENTRE LINE indicates where material is NOT — the axis of a hole, the centreline of a shaft.**

> **A fabricator who read a centre line as a visible edge would machine a step where an axis was intended.**

> **So the line convention is what allows a drawing to be read unambiguously, and departing from it makes a drawing that must be interpreted rather than read.**

**The rules for DRAWING centre lines, since their execution is specified:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **They must EXTEND SLIGHTLY BEYOND the feature — about 2-3 mm** | **So the axis is unmistakably identified** ← |
| **They must CROSS at the LONG dashes, not at a gap** | **Two centre lines meeting at a gap leaves the centre undefined** ← |
| **They should start and end with a LONG dash** | — |
| **A short centre line may be drawn as a continuous THIN line** | Where a chain line would be unreadable |
| **They should not be extended between views unnecessarily** | Clutter |

> **The CROSSING rule is the practical one and it is the mark of a properly drawn drawing: the centre of a hole is defined by the INTERSECTION of two centre lines, and if they cross at a gap the centre is not marked at all.**

> **So the dash pattern must be arranged so that the long dashes cross — which requires the draughtsman to plan the pattern rather than draw it mechanically.**

**The other conventions worth knowing, since this family of questions ranges over them:**

| Convention | Practice |
|---|---|
| **HATCHING (section lines)** | **Continuous THIN lines at 45°, spaced 1-3 mm; adjacent parts hatched in OPPOSITE directions or at different spacings** ← |
| **Parts NOT hatched even when sectioned** | **Shafts, bolts, nuts, rivets, keys, pins, ribs and webs cut longitudinally** ← |
| **Hidden lines behind a section** | **Usually OMITTED, for clarity** |
| **Precedence when lines coincide** | **VISIBLE outline > HIDDEN line > CENTRE line** ← |
| **Small features** | May be shown to an enlarged scale in a detail view |

> **The PRECEDENCE rule resolves the common situation in which two line types fall on the same place: the more important is drawn and the other omitted at that point.**

> **A visible edge coinciding with a hidden edge is drawn as VISIBLE; a hidden edge coinciding with a centre line is drawn as HIDDEN.**

> **That hierarchy is why a well-drawn drawing looks simpler than the object it depicts — the redundant information is suppressed rather than superimposed.**

> **And the NOT-HATCHED list is worth knowing because it looks arbitrary and is not: a rib or a web cut LONGITUDINALLY is not hatched because hatching it would suggest a solid mass of material where in fact the rib is thin.**

> **The convention conveys the truth about the object more clearly than a literal representation would — which is a recurring principle in drawing conventions generally.**

**And the LINE THICKNESSES, since the standard specifies them:**

> **Two line widths are used, in the ratio 2:1 — a THICK line and a THIN line.**

| Standard line widths (mm) | Note |
|---|---|
| **0.25, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.4, 2.0** | **Each is √2 times the previous — the same progression as paper sizes** ← |
| **Typical pair on an A1 drawing** | **0.7 thick / 0.35 thin** |
| **Typical pair on an A4 drawing** | **0.5 thick / 0.25 thin** |

> **The √2 progression matches the paper-size series (A0 to A4), so a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 has its line widths fall to the next standard value and remains correctly proportioned.**

> **That is a neat piece of standard design, and it is why a properly drawn A1 drawing photocopied down to A3 still reads correctly rather than becoming a mass of heavy lines.**

examTip.trick: **A CENTRE LINE is chain thin — long dash ALTERNATING with short dash. A HIDDEN line is UNIFORM short dashes.** The pattern distinguishes them, and option (d) is the hidden line.
examTip.trap: **A centre line indicates where material is NOT** — the axis of a hole. Reading it as a visible edge would produce a wrong part, which is why the convention matters rather than being decorative.
examTip.mnemonic: **Centre lines must CROSS at the LONG dashes** — crossing at a gap leaves the centre undefined. And the PRECEDENCE when lines coincide: VISIBLE > HIDDEN > CENTRE, which is why a good drawing looks simpler than its object.

questions.stem: The dimensioning system in which ALL dimensions are placed so that they can be read from the BOTTOM of the drawing is the:
questions.solution:
**The UNIDIRECTIONAL system.**

**The two systems of placing dimension figures:**

| System | Placement of the figures | Read from |
|---|---|---|
| **ALIGNED system** | **The figure is placed ABOVE the dimension line and ALIGNED WITH IT, so it reads along the dimension** | **The bottom OR the right-hand side, depending on the dimension's direction** ← |
| **UNIDIRECTIONAL system** | **ALL figures are placed HORIZONTALLY, with the dimension line BROKEN at the middle to accommodate them** | **The BOTTOM only** ← |

> **Options (b) and (c) — chain and parallel dimensioning — are ARRANGEMENTS of dimensions, not systems of placing the figures, which makes them the designed distractors.**

> **That is a real distinction: the SYSTEM concerns how the figures are ORIENTED, and the ARRANGEMENT concerns how the dimensions are ORGANISED relative to one another.**

> **A drawing uses one system and may use several arrangements.**

**Why the UNIDIRECTIONAL system is generally preferred:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The drawing need not be TURNED to read it** | **Every figure reads from one position** ← |
| **Suits COMPUTER-AIDED drafting, which places text horizontally by default** | **The decisive practical reason today** ← |
| **Easier for a machine operator or fabricator working at a bench** | The drawing lies flat and is read from one side |
| **Less risk of misreading a figure upside down** | 6 and 9, 68 and 89 |

> **The CAD reason has effectively settled the matter: a drafting system naturally places text horizontally, and the aligned system requires each figure to be rotated to match its dimension line.**

> **So unidirectional dimensioning has become the norm for mechanical and much structural work, while the aligned system persists in architectural and civil drawings where long dimension strings along a building's faces read more naturally when aligned.**

> **Which means both systems remain in use, and the rule is that ONE system must be used CONSISTENTLY throughout a drawing — mixing them is the error, not choosing either.**

**The ARRANGEMENTS of dimensions, since two are offered as options:**

| Arrangement | Description | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **CHAIN dimensioning** | **Successive dimensions in a continuous line, each from the end of the last** | **Errors ACCUMULATE along the chain** ← |
| **PARALLEL (baseline) dimensioning** | **All dimensions measured from ONE common datum, on parallel dimension lines** | **No accumulation — each is independent of the others** ← |
| **COMBINED** | Both, as suits the feature | Common in practice |
| **RUNNING (progressive) dimensioning** | Cumulative dimensions from a datum, on a single line with a common origin mark | Compact form of parallel |
| **Coordinate dimensioning** | A table of x, y coordinates | For many holes |

> **The ACCUMULATION problem with chain dimensioning is the substance of that distinction and it matters in fabrication:**

> **If five dimensions are chained, each with a tolerance of ±0.5 mm, the overall length can be out by ±2.5 mm — the tolerances ADD.**

> **With PARALLEL dimensioning from one datum, each dimension is independent and carries only its own ±0.5 mm, whatever the total length.**

> **So the choice of arrangement determines where the tolerance accumulates, and the rule follows: DIMENSION FROM THE DATUM THAT MATTERS.**

> **If the overall length is critical, dimension the overall length and let the intermediate positions accumulate. If the hole positions are critical, dimension each from a common datum.**

> **A drawing that chains dimensions along a critical direction has, in effect, specified a tolerance far looser than the individual figures suggest — and that is a genuine and common defect.**

**The general dimensioning rules, since they are asked as a set:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each dimension appears ONCE only** | **A dimension repeated in two views can be revised in one and not the other** ← |
| **Dimension the FEATURE in the view where its SHAPE is clearest** | — |
| **Place dimensions OUTSIDE the outline where possible** | Clarity |
| **Smaller dimensions NEARER the object, larger further out** | **So extension lines do not cross dimension lines** ← |
| **Dimension lines should not CROSS one another** | Follows from the above |
| **NEVER use a centre line or an outline as a dimension line** | Though a centre line may be EXTENDED as an extension line |
| **Do NOT over-dimension** | **A closed chain plus an overall dimension is REDUNDANT and may conflict** ← |
| **Give REDUNDANT dimensions as REFERENCE only, in brackets** | Where they help the reader |

> **The OVER-DIMENSIONING rule is the one whose violation causes the most trouble on site: if a chain of dimensions is given AND the overall dimension, the drawing states the same fact twice.**

> **When a revision changes one and not the other, the drawing CONTRADICTS ITSELF — and the fabricator must guess which is intended, or stop and ask.**

> **So the correct practice is to omit one of them, or to mark the redundant figure as REFERENCE in brackets, meaning "provided for convenience, not to be worked to".**

> **That convention resolves the conflict explicitly rather than leaving it to be discovered, and it is why the bracket has a defined meaning in the standard.**

**And the units convention, since it is a source of real error:**

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| **All dimensions in MILLIMETRES, with the unit OMITTED from each figure** | **The standard practice in mechanical and structural drawing** ← |
| **A NOTE stating "ALL DIMENSIONS IN mm UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED"** | **Mandatory, and it is what makes the omission safe** ← |
| **Any dimension in another unit given WITH its unit** | The exception is marked |
| **Civil and architectural drawings often use METRES for levels and mm for details** | **A mixed practice that must be stated clearly** ← |

> **The MIXED PRACTICE in civil drawings is a genuine hazard: levels and site dimensions in metres, member sizes and reinforcement in millimetres, on the same sheet.**

> **A figure of 3.5 could be metres or millimetres, and the difference is a factor of a thousand.**

> **So the convention must be stated on every sheet and followed without exception — and a dimension whose unit is ambiguous must be queried rather than assumed, which is the same discipline as never scaling a drawing.**

examTip.trick: **UNIDIRECTIONAL: all figures HORIZONTAL, read from the bottom, dimension line broken. ALIGNED: figures follow their dimension lines.** Options (b) and (c) are ARRANGEMENTS, not systems.
examTip.trap: **CHAIN dimensioning ACCUMULATES tolerances** — five links at ±0.5 mm give ±2.5 mm overall — while PARALLEL dimensioning from one datum does not. So dimension from the datum that matters.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never OVER-dimension: a chain plus an overall dimension states the same fact twice, and a revision to one makes the drawing contradict itself.** Mark a redundant figure as REFERENCE in brackets. And state the unit convention on every sheet.

questions.stem: At the BREAK-EVEN POINT of a production or project operation:
options: The total revenue equals the total cost and the profit is zero
The total revenue is at its maximum
The variable cost equals the fixed cost
questions.solution:
**The total revenue equals the total cost, and the profit is therefore ZERO.**

**The definition and the computation:**

> **Total cost = FIXED cost + (variable cost per unit × number of units)**

> **Total revenue = selling price per unit × number of units**

> **At break-even the two are equal:**

> **F + v Q = p Q**

> **Q_BE = F / (p − v)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **F** | **FIXED cost — incurred whether or not anything is produced** |
| **v** | **VARIABLE cost per unit** |
| **p** | **Selling price per unit** |
| **(p − v)** | **CONTRIBUTION per unit — what each unit contributes toward the fixed cost** ← |

> **So the break-even quantity is the FIXED COST divided by the CONTRIBUTION PER UNIT, which has a clear meaning: it is the number of units needed for the accumulated contribution to cover the fixed cost.**

**A worked example, since the concept is best seen numerically:**

> **A precast concrete works has fixed costs of Rs 500,000 per month. Each unit costs Rs 300 in materials and labour and sells for Rs 500.**

> **Contribution per unit = 500 − 300 = Rs 200**

> **Q_BE = 500,000/200 = 2,500 units per month**

| Output | Total cost | Total revenue | Profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | **Rs 500,000** | **0** | **−Rs 500,000 — the fixed cost is lost** ← |
| **1,500** | **Rs 950,000** | **Rs 750,000** | **−Rs 200,000** |
| **2,500** | **Rs 1,250,000** | **Rs 1,250,000** | **ZERO — break-even** ← |
| **4,000** | **Rs 1,700,000** | **Rs 2,000,000** | **+Rs 300,000** |

> **Note the operation at zero output: the LOSS equals the whole fixed cost, because fixed costs are incurred regardless.**

> **That is what "fixed" means, and option (c) is precisely wrong: the fixed cost is not zero at break-even, it is the quantity being covered.**

**Why the break-even point matters — what it is used to decide:**

| Decision | Use of the break-even analysis |
|---|---|
| **Whether a project or plant is VIABLE at the expected output** | **If the expected output is below break-even, it loses money** ← |
| **How much SAFETY MARGIN exists** | **See below** ← |
| **Choosing between a HIGH-FIXED-COST and a LOW-FIXED-COST method** | **The most interesting application** ← |
| **Setting a minimum price** | Below (v) no output is worth making |
| **Deciding whether to accept a marginal order** | Any price above (v) contributes |

> **The MARGIN OF SAFETY is the derived quantity worth knowing:**

> **Margin of safety = (expected output − break-even output) / expected output × 100**

> **For an expected 4,000 units: (4,000 − 2,500)/4,000 = 37.5 per cent — meaning output could fall by 37.5 per cent before losses begin.**

> **That single figure is a far better description of an operation's robustness than its profit, because it says how much the assumptions can be wrong.**

**The MOST USEFUL application — comparing methods with different cost structures:**

> **Consider two construction methods for the same work:**

| Method | Fixed cost (plant, setup) | Variable cost per unit |
|---|---|---|
| **A — MANUAL, labour intensive** | **Rs 100,000 (low)** | **Rs 800 (high)** |
| **B — MECHANISED** | **Rs 1,000,000 (high)** | **Rs 400 (low)** ← |

> **Setting the two total costs equal:**

> **100,000 + 800Q = 1,000,000 + 400Q**

> **400Q = 900,000, so Q = 2,250 units**

> **So the CROSSOVER is at 2,250 units:**

| Quantity | Cheaper method |
|---|---|
| **Below 2,250 units** | **MANUAL — the mechanised plant's fixed cost is not recovered** ← |
| **2,250 units** | Indifferent |
| **Above 2,250 units** | **MECHANISED — the lower variable cost repays the plant** ← |

> **That analysis is the standard justification for a plant purchase or hire decision, and it explains a great deal about construction practice:**

> **A SMALL job is done by hand and a LARGE one by machine, and the crossover point is where the plant's fixed cost is recovered by the saving per unit.**

> **Which is why the same contractor uses different methods on different jobs, and why a decision that appears inconsistent is in fact the correct response to a different quantity.**

> **And it is why plant HIRE exists: hiring converts a fixed cost into a variable one, moving the crossover point and making mechanisation viable on smaller quantities.**

**The assumptions of break-even analysis, which limit it:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **The selling price is CONSTANT regardless of quantity** | **Selling more usually requires a lower price** ← |
| **The variable cost per unit is CONSTANT** | **Economies of scale reduce it; overtime and congestion raise it** ← |
| **Fixed costs are genuinely fixed over the range** | **They STEP UP — a second shift, a second machine, a larger site** ← |
| **Costs divide cleanly into fixed and variable** | Many are semi-variable |
| **Everything produced is sold** | Stock accumulates |
| **A single product, or a constant product mix** | — |

> **The STEPPED FIXED COST is the most important departure from the model: fixed costs are fixed only within a CAPACITY RANGE, and beyond it another increment of capacity must be bought.**

> **So a real total-cost curve is a series of segments with jumps between them, and there may be SEVERAL break-even points rather than one.**

> **An operation can be profitable at 2,500 units, unprofitable at 3,000 (having just bought a second machine), and profitable again at 4,000.**

> **Recognising that makes the analysis genuinely useful rather than a textbook exercise, and it explains why expansion decisions are lumpy and why an operation just past a capacity step is the least comfortable place to be.**

examTip.trick: **At break-even, revenue = cost and profit = 0. Q_BE = FIXED COST ÷ CONTRIBUTION per unit (p − v)** — the number of units needed for the contributions to cover the fixed cost.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is precisely wrong: the fixed cost is not zero at break-even — it is the quantity being covered.** At zero output the loss equals the whole fixed cost, which is what "fixed" means.
examTip.mnemonic: **The best use is comparing METHODS: manual (low fixed, high variable) against mechanised (high fixed, low variable).** The crossover quantity decides which is cheaper — and plant HIRE moves that crossover by converting a fixed cost into a variable one.

questions.stem: Two alternatives having DIFFERENT USEFUL LIVES are most properly compared on the basis of:
questions.solution:
**Their EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST (EAC), also called the annual equivalent or annual worth.**

**Why unequal lives create a problem:**

> **Comparing two alternatives by their PRESENT WORTH requires them to serve for the SAME PERIOD — otherwise the comparison is between different amounts of service.**

> **Consider a pump costing Rs 100,000 lasting 5 years against one costing Rs 160,000 lasting 10 years.**

> **Comparing the two capital costs directly is meaningless: the second buys twice the service.**

> **And comparing present worths over unequal periods is equally meaningless for the same reason.**

**The two correct approaches:**

| Method | How it works |
|---|---|
| **EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST** | **Convert each alternative's total cost into an equivalent UNIFORM ANNUAL cost over its OWN life, then compare the annual figures directly** ← |
| **LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE of lives** | **Compare present worths over a period equal to the LCM of the lives, assuming each is replaced identically** |

> **For lives of 5 and 10 years, the LCM method compares present worths over 10 years, with the first alternative replaced once.**

> **The EAC method is generally preferred because it works for ANY combination of lives — including 7 and 11 years, whose LCM is 77 — and because an annual figure is more intelligible to a decision-maker.**

**The computation:**

> **EAC = (capital cost) × (A/P, i, n) + annual operating cost − (salvage value) × (A/F, i, n)**

> **where (A/P, i, n) is the CAPITAL RECOVERY factor:  i(1+i)ⁿ/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1]**

**A worked comparison, to show the method:**

> **At 10 per cent interest:**

| | **Pump A** | **Pump B** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capital cost** | **Rs 100,000** | **Rs 160,000** |
| **Life** | **5 years** | **10 years** |
| **Annual operating cost** | **Rs 30,000** | **Rs 22,000** |
| **Salvage value** | **Rs 10,000** | **Rs 20,000** |
| **(A/P, 10 %, n)** | **0.2638** | **0.1627** |
| **(A/F, 10 %, n)** | **0.1638** | **0.0627** |
| **Capital recovery** | **100,000 × 0.2638 = 26,380** | **160,000 × 0.1627 = 26,032** |
| **Less salvage credit** | **10,000 × 0.1638 = 1,638** | **20,000 × 0.0627 = 1,254** |
| **Plus operating cost** | **30,000** | **22,000** |
| **EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST** | **Rs 54,742** | **Rs 46,778** ← lower |

> **So Pump B is preferable, by about Rs 8,000 a year — and that conclusion could not have been reached from the capital costs, which favour A by Rs 60,000.**

> **The comparison of annual figures is valid because each is the uniform annual cost of providing the same service, over whatever period the equipment lasts.**

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **(a) Total capital cost** | **Ignores the OPERATING cost, the LIFE and the SALVAGE value — it compares the purchase, not the service** ← |
| **(b) Payback period** | **Ignores everything AFTER the payback, including the difference in lives — which is precisely the issue at hand** ← |
| **(c) Equivalent annual cost** | ✓ |
| **(d) First-year operating cost** | **A single year of one component of the cost — the least informative basis available** |

> **Option (a) is the comparison most often made in practice and it is the reason so many poor equipment decisions are taken: the cheapest to buy is frequently the most expensive to own.**

> **The pump example shows it plainly — a machine costing 60 per cent more is 15 per cent cheaper over its life.**

> **That is the essence of LIFE CYCLE COSTING, and it is the correct basis for any procurement decision involving equipment that will be operated and maintained.**

**LIFE CYCLE COSTING, since that is what this method implements:**

> **The total cost of ownership comprises:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Initial CAPITAL cost** | **The only one usually considered, and often the smallest** ← |
| **OPERATING cost — fuel, power, consumables** | **Often the largest over a long life** ← |
| **MAINTENANCE and repair cost** | Rises with age |
| **DOWNTIME cost — the value of production lost** | **Frequently large and usually ignored** ← |
| **Salvage or disposal value** | A credit, or a cost |
| **Cost of financing** | Captured by the discount rate |

> **The DOWNTIME cost is the component most often omitted and it can dominate: a cheaper machine that is unavailable for two weeks in a construction season may cost far more in delay than its purchase saved.**

> **And it is why reliability and the availability of spares and service enter equipment decisions as heavily as price — considerations that a capital-cost comparison cannot represent at all.**

**A caution about the assumption underlying the EAC method:**

> **Converting a cost to an annual equivalent over the equipment's own life implicitly assumes that the equipment will be REPLACED BY SOMETHING SIMILAR when it wears out, indefinitely.**

> **That assumption is reasonable for a pump or a vehicle whose replacement will be much like it.**

> **It is NOT reasonable where:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The need is TEMPORARY — a single project** | **Then the comparison should be over the PROJECT'S life, with the residual value credited** ← |
| **Technology is changing rapidly** | The replacement will not resemble the original |
| **The service will be provided differently in future** | — |

> **So the EAC method's validity rests on an assumption about the future that must be checked — and where it fails, the correct comparison is over the period the service is actually required, with the residual values properly credited.**

> **Which is a good instance of a general point about economic analysis: the arithmetic is straightforward and the ASSUMPTIONS are where the judgement lies, so they must be stated rather than embedded.**

examTip.trick: **Convert each alternative to an EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST over its OWN life, then compare the annual figures.** EAC = capital × (A/P, i, n) + operating − salvage × (A/F, i, n).
examTip.trap: **Option (a) capital cost is the comparison usually made and the reason for poor equipment decisions** — the cheapest to buy is often the most expensive to own. And PAYBACK ignores everything after it, which is exactly the difference in lives.
examTip.mnemonic: **DOWNTIME cost is the life-cycle component most often omitted and can dominate** — a cheap machine unavailable for two weeks in the season costs more in delay than it saved. And the EAC method assumes indefinite similar replacement; check that assumption.

questions.stem: Rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float so that the resource demand is made as uniform as possible, WITHOUT extending the project duration, is called:
questions.solution:
**RESOURCE SMOOTHING**, also called resource levelling.

**The two resource-scheduling problems, which are distinct:**

| Problem | Constraint | Method | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RESOURCE SMOOTHING (levelling)** | **The PROJECT DURATION is fixed and must not be exceeded** | **Shift non-critical activities WITHIN their float** ← | **The duration is preserved; the resource peaks are reduced as far as the float allows** |
| **RESOURCE ALLOCATION (constrained resource scheduling)** | **The RESOURCE LIMIT is fixed and must not be exceeded** | **Delay activities as necessary, even critical ones** | **The PROJECT DURATION may be EXTENDED** ← |

> **So the two differ in WHICH CONSTRAINT IS FIXED, and that determines what may be sacrificed:**

> **SMOOTHING treats the DURATION as inviolable and does the best it can with the resources.**

> **ALLOCATION treats the RESOURCE LIMIT as inviolable and accepts a longer duration.**

> **Option (a) is therefore the other member of the pair, and the distinction is exactly the substance of this question.**

**Why smoothing is worth doing — the problem it solves:**

> **A network scheduled with every activity at its EARLIEST START produces a very uneven resource demand:**
